\chapter*{Introduction}

\section*{Background}

In this book we have attempted to collect most of the consequences of the axiom of choice that have been discovered during the past 90 years. Our goal is to present these statements and the relationships between them in an easily accessible format. Since 1904, when Zermelo introduced the axiom of choice, hundreds of its consequences have appeared in articles by almost as many authors. These articles have explored the complicated pattern of implications between the various consequences. With the introduction of independence proofs by Fraenkel, Mostowski, Specker and Cohen, the pattern of relationships became still more intricate. The results in this area are scattered over a wide spectrum of journals and books. As a result a particular theorem may be proved and reproved by several different authors. For example, Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1988} asked whether or not the axiom of choice for countable families of countable sets implies the countable union theorem. In Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1992} Shannon's question was answered in the negative. Shortly afterward Norbert Brunner, in his review of Howard \cite{bib:1992}, pointed out that the result had already been obtained by Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} in \cite{bib:1974}. This book was begun with the primary purpose of preventing such occurrences. We hope it will also serve as a reference for non-set theorist who need to know the strength of some particular statement relative to the axiom of choice and its consequences.

In some ways our work is similar to that of Herman and Jean Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} (Rubin/Rubin \cite{bib:1985}) which contains equivalents of the axiom of choice. However, our task is complicated by the fact that the statements we consider are not, in general, equivalent. We are concerned with sentences in the language of set theory which can be proved using the axiom of choice but which are not theorems of set theory with that axiom omitted (with the exception of form 0 described below). We call these sentences \emph{forms of the axiom of choice}. The forms are numbered starting with form 0. Form 1 is the axiom of choice and form 0 is $0=0$, provable in set theory without any form of the axiom of choice. The remaining forms are numbered in the order we encountered them as we reviewed the literature.

We consider two versions of set theory. The first is Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory\index{Subject}{Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory} which we denote by $\mathrm{ZF}$. For our purposes any one of the axiomatizations of the theory $\mathrm{ZF}$ will be satisfactory. To be specific we shall use the one given in Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, page 35. The second version of set theory is denoted by $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$\index{Subject}{$\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$}. The theory $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ is the following modification of $\mathrm{ZF}$. A constant symbol $\emptyset$ is added to the language together with the axiom $(\forall x)(x\not\in\emptyset)$. In addition the axioms of extensionality (A1 in Jech \cite{bib:1973b}) and foundation (or regularity) (A8 in Jech \cite{bib:1973b}) are modified to allow the existence of \emph{atoms} (or \emph{urelements}). Each atom $a$ has the property that $a\neq\emptyset$ and $\neg(\exists x)(x\in a)$. Let set$(x)$ be the formula $x=\emptyset \vee(\exists y)(y\in x)$. Then the modified version of the extensionality axiom mentioned above is
\begin{equation*}
(\forall X)(\forall Y)[(\mathrm{set(X)}\wedge \mathrm{set}(Y))\rightarrow((\forall u)(u\in X\leftrightarrow u\in Y)\rightarrow X=Y)].
\end{equation*}
The modified version of the axiom of regularity is
\begin{equation*}
(\forall S)[(S\neq\emptyset \wedge \mathrm{set}(S) \wedge(\forall u\in S)(\mathrm{set}(u)))\rightarrow(\exists x\in S)(x\cap S=\emptyset)].
\end{equation*}

Corresponding to these two theories are two types of models: Cohen models\index{Subject}{Cohen models} of $\mathrm{ZF}$ which use \emph{forcing} to extend a model of $\mathrm{ZF}$ in which the axiom of choice holds to a model in which it fails and Fraenkel-Mostowski (FM) permutation models\index{Subject}{permutation models} of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. Starting with a model of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ in which the axiom of choice is true, and in which the class of atoms is non-empty, $\mathrm{FM}$ models use permutations of the atoms to obtain a submodel in which the axiom of choice is false. Both types of models are described in more detail in part~\ref{pt03:part03} of the book.

Our policy on notation and terminology is (for the most part) to use that of the original articles and books, or standard terminology. However, we are careful to distinguish between the terms ``denumerable'' and ``countable''. We use the term ``denumerable''\index{Subject}{denumerable set} to mean ``countably infinite''. A set $x$ is \emph{denumerable} or \emph{countably infinite} if $x\approx(\omega)$, and a set is \emph{countable}\index{Subject}{countable set} if it is either finite or denumerable.

\section*{Description of the parts of the book}

This book is divided into seven parts

Part~\ref{pt01:part01} is the numerical list of forms. For example, the listing for form 3 is

\noindent \textbf{FORM 3.} $2m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1954a}.

\textbf{[3 A]}\index{Author}{Sierpi\'{n}ski} For all\index{Subject}{countable axiom of choice} cardinals $m$ and $n,\,n\leq m$ and $m$ infinite $\rightarrow m+n=m$. Halpern/Howard\index{Author}{Halpern/Howard} \cite{bib:1970}.

\noindent \textbf{[3 B]} $\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$. Halpern/Howard \cite{bib:1970}.

\noindent \textbf{[3 C]} Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: (For all cardinals $x,\,y$ and $z$) ($x+y=z$ iff ($x\leq z$ and $y\leq z$ and $(\forall u)(x, y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u)$). H\"{a}ussler\index{Author}{H\"{a}ussler} \cite{bib:1983} and Tarski \cite{bib:1949a}.

\noindent \textbf{[3 D]} Every pair of cardinals has a least upper bound in the usual cardinal ordering and for all cardinals $\kappa$ and $\gamma$, if $n\kappa \leq\gamma$ for all $n\in\omega$, then $\aleph_{0}\kappa\leq\gamma$. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1979b}.

\noindent \textbf{[3 E]} $E(IV, V)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m+1=m$ implies $2m=m$. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{[3 F]} $E(III, V)$: For every set $X$, if $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind infinite then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{[3 G]} $E(II, V)$: For every set $X$, if there is a non-empty family of subsets of $X$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ and has no maximal element then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{[3 H]} $E(Ia, V)$: For every set $X$, if $2|X|>|X|$ then $X$ is amorphous. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

In most cases a form's listing contains its number, a name for the form, a precise statement of the form and a reference to the bibliography. Following each form in part~\ref{pt01:part01} is a list of statements known to be equivalent to the form. We also refer to these statements as forms. In the example given above, forms [3 A] through [3 H] are all equivalent to form 3. The listing of each equivalent form ends with a reference to an article (or note) where the proof of equivalence can be found.

Part~\ref{pt02:part02} is the topical list of forms. This listing of the forms by subject matter is the part of the book which is most similar to H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985}. The listing of each form in part~\ref{pt02:part02} contains the same information as its listing in part~\ref{pt01:part01}. One difference between part~\ref{pt01:part01} and part~\ref{pt02:part02} is that in part~\ref{pt02:part02} a form and its equivalents need not occur together. For example, form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) is in the section of algebraic forms while its equivalent form [14 P] (Alaoglu's Theorem) is in the section of forms from analysis.

Part~\ref{pt03:part03}, titled ``Models'', contains a brief description of each model of set theory. These descriptions include the forms that have been proved true in the model and the forms that have been proved false together with a reference to the proof. Each description ends with a list of all forms known to be true in the model and all forms known to be false. For example, in model $\mathcal{M}1$ form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) was proved to be true in Halpern/Levy\index{Author}{Halpern/Levy} \cite{bib:1971}. These facts are included in the description of $\mathcal{M}1$. Since form 14 implies form 30 (the Ordering principle), form 30 is also true in the model and therefore form 30 occurs in the final list of forms which are true in the model. There are two sections in part~\ref{pt03:part03}. Section 1 contains Cohen models for $\mathrm{ZF}$. In most cases the models are denoted by $\mathcal{M}k$, where $k$ is a positive integer. Section 2 contains models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. Our notation for these models is $\mathcal{N}k$, where $k$ is a positive integer.

Part~\ref{pt04:part04}, titled ``Notes'', is a collection of notes which are referred to in other parts of the book. Whenever we consider notation or terminology to be nonstandard we add a note explaining it. Our policy on proofs is to omit them if they are readily available in the literature. However, if a proof is not, in our judgement, readily available, we have included it in a note. Other notes include a survey of the relationships between the (infinitely many) versions of the axiom of choice for sets of $n$ element sets, $n$ a positive integer (note 15), a brief exposition of the transfer theorems of Jech/Sochor and Pincus (note 103), and various properties of and relations between forms (notes 18 and 120).

Part~\ref{pt05:part05} is called ``References for Relationships Between Forms''. To explain part~\ref{pt05:part05} it is helpful to consider an example. A typical line from part~\ref{pt05:part05} is below.

43\quad 63\quad (3)\quad Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1971a} (M2)

The first two numbers are form numbers. The third number which occurs in parentheses is a code number for the status of the implication ``form 43 implies form 63''. The number 3 is the code for ``not provable in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory''. The other code numbers that we use are
\begin{enumerate}
\item[0] for ``The status of the implication is unknown.''
\item[1] for ``The implication is provable.''
\item[2] for ``The implication is provable and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1.''
\item[3] for ``The implication is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}$.''
\item[4] for ``The implication is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}$ and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1 or 3.''
\item[5] for ``The implication is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.''
\item[6] for ``The implication is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are odd.''
\item[7] for ``The status of the implication is unknown and we have found the question asked somewhere in the literature.''
\end{enumerate}

In part~\ref{pt05:part05} the implication codes\index{Subject}{implication codes} are odd numbers for the most part. Following the code number in a typical line of part~\ref{pt05:part05} is a reference to a bibliography item and possibly a note and, in the case of a non-implication, a model number. In the example, Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1971a} refers to a bibliography item in part VI and M2 refers to the model $\mathcal{M}2$ from part~\ref{pt03:part03}.

Part~\ref{pt06:part06}, our bibliography, is a listing of all articles and books we have used arranged alphabetically by author.

Part VII consists of two $(n+1)$ by $(n+1)$ matrices where $n$ is the last form number. (Currently $n=383$.) We refer to these matrices as table 1\index{Subject}{table 1, description} and table 2\index{Subject}{table 2, description}.

Printed copies of table 1 and table 2 are not included. They may be
accessed using the software that is included. In addition the
program maketex.c in the software package will create \TeX\ files
containing copies of table 1 and table 2 which may then be printed.
Tables 1 and 2 are also available at either of the authors' web
sites: \url{http://www.math.purdue.edu/~jer/} or
\url{http://www.emunix.emich.edu/~phoward/}

The natural numbers $0$ through $n$ are the row and column headings in both table 1 and table 2 and are to be thought of as form numbers. Each entry in the body of table 1 is one of the code numbers $0$ through 7 used in part~\ref{pt05:part05}. The code number in row $n$ and column $k$ of table 1 describes the status of the implication ``form $n$ implies form $k$''. Odd entries (1, 3, 5 or 7) mean that the implication or non-implication (or open problem) has a reference listed in part~\ref{pt05:part05}. For example, the entry in row 43, column 39 of table 1 is 3. This means that form 43 does not imply form 39 in $\mathrm{ZF}$ and there is a reference in part~\ref{pt05:part05} to this result. The entry in table 1 at position 8, 40 (that is, row 8, column 40) is 4. This means that form 8 does not imply form 40 in $\mathrm{ZF}$ and this non-implication follows from implications and non-implications that have references in part~\ref{pt05:part05}.

When an even entry is encountered in table 1 it is possible, by studying table 1, to find implications and non-implications from which this even entry follows and which are referenced in part~\ref{pt05:part05}. For example, an examination of table 1 reveals that the entries at positions 43, 8 and 40, 39 are both 1 and that (as noted earlier) the entry at position 43, 39 is a 3. This means that form 43 implies form 8, form 40 implies form 39 and form 43 does not imply form 39 in $\mathrm{ZF}$. Further all these results are referenced in part~\ref{pt05:part05}. It follows from these three results that form 8 does not imply form 40 and hence we have ``reduced'' the non-implication ``form 8 does not imply form 40'' to results that have references in part~\ref{pt05:part05}.

The purpose of table 2 is to provide a direct path to this reduction. In table 2 the non-zero entries are form numbers. These non-zero entries occur only in positions where the corresponding entry in table 1 is 2, 4, or 6. If the table 1 entry at position $m,\,k$ is 2, then the entry in table 2 is a form number $j$ such that form $m$ implies form $j$ and form $j$ implies form $k$. Thus the implication ``form $m$ implies form $k$'' is ``reduced'' to the implications ``form $m$ implies form $j$ ''  and ``form $j$ implies form $k$''. If the table 1 entries at positions $m,\,j$ and $j,\,k$ are both $1$'s then the original implication (``form $m$ implies form $k$'') has been reduced to implications with references in part~\ref{pt05:part05}. If either of the table 1 entries at positions $m,\,j$ or $j,\,k$ is a 2 then the implication corresponding to the 2 can be reduced again using table 2. Similarly, if the entry at position $m,\,k$ of table 1 is a 4 or a 6, the table 2 entry at position $m,\, k$ will be a form number $j$ of a form such that one of two things happens: Either form $j$ implies form $m$ and form $j$ does not imply form $k$ or form $k$ implies form $j$ and form $m$ does not imply form $j$. These two possibilities are illustrated in the diagram below.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{form}\ j\quad {\not\rightarrow}\quad \mathrm{form}\ k &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \mathrm{form}\ k\\
\quad \downarrow & \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\downarrow\\
\mathrm{form}\ m & \qquad \quad\qquad\mathrm{form}\ m\quad \not\rightarrow\quad\mathrm{form}\ j
\end{array}
\end{equation*}
\noindent In either case the non-implication ``form $m$ does not imply form $k$'' has been ``reduced''. Using this method with the 4 at position 8, 40 in table 1 we see that the table 2 entry at position 8, 40 is 231. Referring back to table 1, we see that the entry in position 8, 231 is a 3 and the entry at position 40, 231 is a 1. The non-implication ``form 8 does not imply form 40'' has been reduced to the two facts `` form 8 does not imply form 231'' and ``form 40 implies form 231'' both of which have references in part~\ref{pt05:part05}.

\section*{Software}

This section contains a description\index{Subject}{software description} of the software. The next section contains detailed instructions for its use. All programs and computer files mentioned in this section are on the diskette enclosed inside the back cover. Using the software that is included will eliminate the need for calculations using table 2. The enclosed diskette contains two data files: rfb1.tex and models.dat. The purpose of these files is described later in this section.

The software also includes several programs each of which is described below. There are two versions of each program: A source file with extension .c suitable for compiling on any machine with a c compiler and an executable version with extension .exe which can be run directly on any $\mathrm{PC}$ which runs MS DOS. Here are the descriptions of the c programs
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] mk\_book.c -- This program must be run before any of the others. (From the file rfb1.tex it creates two matrices of size 384 by 384 (which are versions of table 1 and table 2) and stores them in the two files book1 and book2. These files (book1 and book2) are used by the other c programs to extract information about implications among the forms. Each of book1 and book2 uses about .5 megabytes of memory.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{AFTER RUNNING mk-book.c ANY OF THE FOLLOWING CAN BE USED:}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[2.] weakac.c -- This is the main program for obtaining information about the relationships between forms. When you run the program the data files book1 and book2 will be read into memory and then the main menu will appear on the screen. Then menu is show below.

\item[]MAIN MENU

\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] see the meanings of the implication codes

type 1 $<$enter$>$
\item[2.] see what is known about the implication !`form n implies form k?` for any two form numbers n and k

type 2 $<$enter$>$
\item[3.] get information about a single form

type 3 $<$enter$>$
\item[4.] see table 1 restricted to any subset of the forms

type 4 $<$enter$>$
\item[5.] see a submatrix of table 1 consisting of consecutive rows and columns 

type 5 $<$enter$>$
\item[6.] see how an implication or non-implication follows from those with a reference in part~\ref{pt05:part05}

type 6 $<$enter$>$
\item[7.] see the models in which a form is true and those in which it is false

type 7 $<$enter$>$
\item[8.] exit the program

type 8 $<$enter$>$
\end{enumerate}
In order for option 7 to work the file models.dat must be present.

\item[3.] maketex.c -- A program which will create \TeX\ files for table 1 and table 2 from book1 and book2 if you want a hard copy of either of these.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Using the Software}

\textbf{The Setup.} There are three steps in the setup procedure:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] Copy the files from the floppy disk to your computer's memory.
\item[2.] Compile the c programs using a c language compiler. (This step is not necessary if you are working on a computer running MS DOS. We have included complied executable DOS files for each of the c programs.)
\item[3.] Run the program \textbf{mk{\_}book}. This program creates the data files used by the other programs.
\end{enumerate}

The program mk{\_}book takes between 5 and 10 minutes to run. It creates the data files book1 and book2 from the file rfb1.tex. The files copied from the floppy disk together with the data files book1 and book2 occupy about 2.3 megabytes of memory.

To carry out the setup procedure on a DOS machine, put the floppy disk in the disk drive. Assuming that this is drive a:, the following instructions given at the DOS prompt $(\mathrm{C}:\backslash >)$ will create a directory called weakac and copy the files from the disk into that directory.

\noindent md $\mathrm{c}:\backslash $weakac

\noindent copy $\mathrm{a}:^{\ast}\cdot^{\ast}\mathrm{c}:\backslash $weakac

\noindent To complete the setup on a DOS machine change to the weakac directory and run mk\_book with the following two commands.

\noindent cd c:$\backslash$ weakac

\noindent mk\_book

\noindent Answer y to the question ``Do you want to continue?''.

On a non-DOS machine a c language compiler is required. You must compile the c language programs mk\_book.c, weakac.c, and maketex.c. On a UNIX machine, for example, the command

\noindent cc -o mk\_book mk\_book.c

\noindent will compile the c program mk\_book.c and store the executable program in the file mk\_book. The other programs should be compiled similarly. To complete the setup type

\noindent mk\_book

\noindent at the UNIX prompt to run the program mk\_book.

\textbf{Running the Other Programs.} The program \textbf{weakac} is the program that is used for getting information about the relationships between the various consequences of $\mathrm{AC}$. It is described in the previous section. To run it type

\noindent weakac

\noindent at the DOS or UNIX prompt. Follow the instructions on the screen. In particular you are offered the option of writing the program's output in a file.

The program \textbf{maketex} will create \TeX\ files for either table 1 or table 2. At the DOS or UNIX prompt type

\noindent maketex

\noindent You will be prompted with the lines:

\noindent ``Enter the mane of the file to be converted to

\noindent TeX. This will usually be book1 or book2.''

To make a \TeX\ file for table 1 type book1. To make a \TeX\ file for table 2 type book2. You will then be prompted with the question:

\noindent ``To what file name should the TeX file be

\noindent written? Must be different from the input file.''

\noindent At this point you choose the name for the output file. It may be any valid file name other that book1 or book2. For example table1.tex or table2.tex are suitable. A few more lines appear on the screen and you are prompted with the question ``Today's date?'' Enter the date in any format. For example 8/10/97 or August 10, 1997 are suitable responses. The final question is

\noindent ``Will the output be table 1 or table 2?

\noindent respond 1 or 2.''

\noindent Make the appropriate response and the \TeX\ file for table 1 or table 2 will be created. When processed by a \TeX\ program and printed, each of these tables is 144 pages long.

\section*{Final Note}

We have tried to give the original sources of the results. However, this is not always possible. When we give references like Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} \cite{bib:1979}, G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} \cite{bib:1982}, H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985}, etc., it means that information about the results can be found there. It does not necessarily mean that it is the original source. We have also made an effort to check the accuracy of our results, especially when the source is a preprint. As far as we can tell, our results are consistent. However, because of the amount of data that we have, it is virtually impossible to prevent some error from sneaking in. We just hope the errors are not serious and we encourage readers to contact us when they encounter errors or software problems. We would also appreciate hearing of new results in this area. We shall add all additions and corrections to our web pages.

\part{Numerical List of Forms \label{pt01:part01}}

\textbf{FORM 0.} 0 = 0.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ A}] Cardinal successors 2: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\neg\exists p)(m<p<n)$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1954a} and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1966a}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ B}] If $X$ is finite then $X^{\omega}$ is compact. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1984b}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ C}] Closed subspaces of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner \cite{bib:1984b}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ D}] Products of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner \cite{bib:1984b}

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ E}] The box product of a well ordered family of limited amorphous spaces is limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner \cite{bib:1984b} and note 52.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ F}] Cancellation for surjective cardinal equivalence: For every $k\in \omega -\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx=^{\ast} ky$ implies $x=^{\ast}y)$ (The expression $x=^{\ast}y$ means that there is a function $f$ from $x$ onto $y$ and a function $g$ from $y$ onto $x$.) Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1984}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ G}] Cancellation for injective cardinal inequality: For every $k\in\omega -\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx\leq ky$ implies $x\leq y)$ ($\leq$ is the usual (injective) cardinal ordering.) Lindenbaum/Tarski\index{Author}{Lindenbaum/Tarski} \cite{bib:1926}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ H}] F. Riesz Theorem:\index{Subject}{Riesz theorem} A Hilbert space is finite dimensional iff its closed unit ball is compact. Brunner \cite{bib:1983b}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ I}] The following are equivalent in a Hilbert space:

\noindent(a) The closed unit ball is sequentially compact.

\noindent(b) Each unconditionally convergent series converges absolutely.

\noindent(c) Each ortho-normal system is Dedekind finite.

\noindent Brunner \cite{bib:1983b} and note 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ J}] Zermelo's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Zermelo's fixed point theorem} For every partially ordered set $(X, \leq)$, if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} \cite{bib:1988a}, Zermelo\index{Author}{Zermelo} \cite{bib:1908b} and Abian\index{Author}{Abian} \cite{bib:1980}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ K}] For all partially ordered sets $(X, \leq)$, if there is a $\displaystyle \sup$ function $\sigma$ on the well ordered subsets of $X$ then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ L}] Caristi's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Caristi's fixed point theorem} If $(X, \rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi$: $X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering $(x\leq y$ iff $\rho(x, y)\leq\phi(y)-\phi(x))$ every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t \leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Caristi\index{Author}{Caristi} \cite{bib:1976}, Manka \cite{bib:1988a}, and note 38.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ M}] A $T_{1}$ topological space is Dedekind finite if and only if every subspace has a dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ N}] If $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces with dense Dedekind finite subsets so is $X\times Y$. Brunner \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ O}] A Lindel\"{o}f space with a dense, Dedekind finite subset is compact. Brunner \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ P}] A Lindel\"{o}f space with a Dedekind finite basis is compact. Brunner \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Q}] For all cardinal numbers $m$ and $n$ and Dedekind finite cardinals $p$, if $p+m=p+n$ then $m=n$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1949b} and note 94

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ R}] Every infinite Dedekind finite field is the direct limit of a strictly increasing $\omega$-sequence of finite subfields. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1982}, notes 45 and 94.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ S}] If $(P, \leq)$ is a quasi-order such that $P$ is non-empty, well orderable and every antichain is finite then there is a $P$-generic filter. Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1990} and note 47.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ T}] If a set $S$ is hereditarily countable\index{Subject}{hereditarily countable set} (that is, every $y\in TC(S)$ is countable) then the rank of $S$ is $<\omega_{2}$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1982}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ U}] For any class of similar (universal) algebras $K,\,HSP\, K=Mod\,Eq\,K$. (The class of homomorphic images of subalgebras of products of non-empty families of algebras in $K$ is the same as the class of algebras which satisfy the set of equations holding in every algebra in $K$.) Andreka/Nemeti\index{Author}{Andreka/Nemeti} \cite{bib:1981} and note 50.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ V}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP\,K\supseteq PS\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P\,K$ is the class of algebras isomorphic to direct products of algebras in $K$). Andreka/Nemeti \cite{bib:1980}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ W}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP^{r}K\supseteq P^{r}S\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P^{r}K$ is the class of all algebras isomorphic to reduced direct products of algebras in $K$.) Andreka/Nemeti \cite{bib:1980}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ X}] $DC(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{2}^{1})$: If $P\subseteq {^{\omega}}\omega \times {^{\omega}}\omega$ and $P$ has domain ${^{\omega}}\omega,\, P\in\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{1}$, then for any $y\in {^{\omega}}\omega$ there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega\rangle$ of elements of ${^{\omega}}\omega$ with $x_{0}=y$ and $\langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle\in P$ for all $k\in\omega$. Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} \cite{bib:1979} and note 61.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Y}] There is no free complete Boolean algebra over $D$ if $|D|\geq\aleph_{0}$. Stavi\index{Author}{Stavi} \cite{bib:1975}, Gaifman\index{Author}{Gaifman} \cite{bib:1970}, Hales\index{Author}{Hales} \cite{bib:1964}, and note 89.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Z}] Suppose $X$ and $M$ are sets, $F$ is a function from $\mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset\}$ into $M$ and $G$ is a function on $M$ such that $\forall z\in \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset\},\,G(F(z))\in \mathcal{P}(z)-\{\emptyset\}$. Then there are unique $W$ and $R$ such that $W\subseteq M,\,R\subseteq W\times W$ and $R$ is an irreflexive well ordering of $W$, the range of $G|W$ is a partition of $X$, and $\forall w\in W,\,w=F(X -(\bigcup\{G(\nu) :\nu\in W$ and $\nu\, R\,w\}))$. Kruse\index{Author}{Kruse} \cite{bib:1974}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AA}] $CT_{1}$: Restricted Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic I: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable and if each propositional variable occurs in at most one formula in $\Sigma$, then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable. Kolany/Wojtylak\index{Author}{Kolany/Wojtylak} \cite{bib:1991}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AB}] If $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is perfect, then $|X|=2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1974b} and note 28.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AC}] There are $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ perfect subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1974b} and note 28.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AD}] For all ordinals $\beta$, well ordered cardinals $\gamma\geq 1$ and all $n\in\omega$, there is a well ordered cardinal $\kappa$ such that $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{n}$. Erd\"{o}s/Rado\index{Author}{Erd\"{o}s/Rado} \cite{bib:1952} and note 97.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AE}] The number of well ordered subsets of a set: For all $x,\,|x|<|s(x)|$ where $s(x)=$\{ $y\subseteq x:y$ can be well ordered\}. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1939}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AF}] The number of well orderings of a set: For all $x,\,|x|<|w(x)|$ where $w(x)$ is the set of all well orderings of subsets of $x$. Russ \cite{bib:1973d}.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AG}] For any $n\in\omega,\, n\neq 0,\, |s(x)|\not\leq|x^{n}|$ and $|x^{n}|<|w(x)|$ if $|x|$ exceeds some small finite value depending on $n$. $(s(x)$ is the set of well orderable subsets of $x$ and $w(x)$ is the set of well orderings of subsets of $x$.) Truss \cite{bib:1973d}

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AH}] No infinite well orderable set is amorphous.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AI}] Turinici's Fixed Point Theorem\index{Subject}{Turinici's fixed point theorem} for Hausdorff Spaces: If $(X, \leq)$ is a directed, partially ordered set and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ such that

\noindent(a) $(X, \leq)$ is upper semi-continuous with respect to $\tau$,

\noindent(b) Every well ordered subset of $(X, \leq)$ has a unique limit as a net, then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,x\leq f(x)$ has a fixed point. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} \cite{bib:1988b} and note 38.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AJ}] $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is not an inaccessible cardinal for any ordinal $\alpha$. Drake\index{Author}{Drake} \cite{bib:1974} and note 20.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AK}] Every separable metric space is second countable.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AL}] For every set $A$, there is an $\aleph$ which cannot be covered by fewer than $|A|$ sets each of cardinality $<|A|$. Note 131.

[\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AM}] Assume $V$ is a separable vector space, $D$ is a countable dense subset of $V$, and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$, and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx) =tp(x))$. Also assume that $p$ satisfies the following condition:
\begin{equation*}\tag{$^{\ast}$}
(\forall\epsilon>0)(\forall x\in V)(\exists y\in D)\ \text{such that}\ p(x-y)<\epsilon\ \text{and}\ p(y-x)<\epsilon.
\end{equation*}

\noindent Moreover, if $f$ is a linear function from a subspace $S$ of $V$ into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$, then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ so that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. Note 143.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 1.} $C(\infty, \infty)$: The Axiom of Choice:\index{Subject}{axiom of choice} Every set of non-empty sets has a choice function.

[\textbf{1 A}] In every vector space, every generating set contains a basis. Halpern\index{Author}{Halpern} \cite{bib:1966}.

\noindent [\textbf{1 B}] Every commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} \cite{bib:1979}.

\noindent[\textbf{1C}] For all infinite cardinals $m,\,UT(m, m, m)$: If every member of an infinite set $A$ has power $|A|$ then $|\bigcup A|=|A|$. (Note that [1 C] implies $m^{2}=m$ for all infinite cardinals $m$.) Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1994}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 D}] Cardinal successors 3: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\forall p)(m<p\rightarrow n\leq p)$. Tarski \cite{bib:1954a} and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1966a}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 E}] $K(0)$: For every set $S$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a one to one function $f:S\rightarrow\alpha$. (See form $81(n)$).

\noindent[\textbf{1 F}] For all ordinals $\alpha,\,DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$: Given a relation $R$ such that for every subset $Y$ of a set $X$ with $|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$, there is an $x\in X$ with $Y\ R\,x$, then there is a function $f:\aleph_{\alpha}\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall\beta<\aleph_{\alpha},\, \{f(\gamma):\gamma<\beta\}\,R\,f(\beta).)$ Levy\index{Author}{Levy} \cite{bib:1964} and note 133.

\noindent[\textbf{1 G}]\index{Author}{Shannon} Form 163 + form 8. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{1 H}] Form 164 + form 67. Brunner \cite{bib:1982a} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{1 I}] In every metric space ($X,\,d$) there is an $\epsilon$-lattice for some $\epsilon>0$ which is not a strict upper bound of $d$. Brunner \cite{bib:1984e} and note 17.

\noindent[\textbf{1 J}] Form 49 + form 51. Morris\index{Author}{Morris} \cite{bib:1969} and note 121.

\noindent[\textbf{1 K}] Form 133 + form 64. Clear

\noindent[\textbf{1 L}] Hajnal's Free Set Principle:\index{Subject}{Hajnal's free set principle} For every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{<\lambda}$ where $\lambda$ is a well orderable cardinal and $\lambda<|X|$ there is a free set of cardinality $|X|.\, ([X]^{<\lambda}$ is the set of subsets of $X$ of cardinality $<\lambda$. Brunner \cite{bib:1989} and note 22.

\noindent[\textbf{1 M}]\index{Subject}{ramification lemma} The ramification Lemma: If $S:X^{\leq\theta}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E)$ is a ramification system, then for each $g\in E$ there is an $f$ which is maximal (with respect to inclusion) in $\{h\in X^{\leq\theta}:g\in S(h)\}$. Brunner \cite{bib:1989} and note 22.

\noindent[\textbf{1 N}] For every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{WO}$ (well ordered subsets of $X$) there is a co-well-orderable free subset $H$. ($H$ is \emph{co-well-orderable} if $X\,\backslash\, H$ is well orderable). Brunner \cite{bib:1989} and note 22.

\noindent[\textbf{1 O}] $A(D1, C)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X, T)$, if $X$ is covered by a well ordered family of closed, discrete sets then each family $U\subseteq T$ of pairwise disjoint sets is well ordered. Brunner \cite{bib:1983d} and note 26.

\noindent[\textbf{1 P}] $A(P)$: (Depends on $P$ for $P\in\{W1, W2, B1, L1, L2, S, C, H1, A1\})$ Every $T_{2}$ topological space has property $P$. Brunner \cite{bib:1983d} and note 26.

\noindent[\textbf{1 Q}] For any partial order $(X, \leq)$ there is a sup function on the bounded (above), well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 R}] For any partial order $(X, \leq)$ there is a sup function on the bounded subsets of $X$. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 S}] For any partial order $(X, \leq)$ if every well ordered subset of $X$ is bounded then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 T}] For every directed partial order $(X,\, \leq)$ there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 U}] For every directed partial order, if every well ordered subset of $X$ is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 V}] For every partially ordered set $(X, \leq)$, if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka \cite{bib:1988a} and Abian\index{Author}{Abian} \cite{bib:1980}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 W}] Form 133 + form 88. Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 X}] Form 15 + form 91. Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 Y}] Refined Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem:\index{Subject}{Cantor-Bernstein theorem} If $f:X\rightarrow Y$ and $g:Y\rightarrow X$ are onto then there is a bijection $h:X\rightarrow Y$ such that $h\subseteq f \cup g^{-1}$. Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} \cite{bib:1990}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 Z}] If $(P, \leq)$ is a quasi-order and $P\neq\emptyset$ and every antichain is finite, then there is a $P$ generic filter which is well orderable. Shannon \cite{bib:1990} and note 47.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AA}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $f$ is surjective and $R\subseteq S$. Then every mapping $g$ of $S$ into $R$ has the form $g=f\circ h$ for some $h:S\rightarrow S$. Smith\index{Author}{Smith} \cite{bib:1982}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AB}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $f$ is surjective and $R\subseteq S$. Then the mappings of $S$ onto $R$ are precisely the mappings of the form $f\circ h$ where $h:S\rightarrow S$ and $(\forall y\in R)(\exists x\in S)(h(x)\in f^{-1}(\{y\}))$. Smith \cite{bib:1982}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AC}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $R\subseteq S$. Then the retractions of $S$ onto $R$ (that is, the mappings $g : S\rightarrow R$ which are the identity on $R$) are precisely the mappings $f\circ h$ where $h:S\rightarrow S$ and $(\forall y\in R)(h(y)\in f^{-1}(\{y\}))$. Smith \cite{bib:1982}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AD}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP^{g}K \supseteq P^{g}S\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P^{g}K$ is the class of direct products of elements of $K$ not closed under isomorphism). Andreka/Nemeti\index{Author}{Andreka/Nemeti} \cite{bib:1980}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AE}] There is a set $S$ such that $SVC$ holds with $S$ and such that $\mathcal{P}(S)-\{\emptyset\}$ has a choice function. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} and note 59. Also see form 191.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AF}] Form 191 + form 8 + form 193. Blass \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AG}] Form 192 + form 191. Blass \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AH}] $E(V, VI)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$ implies $m^{2}=m$. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AI}] $E(VI, VII)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m^{2}=m$ implies there is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $m=\aleph_{\alpha}$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AJ}] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of mappings of a poset $(X, \leq)$ into itself such that $\forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x$. If for some element $e$ of $X$ each chain in $X$ containing $e$ has a lower bound, then the family $\mathcal{F}$ has a common fixed point. Kasahara\index{Author}{Kasahara} \cite{bib:1976}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AK}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for all cardinals $x,\,\alpha(x+\aleph(x), x\cdot\aleph(x))< \beta$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1973b} and note 98.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AL}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for all cardinals $x,\,\alpha(x, x^{2})<\beta$. Truss \cite{bib:1973b} and note 98.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AM}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for no cardinal $x$ is there a strictly increasing sequence of cardinals $\{y_{\gamma}:\gamma<\beta\}$ such that $y_{\gamma}^{2}=x$. Truss \cite{bib:1973b} and note 98.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AN}] Every lattice ($L, \cap,\,\cup, \subseteq\rangle$ of sets (that is, $L$ is a family of sets and $\cap,\,\cup$ and $\subseteq$ are the usual operations) with a greatest element has a maximal, proper ideal. Bell/Fremlin\index{Author}{Bell}\index{Author}{Bell/Fremlin} \cite{bib:1972}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AO}] Any continuous surjection between compact spaces, where the range space is Hausdorff, has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell \cite{bib:1988} and note 114.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AP}] For any type $\tau$ of the form $\tau =(M)$, every homomorphism of an algebra of type $\tau$ is closed. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} \cite{bib:1989} and note 115.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AQ}] For any type $\tau$ of the form $\tau =(M)$, every homomorphism of an algebra \textbf{A} of type $\tau$ into an algebra \textbf{B} of type $\tau$ maps \textbf{A} onto a subalgebra of \textbf{B}. Diener \cite{bib:1989} and note 105.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AR}] Let $S$ be any family of disjoint non-empty sets and let $\tau =(\bigcup S)$, then any homomorphism from $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;\bigcup S)$ into $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;S)$ maps $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;\bigcup S)$ onto a subalgebra of $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;S)$. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} \cite{bib:1989} and note 115.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AS}] Turinici's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Turinici's fixed point theorem} If $(X, \leq)$ is a directed, partially ordered set and $\tau$ is a topology on $X$ such that

\noindent(a) $(X, \leq)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to $\tau$,

\noindent(b) Every well ordered subset of $(X, \leq)$ is convergent as a net, then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,x\leq f(x)$ has a fixed point. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} \cite{bib:1988b} and note 38.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AT}] For all cardinal numbers $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$, if a graph is both $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ colorable then it is also $\kappa$ colorable for some $\kappa$ such that $\kappa \leq^{\ast}\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa \leq^{\ast}\kappa_{2}$. ($\leq^{\ast}$ is the surjective cardinal ordering). Galvin/Komj\'{a}th\index{Author}{Galvin/Komj\'{a}th} \cite{bib:1991} and note 118.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AU}] Every graph has an irreducible, good coloring. Galvin/Komj\'{a}th \cite{bib:1991} and note 118.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AV}] Every graph of the form $G(A, H(A))$ has an irreducible, good coloring. ($H$ is the Hartogs aleph function.) Galvin/Komj\'{a}th \cite{bib:1991} and note 118.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AW}] Every graph has a chromatic number. Galvin/Komj\'{a}th \cite{bib:1991} and note 118.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AX}] Birkhoff\index{Author}{Birkhoff} Representation Theorem:\index{Subject}{Birkhoff representation theorem} Every algebra is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras. Birkhoff \cite{bib:1944}, Gr\"{a}tzer\index{Author}{Gr\"{a}tzer} \cite{bib:1979} and \cite{bib:1986}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AY}] For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $S_{\lambda}$ be a subset of some topological space $X_{\lambda}$. Then $\mathrm{cl}(\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}S_{\lambda})=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\mathrm{cl}\,(S_{\lambda})$, where the first ``cl'' is closure in the product topology and the second ``cl'' is closure in $X_{\lambda}$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} \cite{bib:1992}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 AZ}] For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$, let $X_{\lambda}$ be a complete uniform space. Then, the product $\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}X_{\lambda}$ equipped with the product uniform structure, is also complete. (See, for example, Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} \cite{bib:1955} pp 176ff for definitions.) Schechter \cite{bib:1992}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BA}] (Depends on the prime \emph{p}) Every group has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1987} and note 24.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BB}] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem\index{Subject}{Nielsen-Schreier theorem} II: If $G$ is a group which is freely generated by $X$ and $U$ is a subgroup of $G$, then there is a subset $A$ of $G$ which freely generates $U$ and is level with respect to $X$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1985} and note 129.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BC}] Assume $P$ is a partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound and $f:P\rightarrow P$ satisfies $\forall x\in f(P)\cup\{a\in P:a$ is an upper bound for some chain in $f(P)\},\, x\leq f(f(x))$. Then $f$ has a fixed apex $u$ (that is, there is some $v\in P$ such that $f(u)=v$ and $f(v)=u$.). Taskovi\'{c}\index{Author}{Taskovi\'{c}} \cite{bib:1988}, \cite{bib:1992a}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BD}] Let $P$ be a partially ordered set in which every increasing sequence has an upper bound and $f:P\rightarrow P$ satisfies $x\leq f(f(x))$ for all $x\in f(P)\cup\{x\in P:x$ is an upper bound for some increasing sequence in $f(P)\}$. Then $f$ has a fixed apex $u$ (that is, $\exists v\in P$, such that $f(u)=v$ and $f(v)=u$). (For purposes of [1 BD], ``sequence'' means a function whose domain is an ordinal.) Taskovi\'{c} \cite{bib:1992b}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BE}] Every unique factorization domain can be mapped homomorphically onto a non-zero subdirectly irreducible ring. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} \cite{bib:1988}, Gr\"{a}tzer\index{Author}{Gr\"{a}tzer} \cite{bib:1979} pp 122-124 and note 84.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BF}] $(\mathrm{D}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is dense in $X$. $(Y$ is \emph{dense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open subset $O\subseteq X$ such that $O\cap Y=\emptyset.)$ McCarten\index{Author}{McCarten} \cite{bib:1988} and note 106.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BG}] $(\mathrm{C}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is codense in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{codense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty closed subset $C\subseteq X$ such that $C\cap Y=\emptyset.)$ McCarten \cite{bib:1988} and note 106.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BH}] $(\mathrm{T}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is thick in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{thick in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset $H\subseteq X$ such that $H\cap Y=\emptyset$.) McCarten \cite{bib:1988} and note 106.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BI}] $(\mathrm{M}T_{0})$: Every topological space has a maximal $T_{0}$ subspace. Schnare\index{Author}{Schnare} \cite{bib:1968} and note 106.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BJ}] In every vector space over the two element field, every generating set contains a basis. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996a}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BK}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X,d$) can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is pairwise disjoint. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} \cite{bib:1997}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BL}] Every family of closed sets in a $T_{2}$ topological space includes a maximal subfamily with the finite intersection property. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985}, p 60,
$M14$.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BM}] For every family $\{(X_{i}, T_{i}):i\in k\}$ of $T_{1}$ topological spaces, the box topology contains an element $\prod_{i\in k}O_{i}$, such that $\emptyset \neq O_{i}$ and $O_{i}\neq X_{i}$ for all $i\in k$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BN}] For every family $\{(X_{i}, T_{i}):i\in k\}$ of disjoint $T_{1}$ topological spaces, the free union contains an open set $O$ such that $\emptyset \neq O\cap X_{i}$ and $O\cap X_{i}\neq X_{i}$ for all $i\in k$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BO}] For every $T_{1}$ topological space $(X, T)$ and every base (subbase) $B$ for $X$ there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal cellular family $Q\subseteq B$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BP}] For every dense in itself topological space $(X, T)$ and every base $B$ for $X$ there exists a nest $N$ included in $B$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BQ}] For every dense in itself topological space $(X, T)$ and every base $B$ for $X$ there exists a tower $R$ included in $B$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BR}] For every $T_{2}$ space $(X, T)$ and every subbase $\mathcal{B}$ for $X$, if $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are cellular families of $X$ included in $\mathcal{B}$, then there is a cellular family $\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$ such that $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are equipollent to subsets of $\mathcal{E}$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BS}] For every Abelian group $(G, +)$, for every $H\subseteq G$, the infinite system of equations
\begin{equation*}
x_{i}+y_{i}=a_{i},\ i\in I,\  a_{i}\in G
\end{equation*}
has a solution in $H$ iff each of its equations has a solution in $H$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996c}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BT}] For every Boolean ring $(B, +, \cdot)$ and every $H\subseteq B$ which is closed under + there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal ideal $Q\subseteq B$ such that $H\cap Q=\{0\}$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996c}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BU}] In every vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, every generating set includes a basis. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1984a} and note 137.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BV}] If $(X, T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $G=\{G_{i}:i\in K\},\,|G_{i}|\geq 2$, is a locally finite family of compact sets with non-empty pairwise disjoint interiors, then there is a continuous real valued function $f$ on $X$ which assumes at least two distinct values on each $G_{i}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1995} and note 43.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BW}] If $(X, T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\},\,|U_{i}|\geq 2$, is a locally finite family of open non-empty pairwise disjoint sets, then there is a continuous real valued function $f$ on $X$ which assumes at least two distinct values on each $U_{i}$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1995} and note 43.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BX}] For every Abelian group $G$ and every subgroup $H$ of $G$ there exists a set of representatives for the quotient $G/H$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996c}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BY}] If $x$ is a set of sets of cardinality at least 2, then there exists a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a finite, non-empty, proper subset of $u$. (Form [1 BY] implies [62 E] $(KW(\infty, <\aleph_{0}))$ and 67 (MC) and $62+67\rightarrow \mathrm{AC}$.) Blass \cite{bib:1979}.

\noindent[\textbf{1 BZ}] Vector Space Multiple Choice: For every family $V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non-trivial vector spaces there is a family $F=\{F_{i}:i\in K\}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,F_{i}$ is a non-empty, finite, independent subset of $V_{i}$. Note 127.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CA}] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem\index{Subject}{Nielsen-Schreier theorem} I: If $G$ is a group which is freely generated by $X$ and $U$ is a subgroup of $G$, then there is a subset $A$ of $G$ which freely generates $U$ and has the Nielsen property with respect to $X$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1985} and note 129.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CB}] For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, if $(X, T)$ is a $T_{2}$ space having a base $B$ such that no $Q\subseteq B,\,|Q|<\kappa$, is a tower, then for every family $\mathcal{D}=\{D_{i}:i\in\kappa\}$ of dense open sets of $X$ there is a filter $F\subseteq T$ such that for every $i\in \kappa$ there is a $b\in F$ with $b\subseteq D_{i}$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996b} and note 77.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CC}] $PC(\aleph_{0}, \mathrm{odd}, \infty)\, +\,MC_{\omega^{+}}$. $PC(\aleph_{0}, \mathrm{odd}, \infty)$ is ``Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.'' and $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ is ``For every natural number $n\geq 1$ and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $u$ such that $|f(u)|$ and $n$ are relatively prime.'' Note 133.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CD}] In a commutative ring, every proper ideal can be extended to a maximal ideal. Krull\index{Author}{Krull} \cite{bib:1929}. ([1 CD] implies [1 B]).

\noindent [\textbf{1 CE}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X,d$) can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is discrete. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} \cite{bib:1997} and note 141.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CF}] If a topological space is $cwH$, then it is $cwH(B)$ for every basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} \cite{bib:1997b} and note 141.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CG}] The disjoint union of $cwH$ spaces is $cwH(B)$ for every basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin \cite{bib:1997b} and note 141.

\noindent[\textbf{1 CH}] If a topological space is $cwN$, then it is $cwH(B)$ for any basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin \cite{bib:1997b} and note 141.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 2.} Existence of successor cardinals: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\forall p<n)(p\leq m)$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1954a}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 3.} $2m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$. Tarski \cite{bib:1954a}.

[\textbf{3 A}] For all cardinals $m$ and $n,\,n\leq m$ and $m$ infinite $\rightarrow m+n=m$. Halpern/Howard\index{Author}{Halpern/Howard} \cite{bib:1970}.

\noindent[\textbf{3 B}] $\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$. Halpern/Howard \cite{bib:1970}.

\noindent[\textbf{3 C}] Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: (For all cardinals $x,\,y$ and $z$) $(x+y=z$ iff $(x\leq z$ and $y\leq z$ and $(\forall u)(x, y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u))$. H\"{a}ussler\index{Author}{H\"{a}ussler} \cite{bib:1983} and Tarski \cite{bib:1949a}.

\noindent[\textbf{3 D}] Every pair of cardinals has a least upper bound in the usual cardinal ordering and for all cardinals $\kappa$ and $\gamma$, if $n\kappa \leq\gamma$ for all $n\in \omega$, then $\aleph_{0}\kappa\leq\gamma$. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1979b}.

\noindent[\textbf{3 E}] $E(IV, V)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m+1=m$ implies $2m=m$. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{3 F}] $E(III, V)$: For every set $X$, if $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind infinite then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{3 G}] $E(II, V)$: For every set $X$, if there is a non-empty family of subsets of $X$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ and has no maximal element then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{3 H}] $E(Ia, V)$: For every set $X$, if $2|X|>|X|$ then $X$ is amorphous. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989}, notes 85(H) and 94.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 4.} Every infinite set is the union of some disjoint family of denumerable subsets. (Denumerable means $\cong\aleph_{0}$.) Whitehead\index{Author}{Whitehead} \cite{bib:1902}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 5.} $C(\aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0}, \mathbb{R})$: Every denumerable set of non-empty denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ has a choice function. Sageev\index{Author}{Sageev} \cite{bib:1975}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 6.} $UT(\aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0}, \mathbb{R})$: The union of a denumerable family of denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is denumerable. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} \cite{bib:1982} and note 3.

[\textbf{6 A}] Every uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ contains a condensation point. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 205 and 324, Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{bib:1918}.

\noindent[\textbf{6 B}] Every uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has two condensation points. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 205 and 324, Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{bib:1918}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 7.} There is no infinite decreasing sequence of cardinals. Schoenflies\index{Author}{Schoenflies} \cite{bib:1908}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 8.} $C(\aleph_{0}, \infty)$: Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{bib:1918}.

[\textbf{8 A}] $PC(\infty, \infty, \infty)$: Every infinite family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1983b}.

\noindent[\textbf{8 B}] $PC(\aleph_{0}, \infty, \infty)$: Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Monro\index{Author}{Monro} \cite{bib:1975}.

\noindent[\textbf{8 C}] Every $\sigma$-compact space is Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner \cite{bib:1982b} and note 43.

\noindent[\textbf{8 D}] Every $\sigma$-compact, locally compact $T_{2}$ space is weakly Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner \cite{bib:1982b} and note 43.

\noindent[\textbf{8 E}] In a metric space every sequentially continuous real valued function is continuous. Brunner \cite{bib:1982c}.

\noindent[\textbf{8 F}] Martin's Axiom\index{Subject}{Martin's axiom} $(\aleph_{0})$: Whenever $(P\leq)$ is a non-empty, ccc quasi-order (ccc means every anti-chain is countable) and $\mathcal{D}$ is a family of $\leq\aleph_{0}$ dense subsets of $P$, then there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter $G$ in $P$. Kunen\index{Author}{Kunen} \cite{bib:1980}, Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1990} and note 47.

\noindent[\textbf{8 G}] Let $R$ be a relation and $R^{\ast}$, the transitive closure of $R$. $(x\,R^{\ast}\,y$ iff there exists a finite ascending $R$-chain connecting $x$ to $y$.) If every ascending $R$-chain is finite, then every ascending $R^{\ast}$-chain is finite. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} \cite{bib:1994}.

\noindent[\textbf{8 H}] A disjoint union of a countable set of compact $T_{2}$ spaces is Lindel\"{o}f. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 I}] A disjoint union of a countable set of Lindel\"{o}f $T_{2}$ spaces is Lindel\"{o}f. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 J}] Hemicompact $T_{2}$ spaces are Lindel\"{o}f. (A \emph{hemicompact} space is a space $(X, T)$ that can be written as a disjoint union $\bigcup\{K_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ such that (i) each $K_{n}$ is a compact set in $X$; (ii) $K_{N}\subseteq K_{n+1}$ for all $n\in\omega$; and (iii) for every compact set $K$ in $X$, there is an $n\in\omega$ such that $K\subseteq K_{n}$.) Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 K}] Hemilindel\"{o}f $T_{2}$ spaces are Lindel\"{o}f. (In [8 J], in the definition of hemicompact replace ``compact'' by ``Lindel\"{o}f'' to get the definition of hemilindel\"{o}f.) Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 L}] Every second countable topological space is separable. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 M}] Form $131+$ form 32. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 N}] $DP$: If $(X, T)$ is a topological space having a countable $\pi$-base, then for every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in\omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$, there is a countable dense set $S\subseteq X$ such that for all $i\in\omega$ and for all but finitely many $s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 O}] $DUCCC$ + form 131. $DUCCC$ is ``If $X$ is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $X$ has the ccc property.'' $(Y$ has the $ccc$ \emph{property} if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 P}] \emph{DUSS} $+$ form 131. \emph{DUSS} is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of separable topological spaces is separable.'' Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 Q}] $DUSC$ + form 131. $DUSC$ is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of second countable topological spaces is second countable.'' Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 R}] \emph{SCDUL} + form 131. \emph{SCDUL} is ``The denumerable disjoint union of second countable spaces is Lindel\"{o}f.'' Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d} and note 132.

\noindent[\textbf{8 S}] $PC(WO, \infty, \infty)$: Every infinite well ordered set of non-empty sets has an infinite subset with a choice function. $([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{S}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{B}])$

\noindent[\textbf{8 T}] $PUT(\aleph_{0}, \infty, \aleph_{0})$: The union of a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has a denumerable subset. $([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{T}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{B}])$

\noindent[\textbf{8 U}] $PUT(WO, \infty, WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has an infinite well ordered subset. $([8\ \mathrm{U}]\leftrightarrow[8\ \mathrm{T}])$

\noindent\textbf{FORM 9.} Finite $\Leftrightarrow$ Dedekind finite: $W_{\aleph_{0}}$ (Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}): $E(I, IV)$ (Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989}): Every Dedekind finite set is finite. Dedekind\index{Author}{Dedekind} \cite{bib:1888} and note 94.

[\textbf{9 A}] For all infinite $x$, if $x$ is Dedekind finite, then $\mathcal{P}(x)$ is is Dedekind finite). Notes 8 and 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 B}] $E(II, IV)$ (Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989}): $(\forall x)(x$ is $T$-finite if and only if $x$ is Dedekind finite). Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 C}] The image of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.2, notes 11 and 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 D}] The union of a Dedekind finite family of finite sets is Dedekind finite. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.4, notes 12 and 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 E}] No Dedekind finite set can be mapped onto $\aleph_{0}$. (See form 160.) Monro\index{Author}{Monro} \cite{bib:1975} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 F}] There is no subset $A$ of the class of Dedekind finite cardinals such that $A$ under the usual cardinal ordering is order isomorphic to $\langle \mathbb{R},\,\leq\rangle$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1965}, Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 6, and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 G}] Every infinite set has a denumerable subset. Cantor\index{Author}{Cantor} \cite{bib:1895} and G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} \cite{bib:1982} p 9.

\noindent[\textbf{9 H}] If $A$ is Dedekind finite and $B$ is Dedekind infinite, then $A\precsim B$. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 28 and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 I}] If $\emptyset \in K$ and for all $A\in K$ and for all $b\not\in A,\,A\, \cup\,\{b\}\in K$, then every Dedekind finite set is in $K$. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 28 and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 J}] The union of a Dedekind infinite family of non-empty sets is Dedekind infinite. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 130 and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 K}] If $A$ is uncountable and $B$ is countable, then $|A-B|=|A|$. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 201.

\noindent[\textbf{9 L}] If $A$ is uncountable and $B$ is countable, then $|A\cup B|=|A|$. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 202.

\noindent[\textbf{9 M}] If $\aleph_{0}<|A|$ and $\aleph_{0}=|B|$, then $\aleph_{0}<|A-B|$. G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 202.

\noindent\textbf{[9 N]} If $\aleph_{0}\leq^{\ast}m$, then $\aleph_{0}\leq m$. Lindenbaum/Tarski\index{Author}{Lindenbaum/Tarski} \cite{bib:1926}, G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 216, and note 69.

\noindent[\textbf{9 O}] $m\leq\aleph_{0}$ or $\aleph_{0}\leq m$. Lindenbaum/Tarski \cite{bib:1926} and G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 216.

\noindent[\textbf{9 P}] If $m+\aleph_{0}<n+\aleph_{0}$, then $m<n$. Lindenbaum/Tarski \cite{bib:1926} and G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 216.

\noindent[\textbf{9 Q}] If $m+\aleph_{0}=n+\aleph_{0}$, then $m=n$ or $m,\,n\leq\aleph_{0}$. Lindenbaum/Tarski \cite{bib:1926} and G. Moore \cite{bib:1982} p 216.

\noindent[\textbf{9 R}] $E(III, IV)$: Every Dedekind finite set has a Dedekind finite power set. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 S}] $E(Ia, IV)$: Every Dedekind finite set is amorphous. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989}, notes 57 and 94.

\noindent[\textbf{9 T}] Restricted Choice: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ such that the collection of non-empty subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco} \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 10.} $C(\aleph_{0}, <\aleph_{0})$: Every denumerable family of non-empty finite sets has a choice function.

[\textbf{10 A}] $UT(\aleph_{0}, <\aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0})$: The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets is denumerable. Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1988} p 569.

\noindent[\textbf{10 B}] Tychonoff's\index{Subject}{Tychonoff's theorem} Compactness Theorem for Countable Families of Finite $T_{2}$ Spaces: The product of a countable family of finite $T_{2}$ spaces is compact. Krom\index{Author}{Krom} \cite{bib:1981}.

\noindent[\textbf{10 C}] Every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{WO}$ on a Dedekind finite, infinite set $X$ has arbitrarily large, finite free subsets. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1989}, notes 22 and 94.

\noindent[\textbf{10 D}] In every Hilbert space with a Dedekind finite orthonormal basis, the closed unit ball is sequentially compact. Brunner \cite{bib:1983b}
and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{10 E}] $PC(\aleph_{0}, <\aleph_{0}, \infty)$: Every denumerable family of finite sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner
\cite{bib:1983b}.

\noindent[\textbf{10 F}] K\"{o}nig's Lemma:\index{Subject}{K\"{o}nig's lemma} Every $\omega$ tree has an infinite chain. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c}, note 21, and note 35.

\noindent[\textbf{10 G}] For all metric spaces $X$ and $Y$ and continuous functions $f$ from $X$ onto $Y$ such that $f^{-1}(y)$ is finite for all $y\in Y$, if $X$ has a dense Dedekind finite subset, then so does $Y$. Brunner \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{10 H}] $\sigma$-compact, paracompact $T_{2}$ spaces are weakly Lindel\"{o}f\index{Author}{Lindel\"{o}f}. Brunner \cite{bib:1982b} and note 43.

\noindent[\textbf{10 I}] Assume $(P, \leq)$ is a partial order such that $P$ is a denumerable union of finite sets and contains a non-empty subset $Q$ relative to which depths are defined for all $x\in \mathrm{P}$. If all $Q$-strong antichains of $P$ are finite then for each denumerable family $\mathcal{D}$ of dense sets there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter. Shannon \cite{bib:1990} and note 47.

\noindent[\textbf{10 J}] Let $S$ be a denumerable set of propositional sentences over an infinite set of propositional letters (in a propositional language where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then $S$ has a model if and only if every finite subset of $S$ has a model. Lolli\index{Author}{Lolli} \cite{bib:1977}.

\noindent[\textbf{10 K}] Let $S$ be a consistent denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then $S$ has a model. Note 19.

\noindent[\textbf{10 L}] Let $S$ be a denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences) such that every finite subset has a model. Then $S$ has a model. Note 19.

\noindent[\textbf{10 M}] $PUT(\aleph_{0}, <\aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0})$: The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets has a denumerable subset.

\noindent[\textbf{10 N}] $PUT(WO, <\aleph_{0}, WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint finite sets has an infinite well ordered subset.

\noindent[\textbf{10 O}] $PC(WO, <\aleph_{0}, \infty)$: Every infinite well ordered family of finite sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 11.} $\mathbb{R}$ is hereditarily Lindel\"{o}f. Lindel\"{o}f
\cite{bib:1905}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 12.} $\mathbb{R}$ is Lindel\"{o}f. Young\index{Author}{Young} \cite{bib:1903}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 13.} Every Dedekind finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is finite. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} \cite{bib:1982} and note 94.

[\textbf{13 A}] $\mathbb{R}$ has no dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

\noindent[\textbf{13 B}] There is a separable topological space $X$ and a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $X^{A\times \omega}$ has no dense, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982d} and note 94.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 14.} BPI: Every Boolean algebra has a prime ideal. M. Stone\index{Author}{M. Stone} \cite{bib:1936}.

[\textbf{14 A}] Ultrafilter Theorem: Every proper filter over a set $S$ (in $\mathcal{P}(S)$) can be extended to an ultrafilter. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 17.

\noindent[\textbf{14 B}] Stone Representation Theorem:\index{Subject}{Stone representation theorem} Every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to a set algebra. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 27 prob 2.12 and M. Stone \cite{bib:1936}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 C}] Every commutative ring with unit has a prime ideal. Scott\index{Author}{Scott} \cite{bib:1954}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 D}] Every ring with unit has a (two sided) prime ideal. (An ideal $P$ in a ring $R$ is prime if $P\neq R$ and for any ideals $A$ and $B$ in $R$, if $AB\subseteq P$ then $A\subseteq P$ or $B\subseteq P.)$ Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1986} and Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1985}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 E}] Almost Maximal Ideal Theorem:\index{Subject}{almost maximal ideal theorem} Every bounded, non-trivial, distributive lattice has an almost maximal ideal. (Definitions: If $D$ is a bounded non-trivial distributive lattice, $I(D)$ is the lattice of ideals of $D$. An \emph{almost maximal ideal} in $D$ is an ideal $P$ of $D$ such that $s(P)=P$ where $s$ is the operation on $I(D)$ defined as follows: If $e$ is the unit of $I(D)$, (i) For $a\in I(D)$ we say $x\in I(D)$ is $a$-\emph{small} if $x\vee b=e$ implies $a\vee b=e$ for all $b\in I(D)$. (ii) For any $a\in I(D)$, $s(a)$ is the join of all a-small elements of $I(D))$. Banaschewski/Harting\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Harting} \cite{bib:1985} and Blass \cite{bib:1986}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 F}] Every non-trivial complete distributive lattice with compact unit has a prime ideal. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1985} and note 29.

\noindent[\textbf{14 G(n)}] $(n\in \omega, n\geq 3)\,P_{n}$: For every graph $G$ if every finite subgraph of $G$ is $n$-colorable then $G$ is $n$-colorable. L\"{a}uchli\index{Author}{L\"{a}uchli} \cite{bib:1971} and note 117.

\noindent[\textbf{14 H}] Compactness Theorem for First Order Logic: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas in a first order language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ has a model then $\Sigma$ has a model. Henkin\index{Author}{Henkin} \cite{bib:1954a} and Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 17.

\noindent[\textbf{14 I}] Consistency Principle:\index{Subject}{consistency principle} For every binary mess $M$ on a set $S$ there is a function $f$ on $S$ which is consistent with $M$. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 17 and note 109.

\noindent[\textbf{14 J}] Tychonoff's\index{Subject}{Tychonoff's theorem} Compactness Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: The product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact. (For many compactness theorems $T$, it is clear that [14 J] implies $T$ implies [14 K].) {\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski\index{Author}{{\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski}
\cite{bib:1954} and Rubin/Scott\index{Author}{Rubin/Scott} \cite{bib:1954}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 K}] Compactness of the Generalized Cantor Space: $\{0,1\}^{I}$ is compact for any I. (For many compactness theorems $T$, it is clear that [14 J] implies $T$ implies [14 K].) Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 28, prob 17 and Mycielski\index{Author}{Mycielski} \cite{bib:1964}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 L}] Stone-\v{C}ech Compactification Theorem:\index{Subject}{Stone-\v{C}ech compactification theorem} For every topological space $X$ there is a pair $(Y, j)$ such that $Y$ is a compact topological space and $j$ is a continuous surjection from $X$ onto $Y$ such that for all topological spaces $Z$ such that $Z$ is compact and completely regular and for all continuous $f:X\rightarrow Z$, there is a unique continuous $h:Y\rightarrow Z$ such that $f=h\circ j$. Rubin/Scott \cite{bib:1954} and note 71.

\noindent[\textbf{14 M}] R. Cowen's Generalization of Konig's Lemma:\index{Subject}{K\"{o}nig's lemma} Let $T$ be a collection of locally finite trees such that for any finite set of levels of $T$, there is a consistent set of vertices piercing those levels. Then there is a consistent set of vertices piercing the entire set of levels of T. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} \cite{bib:1977b} and note 21.

\noindent[\textbf{14 N(n)}] $(n\in\omega,\,n\geq 2)$ [14 M] restricted to families of trees where no tree in the family has a vertex with more than $n$ successors. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} \cite{bib:1977b}, Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1984a}, and note 21.

\noindent[\textbf{14 O}]\index{Subject}{Rado's selection lemma} Let $\{A(i):i\in I\}$\index{Subject}{FIP extension principle} be a collection of finite sets and $R$ a symmetric binary relation on $\bigcup_{i\in I}A(i)$. Suppose that for every finite $W\subseteq I$, there is an $R$-consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in W\}$. Then there is an $R$-consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in I\}$. {\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski\index{Author}{{\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski}
 \cite{bib:1951} and note 109.

\noindent[\textbf{14 P($n$)}] (For $n\geq 3)$ [14 O] restricted to $\{A(i):i\in I\}$ such that for all $i\in I,\,|A(i)|\leq n$. Cowen \cite{bib:1977b} and note 109. (For $n=2$ see form 141.)

\noindent[\textbf{14 Q}] Alaoglu's Theorem:\index{Subject}{Alaoglu's theorem} The unit ball is compact in the weak$^{\ast}$ topology in the dual of a Banach space. (See [52 E].) Johnstone\index{Author}{Johnstone} \cite{bib:1984} and note 23.

\noindent[\textbf{14 R}] Every coherent local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1981} and note 29.

\noindent[\textbf{14 S}] Every compact, regular local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1981} and note 29.

\noindent[\textbf{14 T}] Every regular commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1983} and note 29.

\noindent[\textbf{14 U}] Every closed proper ideal in a Gelfand algebra is contained in some maximal ideal. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1983} and note 29.

\noindent[\textbf{14 V}] FIP Extension Principle: Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{X}$ have the finite intersection property, then $\mathcal{F}\subseteq U$ for some ultrafilter $U$ on $X$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} \cite{bib:1996a}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 W}] Universal Subnet Theorem: Any net has a universal subnet. Schechter \cite{bib:1996a} and note 31.

\noindent[\textbf{14 X}] Cowen-Engler Lemma:\index{Subject}{Cowen-Engler lemma} Let $\Lambda$ and $X$ be sets. Let $\Phi$ be a family of functions from subsets of $\Lambda$ into X. Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\Phi(\lambda)=\{f(\lambda):f\in\Phi$ and $\lambda\in$ dom $f\}$ is finite for each $\lambda\in\Lambda$,
\item[(b)] each finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$ is the domain of at least one $f\in\Phi$, and
\item[(c)] $\Phi$ has finite character, (that is, a function $f$ from a subset of $\Lambda$ into $X$ is in $\Phi$ if and only if every finite subset of $f$ is in $\Phi$).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent Then at least one $f\in\Phi$ has domain $\Lambda$. Schechter \cite{bib:1996a}. (See [14 I].)

\noindent[\textbf{14 Y}] Form 99 + Form 62. Note 33.

\noindent[\textbf{14 Z}] Tychonoff's\index{Subject}{Tychonoff's theorem} Compactness Theorem for Families of Finite Spaces: If $\{X_{i}:i\in I\}$ is a family of finite topological spaces, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_{i}$ is compact. (Cleary [14 Z] implies [14 K] and is implied by [14 J].) Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 28 prob 17, A.A. Lewis\index{Author}{Lewis} \cite{bib:1983}, and Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} \cite{bib:1967}.

\noindent[\textbf{14 AA}] Alexander's Subbase Lemma:\index{Subject}{Alexander's subbase lemma} A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase $S$ for the topology such that every cover by elements of $S$ has a finite subcover. Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} \cite{bib:1955} p 143, A.A. Lewis \cite{bib:1983}, Wolk \cite{bib:1967}, and note 34.

\noindent[\textbf{14 AB}] Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for Sober Spaces: A product of compact, sober topological spaces is compact. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1986}, Johnstone \cite{bib:1984} and note 37.

\noindent[\textbf{14 AC}] (Depends on $k, n\in \omega$ with $k\geq 2,\,n\geq 2$ and $n+k\geq 5$.) $P(k, n)$: If $X$ is a set and $P$ is a property of subsets of $X$ of $n$ character (that is, $\forall y\subseteq X(P(y)$ iff $\forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq n\rightarrow P(z))))$, then if every finite subset of $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets (that is, sets $z$ such that $P(z))$, then $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} \cite{bib:1982}.
