\noindent\textbf{FORM 375.}\index{Subject}{convex domination theorem}\index{Subject}{Gelfand extreme point theorem}\index{Subject}{Hahn-Banach theorem}\index{Subject}{measure extension theorem}\index{Subject}{sandwich theorem}\index{Subject}{support theorem} Tietze-Urysohn\index{Author}{Urysohn} Extension Theorem: If $(X, T)$ is a normal topological space, $A$ is closed in $X$, and $f:A\rightarrow[0,1]$ is continuous, then there exists a continuous function $g:X\rightarrow[0, 1]$ which extends $f$. Urysohn \cite{bib:1924}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 376.} Restricted Kinna Wagner Principle: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ and a function $f$ such that for every $z\subseteq Y$, if $|z|\geq 2$ then $f(z)$ is a non-empty proper subset of $z$. De la Cruz/Di Prisco\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco} \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 377.} Restricted Ordering Principle: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that $Y$ can be linearly ordered. De la Cruz/Di Prisco \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 378.} Restricted Choice for Families of Well Ordered Sets: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that the family of non-empty well orderable subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco \cite{bib:1996}.

[\textbf{378A}] Restricted Choice for Families of Finite Sets: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that the family of non-empty Finite subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 379.} $PKW(\infty, \infty, \infty)$: For every infinite family $X$ of sets each of which has at least two elements, there is an infinite subfamily $Y$ of $X$ and a function $f$ such that for all $y\in Y,\, f(y)$ is a non-empty proper subset of $y$. De la Cruz/Di Prisco \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 380.} $PC(\infty, WO, \infty)$: For every infinite family of non-empty well orderable sets, there is an infinite subfamily $Y$ of $X$ which has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco \cite{bib:1996}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 381.} DUM: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} \cite{bib:1997b}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 382.} DUMN: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin \cite{bib:1997b}.

\noindent\textbf{FORM 383.} MP: Every metric space is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} \cite{bib:1997} and note 141.

[\textbf{383 A}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X, d$) has a refinement $\mathcal{V}$ which covers $X$ and which can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{V_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where each $V_{\alpha}$ is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley \cite{bib:1997} and note 141.

\noindent[\textbf{383 B}] MM: Every metric space is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley \cite{bib:1997} and note 141.

\noindent[\textbf{383 C}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X, d$) has a refinement $\mathcal{V}$ which covers $X$ and which can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{V_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where each $V_{\alpha}$ is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley \cite{bib:1997} and note 141.

\setcounter{chapter}{1}
\chapter{Topical List of Forms}\label{part02}

\section*{ALGEBRAIC FORMS}

\textbf{I. Groups}

[\textbf{1 BA}] (Depends on the prime $p$) Every group has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1987d} and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BB}] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem\index{Subject}{Nielsen-Schreier theorem} II: If $G$ is a group which is freely generated by $X$ and $U$ is a subgroup of $G$, then there is a subset $A$ of $G$ which freely generates $U$ and is level with respect to $X$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1985n} and note 129.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BS}] For every Abelian group $(G,\,+)$, for every $H\subseteq G$, the infinite system of equations
\begin{equation*}
x_{i}+y_{i}=a_{i},\,i\in I,\,a_{i}\in G
\end{equation*}
has a solution in $H$ iff each of its equations has a solution in $H$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996c1}.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BX}] For every Abelian group $G$ and every subgroup $H$ of $G$ there exists a set of representatives for the quotient $G/H$. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996c1}.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CA}] Strong Nielsen-Schreier Theorem I: If $G$ is a group which is freely generated by $X$ and $U$ is a subgroup of $G$, then there is a subset $A$ of $G$ which freely generates $U$ and has the Nielsen property with respect to $X$. Howard \cite{bib:1985n} and note 129.

\noindent [\textbf{62 A}] (Depends on the two primes $p_{1}\neq p_{2}$) Form $308(p_{1})+$ form $308(p_{2})$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1987d}.

\noindent [\textbf{62 B}] (Depends on the prime $p_{1}$) Form $45(p_{1})+$ form $308(p_{1})$. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1987d}.

\noindent [\textbf{62 C}] For every prime $p$, if $\{G_{y}:y\in Y\}$ is a set of finite groups, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}G_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1987d} and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{62 D}] For every prime $p$, if $Y$ is a set of non-empty, finite sets, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}S_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. $(S_{y}$ is the symmetric group on $y$.) Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1987d} and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{67 D}] For every Abelian group $A$, every torsion free divisible subgroup of $A$ is a direct summand of $A$. Armbrust\index{Author}{Armbrust} \cite{bib:1972a} and note 24.

\noindent \textbf{68.} Nielsen-Schreier Theorem: Every subgroup of a free group is free. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p12.

\noindent \textbf{176.} Every infinite, locally finite group has an infinite Abelian subgroup. (\emph{Locally finite} means every finite subset generates a finite subgroup.) Plotkin\index{Author}{Plotkin} \cite{bib:1981i}.

\noindent \textbf{180.} Every Abelian group has a divisible hull. (If $A$ and $B$ are groups, $B$ \emph{is a divisible hull of} $A$ means $B$ is a divisible group, $A$ is a subgroup of $B$ and for every non-zero $b\in B,\,\exists n\in w$ such that $0\neq nb\in A$.) Fuchs\index{Author}{Fuchs} \cite{bib:1970e}, Theorem 24.4 p 107, Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} \cite{bib:1980j}, and note 24.

\noindent \textbf{188.} $EP$ \emph{Ab}: For every Abelian group $A$ there is a projective Abelian group $G$ and a homomorphism from $G$ onto $A$. Blass \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent \textbf{189.} $EI$ \emph{Ab}: For every Abelian group $A$ there is an injective Abelian group $G$ and a one to one homomorphism from $A$ into $G$. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent \textbf{190.} There is a non-trivial injective Abelian group. Blass \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent \textbf{193.} $EFP$ \emph{Ab}: Every Abelian group is a homomorphic image of a free projective Abelian group. Blass \cite{bib:1979} and note 60.

\noindent \textbf{210.} The commutator subgroup of a free group is free. L\"{a}uchli\index{Author}{Lauchli@L\"{a}uchli} \cite{bib:1962d}.

\noindent \textbf{220($p$).} Suppose $p\in\omega$ and $p$ is a prime. Any two elementary Abelian $p$-groups (all non-trivial elements have order \emph{p}) of the same cardinality are isomorphic. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1977b2}.

\noindent \textbf{227.} For all groups $G$, if every finite subgroup of $G$ can be fully ordered then $G$ can be fully ordered. Rav \cite{bib:1977k} and note 79.

\noindent \textbf{228.} Every torsion free Abelian group can be fully ordered. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} \cite{bib:1977k} and note 79.

\noindent \textbf{229.} If $(G,\,\circ,\,\leq)$ is a partially ordered group, then $\leq$ can be extended to a linear order on $G$ if and only if for every finite set $\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}\subseteq G$, with $a_{i}\neq$ the identity for $i=1$ to $n$, the signs $\epsilon_{1},\,\ldots,\,\epsilon_{n}\,(\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1)$ can be chosen so that $P\cap S(a_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}})=\emptyset$ (where $S(b_{1},\, \ldots,\,b_{n})$ is the normal sub-semi-group of $G$ generated by $b_{1},\,\ldots,\,b_{n}$ and $P=\{g\in G:e\leq g\}$ where $e$ is the identity of $G$.) Rav \cite{bib:1977k}.

\noindent \textbf{237.} The order of any group is divisible by the order of any of its subgroups, (i.e., if $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ then there is a set $A$ such that $|H\times A|=|G|$.) Hickman \cite{bib:1976j}.

\noindent \textbf{238.} Every elementary Abelian group (that is, for some prime $p$ every non identity element has order \emph{p}) is the direct sum of cyclic subgroups. Hickman \cite{bib:1976j}.

\noindent \textbf{239.} For all $X$, if $X\neq\emptyset$, then there is a binary operation on $X$ that makes $X$ a group. Hickman \cite{bib:1976j}.

\noindent \textbf{240.} If a group $G$ satisfies ``every ascending chain of subgroups is finite,'' then every subgroup of $G$ is finitely generated. Hickman \cite{bib:1976j}.

\noindent \textbf{251.} The additive groups $(\mathbb{R},\,+)$ and $(\mathbb{C},\,+)$ are isomorphic. Ash\index{Author}{Ash} \cite{bib:1975}.

\noindent \textbf{252.} The additive groups of $\mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are isomorphic. Ash \cite{bib:1975}.

\noindent \textbf{308($p$).} If $p$ is a prime and if $\{G_{y}:y\in Y\}$ is a set of finite groups, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}G_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1987} and note 24.

\noindent \textbf{[308A($p$)]} If $p$ is a prime and if $Y$ is a set of non-empty, finite sets, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}S_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup ($S_{y}$ is the symmetric group on $y$.) Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1987} and note 24.

\noindent \textbf{311.} Abelian groups are amenable. ($G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.) Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{312.} A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable. $(G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A).)$ Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{313.} $\mathbb{Z}$ (the set of integers under addition) is amenable. ($G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.) Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{314.} Every permutation on a non-empty set can be expressed as a product of two reflections. (A reflection is a permutation $\phi$ such that $\phi^{2}$ is the identity.) Degen\index{Author}{Degen} \cite{bib:1988c}.

\noindent [\textbf{333 B}] Every quotient group of an Abelian group each of whose non-unit elements has order 2 has a set of representatives. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996a}.

\noindent \textbf{335 ($n$).} Every quotient group of an Abelian group each of whose elements has order $\leq n$ has a set of representatives. Keremedis \cite{bib:1996c1}.

\noindent \textbf{348.} If $G$ is a group and $X$ and $Y$ both freely generate $G$ then $|X|=|Y|$. Federer/Jonsson\index{Author}{Federer/Jonsson} \cite{bib:1950} and Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1985n}.

\textbf{II. Lattices}

\noindent [\textbf{1 AN}] Every lattice $\langle L, \cap,\,\cup, \subseteq\rangle$ of sets (that is, $L$ is a family of sets and $\cap,\,\cup$ and $\subseteq$ are the usual operations) with a greatest element has a maximal, proper ideal. Bell/Fremlin\index{Author}{Bell/Fremlin} \cite{bib:1972c}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 E}] Almost Maximal Ideal Theorem: Every bounded, non-trivial, distributive lattice has an almost maximal ideal. (Definitions: If $D$ is a bounded non-trivial distributive lattice, $I(D)$ is the lattice of ideals of $D$. An \emph{almost maximal ideal} in $D$ is an ideal $P$ of $D$ such that $s(P)=P$ where $s$ is the operation on $I(D)$ defined as follows: If $e$ is the unit of $I(D)$, (i) For $a\in I(D)$ we say $x\in I(D)$ is $a$-\emph{small} if $x\vee b=e$ implies $a\vee b=e$ for all $b\in I(D)$. (ii) For any $a\in I(D)$, $s(a)$ is the join of all a-small elements of $I(D)$). Banaschewski/Harting\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Harting} \cite{bib:1985d} and Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1986}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 F}] Every non-trivial complete distributive lattice with compact unit has a prime ideal. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1985c} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 R}] Every coherent local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1981b} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 S}] Every compact, regular local lattice is spatial. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1981b} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AE}] For any distributive lattice $D$ with zero and unit, any ideal $J\subseteq D$ and $a\not\in J$, there is a prime filter $F$ such that $a\in F$ and $F\cap J=\emptyset$. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1981b}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AU}] If $Z$ is a real vector lattice with order unit 1 then the set of all positive linear functionals $u$ on $Z$ with $u(1)=1$ is a convex set that has an extreme point. See H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, pages 177 and 182 for definitions. Also see Gardiner\index{Author}{Gardiner} \cite{bib:1974i}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BH}] The sum of finite frames is a spatial frame. Paseka\index{Author}{Paseka} \cite{bib:1989s} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BI}] Every compact, conjunctive frame is spatial. Paseka \cite{bib:1989s} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BJ}] The sum of compact, regular frames is spatial. Paseka \cite{bib:1989s} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BL}] Every compact, 0 dimensional frame is spatial. Paseka \cite{bib:1989s} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BP}] Every non-empty bounded distributive lattice has a prime ideal. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BQ}] Every proper ideal in a bounded distributive lattice is the intersection of the prime ideals containing it. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 79. (Compare with [14 AE]).

\noindent [\textbf{14 BR}] Every $\vee$-compact non trivial lattice has a principal prime ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}, \cite{bib:1985p} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BS}] Every bounded distributive lattice has a prime ideal choice function. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}, \cite{bib:1985p} and note~71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BT}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of bounded, distributive, $\vee$-compact lattices and if $(J_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family such that for all $i\in I,\,J_{i}$ is a proper ideal in $A_{i}$ then there is a family $(P_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for all $i\in I,\,P_{i}$ is a prime principal ideal in $A_{i}$ containing $J_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BU}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of distributive non trivial bounded lattices, then there is a family $(f_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that each $f_{i}$ is a prime ideal choice function on $A_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CH}] For every bounded, distributive lattice $(A, \wedge, \vee)$ in which $0$ is $\wedge$-compact, for all $a\in A,\,a\neq 0$ and for all sequences $(X_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ of subsets of $A$, there is a prime filter in $A$ which contains $a$ and respects each $X_{n}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{50 C}] Every DeMorgan compact regular frame is injective in the category of all such frames. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1988a}, notes 29 and 60.

\noindent [\textbf{50 D}] For any extension $M\supseteq L$ of a compact regular frame $L$, there is an $s\in M$ maximal with respect to the property that $x\vee s=1\rightarrow x=1$ for all $x\in L$. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1988a}, notes 29 and 60.

\noindent [\textbf{86 B($\alpha$)}] The frame envelope of any $\aleph_{\alpha}$ frame is $\aleph_{\alpha}$-Lindel\"{o}f. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1997} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{88 C}] If $m$ is a cardinal number and $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice isomorphic to the lattice of subalgebras of some unary universal algebra (a unary universal algebra is one with only unary or nullary operations) and $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathcal{L}$ of order 2 (that is, $\alpha^{2}$ is the identity) then there is a unary algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ with $|\ \mathrm{domain}\ \mathfrak{A}|\geq m$ and an isomorphism $\rho$ from $\mathcal{L}$ onto the lattice of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ with $\rho(\alpha(x))=(\rho(x))^{-1}(=\{(s,\,t):(t,\,s)\in \rho(x)\})$ for all $x\in \mathcal{L}$. Lampe\index{Author}{Lampe} \cite{bib:1974m}.

\noindent \textbf{268.} If $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice isomorphic to the lattice of subalgebras of some unary universal algebra (a unary universal algebra is one with only unary or nullary operations) and $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathcal{L}$ of order 2 (that is, $\alpha^{2}$ is the identity) then there is a unary algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ and an isomorphism $\rho$ from $\mathcal{L}$ onto the lattice of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ with $\rho(\alpha(x))=(\rho(x))^{-1}(=\{(s,\,t):(t,\,s)\in\rho(x)\})$ for all $x\in \mathcal{L}$. Lampe \cite{bib:1974m}.

\noindent [\textbf{345 C}] Every bounded, distributive lattice has the strong Rasiowa-Sikorski property\index{Subject}{Rasiowa-Sikorski property}. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{345 D}] Every bounded, distributive lattice has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\textbf{III. Rings}

\textbf{A. Boolean Algebras}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Y}] There is no free complete Boolean algebra over $D$ if $|D|\geq\aleph_{0}$. Stavi\index{Author}{Stavi} \cite{bib:1975k}, Gaifman\index{Author}{Gaifman} \cite{bib:1970f}, Hales\index{Author}{Hales} \cite{bib:1964c}, and note 89.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BT}] For every Boolean ring $(B,\,+,\,\cdot)$ and every $H\subseteq B$ which is closed under $+$ there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal ideal $Q\subseteq B$ such that $H\cap Q=\{0\}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996c1}.

\noindent \textbf{14.} BPI: Every Boolean algebra has a prime ideal. M. Stone \cite{bib:1936}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 B}] Stone Representation Theorem:\index{Subject}{Stone representation theorem} Every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to a set algebra. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 27 prob 2.12 and M. Stone \cite{bib:1936}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AV}] Every Boolean algebra has a 2-valued measure. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c1} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BA}] Monteiro's Theorem\index{Subject}{Monteiro's theorem} for Complete Atomic Boolean Algebras: Let $K$ be a complete atomic Boolean algebra, $A$ a subalgebra of the Boolean algebra $B$ and $f$ a homomorphism from $A$ to $K$. Let $d$ be a semimorphism from $B$ into $K$ (that is, $d\,:\,B\rightarrow K,\,d(0)=0,\,d(1)=1$ and for all $x,\,y\in B,\, d(x\vee y)=d(x)\vee d(y)$ ) with $f(x)\leq d(x)$ for all $x\in A$. Then there is a homomorphism $h$ from $B$ to $K$ such that $h(x)\leq d(x)$ for all $x\in B$ and $h/A=f$. Monteiro\index{Author}{Monteiro} \cite{bib:1965g} and Bacsich\index{Author}{Bacsich} \cite{bib:1972b}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BC}] If $m_{0}$ is an additive, real valued measure on a subalgebra $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$ then there exists a measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m=m_{0}$ on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ and the range of $m$ is contained in the closure of the range of $m_{0}$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1930} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BK}] The sum of 4-element Boolean algebras is spatial. Paseka\index{Author}{Paseka} \cite{bib:1989s} and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{43 A}] Tarski's Lemma:\index{Subject}{Tarski's lemma} Let $\{x(n):n\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable collection of subsets of a Boolean algebra $B$ each of which has a meet in B. Then for any $a\neq 0$ in $B$ there is a proper filter $F$ of $B$ that decides $\bigwedge x(n)$ for all $n$ and has $a\in F$. ($F$ \emph{decides} $\bigwedge x(n)$ if either $\bigwedge x(n)\in F$ or $t\not\in F$ for some $t\in x(n)$.) Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985m}.

\noindent \textbf{50.} Sikorski's Extension Theorem:\index{Subject}{Sikorski's extension theorem} Every homomorphism of a subalgebra $B$ of a Boolean algebra $A$ into a complete Boolean algebra $B^{\prime}$ can be extended to a homomorphism of $A$ into $B^{\prime}$. Sikorski\index{Author}{Sikorski} \cite{bib:1964p}, p 141.

\noindent [\textbf{50 A}] Every complete Boolean algebra is injective. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1988a}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 B}] Monteiro's Theorem:\index{Subject}{Monteiro's theorem} Let $K$ be a complete Boolean algebra, $A$ a subalgebra of the Boolean algebra $B$ and $f$ a homomorphism from $A$ to $K$. Let $d$ be a semimorphism from $B$ into $K$ (that is, $d:B\rightarrow K,\,d(0)=0,\,d(1)=1$ and for all $x$ and $y$ in $B,\,d(x\vee y)=d(x)\vee d(y))$ with $f(x)\leq d(x)$ for all $x\in A$. Then there is a homomorphism $h$ from $B$ to $K$ such that $h(x)\leq d(x)$ for all $x\in B$ and $h/A=f$. Monteiro\index{Author}{Monteiro} \cite{bib:1965g} and Bacsich\index{Author}{Bacsich} \cite{bib:1972b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 E}] Form 14 + form 297. Banaschewski \cite{bib:1988a} and Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 F}] For any complete Boolean algebra $B$ and any subalgebra $A$ of $B$, there is a $U\in V^{(B)}$ such that $V^{(B)}\models\ \text{``} U$ is an ultrafilter on $A$ and $U^{B}\subseteq U$''. ($V^{(B)}$ is the Boolean valued universe constructed from $B,\,U^{B}=\{(\hat{x},\,x):x\in B\}$ is the canonical ultrafilter on $B$ and $x\mapsto\hat{x}$ is the canonical embedding of $V$ into $V^{(B)}$.) Bell \cite{bib:1977}  and \cite{bib:1983a}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 G}] For any complete Boolean algebra $B$ and any $C\in V^{(B)}$ such that $V^{(B)}\models \text{``}C$ is a Boolean algebra.'' there is a $U\in V^{(B)}$ such that $V^{(B)}\models \text{``}U$ is an ultrafilter in $C$.'' See [50 F] for definitions. Bell \cite{bib:1983a}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 H}] If $m:A\rightarrow B$ is a monomorphism between Boolean algebras, then there is an $m$-minimal epimorphism $p:B\rightarrow C$ to some Boolean algebra $C$. ($p$ is $m$-minimal if (1) $p\circ m$ is monic and (2) if $q:C\rightarrow D$ is any epimorphism to a Boolean algebra $D$ such that $q\circ p\circ m$ is monic, then $q$ is an isomorphism.) Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 I}] If $A$ is a subalgebra of a Boolean algebra $B$, then there is a $\subseteq$-maximal proper filter $F$ in $B$ such that $F\cap A=\{1\}$. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}

\noindent [\textbf{50 J}] Form 299$+$ form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 K}] Form 300$+$ form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 L}] Form $301+$ form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 M}] Form $302+$ form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{52 A}] On every Boolean algebra there is an additive real valued measure. Luxemburg\index{Author}{Luxemburg} \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 B}] For every proper filter $\mathcal{F}$ of elements of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$, there exists an additive, real valued measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m(x)=1$ for all $x\in \mathcal{F}$. Luxemburg \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 C}] For every non-empty set X and every proper ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ there is a measure $m$ on $\mathcal{P}(X)$ such that $m(x)=0$ for all $x\in \mathcal{I}$. Luxemburg \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 D}] Let $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ be a subalgebra of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$ and $m_{0}$ an additive, real valued measure on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$. Then there is a real valued, additive measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m=m_{0}$ on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ and the range of $m$ is contained in the closed convex hull of the range of $m_{0}$. Luxemburg\index{Author}{Luxemburg} \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{123 A}] Form 70$+$ form 344. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent \textbf{201.} Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras:\index{Subject}{linking axiom} Every Boolean algebra has a maximal linked system. ($L\subseteq B$ is \emph{linked} if $a\wedge b\neq 0$ for all $a$ and $b\in L$.) Schrijver\index{Author}{Schrijver} \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent [\textbf{201 A}] Strong Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras: Each linked system in a Boolean algebra is contained in some maximal linked system. (If $B$ is a Boolean algebra, $L\subseteq B$ is \emph{linked} if $a\wedge b\neq 0$ for all $a$ and $b\in L$.) Schrijver \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent \textbf{247.} Every atomless Boolean algebra is Dedekind infinite. Plotkin\index{Author}{Plotkin} \cite{bib:1976p}, notes 86 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{248.} For any $\kappa,\,\kappa$ is the cardinal number of an infinite complete Boolean algebra if and only if $\kappa^{\aleph_{0}}=\kappa$. Plotkin \cite{bib:1976p} and note 86.

\noindent \textbf{267.} There is no infinite, free complete Boolean algebra. Stavi\index{Author}{Stavi} \cite{bib:1975k} and note 89.

\noindent \textbf{303.} If $B$ is a Boolean algebra, $S\subseteq B$ and $S$ is closed under $\wedge$, then there is a $\subseteq$-maximal proper ideal $I$ of $B$ such that $I \cap S=\{0\}$. H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}.

\noindent \textbf{310.} The Measure Extension Theorem:\index{Subject}{measure extension theorem} Suppose that $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ is a subring (that is, $a,\,b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}\rightarrow a\vee b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}$ and $a-b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}$) of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mu$ is a measure on $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ (that is, $\mu\,:\,\mathcal{A}\rightarrow[0,\,\infty],\,\mu(a\vee b)=\mu(a)+\mu(b)$ for $a\wedge b=0$, and $\mu(0)=0$.) then there is a measure on $\mathcal{A}$ that extends $\mu$. Wagon\index{Author}{Wagon} \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{317.} Weak Sikorski Theorem:\index{Subject}{Sikorski's extension theorem} If $B$ is a complete, well orderable Boolean algebra and $f$ is a homomorphism of the Boolean algebra $A^{\prime}$ into $B$ where $A^{\prime}$ is a subalgebra of the Boolean algebra $A$, then $f$ can be extended to a homomorphism of $A$ into $B$. Howard \cite{bib:1973h}.

\noindent [\textbf{317 A}] If $B$ is a complete, well orderable Boolean algebra and $A$ is a Boolean algebra of which $B$ is a subalgebra, then there is an ideal $I$ of $A$ satisfying $I\cap B =\{0\}$ and $I$ is maximal among those ideals $J$ of $A$ satisfying $J\cap B=\{0\}$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973h}.

\noindent \textbf{344.} If $(E_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of non-empty sets, then there is a family $(U_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that $\forall i\in I,\,U_{i}$ is an ultrafilter on $E_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent \textbf{345.} Rasiowa-Sikorski Axiom:\index{Subject}{Rasiowa-Sikorski axiom} If $(B,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a Boolean algebra, $a$ is a non-zero element of $B$, and $\{X_{n}:n\in w\}$ is a denumerable set of subsets of $B$ then there is a maximal prime filter $F$ of $B$ such that $a\in F$ and for each $n\in \omega$, if $X_{n}\subseteq F$ and $\bigwedge X_{n}$ exists then $\bigwedge X_{n}\in F$. Morillon~\cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{345 A}] Form $14+$ form 43. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{345 B}] Form $14+$ form 106. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{345 E}] Every Boolean algebra has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{370 A}] Measured Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem: If $\mathcal{B}$ is a Boolean algebra and there is a measure on $\mathcal{B}$ then there is an ultrafilter on $\mathcal{B}$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1989r}, \cite{bib:1990e} and note 147.

\textbf{B. Fields (Including Algebraic Properties of} $\mathbb{R}$ \textbf{and} $\mathbb{Q}$) (See note 45.)

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ R}] Every infinite Dedekind finite field is the direct limit of a strictly increasing $\omega$-sequence of finite subfields. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1982f}, notes 45 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BN}] A system of equations over a finite field $F$ has a solution in $F$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $F$. Cowen/Emerson\index{Author}{Cowen/Emerson} \cite{bib:1995} and note 30.

\noindent \textbf{69.} Every field has an algebraic closure. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p~13.

\noindent \textbf{72.} Artin-Schreier Theorem: Every field in which $-1$ is not the sum of squares can be ordered. (The ordering, $\leq$, must satisfy (a) $a\leq b\rightarrow a+c\leq b+c$ for all $c$ and (b) $c\geq 0$ and $a\leq b\rightarrow a\cdot c\leq b\cdot\mathrm{c}$.) Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1954b}].

\noindent \textbf{233.} If a field has an algebraic closure it is unique up to isomorphism. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1977b}].

\noindent \textbf{241.} Every algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ has a real closed subfield. Hodges [\textbf{1976a}], L\"{a}uchli\index{Author}{Lauchli@L\"{a}uchli} [\textbf{1962}] and note 84.

\noindent \textbf{242.} There is, up to an isomorphism, at most one algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} [\textbf{1976a}], L\"{a}uchli [\textbf{1962}] and note 84.

\noindent \textbf{284.} A system of linear equations over a field $F$ has a solution in $F$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $F$. Cowen/Emerson \cite{bib:1995}.

\noindent \textbf{367.} There is a Hamel basis for $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$. Hamel\index{Author}{Hamel} [\textbf{1905}].

\textbf{C. General Rings}

\noindent [\textbf{1 B}] Every commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Hodges [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 CD}] In a commutative ring, every proper ideal can be extended to a maximal ideal. Krull\index{Author}{Krull} [\textbf{1929}]. ([1 CD] implies [1 B]).

\noindent [\textbf{14 C}] Every commutative ring with unit has a prime ideal. Scott\index{Author}{Scott} [\textbf{1954}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 D}] Every ring with unit has a (two sided) prime ideal. (An ideal $P$ in a ring $R$ is prime if $P\neq R$ and for any ideals $A$ and $B$ in $R$, if $AB\subseteq P$ then $A\subseteq P$ or $B\subseteq P$.) Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1986}] and Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} [\textbf{1985}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 T}] Every regular commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Banaschewski [\textbf{1983}] and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 U}] Every closed proper ideal in a Gelfand algebra is contained in some maximal ideal. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} [\textbf{1983}] and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AL}] The radical of a proper ideal $A$ in a commutative ring $R$ with identity is the intersection of all prime ideals in $R$ containing $A$. (The \emph{radical} of $A= \{x\in R:\ \text{for some}\ m\in\omega,\, x^{m}\in A\}.)$ Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}] and note 80.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AM}] Let $A$ be a subring of a commutative ring $R$ and $p$ a prime ideal in $A$ such that $p=Rp\cap A$. Then there is a prime ideal $J$ in $R$ such that $p=J\cap A$. Rav [\textbf{1977}] and note 80.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AN}] In every commutative ring with identity, every proper ideal is included in some prime ideal. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AO}] Suppose $R$ is a commutative ring, $A$ is a proper ideal in $R$, and $S$ is a multiplicative semigroup in $R$ not meeting $A$. Then there is a prime ideal $p$ in $R$ such that $A\subseteq p$ and $p\cap S=\emptyset$. Rav [\textbf{1977}] and note 80.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BM}] A system of equations over a finite ring $R$ has a solution in $R$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $R$. Abian\index{Author}{Abian} [\textbf{1972}] and note 30.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BO}] A system of equations over a finite structure $(A,\,+,\,\cdot)$ has a solution in $A$, if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $A$. note 30.

\noindent \textbf{226.} Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, $B$ a proper subring containing 1 and $q$ a prime ideal in $B$. Then there is a subring $A$ of $R$ and a prime ideal $p$ in $A$ such that (a) $B\subseteq A$ (b) $q=B\cap p$ (c) $R-p$ is multiplicatively closed and (d) if $A\neq R$, then $R-A$ is multiplicatively closed. Rav [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{243.} Every principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} [\textbf{1976a}] and note 84.

\noindent \textbf{244.} Every principal ideal domain has a maximal ideal. Hodges [\textbf{1976a}] and note 84.

\noindent \textbf{278.} In an integral domain $R$, if every ideal is finitely generated then $R$ has a maximal proper ideal. Hodges [\textbf{1974}] and note 45 E.

\textbf{IV. Universal Algebra}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ U}] For any class of similar (universal) algebras $K,\,HSP\,K=Mod\,Eq\,K$. (The class of homomorphic images of subalgebras of products of non-empty families of algebras in $K$ is the same as the class of algebras which satisfy the set of equations holding in every algebra in $K$.) Andreka/Nemeti\index{Author}{Andreka/Nemeti} \cite{bib:1981b} and note 50.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ V}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP\,K\supseteq PS\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P\,K$ is the class of algebras isomorphic to direct products of algebras in $K$). Andreka/Nemeti~[\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ W}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP^{r}K\supseteq P^{r}S\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P^{r}K$ is the class of all algebras isomorphic to reduced direct products of algebras in $K$.) Andreka/Nemeti [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AD}] For every class $K$ of similar algebras $SP^{g}K\supseteq P^{g}S\,K$. (For any class $K$ of similar algebras, $S\,K$ is the class of all subalgebras of elements of $K$ (not closed under isomorphism) and $P^{g}K$ is the class of direct products of elements of $K$ not closed under isomorphism). Andreka/Nemeti [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AP}] For any type $\tau$ of the form $\tau =(M)$, every homomorphism of an algebra of type $\tau$ is closed. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} [\textbf{1989}] and note 115.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AQ}] For any type $\tau$ of the form $\tau =(M)$, every homomorphism of an algebra $\mathbf{A}$ of type $\tau$ into an algebra $\mathbf{B}$ of type $\tau$ maps $\mathbf{A}$ onto a subalgebra of $\mathbf{B}$. Diener [\textbf{1989}] and note 105.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AR}] Let $S$ be any family of disjoint non-empty sets and let $\tau =(\bigcup S)$, then any homomorphism from $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;\bigcup\,S)$ into $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;S)$ maps $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;\bigcup\,S)$ onto a subalgebra of $:\mathfrak{P}(\tau;S)$. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} [\textbf{1989}] and note 115.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AX}] Birkhoff Representation Theorem:\index{Subject}{Birkhoff representation theorem} Every algebra is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras. Birkhoff\index{Author}{Birkhoff} [\textbf{1944}], Gr\"{a}tzer [\textbf{1979}] and [\textbf{1986}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 BE}] Every unique factorization domain can be mapped homomorphically onto a non-zero subdirectly irreducible ring. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1988}], Gr\"{a}tzer\index{Author}{Gratzer@Gr\"{a}tzer} [\textbf{1979}] pp 122-124 and note 84.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AS}] Let $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ be (universal) algebras of type $r$ where $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ have underlying sets $A$ and $B$ respectively and $B$ is finite. Suppose for every finite $C\subseteq A$ there is a partial $r$ homomorphism from $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ with domain $C$. Then there is an $r$ homomorphism from $\mathfrak{A}$ into $\mathfrak{B}$ . van Benthem\index{Author}{Benthem} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent [\textbf{43 N}] $RM1,\,\aleph_{0}$: The representation theorem for multi-algebras with $\aleph_{0}$ unary operations: Assume $(A,\,F)$ is a multi-algebra with $\aleph_{0}$ unary operations (and no other operations), then there is an algebra $(B,\,G)$ with $\aleph_{0}$ unary operations and an equivalence relation $E$ on $B$ such that $(B/E,\,G/E)$ and $(A,\,F)$ are isomorphic multi-algebras. Note 50 and H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} \cite{bib:1981b}.

\noindent [\textbf{43 O}] (Depends on $n\in\omega,\,n\geq 1)\,RM1,\,n$: The representation theorem for multi-algebras with $n$ unary operations: Assume $(A,\,F)$ is a multi-algebra with $n$ unary operations (and no other operations), then there is an algebra $(B,\,G)$ with $n$ unary operations and an equivalence relation $E$ on $B$ such that $(B/E,\,G/E)$ and $(A,\,F)$ are isomorphic multi-algebras. H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} \cite{bib:1981b} and note 50.

\noindent [\textbf{67 E}] For any algebra $\mathbf{A}$ with finitary operations (that is, $\mathbf{A}$ is of type $\tau$ where $\tau=(K_{i})_{i\in I}$ with $K_{i}$ finite for each $i\in I$) and for any generating subset $Z$ of $\mathbf{A}$, there is a function $h:A\rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\omega}(Z)$ ($A$ is the domain of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\omega}(Z)$ is the set of all finite subsets of $Z$.) such that $\forall a\in A,\,a$ is in the subalgebra of $\mathbf{A}$ generated by $h(a)$. Diener [\textbf{1989}] and note 115.

\noindent [\textbf{67 F}] For any algebra $\mathbf{A}$ with one unary operation $f$ and any generating set $Z$ of $\mathbf{A}$, there is a function $h:A\rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\omega}(Z)$ ($A$ is the domain of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\omega}(Z)$ is the set of all finite subsets of $Z$.) such that $\forall a\in A,\,a$ is in the subalgebra of $\mathbf{A}$ generated by $h(a)$. Diener [\textbf{1989}] and note 115.

\noindent [\textbf{88 C}] If $m$ is a cardinal number and $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice isomorphic to the lattice of subalgebras of some unary universal algebra (a unary universal algebra is one with only unary or nullary operations) and $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathcal{L}$ of order 2 (that is, $\alpha^{2}$ is the identity) then there is a unary algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ with $|\,\mathrm{domain}\,(\mathfrak{A})|\geq m$ and an isomorphism $\rho$ from $\mathcal{L}$ onto the lattice of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ with $\rho(\alpha(x))=(\rho(x))^{-1}(=\{(s,\,t):(t,\, s)\in\rho(x)\})$ for all $x\in \mathcal{L}$. Lampe\index{Author}{Lampe} \cite{bib:1974m}.

\noindent [\textbf{88 D}] For any cardinal $m$, there is a unary algebra $\mathfrak{A} =\langle A,\, F\rangle$ (only unary and nullary operations) and a proper subalgebra $\mathfrak{D}$ of $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ has exactly four subalgebras, $\mathfrak{A},\,\emptyset,\,\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\ast}=\{(s,\,t):(t,\,s)\in \mathfrak{D}\}$. Lampe \cite{bib:1974m}.

\noindent [\textbf{159 A}] Every variety has an initial algebra. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1983b}] and note 32.

\noindent [\textbf{159 B}] For every variety $V$ and set $X,\,V$ has a free algebra on $X$. Blass [\textbf{1983b}] and note 32.

\noindent \textbf{174($\alpha$).} $RM1,\,\aleph_{\alpha}$: The representation theorem for multi-algebras with $\aleph_{\alpha}$ unary operations: Assume $(A,\,F)$ is a multi-algebra with $\aleph_{\alpha}$ unary operations (and no other operations). Then there is an algebra $(B,\,G)$ with $\aleph_{\alpha}$ unary operations and an equivalence relation $E$ on $B$ such that $(B/E,\,G/E)$ and $(A,\, F)$ are isomorphic multi-algebras. H\"{o}ft/Howard \cite{bib:1981b} and note 50.

\noindent \textbf{268.} If $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice isomorphic to the lattice of subalgebras of some unary universal algebra (a \emph{unary universal algebra} is one with only unary or nullary operations) and $\alpha$ is an automorphism of $\mathcal{L}$ of order 2 (that is, $\alpha^{2}$ is the identity), then there is a unary algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ and an isomorphism $\rho$ from $\mathcal{L}$ onto the lattice of subalgebras of $\mathfrak{A}^{2}$ with $\rho(\alpha(x))=(\rho(x))^{-1}(=\{(s,\,t):(t,\,s)\in\rho(x)\})$ for all $x\in \mathcal{L}$. Lampe\index{Author}{Lampe} \cite{bib:1974m}.

\textbf{V. Vector Spaces}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AM}] Assume $V$ is a separable vector space, $D$ is a countable dense subset of $V$, and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$, and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x))$. Also assume that $p$ satisfies the following condition:
\begin{equation*}
\tag{$^{\ast}$} (\forall\epsilon>0)(\forall x\in V)(\exists y\in D)\ \text{such that}\ p(x-y)<\epsilon\ \mathrm{and}\ p(y-x)<\epsilon.
\end{equation*}
Moreover, if $f$ is a linear function from a subspace $S$ of $V$ into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$, then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ so that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. Note 143.

\noindent [\textbf{1 A}] In every vector space, every generating set contains a basis. Halpern\index{Author}{Halpern} [\textbf{1966}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 BJ}] In every vector space over the two element field, every generating set contains a basis. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 BU}] In every vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, every generating set includes a basis. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1984a}] and note 137.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BZ}] Vector Space Multiple Choice: For every family $V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non-trivial vector spaces there is a family $F=\{F_{i}:i\in K\}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,F_{i}$ is a non-empty, finite, independent subset of $V_{i}$. Note 127.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AU}] If $Z$ is a real vector lattice with order unit 1 then the set of all positive linear functionals $u$ on $Z$ with $u(1)=1$ is a convex set that has an extreme point. See H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, pages 177 and 182 for definitions. Also see Gardiner\index{Author}{Gardiner} \cite{bib:1974i}.

\noindent [\textbf{43 V}] Every convex-compact set in a Hausdorff topological vector space with a basis of convex open sets is Baire. Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and note 23.

\noindent \textbf{52.} Hahn-Banach Theorem:\index{Subject}{Hahn-Banach theorem} If $V$ is a real vector space and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$ and $(\forall t>0)(p(tx)=tp(x))$ and $S$ is a subspace of $V$ and $f:S\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is linear and satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$ then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. L\'{o}s/Ryll-Nardzewski\index{Author}{Los/Ryll-Nardzewski@{\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski}
 [\textbf{1951}].

\noindent [\textbf{52 F}] If $X$ is a topological vector space then for every continuous sublinear functional $p$ on $E$ there is a linear functional $f$ on $E$ such that $f\leq p$. Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent [\textbf{52 G}] If $X$ is a normed vector space then for every continuous sublinear functional $p$ on $E$ there is alinear functional $f$ on $E$ such that $f\leq p$. Fossy/Morillon [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent [\textbf{52 H}] Existence of Real Valued Banach Limits: For any directed set $(\Delta,\,\sqsubseteq)$ there exists a (real valued) Banach limit. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{52 I}] Real Valued Convex Domination Theorem: For every real vector space $X$, every subspace $X_{0}\subseteq X$, every linear $\lambda_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and every convex $p:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, if $\lambda_{0}\leq p$ on $X_{0}$ then $\lambda_{0}$ can be extended to a linear map $\lambda:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda\leq p$ on $X$. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{52 J}] Support Theorem for Real Valued Convex Functions: For every real vector space $X$, every convex function $p:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a pointwise maximum of affine functions. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{52 K}] Sandwich Theorem for Real Valued Functions: For every real vector space $X$, if $e:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a concave function, $g:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function, and $e\leq g$ everywhere on $X$, then there exists an affine function $f:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $e\leq f\leq g$ everywhere on $X$. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent \textbf{65.} The Krein-Milman Theorem:\index{Subject}{Krein-Milman theorem} Let $K$ be a compact convex set in a locally convex topological vector space $X$. Then $K$ has an extreme point. (An extreme point is a point which is not an interior point of any line segment which lies in $K$.) Royden\index{Author}{Royden} [\textbf{1963}] and H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, p. 177.

\noindent \textbf{66.} Every vector space over a field has a basis. Hamel\index{Author}{Hamel} [\textbf{1905}].

\noindent \textbf{95 ($F$).} Existence of Complementary Subspaces over a Field $F$: If $F$ is a field, then every vector space $V$ over $F$ has the property that if $S\subseteq V$ is a subspace of $V$, then there is a subspace $S^{\prime}\subseteq V$ such that $S\cap S^{\prime}=\{0\}$ and $SUS^{\prime}$ generates $V$. Bleicher\index{Author}{Bleicher} [\textbf{1964}], [\textbf{1965}], H. Rubin/J. Rubin \cite{bib:1985q}, pp 119ff, and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, p 148 prob 10.4.

\noindent \textbf{96.} L\"{o}wig's Theorem.\index{Subject}{L\"{o}wig's theorem} If $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are both bases for the vector space $V$ then $|B_{1}|=|B_{2}|$. L\"{o}wig\index{Author}{Lowig@L\"{o}wig} [\textbf{1934}].

\noindent \textbf{109.} Every field $F$ and every vector space $V$ over $F$ has the property that each linearly independent set $A\subseteq V$ can be extended to a basis. Bleicher [\textbf{1964}], [\textbf{1965}], Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1984a}], H. Rubin/J. Rubin \cite{bib:1985q}, pp 119ff.

\noindent \textbf{110.} Every vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$ has a basis. Blass [\textbf{1984a}].

\noindent \textbf{195.} Every general linear system has a linear global reaction. Note 62 and Harazisville (see Kharazishvili\index{Author}{Kharazishvili} [\textbf{1979}]).

\noindent [\textbf{218 A}] Existence of Complementary Subspaces: For every field $F$, every vector space $V$ over $F$ has the property that if $S\subseteq V$ is a subspace of $V$, then there is a subspace $S^{\prime}\subseteq V$ such that $S\cap S^{\prime}=\{0\}$ and $SUS^{\prime}$ generates $V$. Bleicher [\textbf{1964}], [\textbf{1965}], H. Rubin/J. Rubin \cite{bib:1985q}, pp 123ff, Theorems 6.36, 6.37, and 6.38.

\noindent \textbf{235.} If $V$ is a vector space and $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are bases for $V$ then $|B_{1}|$ and $|B_{2}|$ are comparable. Gross\index{Author}{Gross} [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent \textbf{236.} If $V$ is a vector space with a basis and $S$ is a linearly independent subset of $V$ such that no proper extension of $S$ is a basis for $V$, then $S$ is a basis for $V$. Gross [\textbf{1975}], [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent [\textbf{236 A}] If $V$ is a vector space with a basis, then every linearly independent subset is contained in a basis.

\noindent \textbf{286.} Extended Krein-Milman Theorem:\index{Subject}{Krein-Milman theorem} Let $\mathrm{K}$ be a quasicompact (sometimes called convex-compact), convex subset of a locally convex topological vector space, then $\mathrm{K}$ has an extreme point. H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, p. 177--178 and note 23.

\noindent \textbf{287.} The Hahn-Banach Theorem\index{Subject}{Hahn-Banach theorem} for Separable Normed Linear Spaces: Assume $V$ is a separable normed linear space and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+ p(y)$ and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x))$ and assume $f$ is a linear function from a subspace $S$ of $V$ into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$, then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ so that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. Note 145.

\noindent [\textbf{333 A}] In every vector space $B$ over the two element field, every subspace of $B$ has a complementary subspace. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent \textbf{346.} Vector Space Kinna-Wagner Principle: For every family $V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non-trivial vector spaces there is a family $F=\{F_{i}:i\in K\}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,F_{i}$ is a non-empty, independent subset of $V_{i}$. Note 127.

\noindent \textbf{367.} There is a Hamel\index{Author}{Hamel} basis for $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$. Hamel [\textbf{1905}].

\noindent \textbf{372.} Generalized Hahn-Banach Theorem: Assume that $X$ is a real vector space, $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$ is a Dedekind complete ordered vector space and $X_{0}$ is a subspace of $X$. If $\lambda_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow Z$ is linear and $p:X\rightarrow Z$ is sublinear and if $\lambda_{0}\preccurlyeq p$ on $X_{0}$ then $\lambda_{0}$ can be extended to a linear map $\lambda:X\rightarrow Z$ such that $\lambda\preccurlyeq p$ on $X$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{372 A}] Existence of Banach Limits: For any directed set $(\triangle,\,\sqsubseteq)$ and any Dedekind complete ordered vector space $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$ there exists a $Z$-valued Banach limit. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{372 B}] Generalized Convex Domination Theorem:\index{Subject}{convex domination theorem} For every real vector space $X$, every Dedekind complete ordered vector space $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$, every subspace $X_{0}\subseteq X$, every linear $\lambda_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow Z$ and every convex $p:X\rightarrow Z$, if $\lambda_{0}\preccurlyeq p$ on $X_{0}$ then $\lambda_{0}$ can be extended to a linear map $\lambda:X\rightarrow Z$ such that $\lambda\preccurlyeq p$ on $X$. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{372 C}] Generalized Support Theorem:\index{Subject}{support theorem} For every real vector space $X$ and every Dedekind complete ordered vector space $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$, every convex function $p:X\rightarrow Z$ is a pointwise maximum of affine functions. Schechter [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{372 D}] Generalized Sandwich Theorem: For every real vector space $X$ and every Dedekind complete ordered vector space $(Z,\,\preccurlyeq)$, if $e:X\rightarrow Z$ is a concave function, $g:X\rightarrow Z$ is a convex function, and $e\leq g$ everywhere on $X$, then there exists an affine function $f:X\rightarrow Z$ satisfying $e\leq f\leq g$ everywhere on $X$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996b}] and note 31.

\section*{ANALYSIS (FORMS FROM ANALYSIS)}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ H}] F. Riesz Theorem:\index{Subject}{Riesz theorem} A Hilbert space is finite dimensional iff its closed unit ball is compact. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ I}] The following are equivalent in a Hilbert space:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The closed unit ball is sequentially compact.
\item[(b)] Each unconditionally convergent series converges absolutely.
\item[(c)] Each ortho-normal system is Dedekind finite.
\end{enumerate}
Brunner [\textbf{1983b}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AM}] Assume $V$ is a separable vector space, $D$ is a countable dense subset of $V$, and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$, and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x))$. Also assume that $p$ satisfies the following condition:
\begin{equation*}
\tag{$^{\ast}$} (\forall\epsilon>0)(\forall x\in V)(\exists y\in D)\ \text{such that}\ p(x-y)<\epsilon\ \mathrm{and}\ p(y-x)<\epsilon.
\end{equation*}
Moreover, if $f$ is a linear function from a subspace $S$ of $V$ into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$, then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ so that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. Note 143.

\noindent [\textbf{8 E}] In a metric space every sequentially continuous real valued function is continuous. Brunner [\textbf{1982c}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 D}] In every Hilbert space with a Dedekind finite orthonormal basis, the closed unit ball is sequentially compact. Brunner [\textbf{1983b}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{14 Q}] Alaoglu's Theorem:\index{Subject}{Alaoglu's theorem} The unit ball is compact in the weak$^{\ast}$ topology in the dual of a Banach space. (See [52 E].) Johnstone\index{Author}{Johnstone} [\textbf{1984}] and note 23.

\noindent [\textbf{14 U}] Every closed proper ideal in a Gelfand algebra is contained in some maximal ideal. Banaschewski [\textbf{1983}] and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BY}] For every topological space $X$, every proper ideal in the normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra of continuous bounded functions from $X$ into $\mathbb{R}$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BZ}] Every proper ideal in a non-trivial normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra or $\mathbb{C}$-algebra with identity is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CA}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of non trivial commutative normed algebras with identity then there is a family $(J_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for each $i\in I,\,J_{i}$ is a maximal ideal in $A_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CB}] If $X$ is a topological space and $I$ is a proper ideal in the algebra of all bounded continuous functions from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that every function in $I$ vanishes at at least one point of $X$ then $I$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CL}] Gelfand Extreme Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Gelfand extreme point theorem} If $A$ is a non-trivial Gelfand algebra then the closed unit ball in the dual of $A$ has an extreme point $e$ with $e\neq 0$. Morillon [\textbf{1986}], notes 23 and 29.

\noindent [\textbf{52 E}] The unit ball is convex-compact in the weak$^{\ast}$ topology in the dual of a Banach space. (See [14 Q].) Luxemburg\index{Author}{Luxemburg} \cite{bib:1969d}, H. Rubin /J. Rubin \cite{bib:1985q} p 178, and note 23.

\noindent \textbf{65.} The Krein-Milman Theorem:\index{Subject}{Krein-Milman theorem} Let $K$ be a compact convex set in a locally convex topological vector space $X$. Then $K$ has an extreme point. (An extreme point is a point which is not an interior point of any line segment which lies in $K$.) Royden\index{Author}{Royden} [\textbf{1963}] and H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, p. 177.

\noindent [\textbf{118 V}] If $(L,\,\leq)$ is a linear order and $G=\{[l_{i},\,r_{i}]:i\in K\}$ is a locally finite family of closed intervals of $L$ whose interiors are non-empty and pairwise disjoint, then there exists a continuous real valued function $f:L\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $|f^{-1}(0)\cap[l_{i},\,r_{i}]|\geq 2$ and $|f^{-1}(1) \cap [l_{i},\,r_{i}]|\geq 1$ for all $i\in K$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{118 W}] If $(L,\,\leq)$ is a linear order and $G=\{[l_{i},\,r_{i}]:i\in K\}$ is a locally finite family of closed intervals of $L$ whose interiors are non-empty and pairwise disjoint, then there exists a continuous real valued function $f:L\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,f(l_{i})=f(r_{i})=0$ and $f(x)>0$ for all $x\in(l_{i},\,r_{i})$. Keremedis [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{118 X}] If $(L,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order and $G=\{(l_{i},\,r_{i}):i\in K\}$ is a family of open, non-empty, pairwise disjoint intervals of $L$, then there exists a set $\{f_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non constant continuous real valued functions on $L$ such that for each $i\in K,\,f_{i}$ vanishes outside of $(l_{i},\, r_{i})$. Keremedis [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{124.} Every operator on a Hilbert space with an amorphous base is the direct sum of a finite matrix and a scalar operator. (A set is amorphous if it is not the union of two disjoint infinite sets.) Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984a}].

\noindent [\textbf{126 A}] Every positive functional on a $B$-lattice is continuous. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984d}] and note 16.

\noindent \textbf{153.} The closed unit ball of a Hilbert space is compact in the weak topology. Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and Rudin\index{Author}{Rudin} [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{156.} Theorem of Gelfand and Kolmogoroff:\index{Subject}{Gelfand-Kolmogoroff theorem} Two compact $T_{2}$ spaces are homeomorphic if their rings of real valued continuous functions are isomorphic. Brunner [\textbf{1983a}] and Gelfand/Kolmogoroff\index{Author}{Gelfand/Kolmogoroff} [\textbf{1939}].

\noindent \textbf{157.} Theorem of Goodner:\index{Subject}{Goodner's theorem} A compact $T_{2}$ space is extremally disconnected (the closure of every open set is open) if and only if each non-empty subset of $C(X)$ (set of continuous real valued functions on $X$) which is pointwise bounded has a supremum. Goodner\index{Author}{Goodner} [\textbf{1950}].

\noindent \textbf{158.} In every Hilbert space $H$, if the closed unit ball is sequentially compact, then $H$ has an orthonormal basis. Brunner [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent \textbf{279.} The Closed Graph Theorem\index{Subject}{closed graph theorem} for operations between Fr\'{e}chet Spaces: Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are Fr\'{e}chet spaces, $T:X\rightarrow Y$ is linear and $G=\{(x,\,Tx): x\in X\}$ is closed in $X\times Y$. Then $T$ is continuous. Rudin [\textbf{1991}] p. 51, Wright \cite{bib:1973h}, note 96.

\noindent \textbf{281.} There is a Hilbert space $H$ and an unbounded linear operator on $H$. Wright \cite{bib:1973h}, note 96.

\noindent \textbf{286.} Extended Krein-Milman Theorem:\index{Subject}{Krein-Milman theorem} Let $\mathrm{K}$ be a quasicompact (sometimes called convex-compact), convex subset of a locally convex topological vector space, then $\mathrm{K}$ has an extreme point. H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, p. 177--178 and note 23.

\noindent \textbf{287.} The Hahn-Banach Theorem\index{Subject}{Hahn-Banach theorem} for Separable Normed Linear Spaces: Assume $V$ is a separable normed linear space and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+ p(y)$ and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x))$ and assume $f$ is a linear function from a subspace $S$ of $V$ into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall x\in S)(f(x)\leq p(x))$, then $f$ can be extended to $f^{\ast}:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ so that $f^{\ast}$ is linear and $(\forall x\in V)(f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x))$. Note 145.

\noindent \textbf{370.} Weak Gelfand Extreme Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Gelfand extreme point theorem} If $A$ is a non-trivial Gelfand algebra then the closed unit ball in the dual of $A$ has an extreme point $e$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} [\textbf{1986}], notes 23 and 29.

\section*{CARDINAL NUMBER FORMS}

\textbf{I. Alephs and their Properties}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AL}] For every set $A$, there is an $\aleph$ which cannot be covered by fewer than $|A|$ sets each of cardinality $<|A|$. Note 131.

\noindent \textbf{25.} $\aleph_{\beta+1}$ is regular for all ordinals $\beta$. Feferman/Levy\index{Author}{Feferman/Levy}\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1963}] and Gitik\index{Author}{Gitik} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{34.} $\aleph_{1}$ is regular. Russell\index{Author}{Russell} [\textbf{1906}] and note 3.

\noindent [\textbf{40 B}] For all ordinals $\alpha$, the $\aleph_{\alpha}$ partition principle holds: For every ordinal $\alpha$ and every cardinal $\kappa$, if $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq^{\ast}\kappa$, then $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq\kappa$. Pelc\index{Author}{Pelc} [\textbf{1978}], Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}], and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{41.} $W_{\aleph_{1}}$: For every cardinal $m,\,m\leq\aleph_{1}$ or $\aleph_{1}\leq m$. Jech \cite{bib:1973b}.

\noindent \textbf{54.} For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m$ adj $2^{m}$ implies $m$ is an aleph. ($m\ adj\ n$ iff $m<n$ and $(\neg\exists p)(m<p<n)$.) Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1979}] prob 1337, thm 1338 and prob 1339.

\noindent \textbf{56.} $\aleph(2^{\aleph_{0}})\neq\aleph_{\omega}$. ($\aleph(2^{\aleph_{0}})$ is Hartogs' aleph, the least $\aleph$ not $\leq 2^{\aleph_{0}}$.) Mathias [\textbf{1979}] p 125.

\noindent \textbf{58.} There is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $\aleph(2^{\aleph_{\alpha}})\neq\aleph_{\alpha+1}$. $(\aleph(2^{\aleph_{\alpha}})$ is Hartogs' aleph, the least $\aleph$ not $\leq 2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$.) Mathias [\textbf{1979}] p 126.

\noindent \textbf{71($\alpha$).} $W_{\aleph_{\alpha}}:(\forall x)(|x|\leq\aleph_{\alpha}$ or $|x|\geq\aleph_{\alpha}$). Pelc [\textbf{1978}], Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, page 119 and Levy [\textbf{1964}].

\noindent \textbf{104.} There is a regular uncountable aleph. Jech [\textbf{1966b}] p 165 prob 11.26.

\noindent \textbf{108.} There is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$ is not the union of a denumerable set of denumerable sets. Gitik [\textbf{1985}].

\noindent \textbf{159.} The regular cardinals are cofinal in the class of ordinals. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent \textbf{170.} $\aleph_{1}\leq 2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Bernstein\index{Author}{Bernstein} [\textbf{1908}] and Banaschewski/Moore [\textbf{1990}].

\noindent \textbf{182.} There is an aleph whose cofinality is greater than $\aleph_{0}$. Gitik [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{183($\alpha$).} There are no $\aleph_{\alpha}$ minimal sets. That is, there are no sets $X$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $|X|$ is incomparable with $\aleph_{\alpha}$
\item[(2)] $\aleph_{\beta}<|X|$ for every $\beta<\alpha$ and
\item[(3)] $\forall Y\subseteq X,\,|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$ or $|X-Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$.
\end{enumerate}
Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1980b}] and note 56.

\noindent \textbf{208.} For all ordinals $\alpha,\,\aleph_{\alpha+1}\leq 2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$. Figura\index{Author}{Figura} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{209.} There is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that for all $X$, if $X$ is a denumerable union of denumerable sets then $\mathcal{P}(X)$ cannot be partitioned into $\aleph_{\alpha}$ non-empty sets. Morris\index{Author}{Morris} [\textbf{1970}].

\noindent \textbf{245.} There is a function $f:\omega_{1}\rightarrow\omega_{1}^{\omega}$ such that for every $\alpha,\, 0<\alpha<\omega_{1},\,f(\alpha)$ is a function from $\omega$ onto $\alpha$. Litman\index{Author}{Litman} [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent [\textbf{245 A}] There is a function $g:\omega_{1}\rightarrow\omega_{1}^{\omega}$ such that for all limit ordinals $\alpha<\omega_{1},\,g(\alpha)$ is an increasing function from $\omega$ into $\alpha$ with the range of $g$ cofinal in $\alpha$. Litman [\textbf{1976}]

\noindent [\textbf{245 B}] Every closed set A in $\omega_{1}$ which contains only limit ordinals is a derivative (that is, $\exists B\subseteq\omega_{1}$ such that $A=\{x:x\ \text{is a limit and}\ \{t:t\in B\}\ \text{is cofinal in}\ x\}$.) Litman [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent \textbf{246.} The monadic theory theory $MT(\omega_{1},\,<)$ of $\omega_{1}$ is recursive. Litman [\textbf{1976}] and note 85.

\noindent \textbf{275.} The sequence of cardinals $\langle\aleph_{n}: n\in\omega\rangle$ has a unique minimal upper bound. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1974b}].

\noindent \textbf{315.} $\Omega=\omega_{1}$, where $\Omega=\{\alpha\in\ \mathrm{On}: (\forall\beta\leq\alpha)(\beta=0\vee(\exists\gamma)(\beta=\gamma+ 1) \vee$ there is a sequence $\langle\gamma_{n}: n\in\omega\rangle$ such that for each $n\ \gamma_{n}<\beta$ and $\beta=\bigcup\nolimits_{n<\omega}\gamma_{n}\}$ Gitik\index{Author}{Gitik} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{365.} For every uncountable set $A$, if $A$ has the same cardinality as each of its uncountable subsets then $|A|=\aleph_{1}$. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\textbf{II. Cardinal Arithmetic}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ A}] Cardinal successors 2: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\neg\exists p)(m<p<n)$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1954a}] and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} [\textbf{1966a}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ F}] Cancellation for surjective cardinal equivalence: For every $k\in w-\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx=^{\ast} ky\ \mathrm{implies}\ x=^{\ast} y)$ (The expression $x=^{\ast}y$ means that there is a function $f$ from $x$ onto $y$ and a function $g$ from $y$ onto $x$.) Truss [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ G}] Cancellation for injective cardinal inequality: For every $k\in \omega-\{0\},\,(\forall x\forall y)(kx\leq ky\ \mathrm{implies}\ x\leq y)$ ($\leq$ is the usual (injective) cardinal ordering.) Lindenbaum/Tarski\index{Author}{Lindenbaum/Tarski} [\textbf{1926}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Q}] For all cardinal numbers $m$ and $n$ and Dedekind finite cardinals $p$, if $p+m=p+n$ then $m=n$. Tarski [\textbf{1949b}] and note 94

\noindent [\textbf{1 D}] Cardinal successors 3: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\forall p)(m<p\rightarrow n\leq p)$. Tarski [\textbf{1954a}] and Jech [\textbf{1966a}].

\noindent \textbf{2.} Existence of successor cardinals: For every cardinal $m$ there is a cardinal $n$ such that $m<n$ and $(\forall p<n)(p\leq m)$. Tarski [\textbf{1954a}].

\noindent \textbf{3.} $2m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$. Tarski [\textbf{1954a}].

\noindent [\textbf{3 A}] For all cardinals $m$ and $n,\,n\leq m$ and $m$ infinite $\rightarrow m+n=m$. Halpern/Howard [\textbf{1970}].

\noindent [\textbf{3 B}] $\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,\aleph_{0}\cdot m=m$. Halpern/Howard\index{Author}{Halpern/Howard} [\textbf{1970}].

\noindent [\textbf{3 C}] Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: (For all cardinals $x,\,y$ and $z$) ($x+y=z$ iff ($x\leq z$ and $y\leq z$ and $(\forall u)(x,\,y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u)$). H\"{a}ussler\index{Author}{Haussler@H\"{a}ussler} [\textbf{1983}] and Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1949a}].

\noindent [\textbf{9 F}] There is no subset $A$ of the class of Dedekind finite cardinals such that $A$ under the usual cardinal ordering is order isomorphic to $\langle \mathbb{R}, \leq\rangle$. Tarski [\textbf{1965}], Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 6, and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 K}] If $A$ is uncountable and $B$ is countable, then $|A-B|=|A|$. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] p 201.

\noindent [\textbf{9 L}] If $A$ is uncountable and $B$ is countable, then $|A\cup B|=|A|$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 202.

\noindent [\textbf{9 M}] If $\aleph_{0}<|A|$ and $\aleph_{0}=|B|$, then $\aleph_{0}<|A-B|$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 202.

\noindent \textbf{[9 N]} If $\aleph_{0}\leq^{\ast}m$, then $\aleph_{0}\leq m$. Lindenbaum/Tarski\index{Author}{Lindenbaum/Tarski} [\textbf{1926}], G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 216, and note 69.

\noindent [\textbf{9 O}] $m\leq\aleph_{0}$ or $\aleph_{0}\leq m$. Lindenbaum/Tarski [\textbf{1926}] and G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 216,

\noindent [\textbf{9 P}] If $m+\aleph_{0}<n +\aleph_{0}$, then $m<n$. Lindenbaum/Tarski [\textbf{1926}] and G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 216.

\noindent [\textbf{9 Q}] If $m+\aleph_{0}=n+\aleph_{0}$, then $m=n$ or $m,\,n\leq\aleph_{0}$. Lindenbaum/Tarski [\textbf{1926}] and G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 216.

\noindent \textbf{53.} For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m^{2}\leq 2^{m}$. Mathias [\textbf{1979}] prob 1336.

\noindent \textbf{55.} For all infinite cardinals $m$ and $n$, if $m\cdot n=m+n$ then, $m\leq n$ or $n\leq m$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1979}] p 125.

\noindent \textbf{136($k$).} Surjective Cardinal Cancellation (depends on $k\in\omega-\{0\}$): For all cardinals $x$ and $y,\,kx\leq^{\ast}ky$ implies $x\leq^{\ast}y$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1984}] and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{161.} Definability of cardinal addition in terms of $\leq$: There is a first order formula whose only non-logical symbol is $\leq$ (for cardinals) that defines cardinal addition. H\"{a}ussler~[\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{162.} Non-existence of infinite units: There is no infinite cardinal number $A$ such that $A+A>A$ and for all cardinals $x$ and $y,\,x+y=A\rightarrow x=A$ or $y=A$. H\"{a}ussler~[\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{200.} For all infinite $x,\,|2^{x}|=|x!|$. Dawson/Howard\index{Author}{Dawson/Howard} [\textbf{1976}] and note 64.

\noindent \textbf{204.} For every infinite $X$, there is a function from $X$ onto $2X$. Truss [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{277.} $E(D,\,VII)$: Every non-well-orderable cardinal is decomposable. Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1973a}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{283.} Cardinality of well ordered subsets: For all $n\in\omega$ and for all infinite $x,\,|x^{n}|<|s(x)|$ where $s(x)$ is the set of all well orderable subsets of $x$. Truss [\textbf{1973d}].

\noindent \textbf{290.} For all infinite $x,\,|2^{x}|=|x^{x}|$. Pincus [\textbf{1978}] and note 64.

\noindent \textbf{291.} For all infinite $x,\, |x!|=|x^{x}|$. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1978}] and note 64.

\textbf{III. Cardinality of Unions}

\noindent [\textbf{1 C}] For all infinite cardinals $m,\,UT(m,\,m,\,m)$: If every member of an infinite set $A$ has power $|A|$ then $|\bigcup A|=|A|$. (Note that [1 C] implies $m^{2}=m$ for all infinite cardinals m.) Howard\index{Author}{Howard} [\textbf{1994}].

\noindent \textbf{6.} $UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\mathbb{R})$: The union of a denumerable family of denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is denumerable. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] and note 3.

\noindent [\textbf{8 T}] $PUT(\aleph_{0},\,\infty,\,\aleph_{0})$: The union of a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has a denumerable subset. $([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{T}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{B}])$

\noindent [\textbf{8 U}] $PUT(WO,\,\infty,\,WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets has an infinite well ordered subset. $([8\ \mathrm{U}]\leftrightarrow[8\ \mathrm{T}])$

\noindent [\textbf{10 A}] $UT(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$: The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets is denumerable. Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} [\textbf{1988}] p 569.

\noindent [\textbf{10 M}] $PUT(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$: The union of denumerably many pairwise disjoint finite sets has a denumerable subset.

\noindent [\textbf{10 N}] $PUT(WO,\,<\aleph_{0},\,WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint finite sets has an infinite well ordered subset.

\noindent \textbf{18.} \emph{PUT} $(\aleph_{0},2,\,\aleph_{0})$: The union of a denumerable family of pairwise disjoint pairs has a denumerable subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984f}].

\noindent [\textbf{18 B}] The union of a denumerable family of pairs has a denumerable subset. Note 135.

\noindent [\textbf{18 D}] $PUT(WO,\,2,\,WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered family of pairwise disjoint pairs has an infinite well ordered subset. $([18\ \mathrm{D}\leftrightarrow 18)$

\noindent \textbf{20.} If $\{A_{x}:x\in S\}$ and $\{B_{x}:x\in S\}$ are families of pairwise disjoint sets and $|A_{x}|=|B_{x}|$ for all $x\in S$, then $|\bigcup_{x\in S}A_{x}|= |\bigcup_{x\in S}B_{x}|$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] (1.4.12 and 1.7.8).

\noindent \textbf{21.} If $S$ is well ordered, $\{A_{x}:x\in S\}$ and $\{B_{x}:x\in S\}$ are families of pairwise disjoint sets, and $|A_{x}|=|B_{x}|$ for all $x\in S$, then $|\bigcup_{x\in S}A_{x}|=|\bigcup_{x\in S}B_{x}|$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{22.} $UT(2^{\aleph_{0}},2^{\aleph_{0}},2^{\aleph_{0}})$: If every member of an infinite set of cardinality $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ has power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$, then the union has power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Borel\index{Author}{Borel} [\textbf{1898}] and G. Moore [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{23.} $(\forall\alpha)(UT(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha}))$: For every ordinal $\alpha$, if $A$ and every member of $A$ has cardinality $\aleph_{\alpha}$, then $|\bigcup A|=\aleph_{\alpha}$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{26.} $UT(\aleph_{0},2^{\aleph_{0}},2^{\aleph_{0}})$: The union of denumerably many sets each of power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ has power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Borel [\textbf{1898}].

\noindent \textbf{27.} $(\forall\alpha)(UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha}))$: The union of denumerably many sets each of power $\aleph_{\alpha}$ has power $\aleph_{\alpha}$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 36.

\noindent \textbf{29.} If $|S|=\aleph_{0}$ and $\{A_{x}:x\in S\}$ and $\{B_{x}:x\in S\}$ are families of pairwise disjoint sets and $|A_{x}|=|B_{x}|$ for all $x\in S$, then $|\bigcup_{x\in S}A_{x}|=|\bigcup_{x\in S}B_{x}|$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 324.

\noindent \textbf{31.} $UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$: The countable union theorem: The union of a denumerable set of denumerable sets is denumerable. Cantor\index{Author}{Cantor} [\textbf{1878}].

\noindent [\textbf{38 A}] $UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\neq 2^{\aleph_{0}})$: A denumerable union of denumerable sets does not have cardinality $2^{\aleph_{0}}$.

\noindent [\textbf{80 A}] $UT(\aleph_{0},2,\,\aleph_{0})$: The union of denumerably many pairs is denumerable.

\noindent \textbf{111.} $UT(WO,\,2,\,WO)$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of 2-element sets is an infinite well ordered set.

\noindent [\textbf{122 A}] $UT(WO,\,<\aleph_{0},\,WO)(U_{\aleph_{0}})$: The union of a well ordered set of finite sets is well orderable. Brunner/Howard\index{Author}{Brunner/Howard} [\textbf{1992}]. (See note 27 for more information on $UT(WO,\,\kappa,\,WO),\,\kappa$ a well ordered cardinal. The proof that 122 implies [122 A] is similar to the proof given in Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} [\textbf{1988}] p 569.)

\noindent \textbf{151.} $UT(WO,\,\aleph_{0},\,WO)(U_{\aleph_{1}})$: The union of a well ordered set of denumerable sets is well orderable. Brunner/Howard [\textbf{1992}]. (If $\kappa$ is a well ordered cardinal, see note 27 for $UT(WO,\,\kappa,\, WO)$.)

\noindent \textbf{207($\alpha$).} $UT(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha},\,<2^{\aleph_{\alpha}})$: The union of $\aleph_{\alpha}$ sets each of cardinality $\aleph_{\alpha}$ has cardinality less than $2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$. Figura\index{Author}{Figura}~[\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{231.} $UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO)$: The union of a well ordered collection of well orderable sets is well orderable. Tsukada~[\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{296.} Part-$\infty$: Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets. Gonzalez\index{Author}{Gonzalez} [\textbf{1995b}], Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{359.} If $\{A_{x}:x\in S\}$ and $\{B_{x}:x\in S\}$ are families of pairwise disjoint sets and $|A_{x}|\leq|B_{x}|$ for all $x\in S$, then $|\bigcup_{x\in S}A_{x}|\leq |\bigcup_{x\in S}B_{x}|$. Higasikawa\index{Author}{Higasikawa} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{[373 $\mathbf{B}(n)$]} $PUT(\aleph_{0},\,n,\,\aleph_{0})$ for $n\in \omega-\{0,1\}$: The union of a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint $n$-element sets has a denumerable subset.

\noindent \textbf{[373 $\mathbf{C}(n)$]} $PUT(WO,\,n,\,WO)$ for $n\in\omega -\{0,1\}$: The union of an infinite well ordered set of pairwise disjoint $n$-element sets has an infinite well ordered subset.

\noindent \textbf{374($n$).} $UT(\aleph_{0},\,n,\,\aleph_{0})$ for $n\in\omega -\{0,1\}$: The union of a denumerable set of $n$-element sets is denumerable.

\textbf{IV. Definitions of Finite Including Forms Involving Dedekind Finite}

\noindent [\textbf{1 AH}] $E(V,\,VI)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$ implies $m^{2}=m$. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AI}] $E(VI,\,VII)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m^{2}=m$ implies there is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $m=\aleph_{\alpha}$. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{3 E}] $E(IV,\,V)$: For all infinite cardinals $m,\,m+1=m$ implies $2m=m$. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{3 F}] $E(III,\,V)$: For every set $X$, if $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind infinite then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note~94.

\noindent [\textbf{3 G}] $E(II,\,V)$: For every set $X$, if there is a non-empty family of subsets of $X$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ and has no maximal element then $2|X|=|X|$. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{3 H}] $E(Ia,\,V)$: For every set $X$, if $2|X|>|X|$ then $X$ is amorphous. Howard Yorke [\textbf{1989}], notes 85(H) and 94.

\noindent \textbf{9.} Finite $\Leftrightarrow$ Dedekind finite: $W_{\aleph_{0}}$ (Jech \cite{bib:1973b}): $E(I,\,IV)$ (Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1989}]): Every Dedekind finite set is finite. Dedekind\index{Author}{Dedekind} [\textbf{1888}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 A}] For all infinite $x$, if $x$ is Dedekind finite, then $\mathcal{P}(x)$ is is Dedekind finite). Notes 8 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 B}] $E(II,\,IV)$ (Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}]): $(\forall x)$($x$ is $T$-finite if and only if $x$ is Dedekind finite). Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 C}] The image of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.2, notes 11 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 D}] The union of a Dedekind finite family of finite sets is Dedekind finite. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.4, notes 12 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 G}] Every infinite set has a denumerable subset. Cantor\index{Author}{Cantor} [\textbf{1895}] and G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] p 9.

\noindent [\textbf{9 H}] If $A$ is Dedekind finite and $B$ is Dedekind infinite, then $A\precsim B$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 28 and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 I}] If $\emptyset \in K$ and for all $A\in K$ and for all $b\not\in A,\,A\cup\{b\}\in K$, then every Dedekind finite set is in $K$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 28 and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 J}] The union of a Dedekind infinite family of non-empty sets is Dedekind infinite. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 130 and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{9 R}] $E(III,\,IV)$: Every Dedekind finite set has a Dedekind finite power set. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.
