\noindent [\textbf{9 S}] $E(Ia,\, IV)$: Every Dedekind finite set is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}], notes 57 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{13.} Every Dedekind finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is finite. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{13 A}] $\mathbb{R}$ has no dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{57.} If $x$ and $y$ are Dedekind finite sets then either $|x|\leq|y|$ or $|y|\leq|x|$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1979}] p 125 and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{64.} $E(I,\,Ia)$ (Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}]): There are no amorphous sets. Note 94 and Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1958}], notes 57 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{82.} $E(I,\,III)$ (Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}]): If $X$ is infinite then $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind infinite, ($X$ is finite $\Leftrightarrow \mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind finite.) Levy [\textbf{1958}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{82 A}]. Every infinite set can be mapped onto $\omega$. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}], Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1972}].

\noindent [\textbf{82 B}] $E(Ia,\,III)$: For every set $X$, if $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind finite then $X$ is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}], notes 57 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{83.} $E(I,\,II)$ (Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}]): $T$-finite is equivalent to finite. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1924}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{83 A}] $E(Ia,\,II)$: Every $T$-finite set is amorphous. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}], notes 57 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{84.} $E(II,\,III)$ (Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1989}]): $(\forall x)$ ($x$ is $T$-finite if and only if $\mathcal{P}(x)$ is Dedekind finite). Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1989}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{98.} The set of all finite subsets of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.5 and note~94.

\noindent \textbf{102.} For all Dedekind finite cardinals $p$ and $q$, if $p^{2}=q^{2}$ then $p=q$. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 162 prob 11.12 and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{163.} Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982a}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{164.} Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}], notes 42 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{185.} Every linearly ordered Dedekind finite set is finite. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1979a}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{185 A}] If $X$ is a linearly ordered set and there is neither an increasing nor a decreasing injection $f:\omega \rightarrow X$, then $X$ is finite. Hickman [\textbf{1979a}].

\noindent \textbf{198.} For every set $S$, if the only linearly orderable subsets of $S$ are the finite subsets of $S$, then either $S$ is finite or $S$ has an amorphous subset. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1978b}] and note 57.

\noindent \textbf{199($n$).} (For $n\in\omega-\{0,1\})$ If all $\varSigma_{n}^{1}$, Dedekind finite subsets of $^{\omega}\omega$ are finite, then all $\varPi_{n}^{1}$ Dedekind finite subsets of $^{\omega}\omega$ are finite. Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} [\textbf{1978}], notes 57 and 61.

\noindent \textbf{215.} If $(\forall y\subseteq X)$ ($y$ can be linearly ordered implies $y$ is finite), then $X$ is finite. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1972a}].

\noindent \textbf{276.} $E(V^{\prime\prime},\,III)$: For every set $A,\,\mathcal{P}(A)$ is Dedekind finite if and only if $A=\emptyset$ or $2|\mathcal{P}(A)|>|\mathcal{P}(A)|$. Howard/Spi\u{s}iak\index{Author}{Howard/Spisiak@Howard/Spi\u{s}iak} [\textbf{1994}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{277.} $E(D,\,VII)$: Every non-well-orderable cardinal is decomposable. Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1973a}] and note 94.

\textbf{V. Ordering Cardinals}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AE}] The number of well ordered subsets of a set: For all $x,\,|x|<|s(x)|$ where $s(x)=\{y\subseteq x:y\ \text{can be well ordered}\ \}$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1939}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AF}] The number of well orderings of a set: For all $x,\,|x|<|w(x)|$ where $w(x)$ is the set of all well orderings of subsets of $x$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1973d}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AG}] For any $n\in \omega,\,n\neq 0,\,|s(x)|\not\leq|x^{n}|$ and $|x^{n}|<|w(x)|$ if $|x|$ exceeds some small finite value depending on $n$. ($s(x)$ is the set of well orderable subsets of $x$ and $w(x)$ is the set of well orderings of subsets of $x$.) Truss [\textbf{1973d}]

\noindent [\textbf{1 Y}] Refined Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem:\index{Subject}{Cantor-Bernstein theorem} If $f:X\rightarrow Y$ and $g:Y\rightarrow X$ are onto then there is a bijection $h:X\rightarrow Y$ such that $h\subseteq f\cup g^{-1}$. Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AK}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for all cardinals $x,\,\alpha(x+\aleph(x),\,x\cdot\aleph(x))< \beta$. Truss [\textbf{1973b}] and note 98.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AL}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for all cardinals $x,\,\alpha(x,\,x^{2})<\beta$. Truss [\textbf{1973b}] and note 98.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AM}] There is an ordinal $\beta$ such that for no cardinal $x$ is there a strictly increasing sequence of cardinals $\{y_{\gamma}:\gamma<\beta\}$ such that $y_{\gamma}^{2}=x$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1973b}] and note 98.

\noindent [\textbf{3 C}] Definability of cardinal addition as the least upper bound: ($\forall$ cardinals $x,\,y$ and $z$) ($x+y=z$ iff ($x\leq z$ and $y\leq z$ and $(\forall u)(x,\,y\leq u\rightarrow z\leq u)$)). H\"{a}ussler\index{Author}{Haussler@H\"{a}ussler} [\textbf{1983}] and Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1949a}].

\noindent [\textbf{3 D}] Every pair of cardinals has a least upper bound in the usual cardinal ordering and for all cardinals $\kappa$ and $\gamma$, if $n\kappa \leq\gamma$ for all $n\in w$, then $\aleph_{0}\kappa\leq\gamma$. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1979b}].

\noindent \textbf{7.} There is no infinite decreasing sequence of cardinals. Schoenflies\index{Author}{Schoenflies} [\textbf{1908}].

\noindent [\textbf{9 E}] No Dedekind finite set can be mapped onto $\aleph_{0}$. (See form 160.) Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1975}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{40 B}] For all ordinals $\alpha$, the $\aleph_{\alpha}$ partition principle holds: For every ordinal $\alpha$ and every cardinal $\kappa$, if $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq^{\ast}\kappa$, then $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq\kappa$. Pelc\index{Author}{Pelc} [\textbf{1978}], Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}], and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{59($\leq$).} If $(A,\,\leq)$ is a partial ordering that is not a well ordering, then there is no set $B$ such that $(B,\,\leq)$ (the usual injective cardinal ordering on $B$) is isomorphic to $(A,\,\leq)$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1979}] p 120.

\noindent \textbf{100.} Weak Partition Principle:\index{Subject}{partition principle} For all sets $x$ and $y$, if $x\precsim^{\ast} y$, then it is not the case that $y\prec x$. Lindenbaum/Tarski\index{Author}{Lindenbaum/Tarski} [\textbf{1926}] and note 69.

\noindent [\textbf{100 A}] For every set $A$ and function $f$ it is false that $A\prec f^{\prime\prime}A$. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}], p. 327.

\noindent [\textbf{100 B}] For all sets $x$ and $y$, if $x\precsim^{\ast}y$ and $y\precsim x$, then $x\approx y$. Higasikawa\index{Author}{Higasikawa} [\textbf{1995}] and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{101.} Partition Principle: If $S$ is a partition of $M$, then $s\precsim\ M$. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1947}].

\noindent [\textbf{101 A}] For all sets $x$ and $y,\,x\precsim^{\ast}y$ implies $x\precsim y$. Lindenbaum/Tarski [\textbf{1926}] and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{103.} If $(P,\,<)$ is a linear ordering and $|P|>\aleph_{1}$ then some initial segment of $P$ is uncountable. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 164 prob 11.21.

\noindent \textbf{105.} There is a partially ordered set $(A,\,\leq)$ such that for no set $B$ is $(B,\,\leq)$ (the ordering on $B$ is the usual injective cardinal ordering) isomorphic to $(A,\,\leq)$. Forti/Honsell\index{Author}{Forti/Honsell} [\textbf{1985}] and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} [\textbf{1966c}].

\noindent \textbf{159.} The regular cardinals are cofinal in the class of ordinals. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent \textbf{160.} No Dedekind finite set can be mapped onto an aleph. (See [9 E].) Monro [\textbf{1975}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{161.} Definability of cardinal addition in terms of $\leq$: There is a first order formula whose only non-logical symbol is $\leq$ (for cardinals) that defines cardinal addition. H\"{a}ussler~[\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{162.} Non-existence of infinite units: There is no infinite cardinal number $A$ such that $A+A>A$ and for all cardinals $x$ and $y,\,x+y=A\rightarrow x=A$ or $y=A$. H\"{a}ussler~[\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{168.} Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem:\index{Subject}{Cantor-Bernstein theorem} $(\forall x)(\forall y)(|x|\leq^{\ast}|y|\ \mathrm{and}\ |y|\leq^{\ast}|x|\ \mathrm{implies}\ |x|=|y|)$. Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}] and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{186.} Every pair of cardinal numbers has a least upper bound (in the usual cardinal ordering.) Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1979b}].

\noindent \textbf{187.} Every pair of cardinal numbers has a greatest lower bound (in the usual cardinal ordering.) Hickman [\textbf{1979b}].

\noindent [\textbf{192 A}] $(\forall x)(\exists y)$($x\leq^{\ast}y$ and $y$ indexed choice holds). Blass in Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1977b}], notes 60 and 69.

\noindent \textbf{204.} For every infinite $X$, there is a function from $X$ onto $2X$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{205.} For all cardinals $m$ and $n$, if $m\leq^{\ast}n$ and $\neg(n\leq^{\ast}m)$ then there is a cardinal $k<n$ such that $m\leq^{\ast}k$. Pelc\index{Author}{Pelc} [\textbf{1978}] and note 69.

\noindent \textbf{208.} For all ordinals $\alpha,\,\aleph_{\alpha+1}\leq 2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$. Figura\index{Author}{Figura} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{274.} There is a cardinal number $x$ and an $n\in\omega$ such that $\neg(x\ \mathrm{adj}^{n}\,x^{2})$. (The expression ``$x\ \mathrm{adj}^{n}\ ya^{\prime\prime}$ means there are cardinals $z_{0},\,\ldots,\,z_{n}$ such that $z_{0}=x$ and $z_{n}=y$ and for all $i,\,0\leq i<n,\,z_{i}<z_{i+1}$ and if $z_{i}<z\leq z_{i+1}$, then $z=z_{i+1}$.) (Compare with [0 A]). Truss [\textbf{1974b}].

\noindent \textbf{283.} Cardinality of well ordered subsets: For all $n\in \omega$ and for all infinite $x,\,|x^{n}|<|s(x)|$ where $s(x)$ is the set of all well orderable subsets of $x$. Truss [\textbf{1973d}].

\noindent \textbf{347.} Idemmultiple Partition Principle: If $y$ is idemmultiple $(2\times y\approx y)$ and $x\precsim^{\ast} y$, then $x\precsim y$. Higasikawa\index{Author}{Higasikawa} [\textbf{1995}] and note 69.

\textbf{VI. Inaccessible Cardinals}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AJ}] $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is not an inaccessible cardinal for any ordinal $\alpha$. Drake\index{Author}{Drake} [\textbf{1974}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{117.} If $\kappa$ is a measurable cardinal, then $\kappa$ is the $\kappa$th inaccessible cardinal. Keisler/Tarski\index{Author}{Keisler/Tarski} [\textbf{1964}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{196($\alpha$).} $\aleph_{\alpha}$ and $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ are not both measurable. Bull\index{Author}{Bull} [\textbf{1978}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{318.} $\aleph_{1}$ is not measurable. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} [\textbf{1968a}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{319.} Measurable cardinals are inaccessible. Drake [\textbf{1974}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{320.} No successor cardinal, $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$, is measurable. Drake [\textbf{1974}] and note 20.

\noindent \textbf{321.} There does not exist an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $\aleph_{\alpha}$ is weakly compact and $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is measurable. Bull [\textbf{1978}] and note 20.

\textbf{VII. Miscellaneous Cardinal Number Forms}

\noindent [\textbf{15 A}] $K(1):(\forall M)$($\exists\alpha$ an ordinal) ($|M|=|A|$ for some $A\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\alpha)$). (See form 81($n$).) Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 53 prob 4.12 and Kinna/Wagner\index{Author}{Kinna/Wagner} [\textbf{1955}].

\noindent [\textbf{40 C}] For each idemmultiple set $x\,(2\times x\approx x)$, if there exists a surjection $f$ mapping $x$ onto an ordinal $\lambda$ such that for each $\psi<\lambda,\,f^{-1}[\{\psi\}]$ is Dedekind infinite, then $\lambda\precsim\ x$. Higasikawa [\textbf{1995}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{81($n$).} (For $n\in \omega)\ K(n)$: For every set $S$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a one to one function $f:S\rightarrow \mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha)$. ($\mathcal{P}^{0}(X)=X$ and $\mathcal{P}^{n+1}(X)=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}^{n}(X)$). ($K(0)$ is equivalent to form 1 (AC) and $K(1)$ is equivalent to the selection\index{Subject}{Rado's selection lemma} principle (form 15)). Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1972}], [\textbf{1973b}] and note 90.

\noindent \textbf{97.} Cardinal Representatives:\index{Subject}{cardinal representatives}\index{Subject}{countable axiom of choice} For every set $A$ there is a function $c$ with domain $\mathcal{P}(A)$ such that for all $x,\,y\in \mathcal{P}(A)$, (i) $c(x)=c(y)\leftrightarrow x\approx y$ and (ii) $c(x)\approx x$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p~154.

\noindent [\textbf{97 A}] For every set $\{X_{i}:i\in I\}$ of local cardinal numbers, there is a set $\{x_{i}:i\in I\}$ of sets such that for each $i\in I$ there exists a $y_{i}\in X_{i}$ such that $x_{i}\approx y_{i}$. ($X$ is a \emph{local cardinal number} if for all $x,\,y\in X,\,x\approx y.)$ Higasikawa\index{Author}{Higasikawa} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{175.} Transitivity Condition: For all sets $x$, there is a set $u$ abd a function $f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $f$ is a one to one function from $x$ onto $u$. von Rimscha\index{Author}{Rimscha} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{269.} For every cardinal $m$, there is a set $A$ such that $2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m$ and there is a choice function on the collection of 2-element subsets of $A$. Lampe\index{Author}{Lampe} \cite{bib:1974m}.

\noindent \textbf{296.} Part-$\infty$: Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets. Gonzalez\index{Author}{Gonzalez} [\textbf{1995b}], Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1997}].

\section*{CHOICE FORMS}

\textbf{I. Choosing Single Elements}

\noindent \textbf{1.} $C(\infty,\,\infty)$: The Axiom of Choice:\index{Subject}{axiom of choice} Every set of non-empty sets has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{5.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\mathbb{R})$: Every denumerable set of non-empty denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ has a choice function. Sageev\index{Author}{Sageev} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{8.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent [\textbf{8 M}] Form 131+ form 32. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note~132.

\noindent \textbf{10.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$: Every denumerable family of non-empty finite sets has a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{14 Y}] Form 99+ Form 62. Note 33.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BS}] Every bounded distributive lattice has a prime ideal choice function. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}, \cite{bib:1985p} and note~71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BT}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of bounded, distributive, $\vee$-compact lattices and if $(J_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family such that for all $i\in I,\,J_{i}$ is a proper ideal in $A_{i}$ then there is a family $(P_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for all $i\in I,\,P_{i}$ is a prime principal ideal in $A_{i}$ containing $J_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BU}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of distributive non trivial bounded lattices then there is a family $(f_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that each $f_{i}$ is a prime ideal choice function on $A_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BW}] For every set $E$ there is an ultrafilter choice function on $E$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BX}] If $(E_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of sets and $(F_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family such that for each $i,\,F_{i}$ is a filter in $\mathcal{P}(E_{i})$, then there is a family $(U_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for each $i\in I,\,U_{i}$ is an ultrafilter in $\mathcal{P}(E_{i})$ containing $F_{i}$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note~71.

\noindent \textbf{16.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,\leq 2^{\aleph_{0}})$: Every denumerable collection of non-empty sets each with power $\leq 2^{\aleph_{0}}$ has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{24.} $C(\aleph_{0},2^{(2^{\aleph_{0}})})$: Every denumerable collection of non-empty sets each with power $2^{(2^{\aleph_{0}})}$ has a choice function. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{28.} $C(\aleph_{0},2^{\aleph_{0}})$: Every denumerable collection of non-empty sets each with power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{32.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,\leq\aleph_{0})$: Every denumerable set of non-empty countable sets has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent [\textbf{32 A}] $C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$. Every denumerable set of denumerable sets has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{33($n$).} If $n\in \omega-\{0,1\},\,C(LO,\,n)$: Every linearly ordered set of $n$ element sets has a choice function. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{39.} $C(\aleph_{1},\,\infty)$: Every set $A$ of non-empty sets such that $|A|=\aleph_{1}$ has a choice function. Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1918}], G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p. 202.

\noindent \textbf{40.} $C(WO,\,\infty)$: Every well orderable set of non-empty sets has a choice function. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 325.

\noindent \textbf{45($n$).} If $n\in\omega-\{0,1\},\,C(\infty,\,n)$: Every set of $n$-element sets has a choice function. Mostowski\index{Author}{Mostowski} [\textbf{1945}], Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{46 ($K$)}. If $K$ is a finite subset of $\omega-\{0,\,1\},\,C(\infty,\,K)$: For every $n\in K$, every set of $n$-element sets has a choice function. Mostowski [\textbf{1945}], Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{47($n$).} If $n\in \omega-\{0,1\},\,C(WO,\,n)$: Every well ordered collection of $n$-element sets has a choice function. Mostowski [\textbf{1945}], Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{48($K$).} If $K$ is a finite subset of $\omega-\{0,\,1\},\,C(WO,\,K)$: For every $n\in K,\,C(WO,\,n)$. Mostowski [\textbf{1945}], Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{60.} $C(\infty,\,WO)$: Every set of non-empty, well orderable sets has a choice function. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 125.

\noindent [\textbf{60 A}] $(\forall\alpha)C(\infty,\,\aleph_{\alpha})$: For every ordinal $\alpha$, every family of sets each with power $\aleph_{\alpha}$ has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{61.} $(\forall n\in\omega,\,n\geq 2)(C(\infty,\,n))$: For each $n\in \omega,\,n\geq 2$, every set of $n$ element sets has a choice function. Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1962}].

\noindent \textbf{62.} $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$: Every set of non-empty finite sets has a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{79 A}] $C(\infty,\,\infty,\,\mathbb{R})$: Every set whose elements are non-empty subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ has a choice function. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent \textbf{80.} $C(\aleph_{0},2)$: Every denumerable set of pairs has a choice function. Mostowski [\textbf{1948}].

\noindent \textbf{85.} $C(\infty,\,\aleph_{0})$: Every family of denumerable sets has a choice function. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 115 prob 7.13.

\noindent [\textbf{85 A}] $C(\infty,\,\leq\aleph_{0})$: Every family of non-empty\index{Author}{Freyd} countable sets has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{86($\alpha$).} $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)$: If $X$ is a set of non-empty sets such that $|X|=\aleph_{\alpha}$, then $X$ has a choice function. Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1964}].

\noindent \textbf{88.} $C(\infty,\,2)$: Every family of pairs has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{94.} $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty,\,\mathbb{R})$: Every denumerable family of non-empty sets of reals has a choice function. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 148 prob 10.1.

\noindent [\textbf{111 A}] $C(WO,\,2)$: Every well ordered family of 2-element sets has a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{118 I}] Every linearly ordered set of linear orders, each of which is non-empty and conditionally complete, has a choice function. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}, van Douwen\index{Author}{Douwen} [\textbf{1985}], and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 M}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the family $\{A(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\}$ has a choice function. ($A(a,\,b)$ denotes the set of continuous, order preserving functions from $X$ into $[0,1]$ such that $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=1$.) Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 N}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order then the family $\{A^{\prime}(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\}$ has a choice function. ($A^{\prime}(a, b)$ denotes the set of continuous functions from $X$ into $[0,1]$ such that $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=1.)$ Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 S}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order then there is a choice function $\ast$ for the family of non-empty open intervals of $X$ such that if $a,\,b,\,c\in X$ and either $(a,\,b)\neq\emptyset$ or $(b,\, c)\neq\emptyset$ then $\ast((a,\,c))\in\{\ast((a,\,b)), \ast((b,\,c)), b,\,b^{+}\}$ (where $b^{+}$ is the successor of $b$ if it exists and $b$ otherwise). Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 T}] Every complete linear order has an increasing choice function. Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent \textbf{119.} $C(\aleph_{0},\text{uniformly orderable with order type of the integers})$: Suppose $\{A_{i}: i\in\omega\}$ is a set and there is a function $f$ such that for each $i\in\omega,\,f(i)$ is an ordering of $A_{i}$ of type $\omega^{\ast}+\omega$ (the usual ordering of the integers), then $\{A_{i}:i\in\omega\}$ has a choice function. van Douwen\index{Subject}{van Douwen's choice principle} [\textbf{1985}].

\noindent \textbf{120($K$).} If $K\subseteq\omega-\{0,1\},\,C(LO,\,K)$: Every linearly ordered set of non-empty sets each of whose cardinality is in $K$ has a choice function. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{121.} $C(LO,\,<\aleph_{0})$: Every linearly ordered set of non-empty finite sets has a choice function. Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{122.} $C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0})$: Every well ordered set of non-empty finite sets has a choice function. Truss [\textbf{1973a}].

\noindent \textbf{165.} $C(WO,\,WO)$: Every well ordered family of non-empty, well orderable sets has a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{181.} $C(2^{\aleph_{0}},\,\infty)$: Every set $X$ of non-empty sets such that $|X|=2^{\aleph_{0}}$ has a choice function. Freyd [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{194.} $C(\varPi_{2}^{1})$ or $AC(\varPi_{2}^{1})$: If $P\in\omega \times ^{\omega}\omega,\,P$ has domain $\omega$, and $P$ is in $\varPi_{2}^{1}$, then there is a sequence of elements $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega\rangle$ of $^{\omega}\omega$ with $\langle k,\,x_{k}\rangle\in P$ for all $k\in\omega$. Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} [\textbf{1979}] and note 61.

\noindent \textbf{202.} $C(LO,\,\infty)$: Every linearly ordered family of non-empty sets has a choice function. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{203.} $C(\mathrm{disjoint},\subseteq \mathbb{R})$: Every partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Truss [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{212.} $C(2^{\aleph_{0}},\,\subseteq \mathbb{R})$: If $R$ is a relation on $\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$, there is a $y\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x\,R\,y$, then there is a function $f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb{R},\,x\,R\,f(x)$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1977a}].

\noindent \textbf{213.} $C(\infty,\,\aleph_{1})$: If $(\forall y\in X)(|y|=\aleph_{1})$ then $X$ has a choice function. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1977a}].

\noindent \textbf{250.} $(\forall n\in\omega\,-\{0,1\})(C(WO,\,n))$: For every natural number $n\geq 2$, every well ordered family of $n$ element sets has a choice function. Truss [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{288($n$).} If $n\in\omega\,-\{0,1\},\,C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$: Every denumerable set of $n$-element sets has a choice function. Wi\'{s}niewski~[\textbf{1972}].

\noindent [\textbf{308} $\mathbf{B}(p)$] If $p$ is a prime and if $Y$ is a set of non-empty finite sets such that $(\forall y\in Y)(\mathrm{gcd}(|y|,\,p)=1)$, then $Y$ has a choice function. (This is similar to form 46$(K)$, but in 46$(K)$ the set $K$ is required to be finite.) Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1987}].

\noindent [\textbf{308} $\mathbf{C}(p)$] If $p$ is a prime and if $Y$ is a set of non-empty finite sets such that $(\forall y\in Y)(|y|\equiv 1\mod\,p)$, then $Y$ has a choice function. (This is similar to form 46$(K)$, but in 46$(K)$ the set $K$ is required to be finite.) Howard/Yorke~[\textbf{1987}].

\noindent [\textbf{374} $\mathbf{A}(n)$] For each $i,\,2\leq i\leq n\in \omega-\{0,1\},\,C(\aleph_{0},\,i)$: Every denumerable set of $i$-element sets has a choice function.

\textbf{II. Dependent Choice}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ X}] $DC(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{1})$: If $P\subseteq {^{\omega}\omega} \times{^{\omega}\omega}$ and $P$ has domain ${^{\omega}\omega},\,P\in\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{1}$, then for any $y\in{^{\omega}\omega}$ there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega\rangle$ of elements of $^{\omega}\omega$ with $x_{0}=y$ and $\langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle\in P$ for all $k\in\omega$. Kanovei [\textbf{1979}] and note 61.

\noindent [\textbf{1 F}] For all ordinals $\alpha,\,DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$: Given a relation $R$ such that for every subset $Y$ of a set $X$ with $|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$, there is an $x\in X$ with $YR\,x$, then there is a function $f:\aleph_{\alpha}\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall\beta<\aleph_{\alpha},\, \{f(\gamma):\gamma<\beta\}\,R\,f(\beta)$.) Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1964}] and note 133.

\noindent \textbf{43.} $DC(\omega)$ ($DC$), Principle of Dependent Choices: If $S$ is a relation on a non-empty set $A$ and $(\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(xSy)$ then there is a sequence $a(0), a(1), a(2),\ldots$ of elements of $A$ such that $(\forall n\in\omega) (a(n)\,S\,a(n+1))$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1948}] p 96, Levy [\textbf{1964}] p 136 and note 54.

\noindent [\textbf{43 S}] If $S$ is a relation on $A$ such that $(\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(x\,S\,y)$ and $x_{0}$ is any element of $\mathrm{A}$, then there is a sequence $a(1),a(2),\ldots$ of elements of $A$ such that $a(n)\,S\,a(n+1)$ for all $n\in \omega$ and such that $a(0)=x_{0}$. Notes 101 and~54.

\noindent \textbf{44.} $DC(\aleph_{1})$: Given a relation $R$ such that for every subset $Y$ of a set $X$ with $|Y|<\aleph_{1}$ there is an $x\in X$ with $Y\,R\,x$, then there is a function $f:\aleph_{1}\rightarrow X$ such that $(\forall\beta<\aleph_{1})(\{f(\gamma):\gamma<b\}\,R\,f(\beta))$. Levy [\textbf{1964}].

\noindent \textbf{87($\alpha$).} $DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$: Given a relation $R$ such that for every subset $Y$ of a set $X$ with $|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$, there is an $x\in X$ with $Y\,R\,x$ then there is a function $f:\aleph_{\alpha}\rightarrow X$ such that $(\forall\beta<\aleph_{\alpha})\{f(\gamma):\gamma<\beta\}\,R\,f(\beta)$. Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1964}].

\noindent [\textbf{106 A}] $DMC$: Dependent Multiple Choice: Every tree in which every element has at least one immediate successor has a subtree whose levels are finite and in which every element has at least one immediate successor. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}], Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983c}], Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and note~21.

\noindent [\textbf{106 B}] Weak $\mathrm{DC}$: If $R$ is a binary relation on a non-empty set $E$ such that $(\forall x\in E)(\exists y\in E)(x\,R\,y)$, then there is a sequence $\langle F_{n}\rangle_{n\in\omega}$, of non-empty finite subsets of $E$ such that ($\forall n\in\omega) (\forall x\in F_{n})(\exists y\in F_{n+1})(x\,R\,y)$. (This statement remains equivalent to form 106 if we replace ``binary relation'' by ``transitive binary relation''.) Fossy/Morillon~[\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{211.} $DCR$: Dependent choice for relations on $\mathbb{R}$: If $R\subseteq \mathbb{R}\ \times \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $(\forall x\in \mathbb{R})(\exists y\in \mathbb{R})(x\,R\,y)$ then there is a sequence $\langle x(n): n\in \omega\rangle$ of real numbers such that $(\forall n\in\omega)(x(n)\,R\,x(n+1))$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1977a}].

\textbf{III. Multiple Choice and Kinna-Wagner Principles}

\noindent [\textbf{1 E}] $K(0)$: For every set $S$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a one to one function $f:S\rightarrow\alpha$. (See form 81$(n)$).

\noindent [\textbf{1 BY}] If $x$ is a set of sets of cardinality at least 2, then there exists a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a finite, non-empty, proper subset of $u$. (Form [1 BY] implies [62 E] $(KW(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$) and 67 (MC) and $62+67\rightarrow \mathrm{AC}$.) Blass [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 CC}] $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty) +MC_{\omega^{+}}$. $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty)$ is ``Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.'' and $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ is ``For every natural number $n\geq 1$ and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $u$ such that $|f(u)|$ and $n$ are relatively prime.'' Note 133.

\noindent [\textbf{8 M}] Form 131+ form 32. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 O}] $DUCCC\ +$ form 131. $DUCCC$ is ``If $X$ is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $X$ has the ccc property.'' ($Y$ has the \emph{ccc property} if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 P}] $DUSS\ +$ form 131. $DUSS$ is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of separable topological spaces is separable.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 Q}] $DUSC\ +$ form 131. $DUSC$ is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of second countable topological spaces is second countable.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note~132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 R}] $SCDUL\ +$ form 131. $SCDUL$ is ``The denumerable disjoint union of second countable spaces is Lindel\"{o}f.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AT}] Assume $D$ and $E$ are sets and for all $d\in D,\,d$ is finite. Suppose that for every finite $F\subseteq D$, there is an $S$ such that $(\forall f\in F)(f\cap\,S\in E)$. Then there is an $S$ such that $(\forall d\in D)(d\cap\,S\in E)$. van Benthem\index{Author}{Benthem} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{15.} $KW(\infty,\,\infty)$ (KW), The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle: For every set $M$ there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in M$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. (See form $81(n)$). Kinna/Wagner\index{Author}{Kinna/Wagner} [\textbf{1955}].

\noindent [\textbf{62 E}] $KW(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for families of finite sets: For every set $M$ of finite sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in M$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. Note 70.

\noindent \textbf{67.} $MC(\infty,\,\infty)$ (MC), The Axiom of Multiple Choice: For every set $M$ of non-empty sets there is a function $f$ such that ($\forall x\in M)(\emptyset\neq f(x)\subseteq x$ and $f(x)$ is finite).

\noindent \textbf{76.} $MC_{\omega}(\infty,\,\infty)\ (\omega\text{-}\mathrm{MC})$: For every family $X$ of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $x\in X,\,\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is a non-empty countable subset of $x$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} [\textbf{1997b}].

\noindent [\textbf{106 A}] $DMC$: Dependent Multiple Choice: Every tree in which every element has at least one immediate successor has a subtree whose levels are finite and in which every element has at least one immediate successor. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}], Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983c}], Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and note 21.

\noindent [\textbf{106 D}] For every compact $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ space $(X,\,T)$ and every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in\omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$ there is a regular filter base $\mathcal{F}\subseteq T$ (that is, if $F,\,G\in \mathcal{F}$, then there exists $Q\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $\overline{Q}\subseteq F\cap G$) such that for all $i\in\omega$, for all but finitely many $F\in \mathcal{F},\,\overline{F}\subset D_{i}$. Fossy/Morillon~[\textbf{1995}]

\noindent \textbf{112.} $MC(\infty,\,LO)$: For every family $X$ of non-empty sets each of which can be linearly ordered there is a function $f$ such that for all $y\in X,\,f(y)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $y$. Howard/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Rubin} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{126.} $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$, Countable axiom of multiple choice: For every denumerable set $X$ of non-empty sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $y\in X,\,f(y)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $y$. Brunner [\textbf{1984d}] and Blass [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent [\textbf{126 B}] Form 131+ form 350. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{126 C}] $FSCB\ +$ form 131. FSCB is ``Every separable first countable space $(X,\,T)$ has a denumerable $\pi$-base.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{131.} $MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: For every denumerable family $X$ of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $x\in X,\,\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is a non-empty countable subset of $x$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}].

\noindent \textbf{167.} $PKW(\aleph_{0},\,\geq 2,\,\infty)$, Partial Kinna-Wagner Principle: For every denumerable family $F$ such that for all $x\in F,\,|x|\geq 2$, there is an infinite subset $H\subseteq F$ and a function $f$ such that for all $x\in H,\,\emptyset \neq f(x)\subsetneq x$. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent \textbf{178($n,\,N$).} If $n\in \omega,\,n\geq 2$ and $N\subseteq\{1,2,\,\ldots,\,n-1\},\, N\neq\emptyset,\,MC(\infty,\, n,\,N)$: If $X$ is any set of $n$-element sets then there is a function $f$ with domain $X$ such that for all $A\in X,\,f(A)\subseteq A$ and $|f(A)|\in N$. Zuckerman\index{Author}{Zuckerman} [\textbf{1969a}], \cite{bib:1981b}, and note 53.

\noindent \textbf{214.} $Z(\omega)$: For every family $A$ of infinite sets, there is a function $f$ such that for all $y\in A,\, f(y)$ is a non-empty subset of $y$ and $|f(y)|=\aleph_{0}$. Pincus [\textbf{1977a}].

\noindent \textbf{218.} $(\forall n\in \omega-\{0\})MC$($\infty,\,\infty$, relatively prime to $n$): $\forall n\in \omega-\{0\}$, if $X$ is a set of non-empty sets, then there is a function $f$ such that for all $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a non-empty, finite subset of $x$ and $|f(x)|$ is relatively prime to $n$. Bleicher\index{Author}{Bleicher} [\textbf{1965}].

\noindent \textbf{219.} $(\forall n\in\omega\,-\{0\})MC$($\infty,\,WO$, relatively prime to $n$): For all non-zero $n\in \omega$, if $X$ is a set of non-empty well orderable sets, then there is a function $f$ such that for all $x\in X,\, f(x)$ is a non-empty, finite subset of $x$, and $|f(x)|$ is relatively prime to $n$. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1972a}].

\noindent \textbf{292.} $MC(LO,\,\infty)$: For each linearly ordered family of non-empty sets $X$, there is a function $f$ such that for all $x\in Xf(x)$ is non-empty, finite subset of $x$). Howard/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Rubin} $[\textbf{1977}]$.

\noindent \textbf{322.} $KW(WO,\,\infty)$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a well ordered family of sets: For every well ordered set $X$ there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in M$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. (See form 15). Kinna/Wagner\index{Author}{Kinna/Wagner} [\textbf{1955}], Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent \textbf{323.} $KW(\infty,\,WO)$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a family of well orderable sets: For every set $X$ of well orderable sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. (See form 15.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{324.} $KW(WO,\,WO)$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a well ordered family of well orderable sets: For every well ordered set $X$ of well orderable sets, there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. (See form 15.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{327.} $KW(WO,\,<\aleph_{0})$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a well ordered family of finite sets: For every well ordered set $X$ of finite sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$. (See form 15.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{328.} $MC(WO, \infty)$; For every well ordered set $X$ such that for all $x\in X,\,|x|\geq 1$, there is a function $f$ such that and for every $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$. (See form 67.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{329.} $MC(\infty, WO)$: For every set $M$ of well orderable sets such that for all $x\in X,\,|x|\geq 1$, there is a function $f$ such that for every $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$. (See form 67.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin~[\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{330.} $MC(WO,\,WO)$: For every well ordered set $X$ of well orderable sets such that for all $x\in X,\, |x|\geq 1$, there is a function $f$ such that for every $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$. (See form 67.) Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{333.} $MC(\infty,\,\infty,\,\mathrm{odd})$: For every set $X$ of sets such that for all $x\in X,\,|x|\geq 1$, there is a function $f$ such that for every $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$ and $|f(x)|$ is odd. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent \textbf{334.} $MC$($\infty,\,\infty$, even): For every set $X$ of sets such that for all $x\in X,\,|x|\geq 2$, there is a function $f$ such that for every $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$ and $|f(x)|$ is even. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent \textbf{349.} $MC(\infty,\,\aleph_{0})$: For every set $X$ of non-empty denumerable sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$.

\noindent \textbf{350.} $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$: For every denumerable set $X$ of non-empty denumerable sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $x\in X,\,f(x)$ is a finite, non-empty subset of $x$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{355.} $KW(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a denumerable family of sets: For every denumerable set $X$ there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$.

\noindent \textbf{356.} $KW(\infty,\,\aleph_{0})$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a family of denumerable sets: For every set $X$ of denumerable sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$.

\noindent \textbf{357.} $KW(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a denumerable family of denumerable sets: For every denumerable set $X$ of denumerable sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$.

\noindent \textbf{358.} $KW(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$, The Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle for a denumerable family of finite sets: For every denumerable set $X$ of finite sets there is a function $f$ such that for all $A\in X$, if $|A|>1$ then $\emptyset \neq f(A)\subsetneq A$.

\noindent \textbf{376.} Restricted Kinna Wagner Principle: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ and a function $f$ such that for every $z\subseteq Y$, if $|z|\geq 2$ then $f(z)$ is a non-empty proper subset of $z$. De la Cruz/Di Prisco\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco} [\textbf{1996}].

\textbf{IV. Partial Choice $PC$}

\noindent [\textbf{1 CC}] $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty) +MC_{\omega^{+}}$. $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty)$ is ``Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.'' and $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ is ``For every natural number $n\geq 1$ and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $u$ such that $|f(u)|$ and $n$ are relatively prime.'' Note 133.

\noindent [\textbf{8 A}] $PC(\infty,\,\infty,\,\infty)$: Every infinite family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent [\textbf{8 B}] $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty,\,\infty)$: Every denumerable family of non-empty sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Monro\index{Author}{Monro} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent [\textbf{8 S}] $PC(WO,\,\infty,\,\infty)$: Every infinite well ordered set of non-empty sets has an infinite subset with a choice function. $([8\ \mathrm{A}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{S}]\rightarrow[8\ \mathrm{B}])$

\noindent [\textbf{9 T}] Restricted Choice: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ such that the collection of non-empty subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco~[\textbf{1996}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 E}] $PC(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every denumerable family of finite sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner [\textbf{1983b}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 O}] $PC(WO,\,<\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every infinite well ordered family of finite sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{18 A}] $PC(\aleph_{0},2,\,\infty)$: Every denumerable set of pairs has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{18 C}] $PC(WO,\,2,\,\infty)$: Every infinite well ordered set of pairs has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{32 B}] $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every denumerable set of denumerable sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{32 C}] $PC(WO,\,\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every infinite well ordered set of denumerable sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{126 D}] For every denumerable family $A$ of disjoint non-empty sets there is an infinite set $C\subset\bigcup A$ such that for every $a\in A,\, 0\leq|C\cap a|<\omega$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{132.} $PC(\infty<\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every infinite family of finite sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1977a}] and Kleinberg\index{Author}{Kleinberg} [\textbf{1969}].

\noindent \textbf{150.} $PC(\infty,\,\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: Every infinite set of denumerable sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{166.} $PC(\infty,\,2,\,\infty)$: Every infinite family of pairs has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent \textbf{167.} $PKW(\aleph_{0},\,\geq 2,\,\infty)$, Partial Kinna-Wagner Principle: For every denumerable family $F$ such that for all $x\in F,\,|x|\geq 2$, there is an infinite subset $H\subseteq F$ and a function $f$ such that for all $x\in H,\,\emptyset \neq f(x)\subsetneq x$. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent \textbf{336($n$).} (For $n\in\omega,\,n\geq 2$.) For every infinite set $X$, there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ such that the set of all $n$-element subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. Note 111.

\noindent \textbf{342($n$).} (For $n\in\omega,\,n\geq 2$.) $PC(\infty,\,n,\,\infty)$: Every infinite family of $n$-element sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function. (See form 166.) Note 111.

\noindent \textbf{373($n$).} (For $n\in\omega,\,n\geq 2$.) $PC(\aleph_{0},\,n,\,\infty)$: Every denumerable set of $n$-element sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent [\textbf{373 A($n$)}] (For $n\in \omega,\,n\geq 2$.) $PC(WO,\,n,\,\infty)$: Every infinite well ordered set of $n$-element sets has an infinite subset with a choice function.

\noindent \textbf{378.} Restricted Choice for Families of Well Ordered Sets: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that the family of non-empty well orderable subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco [\textbf{1996}].

\noindent [\textbf{378 A}] Restricted Choice for Families of Finite Sets: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that the family of non-empty finite subsets of $Y$ has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco}  [\textbf{1996}].

\noindent \textbf{379.} $PKW(\infty,\,\infty,\,\infty)$: For every infinite family $X$ of sets each of which has at least two elements, there is an infinite subfamily $Y$ of $X$ and a function $f$ such that for all $y\in Y,\,f(y)$ is a non-empty proper subset of $y$. De la Cruz/Di Prisco [\textbf{1996}].

\noindent \textbf{380.} $PC(\infty,\,WO,\,\infty)$: For every infinite family of non-empty well orderable sets, there is an infinite subfamily $Y$ of $X$ which has a choice function. De la Cruz/Di Prisco~[\textbf{1996}].

\textbf{V. Conditional Choice Including Variations of Rado's Lemma}

\noindent [\textbf{14 I}] Consistency Principle:\index{Subject}{consistency principle} For every binary mess $M$ on a set $S$ there is a function $f$ on $S$ which is consistent with $M$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 17 and note 109.

\noindent [\textbf{14 O}] Let $\{A(i):i\in I\}$ be a collection of finite sets and $R$ a symmetric binary relation on $\bigcup_{i\in I}A(i)$. Suppose that for every finite $W\subseteq I$, there is an $R$-consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in W\}$. Then there is an $R$-consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in I\}$. {\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski\index{Author}{Los/Ryll-Nardzewski@{\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski}
 [\textbf{1951}] and note 109.

\noindent [\textbf{14 $\mathbf{P}(n)$}] (For $n\geq 3$) [14 O] restricted to $\{A(i):i\in I\}$ such that for all $i\in I,\,|A(i)|\leq n$. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1977b}] and note 109. (For $n=2$ see form 141.)

\noindent [\textbf{14 Y}] Form $99$ + form 62. Note 33.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AG}] Topological Rado\index{Author}{Rado} Lemma:\index{Subject}{Rado's selection lemma} Let $\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of compact Hausdorff spaces and suppose for each finite $F\subseteq I$, there is a set $\Phi(F)$ of partial choice functions on $I$ whose domains include $F$ and such that (a) $F_{1}\subseteq F_{2}$ implies $\Phi(F_{2})\subseteq\Phi(F_{1})$ and (b) the set $\{\phi|F:\phi\,\in\Phi(F)\}$ is closed in $\prod\{T_{i}:i\in F\}$ in the product topology. Then there is a choice function $f$ on $I$ satisfying for any finite $F\subseteq I,\,\exists\phi\in\Phi(F)$ such that $f$ and $\phi$ coincide on $F$. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AH}] Principle of Consistent Choices: Let $\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of compact Hausdorf spaces and suppose $R$ is a symmetric binary relation defined for all pairs of elements belonging to distinct $T_{i}$ and such that for all $i\neq j$ in $I$, the set $E(i,j)=\{(x,\,y):x\,R\,y\ \mathrm{and}\ x\in T_{i}\ \mathrm{and}\ y\in T_{j}\}$ is closed in $T_{i}\times T_{j}$. Furthermore suppose that for every finite subset $F\subseteq I$, with at least two elements, $\exists\phi\in\prod\{T_{i}:i\in F\}$ such that $\phi(i)\,R\,\phi(j)$ for all $i\neq j$ in $F$. Then $\exists f\in\prod\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ such that $f(i)\,R\,f(j)$ for all $i\neq j$ in $I$. Rav [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AI}] Engelers Lemma:\index{Subject}{Engelers lemma} Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a family of functions whose domains are subsets of a set $S$ with range $\subseteq\{0,1\}$ and such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For every finite $F\subseteq S,\,\exists\phi\in \mathcal{E}$ with domain F.
\item[(b)] The restriction of any function in $\mathcal{E}$ to any subset of its domain is in $\mathcal{E}$.
\item[(c)] If $\phi$ is any function with domain $\phi \subseteq S$ such that the restriction of $\phi$ to any finite subset of its domain is in $\mathcal{E}$ then $\phi \in \mathcal{E}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\exists f\in \mathcal{E}$ whose domain is $S$. Rav [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AJ}] Robinson's Valuation Lemma:\index{Subject}{Robinson's valuation lemma} Let $\{\phi_{x}:x\in X\}$ be a family of partial valuations on a set $S$. ($\phi$ is a partial valuation on $S$ if the domain of $\phi\subseteq S$ and the range of $\phi \subseteq\{0,1\}.)$ Suppose $\mathfrak{B}$ is a filter base on $X$ such that for every finite $F\subseteq S$ and for every $B\in \mathfrak{B}$ there is $x\in B$ such that $F\subseteq\ \mathrm{dom}\ \phi_{x}$. Then there is a total valuation $f$ on $S$ (that is, $\mathrm{dom}\,f=S$) such that for all finite $F\subseteq S$ and all $B\in \mathfrak{B},\,\exists x\in B$ such that $F\subseteq\ \mathrm{dom}\,\phi_{x}$ and $f|F=\phi_{x}|F$. ($\mathfrak{B}$ is a filter base means $\forall B_{1},\,B_{2}\in \mathfrak{B},\,\exists B_{3}\in \mathfrak{B}$ such that $B_{3}\subseteq B_{1}\cap B_{2}$.) Rav [\textbf{1977}] and Cowen [\textbf{1973}]. Compare with [14 I].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AK}] Let $X$ be a set and $\mathcal{D}=\{Y_{i}:i\in I\}$ a family of finite pairwise disjoint subsets of $\mathcal{P}(X)$. Suppose for every finite subset $\{a,\,b,\,\ldots,\,k\}$ of $I,\,\exists s\in I$ such that $Y_{s}\subseteq Y_{a}\wedge Y_{b}\wedge\ldots\wedge Y_{k}$ (If $Y$ and $Z$ are finite pairwise disjoint sets then $Y\wedge Z= \{A \cap B:A\in Y\ \mathrm{and}\ B\in Z\ \mathrm{and}\ A \cap B\neq\emptyset\}$.) Then there is a choice function $\mu$ whose domain includes $\mathcal{D}$ such that the family $\{\mu(Y_{i}):i\in I\}$ (where $\mu(Y_{i})\in Y_{i})$ of subsets of $X$ is closed under finite intersections. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AP}] Suppose to each finite subset $F$ of a set I there corresponds a set $\Phi(F)$ of functions whose domains are subsets of $I$ including $F$ and such that (a) $F_{1}\subseteq F_{2}$ implies $\Phi(F_{2})\subseteq\Phi(F_{2})$ and (b) $\forall i\in I,\,\{\phi(i):\phi\in\bigcup\{\Phi(F):F$ finite and $F\subseteq I\}\big\}$ is finite. Then there is a function $f$ with domain $I$ such that for all finite $F\subseteq I,\,\exists\phi\in\Phi(F)$ such that $\phi$ and $f$ coincide on F. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}], Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1973}] and note 80.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AQ}] Strong Rado Lemma 1: Let $T$ be a family of finite sets and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a collection of finite subsets of $T$ satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $(\forall K\in T)(\exists S\in \mathcal{F})(K\in S)$
\item[(2)] $(\forall S_{1},\,S_{2}\in \mathcal{F})(\exists S_{3}\in \mathcal{F})(S_{1}\cup S_{2}\subseteq S_{3})$
\end{enumerate}
Assume there is a function $\phi$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ such that for each $S\in \mathcal{F},\,\phi(S)= \phi_{S}$ is a function with domain $S$ and satisfies $(\forall K\in S)(\phi_{S}(K)\in K)$. Then there is a function $f$ with domain $T$ and with the following property: For all $S\in \mathcal{F}$ there is an $S^{\prime}\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $S\subseteq S^{\prime}$ and $f$ and $\phi_{S^{\prime}}$ agree on $S$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} [\textbf{1993}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AR}] Patching Lemma:\index{Subject}{patching lemma} Let $L$ be a local system of $S$ (that is, $L\subseteq \mathcal{P}(S)$ and for each finite $E\subseteq S$, there exists $H\in L$ such that $E\subseteq H$). Let $F$ be a set and $n$ a positive integer. Suppose that for each $H\in L$, there is a function $f_{H}:H^{n}\rightarrow F$ and $\{f_{H}(x):H\in L\}$ is finite for each $x\in S^{n}$. Then there is a function $f:S^{n}\rightarrow F$ such that for any finite subset $K\subseteq S^{n}$, there is an $H\in L$ with $K\subseteq H^{n}$ and $f$ and $f_{H}$ agree on K. Hickin/Plotkin\index{Author}{Hickin/Plotkin} [\textbf{1976}] and note 83.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AY}] Let $F$ be a class of partial functions on $I$ of finite character such that (a) $\{f(\nu):f \in F\}$ is finite for each $\nu\in I$ and (b) for each finite $W \subseteq I$, there exists $f\in F$ with $\mathrm{dom}(f)=W$. Then $F$ contains a function with domain $I$. ($F$ is of finite character means $f\in F$ iff for all finite $\omega\subseteq I,\,f|w\in F$.) Cowen [\textbf{1973}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AZ}] Let $\Phi=\{\phi_{t}\}_{t\in T}$ be a set of partial valuations on a set $S$ (that is, $\mathrm{dom}(\phi_{t})\subseteq S$ and range$(\phi_{t})\subseteq\{0,1\}$) such that for all finite $U\subseteq S$ there is a $t\in T$ for which $U\subseteq\ \mathrm{dom}(\phi_{t})$. Then there is a valuation $\Psi$ with $\mathrm{dom}(\Psi)=S$ and such that for every finite $U\subseteq S$, there is a $t\in T$ with $U\subseteq\, \mathrm{dom}(\phi_{t})$ and $\Psi|U=\phi_{t}|U$. Cowen [\textbf{1973}].

\noindent \textbf{99.} Rado's Selection Lemma:\index{Subject}{Rado's selection lemma} Let $\{K(\lambda):\lambda\in\Lambda\}$ be a family of finite subsets (of $X$) and suppose for each finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$ there is a function $\gamma(S):S\rightarrow X$ such that $(\forall\lambda\in S)(\gamma(S)(\lambda)\in K(\lambda))$. Then there is an $f:\Lambda\rightarrow X$ such that for every finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$ there is a finite $T$ such that $S\subseteq T\subseteq\Lambda$ and such that $f$ and $\gamma(T)$ agree on S. Rado [\textbf{1949}].

\noindent [\textbf{99 A}] Weak Rado Lemma: Let $\Lambda$ be a set. Suppose that $\gamma$ is a function with domain all finite subsets of $\Lambda$ such that for each finite $S\subseteq\Lambda,\,\gamma(S):S\rightarrow\{0,1\}$. Then there is a $\phi$ defined on $\Lambda$ with the property that for every finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$ there is a finite $T\subseteq\Lambda$ such that $S\subseteq T$ and $\gamma(T)$ and $\phi$ agree on $S$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}] and Howard [\textbf{1993}].

\noindent [\textbf{99 B}] Rado's Lemma restricted to families of two element sets: Let $\{k(\lambda):\lambda\in \Lambda\}$ be a family of 2 element subsets of a set $X$ and suppose that for each finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$, there is a function $\gamma(S)$ from $S$ into $X$ such that $(\forall\lambda\in S)(\gamma(S)(\lambda)\in k(\lambda))$. Then there is a function from $\Lambda$ into $X$ such that for every finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$, there is a finite $T$ with $S\subseteq T\subseteq\Lambda$ such that $f$ and $\gamma(T)$ agree on $S$. Rav [\textbf{1977}] and Howard [\textbf{1993}].

\noindent [\textbf{99 C}] Strong Rado Lemma 2: Let $T$ be a family of finite sets and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a collection of finite subsets of $T$ satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $(\forall K\in T)(\exists S\in \mathcal{F})(K\in S)$
\item[(2)] $(\forall S_{1},\,S_{2}\in \mathcal{F})(S_{1}\cup S_{2}\in \mathcal{F})$
\end{enumerate}
Assume there is a function $\phi$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ such that for each $S\in \mathcal{F},\,\phi(S)= \phi_{S}$ is a function with domain $S$ and satisfies $(\forall K\in S)(\phi_{S}(K)\in K)$. Then there is a function $f$ with domain $T$ and with the following property: For all $S\in \mathcal{F}$ there is an $S^{\prime}\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $S\subseteq S^{\prime}$ and $f$ and $\phi_{S^{\prime}}$ agree on $S$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} [\textbf{1993}].

\noindent \textbf{107.} M. Hall's Theorem:\index{Subject}{Hall's theorem} Let $\{S(\alpha):\alpha\in A\}$ be a collection of finite subsets (of a set $X$) then if
\begin{equation*}
\tag{$^{\ast}$} \text{for each finite}\ F\subseteq A\ \text{there is an injective choice function on}\ F
\end{equation*}
then there is an injective choice function on $A$. (That is, a 1-1 function $f$ such that $(\forall\alpha\in A)(f(\alpha)\in S(\alpha))$.) (According to a theorem of P. Hall $(\ast)$ is equivalent to $|\bigcup_{\alpha\in F}S(\alpha)|\geq|F|$. P. Hall's theorem does not require the axiom of choice.) M. Hall\index{Author}{Hall} [\textbf{1948}].

\noindent \textbf{141.} $[14\mathrm{P}(n)]$ with $n=2$: Let $\{A(i):i\in I\}$ be a collection of sets such that $\forall i\in I,\, |A(i)|\leq 2$ and suppose $R$ is a symmetric binary relation on $\bigcup_{i\in I}A(i)$ such that for all finite $W\subseteq I$ there is an $R$ consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in W\}$. Then there is an $R$ consistent choice function for $\{A(i):i\in I\}$. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1977b}] and note 109.

\noindent \textbf{184.} Existence of a double uniformization: For all $X$ and $Y$, for all $E\subseteq X\times Y$, if there is an infinite cardinal $\kappa$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\forall y_{0}\in Y,\,|\{(x,\,y_{0}):x\in X\}\cap E|=\kappa$ and
\item[(2)] $\forall x_{0}\in X,\,|\{(x_{0},\,y):y\in Y\}\cap E|=\kappa$,
\end{enumerate}
then $\exists U\subseteq E$ such that for all $(x,\,y)\in E,\,\exists!z\in X$ such that $(z,\,y)\in U$ and $\exists!z\in Y$ such that $(x,\,z)\in U$. ($U$ is called a \emph{double uniformization}\index{Subject}{double uniformization} of $E$.) Kaniewski/Rogers\index{Author}{Kaniewski/Rogers} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{270 B}] $F_{\mathrm{fin}}$: For any family $\mathcal{F}$ of pairwise disjoint, non-empty, finite sets if $R$ is a symmetric binary relation on $\bigcup \mathcal{F}$ which satisfies (i) the set $\{b\in\bigcup \mathcal{F}:\neg a\,R\,b\}$ is finite for every $a\in\bigcup \mathcal{F}$ and (ii) every finite subfamily of $\mathcal{F}$ has an $R$-consistent choice function, then $\mathcal{F}$ has an $R$-consistent choice function. Kolany/Wojtylak\index{Author}{Kolany/Wojtylak} [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent [\textbf{270 $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{n})$}] $F_{n}^{\mathrm{fin}}$ ($n\geq 3$ a natural number): For any family $\mathcal{F}$ of pairwise disjoint, $n$ element sets if $R$ is a symmetric binary relation on $\bigcup \mathcal{F}$ which satisfies (i) the set $\{b\in\bigcup\,\mathcal{F}:\neg a\,R\,b\}$ is finite for every $a\in\bigcup \mathcal{F}$ and (ii) every finite subfamily of $\mathcal{F}$ has an $R$-consistent choice function, then $\mathcal{F}$ has an $R$-consistent choice function. Kolany\index{Author}{Kolany} [\textbf{1992}].

\textbf{VI. Miscellaneous Choice}

\noindent [\textbf{14 BW}] For every set $E$ there is an ultrafilter choice function on $E$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent \textbf{140.} Let $\Omega$ be the set of all (undirected) infinite cycles of reals (Graphs whose vertices are real numbers, connected, no loops and each vertex adjacent to exactly two others). Then there is a function $f$ on $\Omega$ such that for all $s\in\Omega,\,f(s)$ is a direction along $s$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent [\textbf{170 A}]\index{Author}{Taskovi\'{c}} There is a function that assigns to each denumerable set $D$ of real numbers a real number not in $D$. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1954}].

\noindent \textbf{269.} For every cardinal $m$, there is a set $A$ such that $2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m$ and there is a choice function on the collection of 2-element subsets of $A$. Lampe\index{Author}{Lampe} \cite{bib:1974m}.

\section*{FIXED POINT THEOREMS}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ J}] Zermelo's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Zermelo's fixed point theorem} For every partially ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$, if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}], Zermelo\index{Author}{Zermelo} [\textbf{1908b}] and Abian\index{Author}{Abian} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ K}] For all partially ordered sets $(X,\,\leq)$, if there is a sup function $\sigma$ on the well ordered subsets of $X$ then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ L}] Caristi's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Caristi's fixed point theorem} If $(X,\,\rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering $(x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\, p(x,\,y)\leq\phi(y)-\phi(x))$ every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Caristi\index{Author}{Caristi} [\textbf{1976}], Manka [\textbf{1988a}], and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AI}] Turinici's Fixed Point Theorem\index{Subject}{Turinici's fixed point theorem} for Hausdorff Spaces: If $(X, \leq)$ is a directed, partially ordered set and $\tau$ is a Hausdorff topology on $X$ such that

\noindent (a) $(X,\,\leq)$ is upper semi-continuous with respect to $\tau$,

\noindent (b) Every well ordered subset of $(X,\,\leq)$ has a unique limit as a net, then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,x\leq f(x)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988b}] and note~38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 V}] For every partially ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$, if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and Abian [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AJ}] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of mappings of a poset $(X,\,\leq)$ into itself such that $\forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x$. If for some element $e$ of $X$ each chain in $X$ containing $e$ has a lower bound, then the family $\mathcal{F}$ has a common fixed point. Kasahara\index{Author}{Kasahara} [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AS}] Turinici's Fixed Point Theorem: If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a directed, partially ordered set and $\tau$ is a topology on $X$ such that

\noindent (a) $(X,\,\leq)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to $\tau$,

\noindent (b) Every well ordered subset of $(X,\,\leq)$ is convergent as a net, then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,x\leq f(x)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988b}] and note~38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BC}] Assume $P$ is a partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound and $f:P\rightarrow P$ satisfies $\forall x\in f(P)\cup\{a\in P: a\ \text{is an upper bound for some chain in}\ f(P)\},\, x\leq f(f(x))$. Then $f$ has a fixed apex $u$ (that is, there is some $v\in P$ such that $f(u)=v$ and $f(v)=u$.). Taskovi\'{c} [\textbf{1988}], [\textbf{1992a}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 BD}] Let $P$ be a partially ordered set in which every increasing sequence has an upper bound and $f:P\rightarrow P$ satisfies $x\leq f(f(x))$ for all $x\in f(P)\cup\{x\in P:x$ is an upper bound for some increasing sequence in $f(P)\}$. Then $f$ has a fixed apex $u$ (that is, $\exists v\in P$, such that $f(u)=v$ and $f(v) =u$). (For purposes of [1 BD], ``sequence'' means a function whose domain is an ordinal.) Taskovi\'{c}\index{Author}{Taskovi\'{c}} [\textbf{1992b}].

\noindent \textbf{285.} Let $E$ be a set and $f:E\rightarrow E$, then $f$ has a fixed point if and only if $E$ is not the union of three mutually disjoint sets $E_{1},\,E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$ such that $E_{i}\cap f(E_{i})=\emptyset$ for $i=1,2,3$. Makowski/Wi\'{s}niewski\index{Author}{Makowski/Wisniewski@Makowski/Wi\'{s}niewski} [\textbf{1969}], Abian\index{Author}{Abian} [\textbf{1968}], Baker\index{Author}{Baker} [\textbf{1964}], and Kenyon\index{Author}{Kenyon} [\textbf{1963}].

\noindent \textbf{316.} If a linearly ordered set $(A,\,\leq)$ has the fixed point property then $(A,\,\leq)$ is complete. ($(A,\,\leq)$ has the \emph{fixed point property} if every function $f:A\rightarrow A$ satisfying $(x\leq y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)$) has a fixed point, and ($(A,\,\leq)$ is \emph{complete} if every subset of $A$ has a least upper bound.) H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} [\textbf{1994}].

\section*{GRAPH THEORETIC FORMS}

\noindent [\textbf{1 AT}] For all cardinal numbers $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$, if a graph is both $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ colorable then it is also $\kappa$ colorable for some $\kappa$ such that $\kappa \leq^{\ast}\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa \leq^{\ast}n_{2}$. ($\leq^{\ast}$ is the surjective cardinal ordering). Galvin/Komj\'{a}th\index{Author}{Galvin/Komjath@Galvin/Komj\'{a}th} [\textbf{1991}] and note 118.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AU}] Every graph has an irreducible, good coloring. Galvin/Komj\'{a}th [\textbf{1991}] and note 118.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AV}] Every graph of the form $G(A,\,H(A))$ has an irreducible, good coloring. ($H$ is the Hartogs aleph function.) Galvin/Komj\'{a}th [\textbf{1991}] and note 118.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AW}] Every graph has a chromatic number. Galvin/Komj\'{a}th [\textbf{1991}] and note 118.

\noindent [\textbf{14} $\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{n})$] $(n\in \omega,\,n\geq 3)\,P_{n}$: For every graph $G$ if every finite subgraph of $G$ is $n$-colorable then $G$ is $n$-colorable. L\"{a}uchli\index{Author}{Lauchli@L\"{a}uchli} [\textbf{1971}] and note 117.

\noindent [\textbf{14 M}] R. Cowen's Generalization of Konig's Lemma:\index{Subject}{K\"{o}nig's lemma} Let $T$ be a collection of locally finite trees such that for any finite set of levels of $T$, there is a consistent set of vertices piercing those levels. Then there is a consistent set of vertices piercing the entire set of levels of T. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1977b}] and note 21.

\noindent [\textbf{14} $\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{n})$] $(n\in\omega,\, n\geq 2)$ [14 M] restricted to families of trees where no tree in the family has a vertex with more than $n$ successors. Cowen [\textbf{1977b}], Howard\index{Author}{Howard} [\textbf{1984a}], and note 21.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BD}] Let $H$ be a hypergraph. If every finite subhypergraph has an independent vertex cover then $H$ has an independent vertex cover. Cowen [\textbf{1990}] and note 117.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BE}] Let $H$ be a hypergraph. If every finite subhypergraph is 2-colorable then $H$ is 2-colorable. Cowen [\textbf{1990}] and note 117.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BF}] Let $H$ be a hypergraph whose edges contain at most three vertices. If every finite subhypergraph of $H$ has an independent vertex cover then $H$ has an independent vertex cover. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1990}] and note 117.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BG}] Let $H$ be a hypergraph whose edges contain at most three vertices.
If every finite subhypergraph of $H$ is 2-colorable then $H$ is 2-colorable. Cowen [\textbf{1990}] and note~117.

\noindent [\textbf{88 B}] $G_{2}$: A graph is 2-colorable if every finite subgraph is 2-colorable. Mycielski\index{Author}{Mycielski} [\textbf{1961}] and note 117.

\section*{LOGIC (FORMS FROM LOGIC)}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AA}] $CT_{1}$: Restricted Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic I: If $\Sigma$
is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable and if each propositional variable occurs in at most one formula in $\Sigma$, then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable. Kolany/Wojtylak\index{Author}{Kolany/Wojtylak} [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 J}] Let $S$ be a denumerable set of propositional sentences over an infinite set of propositional letters (in a propositional language where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then $S$ has a model if and only if every finite subset of $S$ has a model. Lolli\index{Author}{Lolli} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 K}] Let $S$ be a consistent denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences). Then $S$ has a model. Note 19.

\noindent [\textbf{10 L}] Let $S$ be a denumerable set of sentences in a first order language (where
conjunction and disjunction are operators on unordered finite sets of sentences)
such that every finite subset has a model. Then $S$ has a model. Note 19.

\noindent [\textbf{14 H}] Compactness Theorem for First Order Logic: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas
in a first order language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ has a model then $\Sigma$ has a model. Henkin\index{Author}{Henkin} [\textbf{1954a}] and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 17.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AW}] The Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable, then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable. Henkin [\textbf{1954b}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AX}] Structural Completeness Theorem for Propositional Logic: Assume \emph{At} is a set of propositional variables and $S$ is the set of propositional formulas generated by \emph{At}. Assume $X \subseteq S$ and $a\in S$ satisfy the following: For any function $e : At \rightarrow S$ if $Cn(\{b[e] : b \in X\}) \subseteq\ Cn(\emptyset)$ then $a[e] \in Cn(\emptyset)$. Then $a\in Cn(X)$. ($Cn(Y)$ is the deductive closure of $Y\cup$ all substitutions of axioms for the classical predicate calculus and for $a\in S,\, a[e]$ is $a$ with each propositional variable $p$ replaced by $e(p)$.) Pogorzelski/Prucnal\index{Author}{Pogorzelski/Prucnal} [\textbf{1974}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 CI}] 3-Sat: Restricted Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic II: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable and if every formula in $\Sigma$ is a disjunction of at most three literals, then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable. (A \emph{literal} is a propositional variable or its negation.) Cowen [\textbf{1990}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 CJ}] The Completeness Theorem for Propositional Logic: Every consistent set of formulas is satisfiable. Henkin [\textbf{1954a}] and [\textbf{1954b}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 CK}] The Completeness Theorem for First Order Logic: Every consistent set of formulas is satisfiable. Henkin [\textbf{1954a}] and [\textbf{1954b}].

\noindent \textbf{42.} L\"{o}wenheim-Skolem Theorem:\index{Subject}{L\"{o}wenheim-Skolem theorem} If a countable family of first order sentences
is satisfiable in a set $M$ then it is satisfiable in a countable subset of $M$. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] p~251.

\noindent [\textbf{43 B}] Countable Henkin Principle:\index{Subject}{Henkin principle} Let $\Phi$ be the class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus. Let $I$ be a countable set of inferences, and $\Gamma$ a consistent subset of $\Phi$ such that $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}$ respects $I$ for each $\psi\in\Phi$. Then for any $\phi\in\Phi$, if $\phi$ is consistent with $\Gamma$ then $\Gamma$ has a finitely consistent extension that contains $\phi$ and decides $I$. Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985m} and note.

\noindent [\textbf{43 P}] The ultraproduct of a well founded structure by a countably complete ultrafilter is well founded. Spector\index{Author}{Spector} [\textbf{1980}] and note 54.

\noindent \textbf{253.} Lo\'{s}' Theorem:\index{Subject}{{\L}os' theorem}
 If $M = \langle A,R_{j}\rangle _{j\in J}$ is a relational system, $X$ any set and $\mathcal{F}$ an ultrafilter in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ then $M$ and $M^{X}/\mathcal{F}$ are elementarily equivalent.
Howard\index{Author}{Howard} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{270.} $CT_{\mathrm{fin}}$: The compactness theorem for propositional logic restricted to sets
of formulas in which each variable occurs only in a finite number of formulas.
Kolany/Wojtylak\index{Author}{Kolany/Wojtylak}\index{Author}{Wojtylak} [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent [\textbf{270 A}] $C(\infty, < \aleph_{0})\wedge CT_{2}$ ($CT_{2}$ is the compactness theorem for propositional logic restricted to sets of formulas in which each variable occurs in at most two formulas. See form 271($n$).) Kolany/Wojtylak [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{271 ($n$).} If $n\in\omega -\{0,1\}, CT_{n}$: The compactness theorem for propositional logic restricted to sets of formulas in which each variable occurs in at most $n$ formulas. Kolany/Wojtylak [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{326.} 2-SAT: Restricted Compactness Theorem for Propositional Logic III: If $\Sigma$ is a set of formulas in a propositional language such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable and if every formula in $\Sigma$ is a disjunction of at most two literals, then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable. (A \emph{literal} is a propositional variable or its negation.) Wojtylak [\textbf{1995}].

\section*{MAXIMAL PRINCIPLES}

\noindent [\textbf{1 B}] Every commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 M}] The ramification Lemma:\index{Subject}{ramification lemma} If $S: X^{\leq\theta}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E)$ is a ramification system, then for each $g\in E$ there is an $f$ which is maximal (with respect to inclusion) in $\{h\in X^{\leq\theta} : g\in S(h)\}$. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1989}] and note 22.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AN}] Every lattice $\langle L,\cap,\cup,\subseteq\rangle$ of sets (that is, $L$ is a family of sets and $\cap,\,\cup$
and $\subseteq$ are the usual operations) with a greatest element has a maximal, proper ideal. Bell/Fremlin\index{Author}{Bell/Fremlin} [\textbf{1972}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 BA}] (Depends on the prime $p$) Every group has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1987}] and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BI}] $(\mathrm{M}T_{0})$: Every topological space has a maximal $T_{0}$ subspace. Schnare\index{Author}{Schnare} [\textbf{1968}] and note 106.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BO}] For every $T_{1}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ and every base (subbase) $B$ for $X$ there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal cellular family $Q\subseteq B$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BT}] For every Boolean ring $(B,+,\cdot)$ and every $H\subseteq B$ which is closed under + there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal ideal $Q\subseteq B$ such that $H\cap Q = \{0\}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996c1}.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CD}] In a commutative ring, every proper ideal can be extended to a maximal ideal. Krull\index{Author}{Krull} [\textbf{1929}]. ([1 CD] implies [1 B]).

\noindent [\textbf{14 A}] Ultrafilter Theorem: Every proper filter over a set $S$ (in $\mathcal{P}(S)$) can be extended to an ultrafilter. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 17.

\noindent [\textbf{14 E}] Almost Maximal Ideal Theorem: Every bounded, non-trivial, distributive lattice has an almost maximal ideal. (Definitions: If $D$ is a bounded non-trivial distributive lattice, $I(D)$ is the lattice of ideals of $D$. An \emph{almost maximal ideal} in $D$ is an ideal $P$ of $D$ such that $s(P) = P$ where s is the operation on $I(D)$ defined as follows: If $e$ is the unit of $I(D)$, (i) For $a \in I(D)$ we say $x \in I(D)$ is \emph{a-small} if $x \vee b = e$ implies $a \vee b = e$ for all $b \in I(D)$. (ii) For any $a\in I(D), s(a)$ is the join of all a-small elements of $I(D)$). Banaschewski/Harting\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Harting} [\textbf{1985}] and Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1986}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 T}] Every regular commutative ring with unit has a maximal ideal. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} [\textbf{1983}] and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 U}] Every closed proper ideal in a Gelfand algebra is contained in some maximal ideal. Banaschewski [\textbf{1983}] and note 29.

\noindent [\textbf{14 V}] FIP Extension Principle:\index{Subject}{FIP extension principle} Let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^{X}$ have the finite intersection property, then $\mathcal{F}\subseteq U$ for some ultrafilter $U$ on $X$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 BV}] For every set $E$ there is an effectively $E$-adequate ultrafilter. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}, \cite{bib:1985p} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BW}] For every set $E$ there is an ultrafilter choice function on $E$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BX}] If $(E_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of sets and $(F_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family such that for each $i, F_{i}$ is a filter in $\mathcal{P}(E_{i})$ then there is a family $(U_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for each $i\in I,\,U_{i}$ is an ultrafilter in $\mathcal{P}(E_{i})$ containing $F_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1985p}, \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BY}] For every topological space X, every proper ideal in the normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra of continuous bounded functions from $X$ into $\mathbb{R}$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BZ}] Every proper ideal in a non-trivial normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra or $\mathbb{C}$-algebra with identity is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CA}] If $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of non trivial commutative normed algebras with identity then there is a family $(J_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that for each $i\in I, J_{i}$ is a maximal ideal in $A_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CB}] If $X$ is a topological space and $I$ is a proper ideal in the algebra of all bounded continuous functions from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that every function in $I$ vanishes at at least one point of $X$ then $I$ is contained in a maximal ideal.
Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{30 G}] Weak Hausdorff Lemma:\index{Subject}{Hausdorff lemma} For every set $X$, every $\subseteq$-chain in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is contained in a maximal $\subseteq$-chain. Note~130.
