\noindent [\textbf{43 L}] $Z_{\omega}$: If every chain in a partially ordered set $P$ is finite, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1948}], Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} [\textbf{1983}], and note 54.

\noindent [\textbf{43 M}] If $(X, \rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi : X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering, $(x < y\ \mathrm{iff}\ \rho(x, y)\leq
\phi(y)-\phi(x))$, there is a maximal element. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1987a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{50 I}] If $A$ is a subalgebra of a Boolean algebra $B$, then there is a $\subseteq$-maximal proper filter $F$ in $B$ such that $F\cap A =\{1\}$. Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b}

\noindent [\textbf{51 B}] $Z(L,\,W)$: Every non-empty linearly ordered set in which every well
ordered subset has an upper bound has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin\index{Author}{Harper/Rubin}
[\textbf{1976}], Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}], H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q} p 37 $M1(L,\,W)$, and note 39.

\noindent [\textbf{62 C}] For every prime $p$, if $\{G_{y}: y\in Y\}$ is a set of finite groups, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y \in Y} G_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1987}] and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{62 D}] For every prime $p$, if $Y$ is a set of non-empty, finite sets, then the weak direct product $\prod _{y\in Y} S_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. ($S_{y}$ is the symmetric group on $y$.) Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1987}] and note 24.

\noindent \textbf{63.} $SPI$: Weak ultrafilter principle: Every infinite set has a non-trivial ultrafilter. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 172 prob 8.5.

\noindent \textbf{70.} There is a non-trivial ultrafilter on $\omega$. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} prob 5.24.

\noindent [\textbf{70 A}] Every Dedekind infinite set has a non-principal ultrafilter.

\noindent [\textbf{87 A($\alpha$)}] $Z_{\aleph_{\alpha}}$: Let $P$ be a partially ordered set in which every well ordered chain has type $<\aleph_{\alpha}$. If every well ordered chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} [\textbf{1983}].

\noindent [\textbf{87 B($\alpha$)}] $Z_{\aleph_{\alpha}}^{\ast}$: Let $P$ be a well-founded partially ordered set (that is, every
chain in $P$ is well ordered.) in which every chain has type $<\aleph_{\alpha}$. If every chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Wolk [\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{89.} Antichain Principle: Every partially ordered set has a maximal antichain. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 133 and Kurepa\index{Author}{Kurepa} [\textbf{1953}].

\noindent [\textbf{89 A}] If $\forall y\in X, y = \langle u,R\rangle$ where $R$ is a partial order on $u$ then there is a function $f$ on $X$ such that $\forall\langle u, R\rangle \in X, f(\langle u,R\rangle)$ is a maximal antichain in $u$. Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} [\textbf{1969}] and Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent \textbf{123.} $SPI^{\ast}$: Uniform weak ultrafilter principle: For each family $F$ of infinite sets $\exists f$ such that $\forall x \in F, f(x)$ is a non-principal ultrafilter on $x$. Halpern\index{Author}{Halpern} [\textbf{1972}]

\noindent \textbf{143.} $H(C,TR)$: If $(X,\,R)$ is a connected relation$ (u\neq v\rightarrow u\,R\,v\ \mathrm{or}\ v\,R\,u)$
then $X$ contains a $\subseteq$-maximal transitive subset. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{201.} Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras:\index{Subject}{linking axiom} Every Boolean algebra has a maximal linked system. ($L \subseteq B$ is \emph{linked} if $a \wedge b\neq 0$ for all $a$ and $b\in L$.) Schrijver\index{Author}{Schrijver} \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent [\textbf{201 A}] Strong Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras: Each linked system in a
Boolean algebra is contained in some maximal linked system. (If $B$ is a Boolean algebra, $L\subseteq B$ is \emph{linked} if $a\wedge b\neq 0$ for all $a$ and $b\in L$.) Schrijver\index{Author}{Schrijver} \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent [\textbf{202 A}] $H(TR\&C,P)$: If $(X,\,R)$ is a transitive, connected relation. Then $X$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin\index{Author}{Harper/Rubin} [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{206.} The existence of a non-principal ultrafilter: There exists an infinite set $X$ and a non-principal ultrafilter on $X$. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1977b}].

\noindent \textbf{225.} Every proper filter on $\omega$ can be extended to an ultrafilter. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent \textbf{244.} Every principal ideal domain has a maximal ideal. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} [\textbf{1976a}] and
note 84.

\noindent \textbf{254.} $Z(D, P, l)$: Every directed relation $(P, R)$ in which ramified subsets have
least upper bounds, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note
39.

\noindent \textbf{255.} $Z(D, R)$: Every directed relation $(P,\,R)$ in which every ramified subset $A$ has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{256.} $Z(P,F)$: Every partially ordered set $(X,\,R)$ in which every forest $A$ has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{257.} $Z(TR,\,P)$: Every transitive relation $(X,\,R)$ in which every partially ordered subset has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{258.} $Z(D,\,L)$: Every directed relation $(X,\,R)$ in which linearly ordered subsets have upper bounds, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{259.} $Z(TR\&C, W)$: If $(X,\,R)$ is a transitive and connected relation in which every well ordered subset has an upper bound, then $(X,\,R)$ has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{260.} $Z(TR\&C,P)$: If $(X,\,R)$ is a transitive and connected relation in which every partially ordered subset has an upper bound, then $(X,\,R)$ has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{261.} $Z(TR,\,T)$: Every transitive relation $(X,\,R)$ in which every subset which is a tree has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{262.} $Z(TR,\,R)$: Every transitive relation $(X, R)$ in which every ramified subset $A$ has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{263.} $H(AS\&C,P)$: Every every relation $(X,\,R)$ which is antisymmetric and connected contains a $\subseteq$-maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{264.} $H(C, P)$: Every connected relation $(X,\,R)$ contains a $\subseteq$-maximal partially ordered set. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{265.} $H(A,\,TR)$: Every relation $(X,\,R)$ contains a $\subseteq$-maximal transitive subset. Harper/Rubin [\textbf{1976}] and note~39.

\noindent \textbf{266.} $H(AS,\,P)$: Every antisymmetric relation contains $\subseteq$-maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin\index{Author}{Harper/Rubin} [\textbf{1976}] and note 39.

\noindent \textbf{278.} In an integral domain $R$, if every ideal is finitely generated then $R$ has a maximal proper ideal. Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} [\textbf{1974}] and note 45 E.

\noindent \textbf{289.} If $S$ is a set of subsets of a countable set and $S$ is closed under chain unions, then $S$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element. Smullyan\index{Author}{Smullyan} [\textbf{1994}] and note 102.

\noindent \textbf{303.} If $B$ is a Boolean algebra, $S\subseteq B$ and $S$ is closed under $\wedge$, then there is a $\subseteq$-maximal proper ideal $I$ of $B$ such that $I \cap S =\{0\}$. H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}.

\noindent \textbf{308($p$).} If $p$ is a prime and if $\{G_{y}:y\in Y\}$ is a set of finite groups, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}G_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. Howard/Yorke [\textbf{1987}] and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{308 A($p$)}] If $p$ is a prime and if $Y$ is a set of non-empty, finite sets, then the weak direct product $\prod_{y\in Y}S_{y}$ has a maximal $p$-subgroup. $(S_{y}$ is the symmetric group on $y$.) Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} [\textbf{1987}] and note 24.

\noindent [\textbf{317 A}] If $B$ is a complete, well orderable Boolean algebra and $A$ is a Boolean algebra of which $B$ is a subalgebra, then there is an ideal $I$ of $A$ satisfying $I\cap B =\{0\}$ and $I$ is maximal among those ideals $J$ of $A$ satisfying $J\cap B=\{0\}$. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973h}.

\noindent \textbf{345.} Rasiowa-Sikorski Axiom:\index{Subject}{Rasiowa-Sikorski axiom} If $(B,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a Boolean algebra, $a$ is a non-zero element of $B$, and $\{X_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ is a denumerable set of subsets of $B$ then there is a maximal prime filter $F$ of $B$ such that $a\in F$ and for each $n\in\omega$, if $X_{n}\subseteq F$ and $\bigwedge X_{n}$ exists then $\bigwedge X_{n}\in F$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}.

\section*{MEASURES (FORMS INVOLVING MEASURES ON SETS)}

\noindent [\textbf{14 AV}] Every Boolean algebra has a 2-valued measure. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c1} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BC}] If $m_{0}$ is an additive, real valued measure on a subalgebra $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$ then there exists a measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m=m_{0}$ on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ and the range of $m$ is contained in the closure of the range of $m_{0}$. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1930} and note 147.

\noindent \textbf{37.} Lebesgue measure is countably additive. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1916}].

\noindent [\textbf{52 A}] On every Boolean algebra there is an additive real valued measure. Luxemburg\index{Author}{Luxemburg} \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 B}] For every proper filter $\mathcal{F}$ of elements of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$, there exists an additive, real valued measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m(x)=1$ for all $x\in \mathcal{F}$. Luxemburg \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 C}] For every non-empty set X and every proper ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ there is a measure $m$ on $\mathcal{P}(X)$ such that $m(x)=0$ for all $x\in \mathcal{I}$. Luxemburg \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{52 D}] Let $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ be a subalgebra of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$ and $m_{0}$ an additive, real valued measure on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$. Then there is a real valued, additive measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ such that $m=m_{0}$ on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ and the range of $m$ is contained in the closed convex hull of the range of $m_{0}$. Luxemburg\index{Author}{Luxemburg} \cite{bib:1969d} and note 147.

\noindent [\textbf{70 C}] There is a 2-valued measure on $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c1} and note 147.

\noindent \textbf{93.} There is a non-measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{221.} For all infinite $X$, there is a non-principal measure on $\mathcal{P}(X)$. Pincus/Solovay [\textbf{1977}] and note 147.

\noindent \textbf{222.} There is a non-principal measure on $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$. Pincus/Solovay\index{Author}{Pincus/Solovay} [\textbf{1977}] and note 147.

\noindent \textbf{223.} There is an infinite set $X$ and a non-principal measure on $\mathcal{P}(X)$. Pincus/Solovay [\textbf{1977}] and note 147.

\noindent \textbf{310.} The Measure Extension Theorem: Suppose that $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ is a subring (that is, $a,\,b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}\rightarrow a\vee b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}$ and $a-b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}$) of a Boolean algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mu$ is a measure on $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ (that is, $\mu\,:\,\mathcal{A}\rightarrow[0,\,\infty],\,\mu(a\vee b)=\mu(a)+\mu(b)$ for $a\wedge b=0$, and $\mu(0)=0$.) then there is a measure on $\mathcal{A}$ that extends $\mu$. Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{311.} Abelian groups are amenable. ($G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.) Wagon~{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{312.} A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable. ($G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.) Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent \textbf{313.} $\mathbb{Z}$ (the set of integers under addition) is amenable. ($G$ is \emph{amenable} if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$.) Wagon \cite{bib:1985u}.

\noindent [\textbf{370 A}] Measured Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem: If $\mathcal{B}$ is a Boolean algebra and there is a measure on $\mathcal{B}$ then there is an ultrafilter on $\mathcal{B}$. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1989r}, \cite{bib:1990e} and note~147.

\section*{MISCELLANEOUS FORMS}

\textbf{0.} $0=0$.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ T}] If a set $S$ is hereditarily countable\index{Subject}{hereditarily countable set} (that is, every $y\in TC(S)$ is countable) then the rank of $S$ is $<\omega_{2}$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AD}] For all ordinals $\beta$, well ordered cardinals $\gamma\geq 1$ and all $n\in \omega$, there is a well ordered cardinal $\kappa$ such that $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{n}$. Erd\"{o}s/Rado\index{Author}{Erdos/Rado@Erd\"{o}s/Rado} [\textbf{1952}] and note 97.

\noindent [\textbf{1 G}] Form $163+$ form 8. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982a}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{1 H}] Form $164+$ form 67. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{1 L}] Hajrial's Free Set Principle:\index{Subject}{Hajnal's free set principle} For every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{<\lambda}$ where $\lambda$ is a well orderable cardinal and $\lambda<|X|$ there is a free set of cardinality $|X|.\, ([X]^{<\lambda}$ is the set of subsets of $X$ of cardinality $<\lambda$. Brunner [\textbf{1989}] and note 22.

\noindent [\textbf{1 M}] The ramification Lemma:\index{Subject}{ramification lemma} If $S:X^{\leq\theta}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E)$ is a ramification system, then for each $g\in E$ there is an $f$ which is maximal (with respect to inclusion) in $\{h\in X^{\leq\theta}:g\in S(h)\}$. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1989}] and note 22.

\noindent [\textbf{1 N}] For every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{WO}$ (well ordered subsets of $X$) there is a co-well-orderable free subset $H$. ($H$ is \emph{co-well-orderable} if $X\backslash H$ is well orderable). Brunner [\textbf{1989}] and note 22.

\noindent [\textbf{1 W}] Form 133 + form 88. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 X}] Form 15 + form 91. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 Y}] Refined Dual Cantor-Bernstein Theorem:\index{Subject}{Cantor-Bernstein theorem} If $f:X\rightarrow Y$ and $g:Y\rightarrow X$ are onto then there is a bijection $h:X\rightarrow Y$ such that $h\subseteq f\cup g^{-1}$. Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AA}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $f$ is surjective and $R\subseteq S$. Then every mapping $g$ of $S$ into $R$ has the form $g=f\circ h$ for some $h:S\rightarrow S$. Smith [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AB}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $f$ is surjective and $R\subseteq S$. Then the mappings of $S$ onto $R$ are precisely the mappings of the form $f\circ h$ where $h:S\rightarrow S$ and $(\forall y\in R)(\exists x\in S)(h(x)\in f^{-1}(\{y\}))$. Smith\index{Author}{Smith} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AC}] Assume $f:S\rightarrow R$ where $R\subseteq S$. Then the retractions of $S$ onto $R$ (that is, the mappings $g\,:\,S\rightarrow R$ which are the identity on $R$) are precisely the mappings $f\circ h$ where $h:S\rightarrow S$ and $(\forall y\in R)(h(y)\in f^{-1}(\{y\}))$. Smith [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AE}] There is a set $S$ such that $SVC$ holds with $S$ and such that $\mathcal{P}(S)-\{\emptyset\}$ has a choice function. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}] and note 59. Also see form 191.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AF}] Form 191 + form 8 + form 193. Blass [\textbf{1979}] and note 60.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AG}] Form 192 + form 191. Blass [\textbf{1979}] and note 60.

\noindent \textbf{4.} Every infinite set is the union of some disjoint family of denumerable subsets. (Denumerable means $\cong\aleph_{0}$.) Whitehead\index{Author}{Whitehead} [\textbf{1902}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 C}] Every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{WO}$ on a Dedekind finite, infinite set $X$ has arbitrarily large, finite free subsets. Brunner [\textbf{1989}], notes 22 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{14 I}] Consistency Principle:\index{Subject}{consistency principle} For every binary mess $M$ on a set $S$ there is a function $f$ on $S$ which is consistent with $M$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 17 and note 109.

\noindent [\textbf{14 X}] Cowen-Engler Lemma:\index{Subject}{Cowen-Engler lemma} Let $\Lambda$ and $X$ be sets. Let $\Phi$ be a family of functions from subsets of $\Lambda$ into $X$. Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\Phi(\lambda)=\{f(\lambda): f\in\Phi\ \mathrm{and}\ \lambda\in \mathrm{dom}\ f\}$ is finite for each $\lambda\in\Lambda$,
\item[(b)] each finite $S\subseteq\Lambda$ is the domain of at least one $f\in\Phi$, and
\item[(c)] $\Phi$ has finite character, (that is, a function $f$ from a subset of $\Lambda$ into $X$ is in $\Phi$ if and only if every finite subset of $f$ is in $\Phi$).
\end{enumerate}
Then at least one $f\in\Phi$ has domain $\Lambda$. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}]. (See 14 I.)

\noindent [\textbf{14 AC}] (Depends on $k,\,n\in\omega$ with $k\geq 2,\,n\geq 2$ and $n+k\geq 5$.) $P(k,\,n)$: If $X$ is a set and $P$ is a property of subsets of $X$ of $n$ character (that is, $\forall y\subseteq X(P(y)$ iff $\forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq n\rightarrow P(z)))$), then if every finite subset of $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets (that is, sets $z$ such that $P(z)$) then $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets. Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AD}] (Depends on $k\in\omega,\,k\geq 2$) $P(k)$: If $X$ is a set and $P$ is a property of subsets of $X$ of finite character (that is, $\forall y\subseteq X(P(y)\ \mathrm{iff}\ \forall z\subseteq y(z\ \mathrm{finite}\ \rightarrow P(z)))$), then if every finite subset of $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets (that is, sets $z$ such that $P(z)$), then $X$ can be partitioned into $k$ or fewer $P$-sets. Cowen [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AF}] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,3): If $X$ is a set, $\mathcal{U}$ is a subset of $\{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ is a subset of $\{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 3\}$ and if for each two finite subsets $\mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V}$ there are transversals $Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ for $\mathcal{U}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{0}$ respectively such that $Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset$, then there are disjoint transversals $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ for $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ respectively. ($Y\subseteq X$ is a transversal for $\mathcal{U}$ if for all $y\in \mathcal{U},\, y\cap Y\neq\emptyset$.) Schrijver\index{Author}{Schrijver} \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AT}] Assume $D$ and $E$ are sets and for all $d\in D,\,d$ is finite. Suppose that for every finite $F\subseteq D$, there is an $S$ such that $(\forall f\in F)(f\cap\,S\in E)$. Then there is an $S$ such that $(\forall d\in D)(d\cap\,S\in E)$. van Benthem\index{Author}{Benthem} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 BB}] Fra\"{\i}ss\'{e}'s Theorem:\index{Subject}{Fra\"{i} ss\'{e}'s theorem} Let $\mathcal{E}$ be inductively ordered (that is, for any $E,\,E^{\prime}\in \mathcal{E},\,\exists E^{\prime\prime}\in \mathcal{E}$ such that $E\cup E^{\prime}\subseteq E^{\prime\prime}$.) For any $E\in \mathcal{E}$, assume $\mathcal{R}_{E}$ is a finite set of $m$-ary relations on $E$. If for any $E,\,E^{\prime}\in \mathcal{E}$ with $E\subseteq E^{\prime}$ we have $\forall R\in \mathcal{R}_{E^{\prime}},\,R/E\in \mathcal{R}_{E}$ then there is an $m$-ary relation $S$ on $\bigcup \mathcal{E}$ such that $S|E\in \mathcal{R}_{E}$ for any $E\in \mathcal{E}$. B\'{e}n\'{e}jam\index{Author}{B\'{e}n\'{e}jam} [\textbf{1970}]. See [14 Y].

\noindent [\textbf{14 CF}] A projective limit of a directed projective system of non-empty sets is non-empty. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note~71.

\noindent \textbf{17.} Ramsey's Theorem\index{Subject}{Ramsey's theorem} I: If $A$ is an infinite set and the family of all 2 element subsets of $A$ is partitioned into 2 sets $X$ and $Y$, then there is an infinite subset $B\subseteq A$ such that all 2 element subsets of $B$ belong to $X$ or all 2 element subsets of $B$ belong to $Y$. (Also, see form 325.) Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 164 prob 11.20 and Ramsey\index{Author}{Ramsey} [\textbf{1929}].

\noindent [\textbf{34 A}] $\exists\alpha<\omega_{2}$ such that there are no hereditarily countable sets of rank $\alpha$. Jech [\textbf{1982}] and note 48.

\noindent [\textbf{43 I}] Form [106 A] + form 10. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent [\textbf{43 P}] The ultraproduct of a well founded structure by a countably complete ultrafilter is well founded. Spector\index{Author}{Spector} [\textbf{1980}] and note 54.

\noindent [\textbf{88 A}] $P(2,2)$: If $X$ is a set and $P$ is a property of subsets of $X$ of 2 character (that is, $\forall y\subseteq X(P(y)\ \mathrm{iff}\,\forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq 2\rightarrow P(z)))$) then if every finite subset of $X$ can be partitioned into two or fewer $P$-sets (that is, sets $z$ such that $P(z)$) then $X$ can be partitioned into two or fewer $P$-sets. Cowen [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent [\textbf{126 F}] Every denumerable family of sets having the sfip also has a pseudo-intersection. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{132 A}] Every set mapping $f:X\rightarrow[X]^{WO}$ (well orderable subsets of $X$) on a Dedekind finite, infinite set $X$ has an infinite free subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1989}]. notes 22 and 94.

\noindent \textbf{137($k$).} Suppose $k\in\omega -\{0\}$. If $f$ is a 1-1 map from $k\times X$ into $k\times Y$ then there are partitions $X=\bigcup_{i<k}X_{i}$ and $Y=\bigcup_{i<k}Y_{i}$ of $X$ and $Y$ such that $f$ maps $\bigcup_{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i})\ \mathrm{onto}\ \bigcup_{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i})$. Truss [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent [\textbf{137 A($k$)}] For all $X$ and $Y\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ form 137($k$) holds. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1984}]

\noindent \textbf{138($k$).} Suppose $k\in\omega$. If $f$ is a partial map from $k\times Y$ onto $k\times X$ (that is, the domain is a subset of $k\times Y$), then there are partitions $X= \bigcup_{i<k}X_{i}$ and $Y=\bigcup_{i<k}Y_{i}$ of $X$ and $Y$ such that $f$ maps $\bigcup_{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i})$ onto $\bigcup_{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i})$. Truss [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent [\textbf{138 A($k$)}] For all standard $X$ and $Y$, form 138$(k)$ holds. Truss [\textbf{1984}]. This is equivalent to 138$(k)$ in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

\noindent [\textbf{140 A}] (Form 137 with $k=2$): If $f$ is a 1-1 map from $2\times X$ into $2\times Y$ then there are partitions $X=X_{0}\cup X_{1}$ and $Y=Y_{0}\cup Y_{1}$ of $X$ and $Y$ such that $f$ maps $(\{0\}\times X_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times X_{1})$ onto $(\{0\}\times Y_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times Y_{1})$. Truss [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent \textbf{152.} $D_{\aleph_{0}}$: Every non-well-orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets. Brunner/Howard\index{Author}{Brunner/Howard} [\textbf{1992}]. (See note 27 for $D_{\kappa},\,\kappa$ a well ordered cardinal.)

\noindent \textbf{172.} For every infinite set $S$, if $S$ is hereditarily countable (that is, every $y\in TC(S)$ is countable) then $|TC(S)|=\aleph_{0}$. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} [\textbf{1982}].

\noindent \textbf{179($\epsilon$).} Suppose $\epsilon>0$ is an ordinal. $\forall x,\,x\in W(\epsilon)$. David\index{Author}{David} [\textbf{1980}] and note 25.

\noindent \textbf{184.} Existence of a double uniformization: For all $X$ and $Y$, for all $E\subseteq X\times Y$, if there is an infinite cardinal $\kappa$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\forall y_{0}\in Y,\,|\{(x,\,y_{0}):x\in X\}\cap E|=\kappa$ and
\item[(2)] $\forall x_{0}\in X,\,|\{(x_{0},\,y):y\in Y\}\cap E|=\kappa$,
\end{enumerate}
then $\exists U\subseteq E$ such that for all $(x,\,y)\in E,\,\exists!z\in X$ such that $(z,\,y)\in U$ and $\exists!z\in Y$ such that $(x,\,z)\in U$. ($U$ is called a \emph{double uniformization} of $E$.) Kaniewski/Rogers\index{Author}{Kaniewski/Rogers} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{191.} $SVC$: There is a set $S$ such that for every set $a$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function from $S\times\alpha$ onto $a$. Blass [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent \textbf{192.} $EP$ sets: For every set $A$ there is a projective set $X$ and a function from $X$ onto $A$. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}] and note 60.

\noindent [\textbf{201 B}] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,2): If $X$ is a set and $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ are subsets of $\{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\}$ and if for each two finite subsets $\mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V}$ there are transversals $Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ for $\mathcal{U}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{0}$ respectively such that $Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset$, then there are disjoint transversals $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ for $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ respectively ($Y\subseteq X$ is a \emph{transversal} for $\mathcal{U}$ if for all $y\in CalU,\, y\cap Y\neq\emptyset$.) Schrijver\index{Author}{Schrijver} \cite{bib:1978j}.

\noindent \textbf{230.} $L^{1}=HOD$. Szczepaniak\index{Author}{Szczepaniak} [\textbf{1977}] and note 82.

\noindent \textbf{234.} There is a non-Ramsey set: There is a set $A$ of infinite subsets of $\omega$ such that for every infinite subset $N$ of $\omega,\,N$ has a subset which is in $A$ and a subset which is not in $A$. Prikry\index{Author}{Prikry} [\textbf{1976}] and Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1968}].

\noindent \textbf{282.} $\omega{\not\rightarrow} (\omega)^{\omega}$. Erd\"{o}s/Rado\index{Author}{Erdos/Rado@Erd\"{o}s/Rado} [\textbf{1952}], Kleinberg/Seiferas\index{Author}{Kleinberg/Seiferas} [\textbf{1973}] and note 97.

\noindent \textbf{309.} The Banach-Tarski Paradox: There are three finite partitions $\{P_{1},\,\ldots,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots,\,Q_{r}\}$ and $\{S_{1},\,\ldots,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots,\,T_{r}\}$ of $B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\}$ such that $P_{i}$ is congruent to $S_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and $Q_{i}$ is congruent to $T_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq r$. Banach/Tarski\index{Author}{Banach/Tarski} [\textbf{1924}].

\noindent \textbf{325.} Ramsey's Theorem\index{Subject}{Ramsey's theorem} II: $\forall n,\,m\in \omega$, if\index{Subject}{Banach-Tarski paradox} A is an infinite set and the family of all $m$ element subsets of $A$ is partitioned into $n$ sets $S_{j},\,1\leq j\leq n$, then there is an infinite subset $B\subseteq A$ such that all $m$ element subsets of $B$ belong to the same $S_{j}$. (Also, see form 17.) Ramsey\index{Author}{Ramsey} [\textbf{1929}].

\section*{ORDERING PRINCIPLES INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF PARTIAL ORDERS}

\textbf{I. Linear And Well Orderings}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ Z}] Suppose $X$ and $M$ are sets, $F$ is a function from $\mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset\}$ into $M$ and $G$ is a function on $M$ such that $\forall z\in \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset\},\,G(F(z))\in \mathcal{P}(z)-\{\emptyset\}$. Then there are unique $W$ and $R$ such that $W\subseteq M,\,R\subseteq W\times W$ and $R$ is an irreflexive well ordering of $W$, the range of $G|W$ is a partition of $X$, and $\forall w\in W,\,w=F(X-\,(\bigcup\{G(\nu)\,:\nu\in W\,\mathrm{and}\,\nu\,R\,w\})$). Kruse\index{Author}{Kruse} [\textbf{1974}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AH}] No infinite well orderable set is amorphous.

\noindent [\textbf{1 J}] Form 49 + form 51. Morris\index{Author}{Morris} [\textbf{1969}] and note 121.

\noindent [\textbf{1 K}] Form 133 + form 64. Clear

\noindent [\textbf{8 G}] Let $R$ be a relation and $R^{\ast}$, the transitive closure of $R$. ($x\,R^{\ast}\,y$ iff there exists a finite ascending $R$-chain connecting $x$ to $y$.) If every ascending $R$-chain is finite, then every ascending $R^{\ast}$-chain is finite. Diener\index{Author}{Diener} [\textbf{1994}].

\noindent [\textbf{15 B}] SDO: For any family $X$ of infinite sets, there is a function $f$ with domain $X$ such that $\forall y\in X,\,f(y)$ is a dense linear ordering of $y$. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{15 C}] SUO: For any family $X$ of infinite sets, there is a function $f$ with domain $X$ such that $\forall y\in X,\,f(y)$ is an unbounded linear ordering of $y$. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{15 D}] SDUO: For any family $X$ of infinite sets, there is a function $f$ with domain $X$ such that $\forall y\in X,\,f(y)$ is a dense unbounded linear ordering of $y$. Pincus [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{30.} Ordering Principle:\index{Subject}{ordering principle} Every set can be linearly ordered. Schr\"{o}der\index{Author}{Schroder@Schr\"{o}der} [\textbf{1988}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 A}] If $R$ is a partial ordering in which the set of predecessors of each element is linearly ordered, then there is a linear ordering extending $R$. Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} [\textbf{1969}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 B}] ADO: Every infinite set differs finitely from a set with a dense linear ordering: for all infinite $x$, there is a $y\subseteq x$ such that $y$ has a dense linear ordering and $x-y$ is finite. Pincus [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 C}] SADO: For every set $F$ there is a function $f$ with domain $F$ such that for all $x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x)$ has a dense linear ordering, and $x-f(x)$ is finite, Pincus [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 D}] UO: There exists an unbounded linear ordering on every infinite set. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus~[\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 E}] ADUO: For all infinite $x$, there exists $y\subseteq x$ such that $y$ has a dense unbounded linear ordering and $x-y$ is finite. Pincus [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{30 F}] SADUO: For every set $F$ there is a function $f$ with domain $F$ such that for all $x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x)$ has a dense unbounded linear ordering, and $x-f(x)$ is finite. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{49.} Order Extension Principle:\index{Subject}{order extension principle} Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1924}] p 78.

\noindent \textbf{51.} Cofinality Principle:\index{Subject}{cofinality principle} Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}] p 117.

\noindent [\textbf{51 A}] For all linear orders $(X,\,\leq)$, there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{51 C}] For every linearly ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$, if every well ordered subset of $X$ is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{67 B}] $MW$: Each set can be covered by a well ordered family of finite sets. Levy\index{Author}{Levy} [\textbf{1962}].

\noindent \textbf{77.} A linear ordering of a set $P$ is a well ordering if and only if $P$ has no infinite descending sequences. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 23.

\noindent [\textbf{77 A}] If a linearly ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$ has no greatest element then it has a subset of order type $\omega$. Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{79.} $\mathbb{R}$ can be well ordered. Hilbert\index{Author}{Hilbert} [\textbf{1900}] p 263.

\noindent \textbf{90.} $LW$: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 133 and Felgner/Jech\index{Author}{Felgner/Jech} [\textbf{1973}].

\noindent \textbf{91.} $PW$: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 133 and H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}.

\noindent \textbf{103.} If $(P,\,<)$ is a linear ordering and $|P|>\aleph_{1}$ then some initial segment of $P$ is uncountable. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 164 prob 11.21.

\noindent [\textbf{118 G}] Each complete linear order admits an extreme choice, that is, if $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order then there is a choice function $f$ on the set of non-empty open interval of $X$ with the property that for all $(a,\,b,\,c)\in X^{3}$ with $a<b<c,\,f((a,\,c))\in\{f((a,\,b)),\,b,\,f((b,\,c))\}$. Morillon~[\textbf{1991a}].

\noindent [\textbf{118 H}] For each linear order $(X,\,\leq)$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a strictly increasing injective map $j$ from $(X,\,\leq)$ to $\{0,1\}^{\alpha}$ with the lexicographic order. Morillon [\textbf{1987}].

\noindent [\textbf{118 I}] Every linearly ordered set of linear orders each of which is non-empty and conditionally complete has a choice function. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}, van Douwen\index{Author}{Douwen} [\textbf{1985}], and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 J}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on $X$ is hereditarily normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}, van Douwen [\textbf{1985}], and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 K}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is highly separated. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 L}] If $X$ is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on $X$ is highly separated. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 M}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the family $\{A(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\}$ has a choice function. ($A(a,\,b)$ denotes the set of continuous, order preserving functions from $X$ into $[0,1]$ such that $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=1$.) Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 N}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the family $\{A^{\prime}(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\}$ has a choice function. ($A^{\prime}(a,\,b)$ denotes the set of continuous functions from $X$ into $[0,1]$ such that $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=1.)$ Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 O}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is effectively normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 P}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is effectively normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 Q}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is hereditarily normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 R}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is monotonely normal. Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 S}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order, then there is a choice function $\ast$ for the family of non-empty open intervals of $X$ such that if $a,\,b,\,c\in X$ and either $(a,\,b)\neq\emptyset$ or $(b,\, c)\neq\emptyset$, then $\ast((a,\,c))\in\{\ast((a,\,b)),\,\ast((b,\,c)),\,b,\,b^{+}\}$ (where $b^{+}$ is the successor of $b$ if it exists and $b$ otherwise). Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 T}] Every complete linear order has an increasing choice function. Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent \textbf{129.} For every infinite set $A,\,A$ admits a partition into sets of order type $\omega^{\ast}+\omega$. (For every infinite $A$, there is a set $\{\langle C_{j},\,<j\rangle:j\in J\}$ such that $\{C_{j}:j\in J\}$ is a partition of $A$ and for each $j\in J, <j$ is an ordering of $C_{j}$ of type $\omega^{\ast}+\omega$.) Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984f}].

\noindent \textbf{130.} $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ is well orderable. Brunner [\textbf{1984f}].

\noindent \textbf{133.} Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}].

\noindent \textbf{163.} Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{164.} Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set. Brunner [\textbf{1982a}], notes 42 and 94.

\noindent [\textbf{170 B}] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier\index{Author}{Raisonnier} [\textbf{1982}] and note 3.

\noindent \textbf{185.} Every linearly ordered Dedekind finite set is finite. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} [\textbf{1979a}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{185 A}] If $X$ is a linearly ordered set and there is neither an increasing nor a decreasing injection $f:\omega\rightarrow X$, then $X$ is finite. Hickman [\textbf{1979a}].

\noindent \textbf{198.} For every set $S$, if the only linearly orderable subsets of $S$ are the finite subsets of $S$, then either $S$ is finite or $S$ has an amorphous subset. Hickman [\textbf{1978b}] and note 57.

\noindent \textbf{227.} For all groups $G$, if every finite subgroup of $G$ can be fully ordered then $G$ can be fully ordered. Rav [\textbf{1977}] and note 79.

\noindent \textbf{228.} Every torsion free Abelian group can be fully ordered. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}] and note 79.

\noindent \textbf{229.} If $(G,\,\circ,\,\leq)$ is a partially ordered group, then $\leq$ can be extended to a linear order on $G$ if and only if for every finite set $\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}\subseteq G$, with $a_{i}\neq$ the identity for $i=1$ to $n$, the signs $\epsilon_{1},\,\ldots,\,\epsilon_{n}\,(\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1)$ can be chosen so that $P\cap S(a_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}})=\emptyset$ (where $S(b_{1},\,\ldots,\, b_{n})$ is the normal sub-semi-group of $G$ generated by $b_{1},\,\ldots,\,b_{n}$ and $P=\{g\in G:e\leq g\}$ where $e$ is the identity of $G$.) Rav~[\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{231 A}] Every almost well orderable set ($W$-set) is well orderable. Note 25.

\noindent \textbf{293.} For all sets $x$ and $y$, if $x$ can be linearly ordered and there is a mapping of $x$ onto $y$, then $y$ can be linearly ordered.

\noindent \textbf{294.} Every linearly ordered $W$-set is well orderable. Morris\index{Author}{Morris} [\textbf{1969}] and note 25.

\noindent \textbf{295.} DO: Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering. Gonzalez\index{Author}{Gonzalez} [\textbf{1995a}].

\noindent [\textbf{295 A}] DUO: Every infinite set has a dense unbounded linear ordering. (An ordering is \emph{unbounded} if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent \textbf{316.} If a linearly ordered set $(A,\,\leq)$ has the fixed point property then $(A,\,\leq)$ is complete. ($(A,\,\leq)$ has the \emph{fixed point property} if every function $f:A\rightarrow A$ satisfying $(x\leq y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)$) has a fixed point, and ($(A,\,\leq)$ is \emph{complete} if every subset of $A$ has a least upper bound.) H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} [\textbf{1994}].

\noindent \textbf{377.} Restricted Ordering Principle: For every infinite set $X$ there is an infinite subset $Y$ of $X$ such that $Y$ can be linearly ordered. De la Cruz/Di Prisco\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco}  [\textbf{1996}].

\section*{{II}. Versions Of Martin's Axiom}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ S}] If $(P,\,\leq)$ is a quasi-order such that $P$ is non-empty, well orderable and every antichain is finite then there is a $P$-generic filter . Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} [\textbf{1990}] and note 47.

\noindent [\textbf{1 Z}] If $(P,\,\leq)$ is a quasi-order and $P\neq\emptyset$ and every antichain is finite, then there is a $P$ generic filter which is well orderable. Shannon [\textbf{1990}] and note~47.

\noindent [\textbf{8 F}] Martin's Axiom\index{Subject}{Martin's axiom} $(\aleph_{0})$: Whenever $(P\leq)$ is a non-empty, ccc quasi-order (ccc means every anti-chain is countable) and $\mathcal{D}$ is a family of $\leq\aleph_{0}$ dense subsets of $P$, then there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter $G$ in $P$. Kunen\index{Author}{Kunen} [\textbf{1980}], Shannon [\textbf{1990}] and note 47.

\noindent [\textbf{10 I}] Assume $(P,\,\leq)$ is a partial order such that $P$ is a denumerable union of finite sets and contains a non-empty subset $Q$ relative to which depths are defined for all $x\in \mathrm{P}$. If all $Q$-strong antichains of $P$ are finite then for each denumerable family $\mathcal{D}$ of dense sets there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter. Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1990f} and note 47.

\noindent [\textbf{43 C}] Existence of a generic set: If $\mathcal{D}$ is a denumerable collection of dense sets in a partial order $(P,\,\leq)$ then for all $p\in P$ there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic $G$ with $p\in G$. Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985m} and note 47.

\noindent [\textbf{43 D}] If $\mathcal{D}$ is a denumerable collection of dense subsets of a partial order $(P,\,\leq)$ then for all $p\in P$ there is a sequence $f:\omega \rightarrow P$ with $f(0)=p$ and $(\forall n\in \omega)(f(n)\geq f(n+1))$ and range $(f)\cap D\neq\emptyset$ for all $D\in \mathcal{D}$. Goldblatt~\cite{bib:1985m}.

\noindent \textbf{171.} If $(P,\,\leq)$ is a partial order such that $P$ is the denumerable union of finite sets and all antichains in $P$ are finite then for each denumerable family $\mathcal{D}$ of dense sets there is a $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter. Shannon \cite{bib:1990f} and note 47.

\textbf{III. Trees}

\noindent [\textbf{10 F}] K\"{o}nig's Lemma:\index{Subject}{K\"{o}nig's lemma} Every $\omega$ tree has an infinite chain. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c1}, note 21, and note 35.

\noindent [\textbf{43 H}] Every tree in which every element has at least one successor has a branch. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1979}] and note note 21.

\noindent [\textbf{86 A($\alpha$)}] If $(P,\,\leq)$ is a tree of height $\lambda\leq\aleph_{\alpha}$ which has fewer than $\lambda$ branches of height $<\lambda$ then one of the following holds for the upside down tree $(P,\, \geq)$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] There is a cardinal $\mu<\lambda$ such that $(P, \geq)$ does not contain a strong antichain of cardinality $\mu$.
\item[(b)] $(P,\,\geq)$ contains a strong antichain of cardinality $\lambda$.
\item[(c)] $(P,\,\geq)$ contains a chain of cardinality $\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
Shannon [\textbf{1992}] and note 119.

\noindent [\textbf{106 A}] $DMC$: Dependent Multiple Choice: Every tree in which every element has at least one immediate successor has a subtree whose levels are finite and in which every element has at least one immediate successor. Blass [\textbf{1979}], Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983c}], Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and note~21.

\noindent \textbf{216.} Every infinite tree has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus [\textbf{1972a}] and note 21.

\noindent \textbf{249.} If $T$ is an infinite tree in which every element has exactly 2 immediate successors then $T$ has an infinite branch. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1975}], note 87 and note 21.

\textbf{IV. Other Partial Ordering Properties (See note 71.)}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ J}] Zermelo's Fixed Point Theorem:\index{Subject}{Zermelo's fixed point theorem} For every partially ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$, if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}], Zermelo\index{Author}{Zermelo} [\textbf{1908b}] and Abian\index{Author}{Abian} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ K}] For all partially ordered sets $(X,\,\leq)$, if there is a sup function $\sigma$ on the well ordered subsets of $X$ then every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ L}] Caristi's Fixed Point Theorem: If $(X,\,\rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi$: $X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering $(x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho(x,\,y)\leq\phi(y)-\phi(x))$ every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t \leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Caristi\index{Author}{Caristi} [\textbf{1976}], Manka [\textbf{1988a}], and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 Q}] For any\index{Subject}{Caristi's fixed point theorem} partial order $(X,\,\leq)$ there is a $\sup$ function on the bounded (above), well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 R}] For any partial order $(X,\,\leq)$ there is a $\sup$ function on the bounded subsets of $X$. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note~38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 S}] For any partial order $(X,\,\leq)$ if every well ordered subset of $X$ is bounded then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 T}] For every directed partial order $(X,\,\leq)$ there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 U}] For every directed partial order, if every well ordered subset of $X$ is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of $X$. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and note~38.

\noindent [\textbf{1 V}] For every partially ordered set $(X,\,\leq)$, if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Manka [\textbf{1988a}] and Abian\index{Author}{Abian} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AJ}] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of mappings of a poset $(X,\,\leq)$ into itself such that $\forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x$. If for some element $e$ of $X$ each chain in $X$ containing $e$ has a lower bound, then the family $\mathcal{F}$ has a common fixed point. Kasahara\index{Author}{Kasahara} [\textbf{1976}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 W}] Universal Subnet Theorem: Any net has a universal subnet. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{43 K}] Let $M$ be a non-empty set partially ordered by $<$ without $<$-minimal elements. Then there is a subset $C$ of $M$ which is linearly ordered by $<$ such that $C$ has no $<$-minimal element. Note 146.

\noindent [\textbf{43 L}] $Z_{\omega}$: If every chain in a partially ordered set $P$ is finite, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} [\textbf{1948}], Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} [\textbf{1983}], and note 54.

\noindent [\textbf{43 M}] If $(X,\,\rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering, $(x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho(x,\,y)\leq \phi(y)-\phi(x))$, there is a maximal element. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1987a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{43 Q}] Matrix$(\omega)$: For every atomless poset $(P,\,\leq)$ and every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ of dense open subsets of $P$, there exists a matrix $C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega\},\, |\bigcup C|=\omega$ of $P$ for $D$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{43 R}] Any partial order $(A,\,\leq)$ with no infinite descending chains is well founded, (that is, for all $X$ such that $\emptyset\,\neq X\subseteq A,\,X$ has a minimal element.) Spector\index{Author}{Spector} [\textbf{1980}] and note 54.

\noindent \textbf{59($\leq$).} If $(A,\,\leq)$ is a partial ordering that is not a well ordering, then there is no set $B$ such that $(B,\,\precsim)$ (the usual injective cardinal ordering on $B$) is isomorphic to $(A,\,\leq)$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1979}] p 120.

\noindent [\textbf{70 B}] Weak Universal Net Theorem: There is a universal net in $\omega$ which is not eventually constant. Schechter [\textbf{1996a}] and note 31.

\noindent [\textbf{87 A($\alpha$)}] $Z_{\aleph_{\alpha}}$: Let $P$ be a partially ordered set in which every well ordered chain has type $<\aleph_{\alpha}$. If every well ordered chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Wolk [\textbf{1983}].

\noindent [\textbf{87 B($\alpha$)}] $Z_{\aleph_{\alpha}}^{\ast}$: Let $P$ be a well-founded partially ordered set, (that is, every chain in $P$ is well ordered), in which every chain has type $<\aleph_{\alpha}$. If every chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ contains a maximal element. Wolk [\textbf{1983}].

\noindent \textbf{89.} Antichain Principle:\index{Subject}{antichain principle} Every partially ordered set has a maximal antichain. Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 133 and Kurepa\index{Author}{Kurepa} [\textbf{1953}].

\noindent \textbf{105.} There is a partially ordered set $(A,\,\leq)$ such that there is no set $(B,\,\precsim)$ ($\precsim$, the usual injective cardinal ordering) isomorphic to $(A,\,\leq)$. Forti/Honsell\index{Author}{Forti/Honsell} [\textbf{1985}] and Jech [\textbf{1966c}].

\noindent \textbf{144.} Every set is almost well orderable. Keisler\index{Author}{Keisler} [\textbf{1970}] and note 25.

\noindent \textbf{217.} Every infinite partially ordered set has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} [\textbf{1972a}].

\section*{TOPOLOGICAL FORMS (INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF $\mathbb{R}$)}

\textbf{I. Baire Category Type Theorems (See note 28.)}

\noindent [\textbf{43 E}] The Baire Category Theorem for \v{C}ech Complete-I Spaces: Every \v{C}ech complete space is Baire. Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985m} and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 F}] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair\index{Author}{Blair} [\textbf{1977}], Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983c}], Goldblatt \cite{bib:1985m}, and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 J}] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [\textbf{1983c}] and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 T}] A sequentially complete metric space is not meager. Note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 U}] Baire Category Theorem for Filter Complete Metric Spaces: Every filter complete metric space is Baire, Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 V}] Every convex-compact set in a Hausdorff topological vector space with a basis of convex open sets is Baire. Fossy/Morillon [\textbf{1995}] and note 23.

\noindent \textbf{106.} Baire Category Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: Every compact Hausdorff space is Baire. Goldblatt \cite{bib:1985m}, G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}], and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{106 C}] Every scattered compact space is a Baire space. Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}] and note 28.

\textbf{II. Product Theorems}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ B}] If $X$ is finite then $X^{\omega}$ is compact. Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ D}] Products of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [\textbf{1984b}]

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ E}] The box product of a well ordered family of limited amorphous spaces is limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [\textbf{1984b}] and note 52.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AY}] For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $S_{\lambda}$ be a subset of some topological space $X_{\lambda}$. Then $\mathrm{cl}( \prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}S_{\lambda})=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\ \mathrm{cl}\ (S_{\lambda})$, where the first ``$\mathrm{cl}$'' is closure in the product topology and the second ``$\mathrm{cl}$'' is closure in $X_{\lambda}$. Schechter [\textbf{1992}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 AZ}] For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$, let $X_{\lambda}$ be a complete uniform space. Then, the product $\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}X_{\lambda}$ equipped with the product uniform structure, is also complete. (See, for example, Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} [\textbf{1955}] pp 176ff for definitions.) Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1992}].

\noindent [\textbf{10 B}] Tychonoff's\index{Subject}{Tychonoff's theorem} Compactness Theorem for Countable Families of Finite $T_{2}$ Spaces: The product of a countable family of finite $T_{2}$ spaces is compact. Krom\index{Author}{Krom} \cite{bib:1981b}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 J}] Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: The product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact. (For many compactness theorems $T$, it is clear that [14 J] implies $T$ implies [14 K].) {\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski\index{Author}{Los/Ryll-Nardzewski@{\L}o\'{s}/Ryll-Nardzewski}
 [\textbf{1954}] and Rubin/Scott\index{Author}{Rubin/Scott} [\textbf{1954}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 K}] Compactness of the Generalized Cantor Space: $\{0,1\}^{I}$ is compact for any I. (For many compactness theorems $T$, it is clear that [14 J] implies $T$ implies [14 K].) Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 28, prob 17 and Mycielski\index{Author}{Mycielski} [\textbf{1964}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 Z}] Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for Families of Finite Spaces: If $\{X_{i}:i\in I\}$ is a family of finite topological spaces, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_{i}$ is compact. (Cleary [14 Z] implies [14 K] and is implied by [14 J].) Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 28 prob 17, A.A. Lewis\index{Author}{Lewis} [\textbf{1983}], and Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} [\textbf{1967}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AB}] Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for Sober Spaces: A product of compact, sober topological spaces is compact. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} [\textbf{1986}], Johnstone\index{Author}{Johnstone} [\textbf{1984}] and note 37.

\noindent [\textbf{43 G}] Form 106 + form 154. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983c}] [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{64 A}] An amorphous power of a compact $T_{2}$ space is compact. Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{64 B}] Finite products of metric $C$ spaces are $C$. (A space is $C$ if each open covering has an amorphous refinement.) Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent \textbf{113.} Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for Countably Many Spaces: The product of a countable set of compact spaces is compact. Brunner [\textbf{1985a}].

\noindent \textbf{115.} The product of weakly Loeb $T_{2}$ spaces is weakly Loeb. (See form 114 for the definition of weakly Loeb.) Brunner [\textbf{1985a}].

\noindent \textbf{127.} An amorphous power of a compact $T_{2}$ space, which as a set is well orderable, is well orderable. Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent \textbf{134.} If $X$ is an infinite $T_{1}$ space and $X^{Y}$ is $T_{5}$, then $Y$ is countable. ($T_{5}$ is ``hereditarily $T_{4}$''.) A. H. Stone\index{Author}{A. H. Stone} [\textbf{1948}].

\noindent \textbf{135.} If $X$ is a $T_{2}$ space with at least two points and $X^{Y}$ is hereditarily metacompact then $Y$ is countable. (A space is \emph{metacompact} if every open cover has an open point finite refinement. If $B$ and $B^{\prime}$ are covers of a space $X$, then $B^{\prime}$ is a \emph{refinement} of $B$ if $(\forall x\in B^{\prime})(\exists y\in B)(x\subseteq y)$. $B$ is \emph{point finite} if $(\forall t\in X)$ there are only finitely many $x\in B$ such that $t\in x$.) van Douwen\index{Author}{Douwen} [\textbf{1980}].

\noindent \textbf{139.} Using the discrete topology on $2,\, 2^{\mathcal{P}(\omega)}$ is compact. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent \textbf{154.} Tychonoff's\index{Subject}{Tychonoff's theorem} Compactness Theorem for Countably Many $T_{2}$ Spaces: The product of countably many $T_{2}$ compact spaces is compact. Brunner [\textbf{1983c}].

\noindent \textbf{177.} An infinite box product of regular $T_{1}$ spaces, each of cardinality greater than 1, is neither first countable nor connected. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1981a}], Knight\index{Author}{Knight} [\textbf{1964}], and note 52.

\noindent \textbf{332.} A product of non-empty compact sober topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent \textbf{343.} A product of non-empty, compact $T_{2}$ topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent \textbf{351.} A countable product of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{352.} A countable product of second countable spaces is second countable. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{353.} A countable product of first countable spaces is first countable. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent \textbf{354.} A countable product of separable $T_{2}$ spaces is separable. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\textbf{III. General Topology}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ C}] Closed subspaces of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ M}] A $T_{1}$ topological space is Dedekind finite if and only if every subspace has a dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ N}] If $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces with dense Dedekind finite subsets so is $X\times Y$. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{1 O}] $A(D1,\,C)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$, if $X$ is covered by a well ordered family of closed, discrete sets then each family $U\subseteq T$ of pairwise disjoint sets is well ordered. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{1 P}] $A(P)$: (Depends on $P$ for $P\in\{W1,\,W2,\,B1,\,L1,\,L2$, $S,\,C,\,H1,\,A1\}$) Every $T_{2}$ topological space has property $P$. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BF}] $(\mathrm{D}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is dense in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{dense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open subset $O\subseteq X$ such that $O\cap Y=\emptyset$.) McCarten\index{Author}{McCarten} [\textbf{1988}] and note 106.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BG}] $(\mathrm{C}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is codense in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{codense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty closed subset $C\subseteq X$ such that $C\cap Y=\emptyset$.) McCarten [\textbf{1988}] and note 106.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BH}] $(\mathrm{T}T_{0})$: Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is thick in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{thick in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset $H\subseteq X$ such that $H\cap Y=\emptyset$.) McCarten [\textbf{1988}] and note 106.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BI}] $(MT_{0})$: Every topological space has a maximal $T_{0}$ subspace. Schnare\index{Author}{Schnare} [\textbf{1968}] and note 106.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BL}] Every family of closed sets in a $T_{2}$ topological space includes a maximal subfamily with the finite intersection property. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985q}, p 60, $M14$.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BM}] For every family $\{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\}$ of $T_{1}$ topological spaces, the box topology contains an element $\prod_{i\in k}O_{i}$, such that $\emptyset \neq O_{i}$ and $O_{i}\neq X_{i}$ for all $i\in k$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BN}] For every family $\{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\}$ of disjoint $T_{1}$ topological spaces, the free union contains an open set $O$ such that $\emptyset \neq O\cap X_{i}$ and $O\cap X_{i}\neq X_{i}$ for all $i\in k$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BO}] For every $T_{1}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ and every base (subbase) $B$ for $X$ there exists a $\subseteq$-maximal cellular family $Q\subseteq B$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BP}] For every dense in itself topological space $(X,\,T)$ and every base $B$ for $X$ there exists a nest $N$ included in $B$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BQ}] For every dense in itself topological space $(X,\,T)$ and every base $B$ for $X$ there exists a tower $R$ included in $B$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BR}] For every $T_{2}$ space $(X,\,T)$ and every subbase $\mathcal{B}$ for $X$, if $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are cellular families of $X$ included in $\mathcal{B}$, then there is a cellular family $\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$ such that $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are equipollent to subsets of $\mathcal{E}$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BW}] If $(X,\,T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\},\,|U_{i}|\geq 2$, is a locally finite family of open non-empty pairwise disjoint sets, then there is a continuous real valued function $f$ on $X$ which assumes at least two distinct values on each $U_{i}$. Keremedis [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CB}] For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, if $(X,\,T)$ is a $T_{2}$ space having a base $B$ such that no $Q\subseteq B,\,|Q|<\kappa$, is a tower, then for every family $\mathcal{D}=\{D_{i}:i\in\kappa\}$ of dense open sets of $X$ there is a filter $F\subseteq T$ such that for every $i\in\kappa$ there is a $b\in F$ with $b\subseteq D_{i}$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CF}] If a topological space is $cwH$, then it is $cwH(B)$ for every basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CG}] The disjoint union of $cwH$ spaces is $cwH(B)$ for every basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{1 CH}] If a topological space is $cwN$, then it is $cwH(B)$ for any basis $B$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{8 C}] Every $\sigma$-compact space is Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner [\textbf{1982b}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{8 D}] Every $\sigma$-compact, locally compact $T_{2}$ space is weakly Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982b}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{8 I}] A disjoint union of a countable set of Lindel\"{o}f $T_{2}$ spaces is Lindel\"{o}f. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 J}] Hemicompact $T_{2}$ spaces are Lindel\"{o}f. (A \emph{hemicompact} space is a space $(X,\,T)$ that can be written as a disjoint union $\bigcup\{K_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ such that (i) each $K_{n}$ is a compact set in $X$; (ii) $K_{N}\subseteq K_{n+1}$ for all $n\in\omega$; and (iii) for every compact set $K$ in $X$, there is an $n\in\omega$ such that $K\subseteq K_{n}$.) Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 K}] Hemilindel\"{o}f $T_{2}$ spaces are Lindel\"{o}f. (In [8 J], in the definition of hemicompact replace ``compact'' by ``Lindel\"{o}f'' to get the definition of hemilindel\"{o}f.) Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 L}] Every second countable topological space is separable. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 N}] $DP$: If $(X,\,T)$ is a topological space having a countable $\pi$-base, then for every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in\omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$, there is a countable dense set $S\subseteq X$ such that for all $i\in \omega$ and for all but finitely many $s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 O}] $DUCCC\ +$ form 131. $DUCCC$ is ``If $X$ is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $X$ has the ccc property.'' $(Y$ has the $ccc$ \emph{property} if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 P}] $DUSS\ +$ form 131. $DUSS$ is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of separable topological spaces is separable.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 Q}] $DUSC\ +$ form 131. $DUSC$ is ``The disjoint union of a denumerable family of second countable topological spaces is second countable.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note~132.

\noindent [\textbf{8 R}] $SCDUL\ +$ form 131. $SCDUL$ is ``The denumerable disjoint union of second countable spaces is Lindel\"{o}f.'' Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{10 H}] $\sigma$-compact, paracompact $T_{2}$ spaces are weakly Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982b}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{13 B}] There is a separable topological space $X$ and a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $X^{A\times\omega}$ has no dense, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{14 BY}] For every topological space $X$, every proper ideal in the normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra of continuous bounded functions from $X$ into $\mathbb{R}$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CB}] If $X$ is a topological space and $I$ is a proper ideal in the algebra of all bounded continuous functions from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that every function in $I$ vanishes at at least one point of $X$, then $I$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}.

\noindent [\textbf{40 A}] $A(L2,\,L1)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\, T)$, if each open cover of $X$ has a well ordered subcover, then each open cover has a well ordered refinement. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{50 L}] Form 301 + form 14. Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{67 A}] $A(A2,\,H2)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ if $(X,\,T)$ is A2, then $(X,\,T)$ is hereditarily $A2$. ($(X,\,T)$ is A2 means if $U\subseteq T$ covers $X$ then $\exists f:X\rightarrow T$ such that for all $x\in X,\,x\in f(x)$ and $f$''$ X$ refines $U$.) Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{67 C}] $A(P)$: (Depends on $P\in\{D1,\,B2,\,B3,\,H2,\,A2\}$.) Every $T_{2}$ topological space has property $P$. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{67 G}] For every $T_{1}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ and every cellular family $\mathcal{O}= \{O_{i}:i\in k\}\subseteq T-\{\emptyset\}$, there is a closed discrete set $\mathcal{I}$ such that for every $i\in k,\, \mathcal{I}\cap O_{i}\neq\emptyset$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996b}] and note 77.

\noindent [\textbf{67 I}] If $(X,\,T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\}$ is a family of non-empty open sets, then there is a family $F=\{f_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non-negative, non-constant, continuous real valued functions on $X$ such that each $f_{i}$ vanishes on $X-U_{i}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent [\textbf{67 J}] If $(X,\,T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\}$ is a family of non-empty open sets, then there is a family $V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\}$ of non-empty closed (compact) sets such that $U_{i}\supseteq V_{i}$ for each $i\in K$. Keremedis [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent [\textbf{67 K}] DUN: The disjoint union of normal topological spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 L}] DUU: If $C$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies Urysohn's lemma\index{Subject}{Urysohn's lemma}, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $C$ satisfies Urysohn's\index{Author}{Urysohn} lemma. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 M}] DUT: If $C$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $C$ satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem. Howard/ Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 N}] DUP: The disjoint union of paracompact spaces is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 O}] DUMET: The disjoint union of metacompact spaces is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 P}] DUPFCS: The disjoint union of PFCS spaces is PFCS. ($X$ is a \emph{PFCS space} iff every point finite open cover of $X$ is shrinkable.) Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 Q}] DUPN: The disjoint union of paracompact spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 R}] DUcwH: The disjoint union of cwH spaces is cwH. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 S}] DUcwN: The disjoint union of cwN spaces is cwN. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 T}] DUcwNN: The disjoint union of cwN spaces is normal. Howard/ Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note~141.

\noindent \textbf{78.} Urysohn's Lemma: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint closed sets in a normal space $S$, then there is a continuous $f:S\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ which is 1 everywhere in $A$ and $0$ everywhere in $B$. Urysohn [\textbf{1925}] pp 290-292.

\noindent [\textbf{91 A}] $A(S,\,W1)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ if $X$ has a dense well ordered subset, then $T$ is well ordered. (Clear) Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent [\textbf{94 A}] The discrete topology on $\omega$ is Lindel\"{o}f. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 40.

\noindent [\textbf{94 B}] There is a Lindel\"{o}f space with a closed, discrete infinite subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982d}] and note 40.

\noindent \textbf{114.} Every A-bounded $T_{2}$ topological space is weakly Loeb. (A-\emph{bounded} means amorphous subsets are relatively compact. \emph{Weakly Loeb} means the set of nonempty closed subsets has a multiple choice function.) Brunner [\textbf{1985a}].

\noindent [\textbf{126 C}] $FSCB\ +$ form 131. \emph{FSCB} is ``Every separable first countable space $(X,\,T)$ has a denumerable $\pi$-base.'' Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{126 E}] If $(X,\,T)$ is a topological space, then for every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$, there is a countable dense set $S\subseteq X$ such that for all $i\in\omega$ and for all but finitely many $s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}$. Keremedis [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.

\noindent [\textbf{126 G}] DUN$(\omega)$: The countable disjoint union of normal topological spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{126 H}] DUU$(\omega)$: If $C$ is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies Urysohn's lemma, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $C$ satisfies Urysohn's lemma. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{126 I}] DUT$(\omega)$: If $C$ is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, then the disjoint union of the spaces in $C$ satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997a}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{126 J}] $F_{\sigma}$ subsets of paracompact spaces are paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note~141.

\noindent [\textbf{126 K}] $F_{\sigma}$ subsets of metacompact spaces are metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}] and note~141.

\noindent \textbf{128.} Aczel's Realization Principle:\index{Subject}{Aczel's Realization Principle} On every infinite set there is a Hausdorff topology with an infinite set of non-isolated points. Brunner [\textbf{1984f}].

\noindent [\textbf{144 A}] Every $p$ space is discrete. (A $p$ \emph{space} is a $T_{2}$ space in which the intersection of any well orderable family of open sets is open). Brunner [\textbf{1984c}].

\noindent \textbf{146.} $A(F,\,A1)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$, if $X$ is a continuous finite to one image of an A1 space then $(X,\,T)$ is an A1 space. ($(X,\,T)$ is A1 means if $U\subseteq T$ covers $X$ then $\exists f:X\rightarrow U$ such that $(\forall x\in X)(x\in f(x))$.) Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent \textbf{147.} $A(D2)$: Every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$ can be covered by a well ordered family of discrete sets. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent \textbf{148.} $A(W2,\,B1)$: For every $T_{2}$ topological space $(X,\,T)$, if $X$ is well ordered, then $X$ has a well ordered base. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent \textbf{149.} $A(F)$: Every $T_{2}$ topological space is a continuous, finite to one image of an A1 space. Brunner [\textbf{1983d}] and note 26.

\noindent \textbf{301.} Any continuous surjection between Boolean spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b} and note 114.

\noindent \textbf{360.} Every second countable topological space is Lindel\"{o}f. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] p 236.

\noindent \textbf{371.} There is an infinite, compact, Hausdorff, extremally disconnected topological space. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} [\textbf{1993}] and note~114.

\noindent \textbf{375.} Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem: If $(X,\,T)$ is a normal topological space, $A$ is closed in $X$, and $f:A\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ is continuous, then there exists a continuous function $g:X\rightarrow[0,\, 1]$ which extends $f$. Urysohn\index{Author}{Urysohn} [\textbf{1924}].

\textbf{IV. Linearly Orderable Spaces}

\noindent [\textbf{34 B}] $\omega_{1}$ with the order topology is not paracompact. Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} [\textbf{1995}] and note 107.

\noindent [\textbf{34 C}] $\omega_{1}$ with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in $\omega_{1}$. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}] and note 107.

\noindent [\textbf{34 D}] $\omega_{1}$ with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}] and note 107.

\noindent [\textbf{34 E}] $\omega_{1}$ with the order topology is not Lindel\"{o}f. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}] and note 107.

\noindent \textbf{118.} Every linearly orderable topological space is normal. Birkhoff\index{Author}{Birkhoff} [\textbf{1967}] p 241.

\noindent [\textbf{118 A}] For each complete linear order, the set of non-empty convex subsets has a choice function, van Douwen\index{Author}{Douwen} [\textbf{1985}].

\noindent [\textbf{118 B}] For each complete linear order, each pairwise disjoint collection of non-empty, convex, open subsets has a choice function, van Douwen [\textbf{1985}].

\noindent [\textbf{118 C}] Every linearly orderable space is collectionwise normal. van Douwen [\textbf{1985}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 D}] Every linearly orderable space is collectionwise Hausdorff. van Douwen [\textbf{1985}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 E}] Every linearly orderable space satisfies Urysohn's lemma, van Douwen [\textbf{1985}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{118 F}] Every linearly orderable space satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, van Douwen [\textbf{1985}] and note~141.

\noindent [\textbf{118 J}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is hereditarily normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h}, van Douwen [\textbf{1985}], and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 K}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is highly separated. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 L}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a complete linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is highly separated. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 O}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is effectively normal. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 R}] If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order, then the order topology on $X$ is monotonely normal. Morillon [\textbf{1987}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{118 U}] Every linearly ordered space is monotonically normal. (A space, $(X,\,<)$ is \emph{monotonically normal} if there is an operator $V$ which assigns to each $x\in X$ and basic open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ a basic open neighborhood $V(x,\,U)$ of $x$ such that $V(x,\,U) \cap V(x^{\prime},\,U^{\prime})\neq\emptyset$ implies $x\in U^{\prime}$ or $x^{\prime}\in U$.) Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{336.} $\omega_{1}$ with the order topology is not paracompact. Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\textbf{V. Compact Spaces}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ O}] A Lindel\"{o}f space with a dense, Dedekind finite subset is compact. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ P}] A Lindel\"{o}f space with a Dedekind finite basis is compact. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{1 AO}] Any continuous surjection between compact spaces, where the range space is Hausdorff, has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b} and note 114.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BV}] If $(X,\,T)$ is a $T_{4}$ topological space and $G=\{G_{i}:i\in K\},\,|G_{i}|\geq 2$, is a locally finite family of compact sets with non-empty pairwise disjoint interiors, then there is a continuous real valued function $f$ on $X$ which assumes at least two distinct values on each $G_{i}$. Keremedis [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{8 H}] A disjoint union of a countable set of compact $T_{2}$ spaces is Lindel\"{o}f. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1996d}] and note 132.
