\noindent [\textbf{14 L}] Stone-\v{C}ech Compactification Theorem: For every topological space $X$ there is a pair $(Y,\,j)$ such that $Y$ is a compact topological space and $j$ is a continuous surjection from $X$ onto $Y$ such that for all topological spaces $Z$ such that $Z$ is compact and completely regular and for all continuous $f:X\rightarrow Z$, there is a unique continuous $h:Y\rightarrow Z$ such that $f=h\circ j$. Rubin/Scott\index{Author}{Rubin/Scott} [\textbf{1954}] and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AA}] Alexander's Subbase Lemma:\index{Subject}{Alexander's subbase lemma} A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase $S$ for the topology such that every cover by elements of $S$ has a finite subcover. Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} [\textbf{1955}] p 143, A.A. Lewis\index{Author}{Lewis} [\textbf{1983}], Wolk\index{Author}{Wolk} [\textbf{1967}], and note 34.

\noindent [\textbf{14 AG}] Topological Rado Lemma: Let $\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of compact Hausdorff spaces and suppose for each finite $F\subseteq I$, there is a set $\Phi(F)$ of partial choice functions on $I$ whose domains include $F$ and such that (a) $F_{1}\subseteq F_{2}$ implies $\Phi(F_{2})\subseteq\Phi(F_{1})$ and (b) the set $\{\phi|F:\phi\in\Phi(F)\}$ is closed in $\prod\{T_{i}:i\in F\}$ in the product topology. Then there is a choice function $f$ on $I$ satisfying for any finite $F\subseteq I,\,\exists\phi\in\Phi(F)$ such that $f$ and $\phi$ coincide on $F$. Rav\index{Author}{Rav} [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 AH}] Principle of Consistent Choices: Let $\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of compact Hausdorf spaces and suppose $R$ is a symmetric binary relation defined for all pairs of elements belonging to distinct $T_{i}$ and such that for all $i\neq j$ in $I$, the set $E(i,\,j)=\{(x,\,y):x\,R\,y\ \mathrm{and}\ x\in T_{i}\ \mathrm{and}\ y\in T_{j}\}$ is closed in $T_{i}\times T_{j}$. Furthermore suppose that for every finite subset $F\subseteq I$, with at least
two elements, $\exists\phi\in\prod\{T_{i}:i\in F\}$ such that $\phi(i)\,R\,\phi(j)$ for all $i\neq j$ in $F$. Then $\exists f\in\prod\{T_{i}:i\in I\}$ such that $f(i)\,R\,f(j)$ for all $i\neq j$ in $I$. Rav [\textbf{1977}].

\noindent [\textbf{14 CC}] A projective limit of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CD}] A projective\index{Subject}{Goodner's theorem} limit of a directed projective system of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CE}] A projective limit of a directed projective system of compact nonempty topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{14 CG}] A projective limit of a directed projective system of finite sets is compact. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\noindent [\textbf{50 E}] Form 14 + form 297. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1988a} and Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 J}] Form 299 + form 14. Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 K}] Form 300 + form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{50 M}] Form 302 + form 14. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}.

\noindent [\textbf{64 C}] $C$ spaces are compact. (A space is \emph{a} $C$ \emph{space} if each open covering has an amorphous refinement.) Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{67 H}] Let $(X,\,T)$ be a $T_{4}$ topological space and let $\{G_{i}:i\in K\}$ be a locally finite family of pairwise disjoint, non-empty, open subsets of $X$. Then there exists a continuous real valued function $f:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,f$ vanishes on the boundary of $G_{i}$ and $f(x_{i})=1$ for some $x_{i}\in G_{i}$. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} [\textbf{1995}] and note 43.

\noindent [\textbf{106 D}] For every compact $T_{2}$ space $(X,\,T)$ and every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$ there is a regular filter base $\mathcal{F}\subseteq T$ (that is, if $F,\,G\in \mathcal{F}$, then there exists $Q\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $\overline{Q}\subseteq F\cap G$) such that $\forall i\in \omega$, for all but finitely many $F\in \mathcal{F},\,\overline{F}\subset D_{i}$. Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{116.} Every compact $T_{2}$ space is weakly Loeb. (See form 114 for the definition of weakly Loeb.) Brunner [\textbf{1985a}].

\noindent \textbf{125.} There does not exist an infinite, compact connected $p$ space. (A $p$ \emph{space} is a $T_{2}$ space in which the intersection of any well orderable family of open sets is open.) Brunner [\textbf{1984c}].

\noindent \textbf{145.} Compact $P_{0}$-spaces are Dedekind finite. (A $P_{0}$-\emph{space} is a topological space in which the intersection of a countable collection of open sets is open.) Brunner [\textbf{1984c}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{155.} $LC$: There are no non-trivial L\"{a}uchli continua. (A \emph{L\"{a}uchli continuum} is a strongly connected continuum. \emph{Continuum} $\equiv$ compact, connected, Hausdorff space; and \emph{strongly connected} $\equiv$ every continuous real valued function is constant.) Brunner [\textbf{1983a}] and L\"{a}uchli\index{Author}{Lauchli@L\"{a}uchli} [\textbf{1962}].

\noindent \textbf{156.} Theorem of Gelfand and Kolmogoroff:\index{Subject}{Gelfand-Kolmogoroff theorem} Two compact $T_{2}$ spaces are homeomorphic if their rings of real valued continuous functions are isomorphic. Brunner [\textbf{1983a}] and Gelfand/Kolmogoroff\index{Author}{Gelfand/Kolmogoroff} [\textbf{1939}].

\noindent \textbf{157.} Theorem of Goodner\index{Author}{Goodner}: A compact $T_{2}$ space is extremally disconnected (the closure of every open set is open) if and only if each non-empty subset of $C(X)$ (set of continuous real valued functions on $X$) which is pointwise bounded, has a supremum. Goodner [\textbf{1950}].

\noindent [\textbf{225 A}] There exists\index{Subject}{Baire's classification} a compact, extremally disconnected topological space having a Dedekind infinite set of clopen subsets. Morillon [\textbf{1993}], notes 94 and 114.

\noindent [\textbf{225 B}] There exists\index{Author}{Feferman/Levy} a compact, $\sigma$-extremally disconnected topological space having a Dedekind infinite set of clopen subsets. Morillon [\textbf{1993}], notes 94 and 114.

\noindent \textbf{297.} Extremally\index{Author}{Jech} disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces are projective in the category of all compact Hausdorff spaces. Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1988a}, Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1988b}, notes 60 and~114.

\noindent \textbf{298.} Every compact Hausdorff space has a Gleason\index{Author}{Gleason} cover. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}, Gleason [\textbf{1958}], and note 114.

\noindent \textbf{299.} Any extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is projective in the category of Boolean topological spaces. Bell \cite{bib:1988b}, notes 60 and 114.

\noindent \textbf{300.} Any continuous surjection between extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell \cite{bib:1988b} and note 114.

\noindent \textbf{302.} Any continuous surjection between compact Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell \cite{bib:1988b} and note 114.

\noindent \textbf{304.} There does not exist a $T_{2}$ topological space $X$ such that every infinite subset of $X$ contains an infinite compact subset. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1985c}].

\noindent \textbf{331.} If $(X_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of compact non-empty topological spaces then there is a family $(F_{i})_{i\in I}$ such that $\forall i\in I,\,F_{i}$ is an irreducible closed subset of $X_{i}$. Morillon \cite{bib:1988h} and note 71.

\textbf{VI. Properties of} $\mathbb{R}$

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AB}] If $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is perfect, then $|X|=2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1974b}] and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AC}] There are $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ perfect subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Truss [\textbf{1974b}] and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{6 A}] Every uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ contains a condensation point. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}] p 205 and 324, Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent [\textbf{6 B}] Every uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has two condensation points. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 205 and 324, Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{11.} $\mathbb{R}$ is hereditarily Lindel\"{o}f\index{Author}{Lindelof@Lindel\"{o}f}. Lindel\"{o}f [\textbf{1905}].

\noindent \textbf{12.} $\mathbb{R}$ is Lindel\"{o}f. Young\index{Author}{Young} [\textbf{1903}].

\noindent \textbf{13.} Every Dedekind finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is finite. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{13 A}] $\mathbb{R}$ has no dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent \textbf{19.} A real function is analytically representable if and only if it is in Baire's classification. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}]~(2.3.1).

\noindent \textbf{35.} The union of countably many meager subsets\index{Author}{Davies} of $\mathbb{R}$ is meager. (Meager sets are the same as sets of the first category.) Feferman/Levy\index{Author}{Feferman/Levy} [\textbf{1963}], Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 7 prob 1.7, and note 28.

\noindent \textbf{36.} If $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $A \bigcap B$ is countable for every bounded $B$ then $A$ is countable. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}] p 36.

\noindent \textbf{37.} Lebesgue measure is countably additive. Sierpi\'{n}ski~[\textbf{1916}].

\noindent \textbf{38.} $\mathbb{R}$ is not the union of a countable family of countable sets. Feferman/Levy [\textbf{1963}] and note 3.

\noindent \textbf{73.} For every $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x\in \mathbb{R}$ the following definitions are equivalent:

(1) $x$ is in the closure of $A$ iff every neighborhood of $x$ intersects $A$.

(2) $x$ is in the closure of $A$ iff there is a sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ such that $\lim x_{n}=x$. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 21.

\noindent [\textbf{73 A}] For all $A\subseteq \mathbb{R},\,x\in A$ and $f:A\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ the following are equivalent:

(1) $(\forall\epsilon>0)(\exists\delta>0)(\forall y\in A)(|y-x|<\delta$ implies $|f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon)$

(2) Whenever $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ and $\lim x_{n}=x$ then $\lim f(x_{n})=f(x)$.
Notes 4, 5 and 6.

\noindent [\textbf{73 B}] $(\forall f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R})(\forall x\in \mathbb{R})$ the following are equivalent:

(1) $(\forall\epsilon>0)(\exists\delta>0)((\forall y\in \mathbb{R}\rangle(|y-x|<\delta\rightarrow|f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon)$

(2) Whenever $\lim x_{n}=x$, then $\lim f(x_{n})=f(x)$.
Note~10.

\noindent \textbf{74.} For every $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ the following are equivalent:

(1) $A$ is closed and bounded.

(2) Every sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ has a convergent subsequence with limit in A. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 21.

\noindent \textbf{79.} $\mathbb{R}$ can be well ordered. Hilbert\index{Author}{Hilbert} [\textbf{1900}] p 263.

\noindent [\textbf{79 A}] $C(\infty,\,\infty,\,\mathbb{R})$: Every set whose elements are non-empty subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ has a choice function. Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} [\textbf{1996a}].

\noindent \textbf{92.} Every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is separable. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 142.

\noindent \textbf{93.} There is a non-measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1918}].

\noindent \textbf{130.} $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ is well orderable. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984f}].

\noindent [\textbf{137 A($k$)}] For all $X$ and $Y\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ form 137$(k)$ holds. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1984}].

\noindent \textbf{142.} $\neg PB$: There is a set of reals without the property of Baire. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 7 and note 28.

\noindent \textbf{169.} There is an uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ without a perfect subset. Banaschewski/Moore\index{Author}{Banaschewski/Moore} [\textbf{1990}], Bernstein\index{Author}{Bernstein} [\textbf{1908}], and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{170 A}] There is a function that assigns to each denumerable set $D$ of reals a real number not in $D$. Sierpi\'{n}ski~[\textbf{1954}].

\noindent [\textbf{170 B}] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier\index{Author}{Raisonnier} [\textbf{1982}] and note 3.

\noindent \textbf{197.} $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is the union of three sets $C$ with the property that for all $x\in C$ there is a straight line $L$ such that $L\cap C=\{x\}$. Davies [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{203.} $C(\mathrm{disjoint},\subseteq \mathbb{R})$: Every partition of $\mathcal{P}(w)$ into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Truss\index{Author}{Truss} [\textbf{1978}].

\noindent \textbf{211.} $DCR$: Dependent\index{Author}{Sierpinski@Sierpi\'{n}ski} Choice\index{Author}{Hamel} for Relations on $\mathbb{R}$: If $R\subseteq \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $(\forall x\in \mathbb{R})(\exists y\in \mathbb{R})(x\ R\ y)$ then there is a sequence $\langle x(n): n\in \omega\rangle$ of real numbers such that $(\forall n\in \omega)(x(n)\,R\,x(n+1))$. Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} [\textbf{1977a}].

\noindent \textbf{212.} $C(2^{\aleph_{0}},\,\subseteq \mathbb{R})$: If $R$ is a relation on $\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$, there is a $y\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x\,R\,y$, then there is a function $f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb{R},\,x\,R\,f(x)$. Mathias [\textbf{1977a}].

\noindent \textbf{224.} There is a partition of the real line into $\aleph_{1}$ Borel sets $\{B_{\alpha}:\alpha<\aleph_{1}\}$ such that for some $\beta<\aleph_{1},\,\forall\alpha<\aleph_{1},\,B_{\alpha}\in G_{\beta}$. ($G_{\beta}$ for $\beta<\aleph_{1}$ is defined by induction, $G_{0}=\{A: A\ \text{is an open subset of}\ \mathbb{R}\}$ and for $\beta>0,\,G_{\beta}=\{\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}A_{i}:(\forall i\in\omega)(\exists\xi<\beta)(A_{i}\in G_{\xi})\}$ if $\beta$ is even and $G_{\beta}=\{\bigcap_{i=0}^{\infty}A_{i}:(\forall i\in \omega)(\exists\xi<\beta)(A_{i}\in G_{\xi})\}$ if $\beta$ is odd.) Stern\index{Author}{Stern} [\textbf{1979}].

\noindent \textbf{251.} The additive groups $(\mathbb{R},\,+)$ and $(\mathbb{C},\,+)$ are isomorphic. Ash [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{252.} The additive groups of $\mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are isomorphic. Ash\index{Author}{Ash} [\textbf{1975}].

\noindent \textbf{272.} There is an $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that neither $X$ nor $\mathbb{R} -X$ has a perfect subset. Truss [\textbf{1974b}] and note 28.

\noindent \textbf{273.} There is a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ which is not Borel. Truss [\textbf{1974b}].

\noindent \textbf{305.} There are $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ Vitali equivalence classes\index{Subject}{Vitali equivalence classes}. (\emph{Vitali equivalence classes} are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation $x\equiv y\leftrightarrow(\exists q\in\mathbb{Q})(x-y=q)$.). Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{306.} The set of Vitali equivalence classes is linearly orderable. (\emph{Vitali equivalence classes} are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation $x\equiv y\leftrightarrow(\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q)$.). Kanovei [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{307.} If $m$ is the cardinality of the set of Vitali equivalence classes, then $H(m)= H(2^{\aleph_{0}})$, where $H$ is Hartogs aleph function and the \emph{Vitali equivalence classes} are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation $x\equiv y\leftrightarrow(\exists q\in\mathbb{Q})(x-y=q)$. Kanovei [\textbf{1991}].

\noindent \textbf{309.} The Banach-Tarski Paradox:\index{Subject}{Banach-Tarski paradox} There are three finite partitions $\{P_{1},\,\ldots,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots,\,Q_{r}\}$ and $\{S_{1},\,\ldots,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots,\,T_{r}\}$ of $B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\}$ such that $P_{i}$ is congruent to $S_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and $Q_{i}$ is congruent to $T_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq r$. Banach/Tarski\index{Author}{Banach/Tarski} [\textbf{1924}].

\noindent \textbf{361.} In $\mathbb{R}$, the union of a denumerable number of analytic sets is analytic. G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} [\textbf{1982}], pp 181 and 325.

\noindent \textbf{362.} In $\mathbb{R}$, every Borel set is analytic. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}], pp 181 and 325.

\noindent \textbf{363.} There are exactly $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ Borel sets in $\mathbb{R}$. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}], p 325.

\noindent \textbf{364.} In $\mathbb{R}$, there is a measurable set that is not Borel. G. Moore [\textbf{1982}], p 325.

\noindent \textbf{366.} There is a discontinuous function $f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real $x$ and $y,\,f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$. Hamel [\textbf{1905}].

\noindent \textbf{367.} There is a Hamel\index{Author}{Jech} basis for $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$. Hamel [\textbf{1905}].

\noindent \textbf{368.} The set of all denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ has power $2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Sierpi\'{n}ski [\textbf{1917}].

\noindent \textbf{369.} If $\mathbb{R}$ is partitioned into two sets, at least one of them has cardinality $2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Luzin/Sierpi\'{n}ski\index{Author}{Luzin/Sierpinski@Luzin/Sierpi\'{n}ski} [\textbf{1917}].

\textbf{VII. Metric Spaces}

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ L}] Caristi's Fixed Point Theorem: If $(X,\,\rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering $(x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\, \rho(x,\,y)\leq\phi(y)-\phi(x))$ every $f:X\rightarrow X$ satisfying $\forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t)$ has a fixed point. Caristi\index{Author}{Caristi} [\textbf{1976}], Manka\index{Author}{Manka} [\textbf{1988a}], and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{$\boldsymbol{0}$ AK}] Every separable metric space is second countable.

\noindent [\textbf{1 I}] In every metric space $(X,\,d)$ there is an $\epsilon$-lattice for some $\epsilon>0$ which is not a strict upper bound of $d$. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} [\textbf{1984e}] and note 17.

\noindent [\textbf{1 BK}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space $(X,\,d)$ can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is pairwise disjoint. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} [\textbf{1997}].

\noindent [\textbf{1 CE}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space $(X,\,d)$ can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is discrete. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{10 G}] For all metric spaces $X$ and $Y$ and continuous functions $f$ from $X$ onto $Y$ such that $f^{-1}(y)$ is finite for all $y\in Y$, if $X$ has a dense Dedekind finite subset, then so does $Y$. Brunner [\textbf{1982d}] and note 94.

\noindent [\textbf{43 F}] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair\index{Author}{Blair} [\textbf{1977}], Brunner [\textbf{1983c}], Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985m} and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 J}] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [\textbf{1983c}] and note 28.

\noindent [\textbf{43 M}] If $(X,\,\rho)$ is a complete metric space and $\phi:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Br{\o}ndsted ordering, $(x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho(x,\,y)\leq \phi(y)-\phi(x)$), there is a maximal element. Brunner [\textbf{1987a}] and note 38.

\noindent [\textbf{64 D}] Metric $C$ spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is $C$ if every open covering has an amorphous refinement. A space is \emph{limited amorphous} if each amorphous subset is relatively compact.) Brunner [\textbf{1984b}].

\noindent [\textbf{67 U}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space $(X,\,d)$ can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{67 V}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X$, \emph{d}) can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent \textbf{75.} Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable. Jech \cite{bib:1973b} p 21.

\noindent [\textbf{76 A}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is locally countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{76 B}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{U_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where $\gamma$ is an ordinal and each $U_{\alpha}$ is point countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent \textbf{173.} MPL: Metric spaces are para-Lindel\"{o}f. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{173 A}] MML: Metric spaces are meta-Lindel\"{o}f. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/ Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent \textbf{232.} Every metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a $\sigma$-point finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 A}] Every metric space has a $\gamma$-point finite base, for some ordinal $\gamma$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 B}] Every metric space has a $\sigma$-locally finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 C}] Every metric space has a $\gamma$-locally finite base, for some ordinal $\gamma$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 D}] Every metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a $\sigma$-discrete base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 E}] Every metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a $\gamma$-discrete base, for some ordinal $\gamma$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 F}] Every metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a $\sigma$-disjoint base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{232 G}] Every metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a $\gamma$-disjoint base for some ordinal $\gamma$. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent \textbf{280.} There is a complete separable metric space with a subset which does not have the Baire property. Wright\index{Author}{Wright} [\textbf{1973}] and note 28.

\noindent \textbf{337.} Every separable metric space is Lindel\"{o}f. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{338.} Every second countable metric space is Lindel\"{o}f. Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{339.} Every second countable metric space is separable. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{340.} Every Lindel\"{o}f metric space is separable. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{341.} Every Lindel\"{o}f metric space is second countable. Good/Tree [\textbf{1995}].

\noindent \textbf{381.} DUM: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin} [\textbf{1997b}].

\noindent \textbf{382.} DUMN: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [\textbf{1997b}].

\noindent \textbf{383.} MP: Every metric space is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{383 A}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space $(X,\,d)$ has a refinement $\mathcal{V}$ which covers $X$ and which can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{V_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where each $V_{\alpha}$ is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{383 B}] MM: Every metric space is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley\index{Author}{Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley} [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\noindent [\textbf{383 C}] Every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space ($X$, \emph{d}) has a refinement $\mathcal{V}$ which covers $X$ and which can be written as a well ordered union $\bigcup\{V_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\gamma\}$ where each $V_{\alpha}$ is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [\textbf{1997}] and note 141.

\setcounter{chapter}{2}
\chapter{Models}\label{part03}

\section*{Introduction}

We consider two types of models: Models of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, ZF, in section I and models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ in section II. These two versions of set theory are described in the introduction to the book. (In what follows, AC is the Axiom of Choice and GCH is the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis.) Our models of ZF are Cohen models\index{Subject}{Cohen models} (or some modern variation) which are obtained from models of ZFC = ZF +AC by using the method of \emph{forcing} to construct an extension which is a model of ZF without AC. The models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ that we use are the permutation models of Fraenkel\index{Author}{Fraenkel} and Mostowski (FM models). We start with a model of $\mathrm{ZF^{0}+ AC}$ which we refer to as the ground model and use a group of permutations of the atoms to construct a submodel in which AC is false. Details on the construction of models for ZF by the method of forcing can be found in Cohen\index{Author}{Cohen} \cite{bib:1966}, Felgner \cite{bib:1971a}, Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, Kunen\index{Author}{Kunen} \cite{bib:1980}, and Solovay\index{Author}{Solovay} \cite{bib:1970}. For more details on permutation models\index{Subject}{permutation models} and the Fraenkel-Mostowski\index{Subject}{Fraenkel-Mostowski (FM) models} method we refer the reader to Felgner \cite{bib:1971a}, Fraenkel\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1922}, Jech \cite{bib:1973b}, and Levy\index{Author}{Levy} \cite{bib:1963a}.

We refer to the statements in the numerical list of forms both by their name (e.g. Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem or BPI) and by their number (e.g. BPI is form 14). Sometimes we refer to a form by a symbol. For example, $C(\infty,\,\infty)$ is AC in the form: ``Every set of non-empty sets has a choice function.'' (form 1); $C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$ is AC for a denumerable set of finite sets (10); $C(WO,\,\infty)$ is AC for a well ordered set of non-empty sets (40); $UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ is ``The union of a denumerable number of denumerable sets is denumerable.'' (The countable union theorem, 31); etc. These and other abbreviations are defined in both the numerical list of forms and the topical list of forms.

\section{Cohen Models, Models of ZF. ($\mathcal{M}$)}\label{pt03:sec1}

There are some weak forms of AC which are true in all Cohen models and some which are false in all Cohen models. These are described briefly below. More information can be found in the notes to which we refer.

Several of our weak forms of AC are known to imply AC in the theory ZF (but not in the theory $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$). More detailed information can be found in notes 18 and 75. Since AC is false in all of our Cohen models of ZF all forms which imply AC in ZF must be false. In the theory $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$, all of these forms are known to imply form 91. Therefore, in the description of each Cohen model, we will say ``91 is false'' and refer to note 75.

Secondly, there are several implications involving more than two forms that are known to hold in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}.$ These are listed with references in note 120. Most are of the form A+B implies C, where A,\,B, and C are form numbers. When it follows from these implications that a certain form is true or false in a model we will, in the description of the model, assert that the form is true (or false) and give a reference to the part of note 120 from which the truth or falsity follows.

\noindent $\mathcal{M}1$: Cohen's original model. Add a denumerable number of generic reals (subsets of $\omega$), $a_{1},\,a_{2},\, \cdots$, along with the set $b$ containing them. It follows from the work of Halpern and Levy that the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (BPI,14) and the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) are true in this model. Cohen\index{Author}{Cohen} proved that in this model there is an infinite subset of the reals that has no denumerable subset (13 is false). Also, the Krein-Milman Theorem (KM, 65) is false because BPI + KM $\rightarrow$ AC and Haddad and Morillon proved that in $\mathcal{M}$1 every orderable topological space is normal (118 is true). Jech\index{Author}{Jech} has shown that the Axiom of Choice for a set of well orderable sets $(C(\infty,\,WO)$, 60) is true and the countable union theorem $(UT(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$, 31) is true. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} proved that Ramsey's Theorem (17) is false. Brunner \cite{bib:1982a} has shown that every set that cannot be well ordered has an infinite Dedekind finite subset (163 is true), but the interval [0, 1] of real numbers is not well orderable and has no infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set (164 is false). It is shown in note 102 that there is a set $S$ consisting of finite unions of sets in $b$, the set of generic reals, that is closed with respect to chain unions, but has no $\subseteq$-maximal element (289 is false). Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1984f} shows that in this model on every infinite set there is a Hausdorff topology with an infinite set of non-isolated points (128 is true). Blass \cite{bib:1979} has shown that in every symmetric model there is a set $X$ such that for each set $a$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function $f$ mapping $X\times\alpha$ onto $a$ (191 is true). (See note 59.) Since BPI is true, it follows from Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1975} that {\L}os' Theorem (253) is false. Monro\index{Author}{Monro} proves that every cardinal that cannot be well ordered is decomposable (i.e. is the sum of two smaller positive cardinals), so 277 is true. In Jech \cite{bib:1973b} (prob 5.20), it is shown that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite (82 is true). David\index{Author}{David} shows that no infinite subset of $b$ is almost well orderable so 144 is false. See note 25 for definitions. By the results of Bell\index{Author}{Bell} \cite{bib:1983}, \cite{bib:1988} and Monro \cite{bib:1972} the following three forms are false in $\mathcal{M}$1: Form 50 (Sikorski's extension theorem on Boolean homomorphisms), form 299 (Any extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is projective in the category of Boolean topological spaces.) and form 300 (Any continuous surjection between extremally disconnected Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain.) See notes 60 and 114 for definitions. Since 154 is true (14 implies 154) and 43 is false (43 implies 13), form 106 (the Baire Category Theorem for compact $T_{2}$ spaces) is false because 106 + 154 implies 43. (See Brunner \cite{bib:1984b} and note 95.) In this model, $\mathbb{R}$ with the order topology is a separable metric space that is not Lindel\"{o}f (337 is false). Also, there is a dense set $K\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ which has no denumerable subset such that $K$ is a second countable metric space that is neither Lindel\"{o}f nor separable (338 and 339 are false). (See Good/Tree \cite{bib:1995}.)

References include Bell \cite{bib:1983}, \cite{bib:1988}, Blass \cite{bib:1979}, \cite{bib:1977a}, Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}, \cite{bib:1984b}, \cite{bib:1984f}, Cohen \cite{bib:1963}, \cite{bib:1966}, David \cite{bib:1980}, Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} \cite{bib:1995}, Halpern/Levy\index{Author}{Halpern/Levy} \cite{bib:1971}, Haddad/Morillon\index{Author}{Haddad/Morillon} \cite{bib:1990}, Howard \cite{bib:1975}, Monro \cite{bib:1972}, \cite{bib:1973a}, Sageev\index{Author}{Sageev} \cite{bib:1981}, Shoenfield\index{Author}{Shoenfield} \cite{bib:1967}, Smullyan\index{Author}{Smullyan} \cite{bib:1994} and note 120(30 and 49). $\mathcal{M}1(\langle(\omega_{1}\rangle)$: Cohen/Pincus Model. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} extends the methods of Cohen and adds a generic $\omega_{1}$-sequence, $\langle I_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\omega_{1}\rangle$, of denumerable sets, where $I_{0}$ is a denumerable set of generic reals, each $I_{\alpha+1}$ is a generic set of enumerations of $I_{\alpha}$, and for a limit ordinal $\lambda,\,I_{\lambda}$ is a generic set of choice functions for $\{I_{\alpha}:\alpha<\lambda\}$. Pincus proves that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true, for each family of infinite sets $x$, there is a function $f$ such that for each $y\in x,\,f(y)\subseteq y$ and $|f(y)|=\aleph_{0}(214)$, is true, every set can be linearly ordered (30) is true, there is a class of cardinal representatives, hence form 97 is true, but $C(\aleph_{1},\,\aleph_{0})$ is false because $<I_{\alpha}:\alpha\in \omega_{1}>$ has no choice function. Therefore, forms 39 $(C(\aleph_{1},\,\infty))$ and 85 $(C(\infty,\,\aleph_{0}))$ are false. Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 163 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) is also false because 43 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a}). Since form 43 implies form 296 (Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets.) it follows from Pincus \cite{bib:1997} that form 295 (Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering.) is also true. (30 + 296 implies 295.) Form 62 $(C(\infty,\, <\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 295 implies 62 and form 60 $(C(\infty,\,WO))$ is false because 60 implies 85. Therefore, form 329 $(MC(\infty,\,WO))$ is false because 62 + 329 $\rightarrow$ 60.

$\mathcal{M}1(\langle\omega_{1}\rangle) \models$ 30, 43, 97, 214, and 295, but 20, 39, 85, 91, 133, 151, 163, 328, and 329 are false. References Pincus \cite{bib:1977a}, \cite{bib:1997}, Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}, note 18, and note 120(32, 43, and 47).

$\mathcal{M}2$: Feferman's model. Add a denumerable number of generic reals to the base model, but do not collect them. Feferman\index{Author}{Feferman} has shown that in this model there is an infinite set of pairs with no choice function (88 is false), there is a partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ with no choice function (203 is false) and the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is false. Truss \cite{bib:1978}\index{Author}{Truss} has shown that in this model $C(WO,\, \infty)$ (40) is true. (He gives credit to Solovay for the proof.) In Truss \cite{bib:1978} it is also shown that $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ does not have a non-trivial ultrafilter (70 is false), and for every infinite set $x$ there is a mapping of $x$ onto $2\times x$ (204) is true. (See note 65.) Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} shows that there is a set of reals that does not have the property of Baire (142 is true), but $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ has no nontrivial real valued measure which is 0 on finite sets (222 is false). (The proof of form 142 requires that the Continuum Hypothesis holds in the outer model.) Since 40 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Truss \cite{bib:1974b} proves that there is a sequence $x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\cdots$ of cardinals such that for each $n,\, x_{n}=\aleph_{n+1}+2^{\aleph_{0}}$ adj $\aleph_{n+1}+\aleph_{2}\cdot2^{\aleph_{0}}$ adj $\aleph_{n+1}+\aleph_{3}\cdot2^{\aleph_{0}}$ adj $\cdots$ adj $\aleph_{n+1}+\aleph_{n+1}\cdot 2^{\aleph_{0}}=x_{n}^{2}$. (The symbol $x$ adj $y$ means $x<y$ and there is nothing between $x$ and $y$.) It follows that 274 is false.

$\mathcal{M}2 \models$ 40, 142, 165, and 204, but 70, 88, 152, 163, 203, 222, and 274 are false. References Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}, Feferman \cite{bib:1965}, Pincus \cite{bib:1972c}, Truss \cite{bib:1978}, \cite{bib:1974b}, note 65, and note 120(34 and 46). (See also Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1971a} pp 160-166 where credit for some of the proofs is given to D. Scott and R. Solovay.)

$\mathcal{M}2(\kappa)$: Feferman/Pincus Model. This is an extension of $\mathcal{M}2$ in which there are $\kappa$ generic sets, where $\kappa$ is a regular cardinal. ($\mathcal{M}2$ is $\mathcal{M}2(\aleph_{0}).)$ Pincus proves that the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) is false in this model. If $\kappa$ is sufficiently large, then there is a non-trivial measure on $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ which is 0 on finite sets (222 is true). $\kappa$ has to be large enough so that form 222 is boundable in sets of rank $\mu$, where $\mu$ is less than $\kappa.$

$\mathcal{M}2(\kappa) \models$ 222, but 52, and 91 are false. References Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972c} and note 18.

$\mathcal{M}2(\langle\omega_{2}\rangle)$: Feferman/Truss\index{Author}{Truss} Model. This is another extension of $\mathcal{M}2$. The set of all sequences of generic reals of length less than $\omega_{2}$ are added to a countable transitive model of ZFC + V = L. Truss proves that $C(|\mathbb{R}|,\,\infty)$ (181) is true, but there is a partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ that has no choice function (203 is false). Since the Axiom of choice is false, it follows that all forms that imply AC in ZF are also false. In particular, $C(LO,\,\infty)$ (202), is false. (See the first paragraph of section I.) Form 163 (every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset) is also false because 181 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a}).

$\mathcal{M}2(\langle \omega_{2}\rangle) \models$ 181, but 163, 202, and 203 are false. References Truss \cite{bib:1978} and Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}.

$\mathcal{M}3$: Mathias' model. Mathias proves that the FM model $\mathcal{N}4$ can be transformed into a model of ZF, $\mathcal{M}3$. $\mathcal{M}3$ is an extension of $\mathcal{M}1$ in which a universal homogeneous partial ordering is defined on $b$, the set of generic reals. (See Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 101 for definitions.) Mathias then proves that the partial ordering on $b$ cannot be extended to a linear ordering (49 is false), but every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true). Also, in this model, every set of well orderable sets has a choice function (60) and the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) are true. Form 60 implies 294 (Every linearly ordered $W$-set is well orderable.), and 30 + 294 + 144 (Every set is a $W$-set.) implies AC. It follows that 144 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.) Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (15 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false because 64 + 133 implies AC. The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is false because 14 implies 49, and $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ (62) is true because 15 implies 62. It was shown by Blass (see note 33) that 62 + 99 (Rado's Selection Lemma) implies 14, so form 99 is false.

$\mathcal{M}3 \models$ 15, 60, and 165, but 49, 91, 99, 144, 152, and 133 are false. References Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} \cite{bib:1967}, notes 25, 33 and 120(6, 34 and 43). Also, see Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1971a} (pp 114--128) and Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} (p 113, prob 8).

$\mathcal{M}4$: Pincus' Model I. This model has many of the properties of the model given in Cohen\index{Author}{Cohen} \cite{bib:1966} (p 143). The ground model, $\mathcal{M}$, is a model of ZF + V = L. Forcing conditions are functions from countable subsets of $\omega_{1}$ to $\{0, 1\}$. $\mathcal{M}4$ is a symmetric submodel of the corresponding generic extension of $\mathcal{M}$. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} proves that the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) is true, but there is an infinite set with no denumerable subset (9 is false), and there is a denumerable family of pairs that has no choice function. It follows that $KW(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$ (358) and $C(\infty,\,2)$ (88) are false. Pincus also proves that the Krein-Milman Theorem (65) is false. (Since BPI (form 14) implies 358, BPI is also false.)

$\mathcal{M}4 \models$ 52, but 65, 88, 91, and 358 are false. References Pincus \cite{bib:1972c} and note 18.

$\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$: Solovay's Model. An inaccessible cardinal $\aleph$ is collapsed to $\aleph_{1}$ in the outer model and then $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$ is the smallest model containing the ordinals and $\mathbb{R}$. (The method of collapsing cardinals that is used in the model and some of the proofs are due to A. Levy. An inaccessible cardinal is used to construct the model. See, for example, Drake\index{Author}{Drake} \cite{bib:1974}, Kanamori/Magador\index{Author}{Kanamori/Magador} \cite{bib:1978} or Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori\index{Author}{Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori} \cite{bib:1978} for information about large cardinals.) In this model, The Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true and every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable (93 is false). Moreover, if $\aleph$ is a measurable cardinal, then so is $\aleph_{1}$ (318 is false). (Also, see Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1968a}.) (It has been shown by Shelah\index{Author}{Shelah} \cite{bib:1984} and Raisonnier \cite{bib:1984} that if ZF + $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)(8)+\neg\ 93$ is consistent (43 implies 8), then so is ZFC + ``there exists an inaccessible cardinal''. Thus, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is necessary for this result.) Moreover, in $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$, every set of reals has the Baire property (142 is false) and the cardinal $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ is not well orderable and is not decomposable (the sum of two smaller positive cardinals) so 277 is false. Also, the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) and the Axiom of Choice for pairs (88) are false. Every uncountable set of reals contains a perfect subset (169 is false). The following two statements are also false in this model: There is a complete separable metric space with a non meager subset (280) and there is a Hilbert space $H$ and an unbounded linear operator on $H$ (281). (See also note 96.) Stern\index{Author}{Stern} proves that in this model, every infinite sequence of Borel sets of the same rank is countable (224 is false). (Truss\index{Author}{Truss} has shown that if the same construction is used with $\aleph$ a limit cardinal then 169 is still false, but 43 is also false. See $\mathcal{M}12(\aleph).)$ Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} has shown that there is no non-Ramsey set (234 is false). According to Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} \cite{bib:1991}, if $m$ is the cardinality of the set of Vitali equivalence classes, then, in $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$, $H(m)=H(2^{\aleph_{0}})$, where $H$ is Hartogs' function (307 is true). $(H(x)$ is the smallest ordinal that is not similar to a subset of $x$ and the Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation $x\equiv y\leftrightarrow(\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).)$ Since 43 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) In Wagon\index{Author}{Wagon} \cite{bib:1985}, it is shown that $\mathbb{Z}$ is not amenable in $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$ (313 is false) and that there is an amenable group with a non-amenable subgroup in $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$ (312 is false). ($G$ is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A).)$

$\mathcal{M}5(\aleph) \models$ 43 and 307, but 88, 93, 142, 163, 169, 224, 234, 277, 280, 281, 312, 313, and 318 are false. $\mathcal{M}6$: Sageev's Model I. Using iterated forcing, Sageev\index{Author}{Sageev} constructs $\mathcal{M}6$ by adding a denumerable number of generic tree-like structures to the ground model, a model of ZF + V = L. He proves that in $\mathcal{M}6$, every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true) and the $2m=m$ principle (3) holds, but the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable set of denumerable subsets of the reals (5) is false. Gonzalez has shown that every infinite set has a dense linear ordering in $\mathcal{M}6$ (295 is true). Form 3 implies form 10 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0}))$ and form 231 $(UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO))$ implies form 5. Thus, form 10 is true and form 231 is false. It is shown in note 123 that 10 + 163 (Every non well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) implies 231. Consequently, form 163 is false. (Halpern/Howard\index{Author}{Halpern/Howard} \cite{bib:1970} have shown using a permutation model that the $2m=m$ principle does not imply the Axiom of Choice in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ See $\mathcal{N}9$.) Form 165 $(C(WO,\,WO))$ is false because 165 implies 5 and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 295 implies 122. Therefore, form 330 $(MC(WO,\,WO))$ is false because 122 + 330 $\rightarrow$ 165. In addition, 126 $(MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$ is false because 30 is true and 5 is false. $(8\,(C(\aleph_{0},\, \infty))$ implies 5 and 30 + 126 implies 8.)

$\mathcal{M}7$: Cohen's Second Model. In this model there are two denumerable sets $U = \{U_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ and $V=\{V_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ such that for each $i\in \omega,\,U_{i}$ and $V_{i}$ cannot be distinguished. Therefore, in this model there is a denumerable set of pairs whose union has no denumerable subset, so form 18 is false, and $KW(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$ (358) is also false. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} has shown that in every symmetric model there is a set $X$ such that for each set $a$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function $f$ mapping $X\times\alpha$ onto $a$ (191 is true). (See note 59.) It is shown in Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} \cite{bib:1995} that in this model there is a Lindel\"{o}f metric space that is neither second countable nor separable (340 and 341 are false).

$\mathcal{M}8$: Apter's Model. Suppose $\mathcal{M} \models$ ZFC $+$ ``There are cardinals $\kappa <\delta< \lambda$ such that $\kappa$ is a supercompact limit of supercompact cardinals, $\lambda$ is a measurable cardinal, and $\delta$ is $\lambda$ supercompact.'' (See, for example, Drake\index{Author}{Drake} \cite{bib:1974}, Kanamori/Magador\index{Author}{Kanamori/Magador} \cite{bib:1978}, or Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori\index{Author}{Solovay/Reinhardt/Kanamori} \cite{bib:1978} for information about large cardinals.) $\mathcal{M}8$ is constructed by first forcing over the ground model $\mathcal{M}$, constructing an inner model $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, doing an additional forcing argument over $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, and then constructing the final inner model $\mathcal{M}8$. In this model $\aleph_{n}$, for $3\leq n\leq\omega$ are singular cardinals so 25 ($\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is regular for all ordinals $\alpha$.) is false. Also, the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable number of sets, 8, is false. (Supercompact and measurable cardinals are used to construct the model.)

In $\mathcal{M}8$, forms 8, 25, and 91 are false. References Apter\index{Author}{Apter} \cite{bib:1985a}, notes 18 and 20.

$\mathcal{M}9$: Feferman/Levy Model. Assume the ground model, $\mathcal{M}$, satisfies ZF + GCH (the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis). Let $P$, the set of forcing conditions, be the set of all finite sets $p$ of triples $(n,\,i,\, \alpha)$ that satisfy: (i) $n\in \omega,\,i\in\omega, \alpha\in\omega_{n}$; and (ii) $(n,\,i,\,\alpha)$, $(n,\,i,\,\beta)\in p$ implies $\alpha=\beta$. Let $G$ be a generic subset of $P$ and let $\mathcal{M}[G]$ be the corresponding generic extension of $\mathcal{M}$. $\mathcal{M}9$ is a symmetric submodel of $\mathcal{M}[G]$. In this model, $\mathbb{R}\subseteq\bigcup\{R_{n}:n\in \omega\}$, where $|R_{n}|=\aleph_{n+1}$ for $n\in \omega$, and $|\aleph_{n}|=|\aleph_{0}|$ for each $n\in \omega$. Therefore, the set of real numbers is a countable union of countable sets (38 is false).

In $\mathcal{M}$9, form 38 is false. References Feferman/Levy\index{Author}{Feferman/Levy} \cite{bib:1963}, Cohen\index{Author}{Cohen} \cite{bib:1966} (p 143), Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} (p 142).

$\mathcal{M}10$: Derrick/Drake\index{Author}{Derrick/Drake} Model. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a model of ZF
+ GCH. Add to $\mathcal{M}$ generic functions $f_{n}$ for each $n\in \omega$, where $f_{n}:\omega_{n}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(w)$, but do not add $\{f_{n}:n\in \omega\}$. It is shown that in this model $\aleph(2^{\aleph_{0}})=\aleph_{\omega}$ (56 is false). $(\aleph(x)$ is the smallest ordinal that is not similar to a subset of $x$, Hartogs' function.) (In fact, for every $\alpha>0$, it is consistent with ZF that $\aleph(2^{\aleph_{0}})=\aleph_{\alpha}.)$ It is shown by Truss\index{Author}{Truss} that in $\mathcal{M}10$ the sequence $\{\aleph_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ has two distinct minimal upper bounds $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ and $\aleph_{\omega}$. $\mathcal{M}11$: Forti/Honsell Model. Using a model of ZF + V = L for the ground model, the authors construct a generic extension, $\mathcal{M}$, using Easton\index{Author}{Easton} forcing which adds $\kappa$ generic subsets to each regular cardinal $\kappa$. (See Easton \cite{bib:1970}.) Then, $\mathcal{M}11$ is a symmetric submodel of $\mathcal{M}$. In this model, the Kinna-Wagner Principle (15) and the Axiom of Choice for a family of well orderable sets (60) are true, but for any partially ordered set $(X,\,\precsim)$ there is a bijection $f:X\rightarrow Y$ such that for all $x,\, y\in X,\,x\precsim\ y\leftrightarrow|f(x)|\leq|f(y)|$ (105 is false). Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 163 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) is also false because 43 implies 8 and 8 + 163 implies AC (Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a}). Form 15 implies the Ordering Principle (30) and form 60 implies that every linearly ordered set that is almost well orderable is well orderable (294). (See note 25 for definitions.) However, 30 + 144 (Every set is almost well orderable.) + 231 iff AC. Thus, form 144 is false.

$\mathcal{M}12(\aleph)$: Truss'\index{Author}{Truss} Model I. This is a variation of Solovay's model, $\mathcal{M}5(\aleph)$ in which $\aleph$ is singular. (Truss uses the method of collapsing cardinal which is due to A. Levy, but, unlike $\mathcal{M}5$, $\aleph$ is not an inaccessible cardinal.) Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a countable model of ZF + V = L and let $\aleph$ be a limit cardinal in $\mathcal{M}$. For each ordinal $\alpha$, the set of conditions $Q^{\alpha}$ is the set of finite sets $p$ of triples, $(\beta,\,n,\,\gamma)$ where $\gamma<\beta<\alpha$ and $n\in \omega$ such that if $(\beta,\,n,\,\gamma_{1})$, $(\beta,\,n,\,\gamma_{2})\in p$, then $\gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}$. $Q_{\alpha}$ is the set of finite sets $p$ of pairs of the form $(n,\,\gamma)$ where $\gamma<\alpha$ and $n\in \omega$ such that if $(n,\,\gamma_{1})$, $(n,\, \gamma_{2})\in p$ then $\gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}$.
A function $f: \omega\rightarrow\alpha$ is called an $\mathcal{M}$-\emph{generic collapsing map} if the set of finite subsets of $\{(n,\,\gamma):f(n)=\gamma\}$ is an $\mathcal{M}$-generic subset of $Q_{\alpha}$. Let $G$ be an $\mathcal{M}$-generic subset of $Q^{\aleph}$ then, $G_{\alpha}$, the projection of $G$ onto $Q_{\alpha}$ is an $\mathcal{M}$-generic subset of $Q_{\alpha}$, for each $\alpha< \aleph$. Let $f_{\alpha}=\bigcup G_{\alpha}$. Then $\mathcal{M}12(\aleph)$ is the smallest model of ZF containing the same ordinals as $\mathcal{M}$ and each $\langle f_{\beta}:\beta<\alpha\rangle$ for $\alpha<\aleph$. In $\mathcal{M}12(\aleph)$, $\aleph=\omega_{1}$. If $\aleph$ is singular, $\omega_{1}$ is singular so 34 is false. On the other hand, the union of a denumerable set of denumerable sets of reals is denumerable (6 is true) and the union of a well ordered set of well orderable sets can be well ordered (231 is true). $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\omega))$ cannot be linearly ordered, so 30 is false. Truss also proves that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is false, every set of reals is Borel (273 is false), and every uncountable set of reals has a perfect subset (169 is false). Form 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 40 implies 31 and form 122 $(C(WO,\, <\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 231 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 $(MC(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 122 + 328 $\rightarrow$ 40

$\mathcal{M}12(\aleph)\models$ 6 and 231, but 30, 31, 34, 43, 106, 152, 169, 273, and 328 are false. References Truss \cite{bib:1974b} and note 43 and 120(43 and 55).

$\mathcal{M}14$: Morris'\index{Author}{Morris} Model. This is an extension of Mathias' model, $\mathcal{M}3$. Morris shows that the cofinal subsets of the partially ordered set $b$, the set of generic reals, can be systematically well ordered. He then proves that in this model, the Cofinality Principle (51) and the Ordering Principle (30) are true, but the Order Extension Principle (49) is false. Forms 30 and 294 (Every linearly ordered $W$-set is well orderable.) are both true in this model (51 implies 294). Since 30 + 294 + 144 (Every set is a $W$-set.) implies AC, it follows that 144 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.) Moreover, form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), so form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false because 64 + 133 implies AC. The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is false because 14 implies 49, and $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})(62)$ is true because 30 implies 62. It was shown by Blass (see note 33) that 62 +
99 (Rado's Selection Lemma) implies 14, so form 99 is false.

$\mathcal{M}15$: Feferman/Blass Model. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} constructs a model similar to Feferman's model, $\mathcal{M}2$. Suppose $\mathcal{M}$ = ZF + V = L. By forcing with finite partial functions from $\omega \times \omega$ into 2, a generic extension $\mathcal{M}[G]$ of $\mathcal{M}$ is obtained that contains an $\omega$-sequence of generic reals $a_{n}\subseteq \omega$. For each $x\subseteq\omega$,
let $\delta(x)$ be the set of reals whose symmetric difference with $x$ is finite. Let $f$ be the function in $\mathcal{M}[G]$ such that for all $n\in\omega,\,f(n)=\{\delta(a_{n}),\, \delta(\omega-a_{n})\}$. Let $S=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}(\delta(a_{n})\cup\delta(\omega-a_{n}))\cup\{f\}$. $\mathcal{M}15$ is the submodel of $\mathcal{M}[G]$ that is hereditarily ordinal definable from $S$ and $\bigcup\ S$. In this model, every set is almost well orderable (144 is true) and all ultrafilters are principal (206 is false). Howard\index{Author}{Howard} has shown that if form 206 is false, then {\L}os' Theorem (253) is true.

$\mathcal{M}15 \models$ 144 and 253, but 206 is false. References Blass \cite{bib:1977b}, Feferman\index{Author}{Feferman} \cite{bib:1965}, Howard \cite{bib:1975}.

$\mathcal{M}16(n)$: Monro's Model I. Monro has constructed an $\omega$-sequence of models of ZF such that,

$(\ast)$ For each ordinal $\alpha,\,\mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha)$ is the same in the $n$th model and the $n + 1$st model.

\noindent $(\mathcal{P}^{0}(\alpha)=\alpha$, and $\mathcal{P}^{n+1}(\alpha)=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha)).)$ He starts with a countable transitive model $\mathcal{M} \models$ ZF + V
= L. Let $H_{\kappa}(A,\,B)$ be the set of all functions $f\subseteq A\times B$ such that $|\mathrm{dom}(f)|<\kappa$. Let $\mathcal{M}^{0}=\mathcal{M}$ and $J^{0}=\omega$. Then $\mathcal{M}^{k+1}$ is obtained from $\mathcal{M}^{k}$ as follows. Let $G^{k+1}$ be $H_{\omega}(J^{k}\times J^{k},\,2)$-generic over $\mathcal{M}_{k}$. For $r\in J^{k}$, let $G_{r}^{k+1}= \{(s,\,a):(r,\,s,\,a)\in\bigcup(G^{k+1}\}$. $(G_{r}^{k+1}:J^{k}\rightarrow 2.)$ Then $J^{k+1}=\{G_{r}^{k+1}:r\in J^{k}\}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{k+1}=\mathcal{M}^{k}[G^{k+1}]$. Let $K(n)$ be the statement: For every set $x$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a 1-1 function $f:x\longrightarrow \mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha)$. $(K(n)$ is form $81(n)$; $K(0)$ is equivalent to AC; and $K(1)$ is equivalent to the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle, form 15.) Monro proves that if $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ are two models such that for each $\alpha,\,\mathcal{P}^{n}(\alpha)$ is the same in each model and, in addition, $\mathcal{M}_{1}\neq \mathcal{M}_{2}$, then $K(n-1)$ is false in each model. Since, each successive pair of models in the sequence constructed has the property $(\ast)$, it follows that for each $n\in \omega$, there is a model of ZF in which 81$(n)$ is false. Monro also proves that for each $n\in \omega$, $\mathcal{M}^{n}\models K(n+1)$. Consequently, it follows that for all $n>0,\,K(n+1) \not\rightarrow\ K(n-1)$.

In $\mathcal{M}16(n)$, forms 15, 81$(n)$, and 91 are false. References Monro \cite{bib:1972}, \cite{bib:1973b}, note 18.

$\mathcal{M}17$: Gitik's Model. Using the assumption that for every ordinal $\alpha$ there is a strongly compact cardinal $\kappa$ such that $\kappa >\alpha$, Gitik\index{Author}{Gitik} extends the universe $V$ by a filter $G$ generic over a proper class of forcing conditions. (Inaccessible cardinals are used in the construction.) In $V[G]$, he constructs a symmetric submodel $\mathcal{M}17$ in which every infinite set is a countable union of sets of smaller cardinality. Thus, there is no regular uncountable cardinal (104 is false), there is no aleph whose cofinality is greater than $\aleph_{0}$ (182 is false), and $\Omega=$ On (315 is false). See note 55. $\mathcal{M}19(\aleph)$: Monro's Model II. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a countable transitive model of ZF + V = L and let $\aleph$ be a regular cardinal in $\mathcal{M}$. A forcing condition is a partial function, $p$, of cardinality less than $\aleph$ such that $p:\aleph\times\aleph\rightarrow 2$. Let $G$ be a generic subset of the set of forcing conditions and let $\mathcal{M}[G]$ be the corresponding generic extension.

Let $p(\mu)=\{(\nu,\,i):(\mu,\,\nu,\,i)\in p\}$, for each $\mu<\aleph$, let $G_{\mu}=\{p(\mu):p\in G\}$, and $G^{\ast}=\{G_{\mu}:\mu<\aleph\}$. Then $\mathcal{M}19(\aleph)$ is the set of all sets in $\mathcal{M}[G]$ that are constructible from $G^{\ast}.$ Monro\index{Author}{Monro} proves that $\mathcal{M}19(\aleph)$ has the same ordinals and alephs as $\mathcal{M}$ and that $G^{\ast}$ is an infinite Dedekind finite set in $\mathcal{M}19(\aleph)$. He also proves that if $x$ is any set that cannot be well ordered, then x can be mapped onto $\aleph$. Thus, $G^{\ast}$ can be mapped onto $\aleph$ so form 160 is false.

In $\mathcal{M}19(\aleph)$, forms 91 and 160 are false. References Monro \cite{bib:1975} and note 18.

$\mathcal{M}20$: Felgner's Model I. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a model of ZF +
V = L. Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} defines forcing conditions that force $\aleph_{\omega}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ to be $\aleph_{1}$. He then proves that in the resulting model, $\mathcal{M}20$, every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true) and the union of a well ordered set of well orderable sets can be well ordered (231 is true), but there is a denumerable set of denumerable sets which does not have a denumerable union (31 is false). Also, in this model every set of well orderable sets has a choice function (60 is true). Form 60 implies 294 (Every linearly ordered $W$-set is well orderable.), and 30 + 294 + 144 (Every set is a $W$-set.) implies AC. It follows that 144 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.) Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 40 implies 31 and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 30 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 $(MC(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 122 + 328 $\rightarrow$ 40.

$\mathcal{M}20 \models$ 30, 60, 165, and 231, but 31, 91, 131, 133, 144, 152, and 328 are false. References Felgner \cite{bib:1974}, notes 18, 25, and 120(34, 43, and 49).

$\mathcal{M}22$: Plotkin's Model I. Let $T$ be a complete first order theory with equality which has infinite models and is $\aleph_{0}$-categorical. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a countable standard transitive model of ZFC which contains a countable model $\mathfrak{A}$ of $T$. It is shown in Plotkin\index{Author}{Plotkin} \cite{bib:1969} that there is a generic extension of $\mathcal{M}$ that contains an isomorphic copy, $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$, of $\mathfrak{A}$, such that in the symmetric submodel constructed, $\mathfrak{A}^{\prime}$ is infinite, Dedekind finite, and the relations of $T$ are definable. Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $T$ be the first order theory of an infinite extra-special $p$-group of exponent $p$. (See note 24 for definitions.) It is shown in Felgner \cite{bib:1975} that this theory is complete and $\aleph_{0}$-categorical. $\mathcal{M}22$ is the resulting model. Plotkin \cite{bib:1981} proves the countable extra-special $p$-groups of exponent $p$ in $\mathcal{M}22$ are all locally finite and have no infinite Abelian subgroups. (Locally finite means that every finite subset generates a finite subgroup.) Thus, form 176 is false. (Since the groups constructed are infinite and Dedekind finite, form 9 is also false.)

In $\mathcal{M}22$, forms 9, 91 and 176 are false. References Plotkin \cite{bib:1969}, \cite{bib:1981}, Felgner \cite{bib:1975}, notes 18 and 24.

$\mathcal{M}23$: Hodges' Model. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a countable transitive model of ZFC + V = L and let $\kappa$ be a regular cardinal in $\mathcal{M}$. Let $A=\sum\nolimits_{\alpha<\kappa}A_{\alpha}$, where each $A_{\alpha}$ is a copy of the cyclic group $Z(4)$. Using forcing conditions of the form $p:A\times\kappa \times\kappa \rightarrow 2$, where $p$ is a partial function with domain of cardinality less than $\kappa$, it is shown in Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} \cite{bib:1976b} that there is a generic extension $\mathcal{M}[G]$ in which there is a generic copy of $A$. It is also shown in Hodges \cite{bib:1976b} that $\mathcal{M}[G]$ can be cut down to a transitive model of ZF which contains $A$ and all elements are definable from elements of $\mathcal{M}$ and sequences of generic sets of length less than $\kappa$. This is the model $\mathcal{M}23$, It is shown in Hodges \cite{bib:1980} that in $\mathcal{M}23,\,A$ is an Abelian group with no divisible hull (180 is false). (If $A$ and $B$ are groups, ``$B$ is a divisible hull of $A$'' means $B$ is a divisible group, $A$ is a subgroup of $B$ and for every non-zero $b\in B,\,\exists n\in w$ such that $0\neq nb\in A$. An Abelian group $B$ is divisible if $n$ divides $a$ for all $a\in B$ and positive $n\in\omega.)$

In $\mathcal{M}23$, forms 91 and 180 are false. References Hodges\index{Author}{Hodges} \cite{bib:1976b}, \cite{bib:1980}, and note 18.

\noindent $\mathcal{M}24$: Blass' Model. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a countable transitive model of ZFC + V = L. For each regular cardinal $\xi$ adjoin generic sets $b_{\xi}^{i}\subseteq\xi$ for each $i\in \mathbb{Z}$ using Easton forcing. (See Easton\index{Author}{Easton} \cite{bib:1970}. There is a proper class of generic sets.) Call the resulting forcing extension $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$. In $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, let $a_{\xi}^{i}$ be the set of all subsets of $\xi$ whose symmetric difference with $b_{\xi}^{i}$ is a constructible set of cardinality less than $\xi$. For each regular $\xi$ and each $i\in \mathbb{Z}$, define $S(a_{\xi}^{i})=a_{\xi}^{i+1}.$ Let $\mathcal{M}24$ be the submodel of $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ consisting of all sets that are hereditarily ordinal definable from $S$ and the $b_{\xi}^{i}$'s. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} has shown that in this model there is no non-trivial injective Abelian group. (See note 60 for definitions.)

In $\mathcal{M}24$, forms 91 and 190 are false. References Blass \cite{bib:1979}, Easton \cite{bib:1970}, notes 18 and 60.

$\mathcal{M}25:$ Freyd's\index{Author}{Freyd} Model. Using topos-theoretic methods due to Fourman\index{Author}{Fourman}, Freyd constructs a Boolean-valued model of ZF in which every well ordered family of sets has a choice function (40 is true), but $C(|\mathbb{R}|,\,\infty)(181)$ is false. Freyd describes an algebraic theory with two constants, three unary operations, and two binary operations. (See Freyd \cite{bib:1980}, p 112.) Let $F$ be the free algebra generated by the two constants and let $\mathcal{B}(F)$ be the corresponding category of Boolean sheaves. The Fourman interpretation arising from $\mathcal{B}(F)$ is the desired model. (See, for example, MacLane\index{Author}{MacLane} \cite{bib:1971} and Johnstone\index{Author}{Johnstone} \cite{bib:1977} for background information on category theory.)

Since 40 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.)

$\mathcal{M}27$: Pincus/Solovay Model I. Let $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ be a model of ZFC + V = L. $R\in 2^{x}$ is said to be \emph{random} if $R\in b$ for every constructible Borel set $b$ which has Lebesgue measure 1. Let $\mathcal{M}_{2}=L(R)$, where $R$ is a random element of $2^{\omega^{L}_{1}}.$ (Models like this were also discussed in Sacks\index{Author}{Sacks} \cite{bib:1969} and Solovay\index{Author}{Solovay} \cite{bib:1971}.) In $\mathcal{M}_{2}$, for each $\alpha\in \omega_{1}$, let $r_{\alpha}=R|\alpha\cdot \omega$. Let $G_{\alpha}^{\ast}$ be the set of all subsets of $\alpha\cdot \omega$ which are finite unions of half open intervals of the form $[\gamma\cdot\omega,\,(\gamma+1)\cdot \omega)$, and $G_{\alpha}$ is the set of subsets of $\alpha\cdot \omega$ which differ finitely from a member of $G_{\alpha}^{\ast}$ . $G_{\alpha}$ is an Abelian group under the operation of symmetric difference. Let $F$ be the function on $\omega_{1}$ such that for each $\alpha\in \omega_{1},\,F(\alpha)$ is the orbit of $r_{\alpha}$ under the action of the group $G_{\alpha}$. Then, $\mathcal{M}27$ is the smallest model of ZF containing $F$. Solovay proves that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) and the Hahn-Banach Theorem (52) are true in $\mathcal{M}27$, but all ultrafilters are principal in this model so 206 is false. Since 43 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1975} has shown that if form 206 is false, then {\L}o\'{s}' Theorem (253) is true. Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1993} has shown that if form 9 is true and form 206 is false then there does not exist an infinite, compact, Hausdorff, extremally disconnected topological space so form 371 is false.

$\mathcal{M}27 \models$ 43, 52, and 253, but 163, 206, 286, and 371 are false. $\mathcal{M}29$: Pincus' Model II. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} constructs a generic extension $M[I]$ of a model $M$ of ZF + class choice + GCH in which $I=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}I_{n},\,I_{-1}=2$ and $I_{n+1}$ is a denumerable set of independent functions from $\omega$ onto $I_{n}$. In this model $\{I_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ is a denumerable set of denumerable sets which has neither a choice function (32 is false), nor a Kinna-Wagner selection function $(KW(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$, 357 is false), nor a multiple choice function $(MC(\aleph_{0},\, \aleph_{0})$, 350 is false); $|I|<|2\times I|$ (3 is false); every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true); every infinite set has a denumerable subset (9 is true); and for all infinite $x,\, |x!|=|2^{x}|=|x^{x}|$ (200, 290, and 291 are true). Pincus also proves that if $x$ is a set of infinite sets, then there is a function $f$ with domain $x$ such that for each $y\in x,\,f(y)\subseteq y$, and $|f(y)|=\aleph_{0}$ (214 is true). In this model form 10 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true (30 implies 10) and form 165 $(C(WO,\,WO))$ is false (165 implies 32). Thus, form 163 (Every non well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) is false because Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} shows that 10 + 163 implies 165. Since form 30 is true and form 214 implies form 296 (Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets.), it follows from Pincus \cite{bib:1997} that form 295 (Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering.) is true.

$\mathcal{M}30$: Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus}/Solovay Model II. In this construction, an $\omega_{1}$ sequence of generic reals is added to a model of ZFC in such a way that the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true, but no nonprincipal measure exists (223 is false). (The construction is similar to that given for $\mathcal{M}27$.) Since 43 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1975} has shown that if form 206 (There exists a nonprincipal ultrafilter.) is false (206 implies 223), then {\L}os' Theorem (253) is true. By results of Wagon\index{Author}{Wagon} \cite{bib:1985}, the amenable groups in $\mathcal{M}30$ are the finite groups and therefore 312 (A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable.) is true and 313 ($\mathbb{Z}$ (the set of integers under addition) is amenable.) is false. $(G$ is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{P}(G)$ such that $\mu(G)=1$ and $\forall A\subseteq G,\, \forall g\in G,\,\mu(gA)=\mu(A).)$

$\mathcal{M}30 \models$ 43, 253, and 312, but 163, 223, and 313 are false. References Pincus/Solovay\index{Author}{Pincus/Solovay} \cite{bib:1977}, Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}, Howard \cite{bib:1975}, and Wagon \cite{bib:1985}.

$\mathcal{M}31$: Szczepaniak's\index{Author}{Szczepaniak} Model. Two models of ZF, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2},\,M_{1}\subseteq M_{2}$, are constructed with the same ordinals (so $L^{1}$ in $M_{1}$ is the same as $L^{1}$ in $M_{2}$), and a generic real $a\in M_{1}$ so that $a\not\in HOD$ in $M_{1}$, but $a\in HOD$ in $M_{2}$. Thus, in at least one of these models $L^{1}\neq HOD$ and that is the model we call $\mathcal{M}31$. (See note 82 for definitions.)

In $\mathcal{M}31$, forms 91 and 230 are false. References Szczepaniak \cite{bib:1977}, notes 18 and 82.

$\mathcal{M}32$: Sageev's Model II. Starting with a model $\mathcal{M}$ of ZF + V = L, Sageev constructs a sequence of models $\mathcal{M}\ \subseteq N_{0}\subseteq N_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq N_{\kappa}$ where $\kappa$ is an inaccessible cardinal, $N_{0}$ is Cohen's model $\mathcal{M}1$, and $N_{\kappa}$ is $\mathcal{M}32$. In this model, every set can be linearly ordered (30 is true); if $\Delta$ is the set of Dedekind finite cardinals, then $2^{\aleph_{0}}<|\Delta|\leq 2^{2^{\aleph_{0}}}$ (9 is false) and each pair of cardinals in $\Delta$ is comparable (57 is true). Sageev\index{Author}{Sageev} also shows that $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ (62) is true. Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 40 implies 9 and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 30 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 $(MC(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 122 + 328 $\rightarrow$ 40. In addition, 126 $(MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$ is false because 30 is true and 8 is false. $(8(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$ implies 9 and 30 + 126 implies 8).

$\mathcal{M}32 \models$ 30, 57, and 62, but 9, 91, 126, 133, and 328 are false. References Sageev \cite{bib:1981}, notes 18 and 120(9).

$\mathcal{M}33$: Plotkin's Model II. The construction is similar to the construction of $\mathcal{M}22.$ An atomless Boolean algebra in a countable standard modell $\mathcal{M}$ of ZF + V = L is embedded in a generic extension, $\mathcal{M}33$, of $\mathcal{M}$ in such a way that the isomorphic copy, $B$, of the Boolean algebra has the property that it is infinite, atomless, and Dedekind finite (9 and 247 are false) and $|B|^{\aleph_{0}}>|B|$ (248 is false). Plotkin also proves that $C(\infty,\,2)$ (88) is false in this model. Additional properties of $B$ include the following: Every filter in $B$ is principal; $B$ has no infinite free subalgebra; $B$ is not the direct union of complete weakly homogeneous Boolean algebras; $B$ is not inversely reducible. See Plotkin \cite{bib:1976} for definitions.

In $\mathcal{M}33$, forms 9, 88, 91, 247 and 248 are false. References Plotkin\index{Author}{Plotkin} \cite{bib:1969}, \cite{bib:1976}, and note 18.

$\mathcal{M}34(\aleph_{1})$: Pincus' Model III. Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} proves that Cohen's model $\mathcal{M}1$ can be extended by adding $\aleph_{1}$ generic sets along with the set $b$ containing them and well orderings of all countable subsets of $b$. The model is constructed in such a way that every collection of denumerable sets has a choice function (85 is true), but there is a denumerable collection of sets of cardinality $\aleph_{1}$ which does not have a choice function. Therefore, both $C(WO,\,WO)$ (165) and $C(\infty,\, \aleph_{1})$ (213) are false. Pincus also shows that the Kinna-Wagner Principle (15) and the Ordering Principle (30) are true. Since form 64 (There is no amorphous set.) is true (30 implies 64), form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset.) is false. Form 165 is false and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 15 implies 122. Therefore, form 330 $(MC(WO,\,WO))$ is false because 122 + 330 $\rightarrow$ 165.

$\mathcal{M}34 \models$ 15, 30 and 85, but 91, 133, 163, 165, 213, and 330 are false. References Pincus \cite{bib:1977a}, notes 74 and 120(6 and 30).

$\mathcal{M}35(\epsilon)$: David's Model. In Cohen's model $\mathcal{M}1$, define sets $B_{n}=\{x\subset\omega:|x\,\Delta\,a_{n}|<\omega \vee|x\,\Delta\, \omega -a_{n}|<\omega\}$ (where $\Delta$ is the symmetric difference). Let $C$ be the function on $\omega$ such that for each $n\in\omega$, $C(n)=B_{n}$. The symmetric submodel, $N$, of $\mathcal{M}1$ which is the set of all sets that are hereditarily ordinal definable from $\{C\}\cup\{a_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ has the property that $(\forall x\in N)(x\in W(1))$, but it is not the case that all sets are in $W(0)$, the set of all well orderable sets. (See note 25.) David proves that this procedure can be generalized so that for any ordinal $\epsilon$ there is a model, $\mathcal{M}35(\epsilon)$, such that for each set $x$ in the model, $x\in W(\epsilon)$, and $\epsilon$ is the smallest ordinal with this property. Thus, form $179(\epsilon)$ is true, so every set is almost well orderable (144) is true, but form $179(\beta)$, $\beta<\epsilon$, is false.

$\mathcal{M}35(\epsilon)\models$ 144 and $179(\epsilon)$, but 91 and $179(\beta)$, $\beta<\epsilon$, are false. References David\index{Author}{David} \cite{bib:1980}, notes 18 and 25.

$\mathcal{M}36$: Figura's Model. Starting with a countable, standard model, $\mathcal{M}$, of ZFC + 2$^{\aleph_{0}}=\aleph_{\omega+1}$, Figura\index{Author}{Figura} uses forcing conditions that are functions from a subset of $\omega\times\omega$ to $\omega_{\omega}$ to construct a symmetric extension of $\mathcal{M}$ in which there is an uncountable well ordered subset of the reals (170 is true), but $\aleph_{1}=\aleph_{\omega}$ so $\aleph_{1}$ is singular (34 is false). (In fact, Figura proves this result for any two cardinals $\kappa$ (replacing $\aleph_{0})$ and $\mu$ (replacing $\aleph_{\omega)}$) such that cf$(\kappa)=\kappa \leq \mathrm{cf}(\mu)<\mu$ and $2^{\kappa}=\mu^{+}$ in $\mathcal{M}$. See note 3.)

$\mathcal{M}36 \models$ 170, but 34 and 91 are false. References Figura \cite{bib:1981}, notes 3 and 18.

$\mathcal{M}37$: Monro's Model III. This is a generic extension of $\mathcal{M}1$ in which there is an amorphous set (64 is false) and $C(\infty,\,2)$ (88) is false. The model is constructed as follows: If $b$ is the countable set of generic reals from which $\mathcal{M}1$ is constructed, define a partial ordering $(Q,\,\leq)$ in $\mathcal{M}1$ where $Q$ is the set of ordered pair $(A,\,p)$ such that $A$ is a finite subset of $b$ and $\rho$: $A^{2}\rightarrow\{0, 1\}$ satisfies $\{(a,\,b):\rho(a,\,b)=1\}$ is an equivalence relation on $A$. The ordering $\leq$ is defined by $(B,\,\sigma)\leq(A,\,\rho)$ if and only if $A\subseteq B$ and $\sigma$ extends $\rho$. Let $F$ be $Q$ generic over $\mathcal{M}1$. Then Monro's model, $\mathcal{M}37$, is $\mathcal{M}1[F]$. In Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1993} it is shown that if form 64 is false then there is an infinite, compact, Hausdorff, extremally disconnected topological space and therefore 371 is true.

$\mathcal{M}37 \models$ 371 but 64, 88, and 91 are false. References Monro\index{Author}{Monro} \cite{bib:1972}, Morillon \cite{bib:1993}, and note 18.

$\mathcal{M}38$: Shelah's Model II. In a model of ZFC + $``\kappa$ is a strongly inaccessible cardinal'', Shelah\index{Author}{Shelah} uses Levy's method of collapsing cardinals to collapse $\kappa$ to $\aleph_{1}$ similarly to Solovay\index{Author}{Solovay} \cite{bib:1970}. (See $\mathcal{M}5$ and $\mathcal{M}12(\aleph)$.) He then builds a special forcing notion and constructs a model in which the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true and every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable (93 is false) just as in $\mathcal{M}5$. However, unlike $\mathcal{M}5$, in Shelah's model there is a set of reals without the Baire property (142 is true) and there is an uncountable set of reals with no perfect set (169 is true). Since 43 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.)
