\noindent $\mathcal{N}36(\beta)$: Brunner/Howard\index{Author}{Brunner/Howard} Model III. This model is a modification of $\mathcal{N}15$. $A= \{a_{i,\alpha}:i\in \omega\wedge\alpha\in \omega_{\beta+1}\}$. Let $\Gamma$ be the group of all permutations on $\omega$. Then $\mathcal{G}=\{g:(\exists\gamma\in\Gamma)(\forall i\in\omega))(\forall\alpha\in \omega_{\beta+1})g(a_{i,\alpha})=a_{\gamma(i),\alpha}\}$. $S$ is the set of all subsets of $A$ of cardinality at most $\aleph_{\beta}$. In this model $C(\aleph_{\beta},\,\infty)(86(\beta)$ is true and, therefore, $C(\aleph_{1},\,\infty)$ (39) is true if $\beta\geq 1$. The union of a denumerable set of finite sets is well orderable ([122 A] is true), but there is an infinite set that is not the union of a disjoint well orderable family of denumerable sets (152 is false). Since 39 implies 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\, \infty))$, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Since 8 implies 9 (Every Dedekind finite set is finite.) and 70 (There is a non-trivial ultrafilter on $\omega$.) is true in every FM model, it follows that 63 (Every infinite set has a non-trivial ultrafilter.) is also true. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} has shown that 191 (There is a set $X$ such that for each set $a$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function $f$ mapping $X\times\alpha$ onto $a$.) is true in every permutation model with a set of atoms. He has also shown that 8 + 191 + 193 (Every Abelian group is a homomorphic image of a free projective Abelian group.) iff AC. Thus, form 193 must be false. (See note 60 for definitions.) In note 144 we show dependent choice (form 43) if true.

References Brunner/Howard \cite{bib:1992}, Blass \cite{bib:1979}, Brunner \cite{bib:1982a}, notes 18, 60, 120(4 and 41), and 144.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}37$: A variation of Blass' model, $\mathcal{N}28$. Let $A=\{a_{i,j}:i\in \omega,\,j\in \mathbb{Z}\}$. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of permutations of $A$ generated by $\{\phi_{i}:i\in\omega\}$, where $\phi_{i}(a_{i,j})=a_{i,j+1}$ and if $k\neq i,\,\phi_{i}(a_{k,j})=a_{k,j}$. $S$ is the set of finite subsets of $A$. For each $i\in\omega$, let $E_{i}=\{a_{i,2j}:j\in \mathbb{Z}\}$ and $O_{i}=\{a_{i,2j+1}:j\in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Then $B=\{E_{i}:i\in\omega\}\cup\{O_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ is a partition of $A$. We define a linear ordering $\precsim$ on $A$ such that $a_{i,j}\precsim a_{k,l}$ if $i<k$, or $i=k$ and $j\leq l$, the lexicographical ordering. Note that $\{a_{i,0}\}$ is a support for $E_{i}$ and $O_{i}$, while the empty set is a support for $(A,\,\precsim)$ and $B$. Thus, $A$ can be linearly ordered, but $B$ cannot be linearly ordered (293 is false). $B$ is also an infinite set which does not admit a partition into sets of order type $^{\ast} \omega+\omega$ so form 129 is false. In H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} \cite{bib:1981} it is shown that $(A,\precsim)$ has no cofinal well ordered subset (form 51 is false) and that every linear ordering with the fixed point property is complete (316 is true). $((A,\, \precsim)$ has the \emph{fixed point} property if every function $f:A\rightarrow A$ satisfying $(x\precsim y\Rightarrow f(x)\precsim f(y))$ has a fixed point, and $((A,\precsim)$ is \emph{complete} if every non-empty subset of $A$ has a least upper bound.)

\noindent $\mathcal{N}38$: Howard/Rubin Model I. Let $(A,\,\leq)$ be an ordered set of atoms which is order isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}^{\omega}$, the set of all functions from $\omega$ into $\mathbb{Q}$ ordered by the lexicographic ordering. That is, if $a,\,b\in \mathbb{Q}^{\omega}$ then $a<b$ if and only if there is some $n\in \omega$ such that $(\forall j<n)(a_{j}=b_{j})$ and $a_{n}<b_{n}$.

For each $b\in A$ and $n\in \omega$,
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $A_{b}^{n}=\{a\in A|a_{i}=b_{i}$ for $0\leq i\leq n\}$ is the $n-$\emph{level block containing} $b$.
($A_{b}^{n}$ will not be in the model we are defining.)
\item[2.] The sequence $\langle b_{n+1},\,b_{n+2},\ldots\rangle$ is the \emph{position of} $b$ \emph{in its} $n-$\emph{level block}.
\item[3.] $\mathscr{B}^{n}=\{A_{a}^{n}|a\in A\}$ is the set of $n-$level blocks.
\item[4.] $\leq_{n}$ is the relation on $\mathscr{B}^{n}$ define by $A_{a}^{n}\leq_{n}A_{b}^{n}$ if and only if $a\leq b$.
\item[5.] Let $f$ be an order automorphism of $(\mathscr{B}^{n},\,\leq_{n})$. (See lemmas A and B in Howard/Rubin \cite{bib:1996}.) We define $\phi_{f}$ to be the unique order automorphism of $(A,\,\leq)$ which satisfies $\phi_{f}^{\prime\prime}A_{a}^{n}=f(A_{a}^{n})$ for all $a\in A$ and such that for all $a\in A,\,a$ and $\phi_{f}(a)$ have the same position in their $n$-level blocks. (By 2 above, this means that $(\forall a\in A)(\forall i>n)(a_{i}=\phi_{f}(a)_{i})$.)
\item[6.] For $n\in \omega,\,G_{n}$ is the group $\{\phi_{f}:f$ is an order automorphism of $(\mathscr{B}^{n},\,\leq_{n})\}$.
\end{enumerate}

$\mathcal{G}$ is the group $\bigcup_{n\in\omega}G_{n}$. (Note that for $n<m,\,G_{n}\subseteq G_{m}$.) $S$ is the set of all $E\subseteq A$ which satisfy the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $E$ is well ordered by the ordering $\leq$ on $A$.
\item[(b)] $(\forall n\in \omega)$ ($ E\cap A_{a}^{n}\neq\emptyset$ for only finitely many $a\in A$)
\item[(c)] $E$ is countable.
\end{enumerate}

It is shown in Howard/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Rubin} \cite{bib:1996} that the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) and the Axiom of Choice for a denumerable family of sets (8) are true, but both the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) and the Axiom of Choice for families of cardinality $2^{\aleph_{0}}$ (181) are false. By using a slight modification of the proof of the Tychonoff Compactness Theorem (see, for example, Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} \cite{bib:1955}, p 143), it can be shown that 14 + 8 implies that the product of a countable number of compact spaces is compact (113). It follows from note 104, that the $2m=m$ principle (3) is false. Using the fact that the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) is false and that the Ordering Principle (30) is true (14 implies 30), Krom proves that there is an ordered topological space that is not normal (118 is false). Since 8 is true, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Since form [154 A] (If $X$ is a compact $T_{2}$ topological space, then $X^{\omega}$ is compact.) is true (14 implies 154) and 43 is false, 106 (the Baire Category Theorem for compact $T_{2}$ spaces) is false because 106 + 154 implies 43. (See Brunner \cite{bib:1984b} and note 95.) Form 14 implies 49 (Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering.) and 49 + 51 (Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering.) iff AC. (See Morris\index{Author}{Morris} \cite{bib:1969} and note 121.) Thus, form 51 is false. Since form 14 implies form 30 (Ordering Principle) and form 113 implies form 296 (Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets.), it follows from Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1997} that form 295 (Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering.) is true. Form 14 implies 62 $(C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ and Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973} has shown that in every FM model, 62 implies 60 $(C(\infty,\,WO))$. Thus, 60 is true. It is also proved in Howard \cite{bib:1973} that in every FM model 14 implies the Weak Sikorski Theorem (317), so 317 is also true. Form 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 40 implies 106 and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true because 60 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 $(MC(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 122 + 328 $\rightarrow$ 40.

$\mathcal{N}39$: Howard's Model II. $A$ is denumerable and is a disjoint union $\bigcup_{i\in\omega}B_{i}\cup\bigcup_{i\in\omega}C_{i}$, where for all $i\in\omega$, $|B_{i}|=|C_{i}|=\aleph_{0}$. Let $f_{i}$ be a fixed bijection from $B_{i}$ onto $C_{i}$ for each $i\in \omega$. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of all permutations $\phi$ of $A$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $\phi(B_{i})=B_{i}$ and $\phi(C_{i})=C_{i})$, $\forall i\in \omega$.
\item[2.] $\{a\in A:\phi(a)\neq a\}$ is finite.
\item[3.] $\phi|B_{i}$ and $\phi|C_{i}$ are even permutations, $\forall i\in \omega$.
\end{enumerate}
For each finite $x\subseteq \omega$ and each finite $E\subseteq A$, define
\begin{equation*}
G(x,\,E)=\{\phi\in \mathrm{fix}(E):(\forall i\in x)(\phi(f_{i})=f_{i})\}
\end{equation*}
Let $\Gamma$ be the filter of subgroups of $\mathcal{G}$ generated by the $G(x,\,E)$, where $x$ is a finite subset of $\omega$ and $E$ is a finite subset of $A$. (The filter is easier to describe for this model than the supports.) $\mathcal{N}39$ is the model determined by $A,\,\mathcal{G}$, and the filter $\Gamma$. It is shown in Howard \cite{bib:1994} that $|B_{i}|=|C_{i}|$ for all $i\in \omega$, but $|\bigcup_{i\in \omega}B_{i}|\neq |\bigcup_{i\in\omega}C_{i}|$, so 29 is false. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} also proves that the union of a well ordered collection of well orderable sets is well orderable $(UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO)$, form 231) is true. However, in every FM model, 231 implies $(\forall\alpha)UT(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha},\,\aleph_{\alpha})$ so form 23 is also true. $C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0})$ (122) is true (231 implies 122) and 122 + 67 (MC) implies AC (see [67 B]), so it follows that MC is false. Since form 165 $(C(WO,\,WO))$ is true, (231 implies 165) it follows from note 2(8 and 9) that 16 and 24 are also true.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}40$: Howard/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Rubin} Model II. A variation of $\mathcal{N}38$. $A$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are the same as in $\mathcal{N}38$, but $S$ is the set of all subsets of $A$ that satisfy conditions (b) and (c) in the definition of $S$ in $\mathcal{N}38$. Thus, we no longer require supports to be well ordered by $\leq$. $\mathcal{N}40$ has many of the same properties as $\mathcal{N}38$, BPI (14) and $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (8) are true, but $C(2^{\aleph_{0}},\,\infty)$ (181) and the $2m=m$ principle (3) are false. (See note 104.) Form 113 (Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for countably many spaces) is true here also, because 14 + 8 implies 113. However, in this model, the Principle of Dependent Choices (43) is true. See Howard/Rubin \cite{bib:1996} for proofs. Using the fact that the Kinna-Wagner Selection Principle (15) is false and the Ordering Principle (30) is true (14 implies 30), Krom\index{Author}{Krom} proves that there is an ordered topological space that is not normal (118 is false). Since 8 is true, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that in this model there is a set that cannot be well ordered and does not have an infinite Dedekind finite subset, (163 is false). (Form 8 plus form 163 iff AC.) Form 14 implies 49 (Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering.) and 49 + 51 (Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering.) iff AC. (See Morris\index{Author}{Morris} \cite{bib:1969} and note 121.) Thus, form 51 is false. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} has shown that 191 (There is a set $X$ such that for each set $a$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function $f$ mapping $X\times\alpha$ onto $a$.) is true in every permutation model with a set of atoms. He has also shown that 8 + 191 + 193 (Every Abelian group is a homomorphic image of a free projective Abelian group.) iff AC. Thus, 193 is false. (See note 60 for definitions.) Since form 14 implies form 30 (Ordering Principle) and form 43 implies form 296 (Every infinite set is the disjoint union of infinitely many infinite sets.), it follows from Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1997} that form 295 (Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering.) is true. Form 14 implies 62 $(C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ and Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973} has shown that in every FM model, 62 implies 60 $(C(\infty,\,WO))$. Thus, 60 is true. Moreover, in every FM model, 60 + 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$ implies AC, so 40 is false. (See Howard/Rubin \cite{bib:1995b}.) It is also shown in Howard \cite{bib:1973} that in every FM model 14 implies the Weak Sikorski Theorem (317), so 317 is true. Form 40 is false and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\infty))$ is true because 60 implies 122. Therefore, form 328 $(MC(WO,\,\infty))$ is false because 122 + 328 $\rightarrow$ 40. Since 43 + 14 is equivalent to 345 ([345 A]), form 345 is true.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}41$: Another variation of $\mathcal{N}3$. $A=\bigcup\{B_{n};n\in\omega\}$ is a disjoint union, where each $B_{n}$ is denumerable and ordered like the rationals by $\leq_{n}$. Thus, for each $n \in \omega,\,(B_{n},\, \leq_{n})\cong(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of all permutations on $A$ such for all $n\in\omega$, and all $\phi\in \mathcal{G},\,\phi$ is an order automorphism of $(B_{n},\,\leq_{n})$. $S$ is the set of all finite unions of the $B_{n}$'s. It follows that $A$ can be linearly ordered in this model, for if $a\in B_{m}$ and $b\in B_{n},\,a\leq b$ if $m<n$ or $m=n$ and $a\leq_{n}b$. For each $n \in \omega,\,B_{n}$ can be well ordered so $A$ is the union of a well ordered set of well orderable sets. Since $A$ can be linearly ordered and not well ordered, it follows that 294 is false. (See note 25 for definitions.) Let $C_{j}$ be the set of all pairs of countable subsets of $B_{j}$, and let $D=\bigcup_{j\in\omega}C_{j}$. Then $D$ has no choice function. (Let $\{E_{j},\,O_{j}\}\in C_{j}$ such that $E_{j}=\{a_{2i}^{j}:i\in \mathbb{Z}\}$ and $O_{j}=\{a_{2i+1}^{j}:i\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of integers. (If $m,\,n\in \mathbb{Q},\,a_{m}^{j}\leq a_{n}^{j}$ iff $m\leq n$.) If $f$ were a choice function on $D$ with support $F$, then there is a $\phi\in$ fix $(F)$ and a $j\in \omega$ such that $\phi$ interchanges $E_{j}$ and $O_{j}$.) Thus, $C(\infty,\,2)$ (88) is false. Also, in this model every infinite set has a countably infinite subset (9) is true and the axiom of choice for well orderable families of finite sets (122) is true. See note 112. Since 70 (There is a non-trivial ultrafilter on $\omega$) is true in every FM model and 9 + 70 implies 63 (Every infinite set has a non-trivial ultrafilter.) it follows that 63 is true. Form 10 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true (9 implies 10) and form 231 $(UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO))$ is false (231 implies 294). It follows that form 163 (Every non well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset) is false. (10 + 163 implies 231. See note 123.) The set $\{B_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ is a denumerable set of denumerable sets that has no Kinna-Wagner selection function and no multiple choice function so $KW(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ (357) and $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ (350) are both false.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}42(p)$: Hickman's Model IV. This model is an extension of $\mathcal{N}32$. Let $A$ be the disjoint union of two denumerable sets $B_{0}$ and $B_{1}$, where $B_{0}$ and $B_{1}$ are both Abelian $p$-groups (each non-identity element has order \emph{p}) for some prime $p\geq 5$. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be the group of all permutations $\phi$ of $A$ such that for $i=0, 1,\,\phi(B_{i})=B_{i}$ and $\phi$ is an automorphism on $B_{i}$. Moreover, for each $\phi\in \mathcal{G}$ and each $b\in B_{0},\,(\ast) \phi(f(b))=f(\phi(b))$, where $f$ is a bijection from $B_{0}$ onto $B_{1}$ in the outer model which is proved to exist if $p\geq 5$. $S$ is the set of all finite subsets of $A$. Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} proves using condition $(\ast)$ that $f$ is in $\mathcal{N}42(p)$ so that $|B_{0}|=|B_{1}|$, but $B_{0}$ and $B_{1}$ are not isomorphic ($220(p)$ is false).

\noindent $\mathcal{N}43$: Brunner's Model II. The set of atoms $A=\bigcup\{P_{n}:n\in\omega\}$, where $|P_{n}|=n+1$ for each $n\in \omega$ and the $P_{n}$'s are pairwise disjoint. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of all permutations $\phi$, on $A$ that $\phi(P_{n})=P_{n}$, for each $n\in \omega$. $S$ is the set of all subsets, $E$, of $A$ such that $\sup\{|E\cap\,P_{n}|:n\in \omega\}$ is finite. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} proves that if $X=\prod\{P_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ and $F$ is an ultrafilter on $\omega$, then the ultraproduct $X/F$ is amorphous (form 64 is false) even though every Dedekind finite subset of $X$ is finite. It is shown in note 122 that both $C(\aleph_{0},2)$ (80) and $MC(\infty,\, \infty)$ (67) are false.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}44$: Gross' model. $A$ is a vector space over a finite field with basis $B=\bigcup_{i\in \omega}B_{i}$ where the $B_{i}$ are pairwise disjoint and $|B_{i}|=4$ for each $i\in \omega$. Let $B_{i}= \{b_{i1},\, \ldots,\,b_{i4}\}.\,G$ is the group of vector space automorphisms $\phi$ of $A$ such that there is a permutation $\pi$ of $\omega$ and for each $i\in \omega$ there is a permutation $\alpha_{i}$ of \{1, 2, 3, 4\} in the group generated by the permutations (1, 2), (3, 4), and (1, 3)(2, 4) such that for all $i\in \omega$ and $j\in\{1,2,3,4\},\,\phi(b_{ij})=b_{\pi(i)\alpha_{i}(j)}$. $S$ is the set of finite subsets of $A$. In Gross\index{Author}{Gross} \cite{bib:1975} it is shown that, in $\mathcal{N}44$, there is a vector space $V$ with a basis and a subset $T\subseteq V$ such that no finite extension of $T$ is a basis and no infinite extension of $T$ is independent. (Hence, form 236 is false).

\noindent $\mathcal{N}45(p)$: Howard/Rubin Model III. Let $p$ be a prime. The set of atoms $A$ is a disjoint union,
\begin{equation*}
A=\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}B_{i}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}C_{i}\cup D
\end{equation*}
where $B_{i}=\{b_{n,\alpha}^{i}:n\,\in\omega\,\wedge\alpha<\aleph_{1}\},\, C_{i}=\{c_{n,\alpha}^{i}:n\in\omega\wedge\alpha<\aleph_{1}\}$, and $D=\{d_{n,\alpha}:n\in \omega\wedge\alpha<\aleph_{1}\}$. For each $\lambda<\aleph_{1}$, let
\begin{equation*}
A_{\lambda}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}B_{i,\lambda}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}C_{i,\lambda}\cup D_{\lambda}
\end{equation*}
where $B_{i,\lambda}=\{b_{n,\lambda}^{i}:n\in \omega\},\,C_{i,\lambda}=\{c_{n,\lambda}^{i}:n\in \omega\}$ and $D_{\lambda}=\{d_{n,\lambda}:n\in \omega\}$. Let $\phi_{\lambda}$ be the permutation of $A$ which is the product of the cycles,
\begin{equation*}
\phi_{\lambda}=\prod_{n\in \omega}(b_{n,\lambda}^{0},\,b_{n,\lambda}^{1},\,\cdots,\, b_{n,\lambda}^{p-1})(c_{n,\lambda}^{0},\,c_{n,\lambda}^{1},\,\cdots,\,c_{n,\lambda}^{p-1}).
\end{equation*}
(Note that $\phi_{\lambda}(d_{n,\lambda})=d_{n,\lambda}$ for each $n\in\omega$ and $\phi_{\lambda}(a)=a,$ for each $a\in A-A_{\lambda}.)$ The group $\mathcal{G}$ is the group generated by the $\phi_{\lambda}$ for $\lambda<\aleph_{1}$ and $S$ is the set of all finite subsets of $A$.

An elementary Abelian $p$-group is an Abelian group such that every nonidentity element has order $p$. (Note that an elementary Abelian $p$-group is just a vector space over the $p$-element field $\{0, 1,\, \cdots,p-1\}.)$ Let $G_{1}$ be the vector space over the $p$-element field $\{0, 1,\,\cdots,p-1\}$ with basis $\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}B_{i,\lambda}$ and $G_{2}$ be the vector space over the same $p$-element field with basis $\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}C_{i}\cup D$. It is shown that $|G_{1}|=|G_{2}|$, but $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ are not isomorphic. Thus, form 220$(p)$ is false in this model. (This extends the result of Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1977b} to $p=2$ and 3. See $\mathcal{N}42(p)$.)

\noindent $\mathcal{N}46$: H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{Hoft/Howard@H\"{o}ft/Howard} Model I. The set $A$ of atoms is denumerable and ordered by $\leq$ so that $(A,\, \leq)$ is order isomorphic to the rationals. $A$ is written as the union $A=D_{1}\cup D_{2}\cup D_{3}$ of three dense disjoint subsets. $G$ is the group of all order automorphisms $\phi$ of $A$ such that $\phi(D_{i})=D_{i}$ for $i=1,2,3$. $S$ is the set of all subsets $E$ of $A$ which satisfy the following three conditions: (a) $E\cap D_{1}$ is finite, (b) $E\cap D_{2}$ is well ordered by $\leq$ and (c) If $b:\alpha\rightarrow E\cap D_{2}$ is an order preserving bijection from an ordinal $\alpha$ onto $E\cap D_{2}$ and $\lambda\leq\alpha$ is a limit ordinal, then the least upper bound of $\{b(\gamma):\gamma<\lambda\}$ in $(A,\,\leq)$ exists and is in $D_{3}$. In H\"{o}ft/Howard \cite{bib:1994}, it is shown that in $\mathcal{N}46,\,D_{1}$ is an infinite linearly orderable set which is Dedekind finite (form 185 is false) and that $\forall X$, if $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is Dedekind finite then every subset of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ has a maximum element (form 84 is true).

\noindent $\mathcal{N}47$: H\"{o}ft/Howard Model II. This model is similar to $\mathcal{N}33$. The atoms $A$ are ordered by $\leq$ so that they have order type that of the real numbers $\mathbb{R} (|A|=2^{\aleph_{0}})$. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of all order automorphisms of $(A,\,\leq)$ and $S$ is the set of bounded subsets of $A$. It is shown in H\"{o}ft/Howard \cite{bib:1994} that in $\mathcal{N}47$ a linear ordering with no infinite descending sequences is a well ordering (form 77 is true) and that $(A,\,\leq)$ has the fixed point property but is not complete (since $A$ has no least upper bound). It follows that form 316 is false.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}48$: Pincus' Model XI. $\mathcal{A}= (A,\,<,\,C_{0},\,C_{1},\,\ldots)$ is called an \emph{ordered colored set} (OC set) if $<$ is a linear ordering on $A$ and the $C_{i}$, for $i\in \omega$ are subsets of $A$ such that for each $a\in A$ there is exactly one $n\in \omega$ such that $a\in C_{n}$. If $a\in C_{n},\,C_{n}$ is called the \emph{color} of $a$. In this model we take the set of atoms to be a denumerable, universal, homogeneous OC set. (See Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p101 for definitions.) It follows that $<$ is a dense unbounded linear ordering such that between any two distinct elements of $A$ there are elements of every color. $\mathcal{G}$ is the group of automorphisms of $\mathcal{A}$ and $S$ is the set of all finite subsets of $A$. Pincus proves that each $C_{i}$, where $i\in \omega$, is an infinite set which is not the union of an infinite number of pairwise disjoint infinite sets (296 is false). Pincus also proves that there is a dense linear ordering on every set (295 is true) and the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem (14) is true. Form 14 implies 49 (Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering.) and 49 + 51 (Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering.) iff AC. (See Morris\index{Author}{Morris} \cite{bib:1969} and note 121.) Thus, form 51 is false. Form 154 (Tychonoff's compactness theorem for countably many $T_{2}$ spaces) is true (14 implies 154) and 43 is false (43 implies 296). Thus, it follows from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1983c} and note 95 that 106 (the Baire category theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces) is false (106 + 154 iff 43). Form 14 implies the Ordering Principle (30) and the Kinna-Wagner Principle (15) is false in every FM model. It is shown in Krom\index{Author}{Krom} \cite{bib:1986} that there is an orderable topological space that is not normal (118 is false). Form 14 implies 62 $(C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ and Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973} has shown that in every FM model 62 implies 60 $(C(\infty,\,WO))$. Thus, 60 is true. It is also shown in Howard \cite{bib:1973} that in every FM model 14 implies the Weak Sikorski Theorem (317), so 317 is true. Form 30 (Ordering Principle) $+$ form 126 $(MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$ implies form 8 $(C(\aleph_{0},\, \infty))$. Since 30 is true and 8 is false, it follows that 126 is false. Since form 165 $(C(WO,\,WO))$ is true, (60 implies 165) it follows from note 2(8 and 9) that 16 and 24 are also true.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}49$: De la Cruz/Di Prisco Model\index{Author}{De la Cruz/Di Prisco}. Let $A=\{a(i,p):i\in \omega\wedge p\in \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\}$. $(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ denotes the additive group.) For each $i\in \omega$, let $A_{i}=\{a(i,p):p\in \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\}$ and for each $i\in \omega$ and $p\in \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$, let $\pi_{i}^{p}: A\rightarrow A$ be defined by $\pi_{i}^{p}(a(j,\,q))= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
a(j,p+q) & \mathrm{if}\,j=i\\ a(j,\,q) & \mathrm{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.$. $G$ is the group generated by the permutations $\pi_{i}^{p}$ for $i\in \omega$ and $p\in \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$. $S$ is the set of finite supports. De la Cruz and Di Prisco have shown that every infinite set in this model is Dedekind infinite (9 is true) and that $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ is a countable family of well orderable sets such that no infinite subfamily has Kinna-Wagner selection function. It follows that 167 and 380 are false. In addition De la Cruz and Di Prisco have shown that for every $n\in\omega, n\geq 2$, there is a set of $n$ elements sets in the model with no choice function (47(n) is false).

\noindent $\mathcal{N}50(E)$: Brunner's Model III. $E$ is a finite set of prime numbers. For each $p\in E$ and $n\in \omega$, let $A_{p,n}$ be a set of atoms of cardinality $p^{n}$. $A$ is the disjoint union $A=\bigcup_{p\in E,n\in\omega}A_{p,n}$. For each $p\in E$ and $n\in \omega$, let $\eta_{p,n}$ be a permutation of $A_{p,n}$ consisting of a single cycle of length $p^{n}$. For each $p\in E$ let $\eta_{p}$ be the permutation of $A$ defined by $\eta_{p}(a)=\eta_{p,n}(a)$ if $a\in A_{p,n}$ and $\eta_{p}(a)=a$ for $a\not\in\bigcup_{n\in\omega}A_{p,n}$.
$\mathcal{G}$ is the group of permutations of $A$ generated by $\{\eta_{p}:p\in E\}$. $S$ is the ideal of finite subsets of $A$. This is the model of the lemma on page 72 of Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1990}. In Brunner \cite{bib:1990} it is shown that $MC(\infty,\,\infty)$ (form 67) and $KW(WO, \infty)$ (form 322) are true and that $PC(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form [10
E]) and $PC(\infty, n,\,\infty)$ (form $45(n))$ (for $n=\sum\nolimits_{p\in E}n_{p}\cdot p$ where $n_{p}\in \omega$ for $p\in E$) are false.

322, 361, and 363 but 10, 154, 164, 342(n) (for $n$ as described above) and 344 are false. References Brunner \cite{bib:1990}, notes 18 and 120(2, 10, and 56).

\noindent $\mathcal{N}51$: W\c{e}glorz\index{Author}{W\c{e}glorz}/Brunner Model. Let $A$ be denumerable and $\mathcal{G}$ be the group of all permutations of $A$. \noindent $\mathcal{N}52$: Felgner/Truss Model. Let $(\mathcal{B},\,\prec)$ be a countable universal homogeneous linearly ordered Boolean algebra, (i.e., $<$ is a linear ordering extending the Boolean partial ordering on $B$). Let $A=\{a_{x}:x\in \mathcal{B}\}$; let $\mathcal{G}$ be the group of all permutations on $A$ which preserve the structure (a linearly ordered Boolean algebra); and let $S$ be the set of finite subsets of $A$. It is shown in Felgner/Truss \cite{bib:1996} that $A$ has no prime ideal so form 14 is false. It is also shown that every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering so form 49 is true.

$\mathcal{N}53$: Good/Tree/Watson\index{Author}{Good/Tree/Watson} Model I. Let $A=\bigcup\{Q_{n}:n\in \omega\}$, where $Q_{n}=\{a_{n,q}$: $q\in \mathbb{Q}\}$. Suppose $<$ is the lexicographic ordering on $A$, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
a_{n,q}<a_{m,p}\,\mathrm{if}\ n<m,\ \mathrm{or}\ n=m\ \mathrm{and}\ q<p.
\end{equation*}
The group of permutations $\mathcal{G}$, is the group of all permutations on $A$ which are a rational translation on $Q_{n}$, i.e. if $\phi\in G$, then $\phi|Q_{n}(a_{n,q})=a_{n,q+r_{n}}$ for some $r_{n}\in \mathbb{Q}$, and supports are finite. Let $d$ be the metric on $A$ given by:
\begin{equation*}
d(a_{n,q},\,a_{m,p})=1\ \mathrm{if}\ n\neq m
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
d(a_{n,q},\,a_{m,p})=|q-p|/(1+|q-p|)\ \mathrm{if}\ n=m.
\end{equation*}
It is shown in Good/Tree/Watson \cite{bib:1996} that $(A,\,d)$ is a linearly ordered, zero dimensional, metric space, but is not paracompact (MP, form 383 is false). Each $Q_{n}$, being a second countable metric space, is paracompact, and the disjoint union topology on $A$ coincides With the metric topology which is normal. Hence, $A$ can be considered as a normal non paracompact disjoint union of paracompact spaces. Thus, DUP ([67 N]) is false. It is shown in Howard\index{Author}{Howard}/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin \cite{bib:1997b} that MM (383), DUMN (382), and $C(\infty,\,2)$ (88) are each false, but every infinite set does have a countably infinite subset so form 9 is true.

\noindent $\mathcal{N}54$: Good/Tree/Watson Model II. This model is a variation of $\mathcal{N}53$. The set of atoms $A=\bigcup\{Q_{n}:\,n\in \omega\}$, where $Q_{n}=\{a_{n,q}:q\in \mathbb{R}\}$. We let $<$ be the lexicographic ordering on $A$. The group of permutations $\mathcal{G}$, is the group of all permutations on $A$ which are a translation on $Q_{n}$, that is, if $\phi\in \mathcal{G}$, then $\phi|Q_{n}(a_{n,q})=a_{n,q+r_{n}}$ for some $r_{n}\in \mathbb{R}$. Supports are finite. Let $d$ be the metric on $A$ given by:
\begin{equation*}
d(a_{n,q},\,a_{m,p})=1\,\mathrm{if}\ n\neq m

and
\begin{equation*}
d(a_{n,q},\,a_{m,p})=|q-p|/(1+|q-p|)\,\mathrm{if}\,n=m.
\end{equation*}
It is shown in Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley \cite{bib:1997} that $(A,\,d)$ is a metric space that is not meta-Lindel\"{o}f (173 is false).

\section*{NOTE 2}

In this note we list implications that hold in every Fraenkel-Mostowski model. None of the implications listed are known to be theorems of ZF. In each case we list the implication and a reference if one is available.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $231\rightarrow 23$, this is reasonably clear.
\item[2.] $40+60\rightarrow 1$, Howard/Rubin \cite{bib:1995b}.
\item[3.] $62\rightarrow 60$, Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973}.
\item[4.] $14\rightarrow 317$, Howard \cite{bib:1973}.
\item[5.] $165\rightarrow 231$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
If $X$\index{Author}{Brunner/Rubin} is a set of well orderable sets in a Fraenkel-Mostowski model $\mathcal{N}$, then for each $y\in X$, the set $y^{\prime}$ of well orderings of $y$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}$ since any permutation fixing $y$ pointwise also fixes $y^{\prime}$ pointwise. Therefore, by form 165 $(C(WO,\,WO))$, the set $X^{\prime}=\{y^{\prime}:y\in X\}$ has a choice function. Using this choice function and a well ordering of $X$ a well ordering of $\bigcup X$ can be constructed.
\end{proof}

\begin{enumerate}
\item[6.] $323\rightarrow 60$, because $323\rightarrow 62$ is a theorem of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$, and, by 3 above, $62\rightarrow 60$ in every Fraenkel-Mostowski model. Howard\index{Author}{Howard} \cite{bib:1973}.
\item[7.] $8+67\leftrightarrow 1$, Brunner/Rubin \cite{bib:1986}.
\item[8.] $165\rightarrow 24$, K. Keremedis. (In every FM model $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ can be well ordered, form 130 is true, and $|\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})|=2^{(2^{\aleph_{0}})}.)$
\item[9.] $165\rightarrow 16$. (In every FM model, $\mathbb{R}$ can be well ordered, form 79 is true, and $|\mathbb{R}|=2^{\aleph_{0}}.)$
\item[10.] $165\rightarrow 212$. (See 9.)
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 3}

From Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} \cite{bib:1979} p 124:

\begin{theorem*}
(Solovay) $Con\text{(}ZF\text{)}\rightarrow Con\text{(}ZF+\text{43}\ \text{(}DC(\omega)\text{)}\
\text{+}$ Every endomorphism of the additive group of the real line is continuous)
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
(Levy) $Con\text{(}ZF\text{)}\rightarrow Con\text{(}ZF \text{+}\ \text{cf}\text{(}\omega_{1})=\omega +\mathbb{R}$ is the denumerable union of denumerable sets $\text{+}\ \neg\Sigma_{3}^{1}-AC$).
\end{theorem*}

In Figura\index{Author}{Figura} \cite{bib:1981} a summary of these results is given. In addition Figura generalizes form 34 ($\aleph_{1}$ is regular), form 38 ($\mathbb{R}$ is not a countable union of countable sets) and form 170 ($\mathbb{R}$ has an uncountable well orderable subset.) These generalizations for regular cardinals $\kappa$, are respectively, (in the notation of Figura \cite{bib:1981}):

$\neg CP(\kappa):\kappa^{+}$ is regular.

$\neg WOP(\kappa):\mathcal{P}(\kappa)$ has a well ordered subset of power not $\leq \kappa$.

$\neg DP(\kappa):\mathcal{P}(\kappa)$ is not the union of $\kappa$ sets of power $\leq \kappa$.

\noindent In summary, the results are
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $DP(\kappa)$ implies $WOP(\kappa)$ and $DP(\kappa)$ implies $CP(\kappa)$.
\item[2.] $\mathrm{Con}(\mathrm{ZF}+CP(\kappa)\,+WOP(\kappa)+DP(\kappa))$
\item[3.] $\mathrm{Con(ZF}+CP(\kappa)+\neg WOP(\kappa)\,+\neg DP(\kappa))$
\item[4.] $\mathrm{Con(ZF}+CP(\kappa)\,+WOP(\kappa)\,+\neg DP(\kappa))$
\item[5.] $\mathrm{Con(ZF}+WOP(\kappa)\,+\neg CP(\kappa)+\neg DP(\kappa))$
\item[6.] $\mathrm{Con(ZF}+\{\kappa:DP(\kappa)\}$ is a proper class)
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 4}

Form 73 $\rightarrow$ [73 A]. (Form 73 is: For every $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x\in \mathbb{R}$ the following definitions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $x$ is in the closure of $A$ iff every neighborhood of $x$ intersects $A$.
\item[(2)] $x$ is in the closure of $A$ if there is a sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ such that $\lim x_{n}=x$.
\end{enumerate}
and form [73 A] is: For all $A\subseteq \mathbb{R},\,x\in A$ and $f: A\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $(\forall\epsilon)(\exists\delta)(\forall y\in A)(|y-x|<\delta$ implies $|f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon)$
\item[(2)] Whenever $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ and $\lim x_{n}=x$ then $\lim f(x_{n})=f(x).)$
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Assume Form 73. Fix $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x\in A$. The fact that part (1) of [73 A] implies part (2) of [73 A] is clear. Assume (2) of [73 A] and $\neg(1)$ of [73 A]. Then $\exists\epsilon\,\forall\delta\,\exists y\in A$ such that $|y-x|<\delta$ and $|f(x)-f(y)|\geq\epsilon$. Let $B=\{y\in A:|f(x)-f(y)|\geq\epsilon\}$. Every neighborhood of $x$ intersects $B$. By form 73, $x= \lim x_{n}$ for some sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq B(\subseteq A)$. But $\lim f(x_{n})\neq f(x)$ contradicting part (2) of [73 A].
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 5}

[73 A] $\rightarrow$ form 74. (See note 4 for a statement of [73 A]. Form 74 is: For every $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $A$ is closed and bounded.
\item[(2)] Every sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ has a convergent subsequence with limit in A.)
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Assume [73 A]. The usual proof that part (1) of form 74 implies part (2) doesn't require any choice. So assume $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $A$ satisfies (2) of 74 but not (1) of 74. Assume first that $A$ is bounded. Then $A$ is not closed so there is an $x_{0}\not\in A$ such that every neighborhood of $x_{0}$ intersects $A$. Define $f: A\cup \{x_{0}\}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by $f(x)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $f(x)=0$ if $x=x_{0}$. Then (1) of [73 A] fails (with $\epsilon=1)$ so there is a sequence $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A \cup\{x_{0}\}$ such that $\lim f(x_{n})\neq f(x_{0})$. This means we can assume $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A$ (replacing $\{x_{n}\}$ by a subsequence if necessary). By (2) of form 74, $\lim x_{n}\in A$ that is $x_{0}\in A$, a contradiction. Now assume that $A$ is unbounded. Let $f$ be a monotone, increasing function from the interval $(-1,1)$ one to one, onto $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies $(\forall a,\,b\in(-1,1))(|a-b|\leq|f(a)-f(b)|)$. (For example, $f(x)=\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}$ would work.) Then $f^{-1}(A)$ is bounded and satisfies (2) of 74 because if $\{x_{n}\}$ is a sequence in $f^{-1}(A)$, then $\{f(x_{n})\}$ is a sequence in $A$. Since $A$ satisfies (2) of 74, $\{f(x_{n})\}$ has a convergent subsequence with limit in $A$. Using the property which we required $f$ to have we infer that $f^{-1}$ applied to the convergent subsequence mentioned above gives a convergent subsequence of $\{x_{n}\}$ with limit in $f^{-1}(A)$. Since we have proved (2) of 74 implies (1) of 74 for bounded sets we conclude that $f^{-1}(A)$ is closed. Hence there are numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $-1<a<b<1$ and $(\forall x\in f^{-1}(A))(a<x<b)$. Since $f$ is monotone increasing $(\forall x\in A)(f(a)<x<f(b))$. Hence $A$ is bounded. 
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 6}

[73 A] $\rightarrow$ form 73. (See note 4 for a statements of forms 73 and [73 A].)

\begin{proof}
Assume [73 A] and assume $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy part (1) of 73 but not (2) of 73 (This means $x_{0}\not\in A$). Then
\begin{equation*}
\text{For every sequence}\ \{x_{n}\}\ \mathrm{from}\ A,\ \lim x_{n}\neq x_{0} \qquad\qquad\qquad (\ast)
\end{equation*}
 Define $f:A \cup\{x_{0}\}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by $f(x)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $f(x)=0$ if $x=x_{0}$. By $(\ast)$, if $\{x_{n}\}$ converges to $x_{0}$ and $\{x_{n}\}\subseteq A \cup\{x_{0}\}$ then $\{x_{n}\}$ is eventually constant and equal to $x_{0}$. Therefore, $\lim f(x_{n})=f(x_{0})$. Therefore, (2) of [73 A] holds (with $A$ of [73 A] equal to $A \cup\{x_{0}\}$ of the present proof). Hence (1) of [73 A] holds, which means $(\exists\delta>0)(\forall x\in A\cup\{x_{0}\})(|x-x_{0}|<\delta\rightarrow|f(x)-f(x_{0})|<1)$. But by (1) of 73, the set $B=\{x:|x-x_{0}|<\delta\}\cap A\neq\emptyset$. Choose $y\in B$, then $y\neq x_{0},\, y\in A$ and $|1-0|=|f(y)-f(x)|<1$, a contradiction. 
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 7}

In this note we prove that form 43 (Dependent Choice) implies form 113 (A countable product of compact topological spaces is compact.) Our proof is based on the proof of theorem 6.1 in Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree} \cite{bib:1995}. Let $\{X_{\alpha}:\alpha<\omega\}$ be a countable set of compact topological spaces. Let $X=\prod_{\alpha\in\omega}X_{\alpha}$ and for $\beta<\omega$ define $p_{\beta}:X\rightarrow\prod_{\alpha\leq\beta}X_{\alpha}$ by $p_{\beta} (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots) =(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots,\,x_{\beta})$. To show that $X$ is compact let $\mathcal{C}$ be a collection of closed sets in $X$ with the finite intersection property. We will use Dependent Choice to choose a sequence $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots)$ with the property that for all $\alpha<\omega,\,(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{\alpha})\in\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$. Then we will prove, as in Good/Tree \cite{bib:1995}, that
$(x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots) \in\bigcap \mathcal{C}$.

\begin{definition*}
If $x_{0}\in X_{0}$ and $\alpha<\kappa$ we say $x_{0}$ \emph{can be extended to level} $\alpha$ if there is a sequence $(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{\alpha})$ such that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{\alpha})\in\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$. Similarly, if $\alpha<\beta<\kappa$ and $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots,\,x_{\alpha})\in\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$ then we say $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{\alpha})$ can be extended to level $\beta$ if there is a sequence $(y_{\alpha+1},\,\ldots,\,y_{\beta})$ such that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{\alpha},\,y_{\alpha+1},\,\ldots,\, y_{\beta})\in\cap\{\overline{p_{\beta}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If $\beta\leq\gamma<\kappa$ define
\begin{equation*}
p_{\beta,\gamma}:\prod_{\alpha\leq\gamma}X_{\alpha}\rightarrow\prod_{\alpha\leq\beta}X_{\alpha}
\end{equation*}
by
\begin{equation*}
p_{\beta,\gamma}\,(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,\ldots,\,x_{\gamma})=(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{\beta}).
\end{equation*}

For every $\alpha<\kappa$, let $X_{0,\alpha}=\{x\in X_{0}:x$ can be extended to level $\alpha$\}. $X_{0,\alpha}$ is closed in $X_{0}$ because $X_{0,\alpha}=p_{0,\alpha} (\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\})$ and
\begin{enumerate}
\item[A.] $\prod_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}X_{\beta}=X_{0}\times\prod_{1\leq\beta\leq\alpha}X_{\beta}$ is compact.
\item[B.] $\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$ is closed in $\prod_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}X_{\beta}$.
\item[C.] If $Y$ and $Z$ are compact topological spaces and $D$ is closed in $Y\times Z$ then the projection of $D$ onto $Y$ is closed.
\end{enumerate}

We also note that $X_{0,\alpha}\neq\emptyset$ since $\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$ is non-empty (by the compactness of $\prod_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}X_{\beta}$). We can conclude that the family $\{X_{0,\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\}$ has the finite intersection property since $X_{0,\alpha_{1}} \cap\ldots\cap X_{0,\alpha_{k}}=X_{0,\alpha}$ where $\alpha=\max\{\alpha_{1},\,\ldots,\,\alpha_{k}\}$. Since $X_{0}$ is compact $\bigcap_{\alpha<\kappa}X_{0,\alpha}\neq\emptyset$. Choose $x_{0} \in\bigcap_{\alpha<\kappa}X_{0,\alpha}$.

Assume that $x_{0},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta}$ have been chosen so that $(x_{0},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta})$ is extendible to level $\alpha$ for every $\alpha$ such that $\beta<\alpha<\kappa$. For every such $\alpha$, let $X_{\beta+1,\alpha}=\{x\in X_{\beta+1}:(x_{0},\, \ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,x)$ is extendible to level $\alpha$\}.
\end{definition*}

\begin{claim*}
$X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$ is closed.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
First note that
\begin{equation*}
X_{\beta+1,\alpha}=\{x\in X_{\beta+1}:(x_{0},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,x)\in p_{\beta+1,\alpha}(\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}).
\end{equation*}
$\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$ is closed in $\prod_{\gamma\leq\alpha}X_{\gamma}=\Big(\prod_{\gamma\leq\beta+1}X_{\gamma}\Big)\times\Big(\coprod_{\beta+1<\gamma\leq\alpha}X_{\gamma}\Big)$. Therefore, by C. above, $p_{\beta+1,\alpha} (\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\})$ is closed. Assume $y\in X_{\beta+1}$ is in the closure of $X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$. We will complete the proof of the claim by showing that $y\in X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$. Let $N$ be a neighborhood of $(x_{0},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,y)$ in $\prod_{\gamma\leq\beta+1}X_{\gamma}$. Then the projection of $N$ onto $X_{\beta+1}$ is a neighborhood of $y$. Therefore there is an $x\in X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$ such that $x$ is in this projection and therefore, the sequence $(x_{0},\,\ldots,\, x_{\beta},\,x)$ is in $N$. Also $(x_{0},\,\ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,x)$ is in $p_{\beta+1,\alpha}(\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\})$. This shows that $(x_{0},\,\ldots,\, x_{\beta},\,y)$ is in the closure of $p_{\beta+1,\alpha}(\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\})$ and hence $(x_{0},\, \ldots,\,x_{\beta},\,y)$ is in $p_{\beta+1,\alpha}(\bigcap\{\overline{p_{\alpha}(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\})$. $y$ is therefore in $X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$.
\end{proof}

As above, the family $\{X_{\beta+1,\alpha}:\beta<\alpha<\kappa\}$ has the finite intersection property. Since $X_{\beta+1}$ is compact, $\bigcap_{\beta<\alpha<\kappa}X_{\beta+1,\alpha}\neq\emptyset$. Choose $x_{\beta+1}\in\bigcap_{\beta<\alpha<\kappa}X_{\beta+1,\alpha}$.

The argument that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots)$ is in $\bigcap \mathcal{C}$ is by contradiction. Suppose the assertion is false. Then there is an open set $U=\prod_{\alpha<\omega}U_{\alpha}$ and $C\in \mathcal{C}$ such that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots) \in U$ and $U\cap C=\emptyset$. Choose $\gamma\in \omega$ so that $U_{\alpha}=X_{\alpha}$ whenever $\alpha>\gamma$, and let $V=\prod_{\alpha\leq\gamma}U_{\alpha}$. $V$ is open in $\prod_{\alpha\leq\gamma}X_{\alpha}$. Further $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{\gamma})\in V$ hence $V\cap p_{\gamma}(C)\neq\emptyset$.
This means that there is some sequence $(y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots) \in C$ with $(y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{\gamma})\in V$. Which (by definition of $V$) implies that $(y_{0},\, y_{1},\,\ldots) \in U$. This contradicts $U\cap C=\emptyset$.

\section*{NOTE 8}

[9 A] (The statement
\begin{equation*}
(\forall x)((x\ \text{infinite and}\ x\ \text{Dedekind finite) implies}\ \mathcal{P}(x)\ \text{is Dedekind finite)}\qquad (\ast))
\end{equation*}
is equivalent to form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite).

\begin{proof}
Assume $(\ast)$ and suppose that $x$ is a set which is infinite and not Dedekind infinite. Then by $(\ast)$, $Y=\mathcal{P}(x)$ is infinite and Dedekind finite. Applying $(\ast)$ again, $z=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(x))$ is infinite and Dedekind finite. But $\{A_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ is a denumerable subset of $z$ where $A_{n}=\{t\subseteq x:|t|=n\}$, a contradiction. Conversely assuming form 9, the hypotheses of $(\ast)$ are never true.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 10}

[73 A] is equivalent to [73 B]. (See note 4 for a statement of [73 A]. Form [73 B] is: $(\forall f:\mathbb{R}\,\rightarrow \mathbb{R})(\forall x\in \mathbb{R})$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $(\forall\epsilon>0)(\exists\delta>0)((\forall y)(|y-x|<\delta\rightarrow|f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon)$
\item[(2)] Whenever $\lim x_{n}=x$, then $\lim f(x_{n})=f(x).)$
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Clearly [73 A] implies [73 B]. Assume [73 B] and assume that [73 A] fails. Then $\exists A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\, \exists x_{0}\in A$ and $\exists f:A\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that (2) of [73 A] holds but (1) of [73 A] fails. Define $g:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by $g(x)=f(x)$ if $x\in A$ and $g(x)=f(x_{0})$ if $x\not\in A$. Then (2) of [73 B] holds for $g$ so (1) of [73 B] holds for $g$. This implies that (1) of [73 A] holds for $f$.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 11}

Form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite) is equivalent to [9 C] (The image of a Dedekind finite set is Dedekind finite.)

\begin{proof}
Clearly form 9 implies [9 C]. By note 8 (above) to prove [9 C] implies 9, it suffices to prove [9 C] implies [9 A]. Assume [9 C] and that $x$ is an infinite, Dedekind finite set and that $\mathcal{P}(x)$ is Dedekind infinite. Then there is a one to one function $f:\omega \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma*}
We may assume that $(\forall i,\,j\in \omega)(i\neq j$ implies $f(i) \cap f(j)=\emptyset)$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
If $g:\omega\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x)$ is one to one, then we define $f:\omega\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x)$ by induction so that for each $i\in\omega,\,f(i)\cap f(j)=\emptyset$ for all $j<i$, and such that the set algebra generated by $\{g(k)\cap(x-\bigcup_{j\leq i}f(j)):k>j\}$ is infinite, $f(0)$ is defined as follows: Either the set algebra generated by $\{g(k)\,\cap\,g(0):k>0\}$ is infinite or the set algebra generated by $\{g(k)\,\cap\,(x-g(0)):k>0\}$ is infinite. If the latter is true then $f(0)=g(0)$. If the latter is false then $f(0)=x-g(0)$. Suppose that $f(i)$ has been defined for every $i<n$ satisfying the required conditions. Then for some $k$ (and we take the least such) $g(k) \cap (x-\bigcup_{j<n}f(j))\neq\emptyset$ (call this set $A$) and $(x-\bigcup_{j<n}f(j))-g(k)\neq\emptyset$ (call this set $B$). Since $A\cup B=(x-\bigcup_{j<n}f(j))$, one of the two set algebras, either that generated by $\{g(k)\,\cap\,A:k>n\}$ or that generated by $\{g(k)\,\cap\, B:k>n\}$, is infinite. If the latter is the case, let $f(k)=A$. If the latter fails, let $f(k)=B$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

Now define $h:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x)$ by
\begin{equation*}
h(t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
f(i), & \mathrm{if}\ t\in f(i)\\
\emptyset\ & \mathrm{otherwise}.
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
By [9 C] the image of $X$ under $h$ is Dedekind finite, a contradiction.

\section*{NOTE 12}

Form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite) and [9 D] (The union of a Dedekind finite family of finite sets is Dedekind finite) are equivalent.

\begin{proof}
It is clear that form 9 implies [9 D]. Since 9 and [9 A] are equivalent (see note 8.) it suffices to show that [9 D] implies [9 A]. Assume [9 D] and that $x$ is a set which is Dedekind finite such that $\mathcal{P}(x)$ is Dedekind infinite. Then there is a one to one function $f:\omega\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(x)$ and, as in note 11, we may assume that $(\forall i,\,j\in \omega)(i\neq j$ implies $f(i) \cap f(j)=\emptyset)$. It is also no loss of generality to assume $(\forall i\in \omega)(f(i)\neq\emptyset)$. Let
\begin{equation*}
W=\{\{i,\,t\}:i\in\omega\wedge t\in f(i)\}.
\end{equation*}
Then $W$ is Dedekind finite since $x$ is. But $\omega\subseteq\bigcup W$, a contradiction. $\square$(See Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b} p 161 prob 11.4.)
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 13}

The fact that form 39 does not imply form 43 follows from the theorem of Jensen mentioned in Mathias\index{Author}{Mathias} \cite{bib:1979} p. 123 and proved in Felgner\index{Author}{Felgner} \cite{bib:1971a}:

\begin{theorem*}
If $\alpha$\index{Subject}{Gauntt's condition $L(n,\, Z)$} is an infinite cardinal in a countable standard model $M$ of $ZF+V=L$ then $M$ can be extended to an model $N$ of $ZF$ with the same ordinals and (well ordered) cardinals as $M$ in which $C(\alpha,\,\infty)$ (form 39) is true and $DC(\omega)$ (form 43) is false.
\end{theorem*}

\section*{NOTE 14}

Form 40 does not imply form 44 by the following theorem which is proved in Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1966b}:

\begin{theorem*}
Let $M$ be a countable standard model for $ZF+AC$ and $\alpha$ a regular, infinite cardinal in $M$. Then there is a model $N$ of $ZF$ containing $M$ with the same ordinals as $M$ such that in $N,\,\neg DC(\alpha)$ (see form 87), $\neg C(\alpha,\,2)$ and there is a cardinal incomparable with $\alpha$. But for every $\beta<\alpha,\,DC(\beta)$ and $C(\beta,\,\infty)$ hold and $\beta$ is comparable with every cardinal.
\end{theorem*}

\section*{NOTE 15}

Finite axioms of choice:\index{Subject}{finite axioms of choice} $C(\infty,\,n),C(LO,\,n),C(WO,\,n),C(\infty,\,\in Z),C(LO, \in Z),C(WO,\,\in Z)$ and $C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$, (forms 45, 33, 47, 46, 120, 48, and 288 respectively) and generalizations have been studied extensively in Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1984b}, Conway\index{Author}{Conway} \cite{bib:1971}, Gauntt\index{Author}{Gauntt} \cite{bib:1970} and \cite{bib:1968}, Mostowski\index{Author}{Mostowski} \cite{bib:1958}, Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1973a}, Wi\'{s}niewski\index{Author}{Wi\'{s}niewski} \cite{bib:1972} and Zuckerman\index{Author}{Zuckerman} \cite{bib:1971}. Here is a summary of the results. (See Truss \cite{bib:1973a} for more details.)

Until further notice $n\in \omega$ and $Z$ is a finite subset of $\omega$. The first two of the following conditions on the pair $(n,\,Z)$ were introduced by Mostowski\index{Subject}{Mostowski's condition $D(n,\,Z)$} in \cite{bib:1958} and the third by Gauntt in \cite{bib:1970}.

$D(n,\,Z)$. For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ (the symmetric group on n) without fixed points, there is a subgroup $H$ of $G$ and proper subgroups $K_{1},\,\ldots,\,K_{r}$of $H$ such that $\Sigma|H:K_{i}|\in Z$.

$K(n,\,Z)$.\index{Subject}{Mostowski's condition $K(n,\,Z)$} For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ without fixed points, there is a subgroup $H$ of $G^{\omega}$ (the restricted direct product of countably many copies of $G$) and proper subgroups $K_{1},\,\ldots,\, K_{r}$ of $H$ such that $\Sigma|H:K_{i}|\in Z$

$L(n,\,Z)$. For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ without fixed points, there are proper subgroups $K_{1},\, \ldots,\,K_{r}$ of $G$ such that $\Sigma|G:K_{i}|\in Z$.

Blass \cite{bib:1984b} has noticed that $L(n,\,Z)$ is can be formulated as follows:

Every group that can act without fixed points on an $n$ element set can also act without fixed points on a $k$ element set for at least one $k\in Z$.

\noindent The equivalence of the two conditions is based on the following:

\begin{lemma*}
Suppose that $H$ is a group and $A$ is a set of cardinality $k$ then $H$ acts without fixed points on $A\Leftrightarrow$ there are proper subgroups $J_{1},\,\ldots,\, J_{r}$ of $H$ (not necessarily distinct) such that $\Sigma|H:J_{i}|=k$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
(Outline) $(\Rightarrow)$ If $H$ acts without fixed points on $A$, let $A_{1},\,\ldots,\,A_{r}$ be the orbits of elements of A under the action. Then $|A_{i}|\geq 2$ and $\Sigma|A_{i}|=k$. If, for each $i,\, 1\leq i\leq r$ we choose $a_{i}\in A_{i}$ and let $J_{i}$ be the subgroup of $H$ consisting of those elements that fix $a_{i}$ then $J_{i}$ is proper and $|H:J_{i}|=|A_{i}|$.

\noindent$(\Leftarrow)$ Let $A$ be the disjoint union of the left cosets of the $J_{i},\,1\leq i\leq r$. Then $H$ acts on $A$ without fixed points.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}
$D(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty,\,Z)\rightarrow C(\infty,\,n)$. $(\Leftarrow$ Gauntt\index{Author}{Gauntt} \emph{\cite{bib:1970}}, $\Rightarrow$ Mostowski\index{Author}{Mostowski} \emph{\cite{bib:1958}})
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
$L(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(WO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n)$. (Gauntt \emph{\cite{bib:1968}})
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
$K(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n)$. ($\Rightarrow$ Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \emph{\cite{bib:1973a}}, $\Leftarrow$ Mostowski \emph{\cite{bib:1958}})
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
$L(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(LO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(LO,\,n)$. (Truss \emph{\cite{bib:1973a}})
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
$ZF\vdash C(LO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(WO,\,Z)\rightarrow C(WO,\,n)$. (Truss \emph{\cite{bib:1973a}})
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
$ZF\vdash C(\infty,\,Z)\rightarrow C(LO,\,n)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash C(\infty,\,Z)\rightarrow C(\infty,\,n)$. (Truss \emph{\cite{bib:1973a}})
\end{theorem*}

\noindent Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1984b} has introduced the following forms each depending on the set I:

$C(I,\,n)$. Every $I$ indexed family of $n$ element sets has a choice function. (Depends on $n\in \omega$.)

$C(I,\,\in Z)$. $(\forall n\in Z)(C(I,\,n))$. (Depends on finite $Z\subseteq \omega$.) and has shown

\begin{theorem*}
$L(n,\,Z)\Leftrightarrow ZF\vdash(\forall I)(C(I,\,\in Z)\rightarrow C(I,\,n))$.
\end{theorem*}

We now turn to some generalizations of the finite axioms of choice due to Truss \cite{bib:1973a}. Some definitions are necessary. For any set $X$ let $e(X)$ be the set of nonempty finite subsets of $X$ and define $e(0,\, X)=X$ and $e(n+1,\,X)=e(e(n,\,X))$. (We assume that $e(k,\,X) \cap e(j,\,X)=\emptyset$ for $j\neq k$. If this is not the case we replace $e(n,\,X)$ by $\{e(n,\,X)\}\times e(n,\,X)$ for each $n\in \omega$.) Let $V(m,\, X)$ be the set of equivalence classes on $e(m,\,X)$ under the equivalence relation $aRb$ iff $\exists$ a permutation $\phi$ of $X$ such that (the extension of) $\phi(a)=\mathrm{b}$. If $|X|=n\in\omega$ then there is a natural 1-1 correspondence between $V(m,\,n)$ and $V(m,\,X).(\nu\rightarrow f(\nu)$ where $f$ is (the extension of) any one to one correspondence between $X$ and $n$.) For $\nu\in V(m,\,n)$ we denote the corresponding equivalence class in $V(m,\,X)$ by $\nu(X)$. Let $V=\bigcup\{V(m,\,n):m,\,n\in \omega,\, n\neq 0\}$. For any $Z\subseteq V$, Truss defines the following choice axioms: ($Z$ no longer denotes a finite subset of $\omega$.)

$C(\infty,\,Z)$. For any set $Y,\,\{\nu(X):\nu\in Z$ and $X\in Y$ and $\nu\in V(m,\,|X|)$ for some $m\in \omega$\} has a choice function.

$C(LO,\,Z)$. For any linearly ordered set $Y$, same as above.

$C(WO,\,Z)$. For any well ordered set $Y$, same as above.

If $\nu\in V$, then we let $C(\infty,\,\nu)$, $C(LO,\,\nu)$ and $C(WO,\,\nu)$ denote respectively $C(\infty,\,\{\nu\})$, $C(LO,\,\{\nu\})$ and $C(WO,\,\{\nu\})$.

\noindent For example, if $Z=\{\nu\}$ where $\nu$ is the set of all pairs of elements of $n$ then $C(\infty,\, \{\nu\})\equiv C(\infty,\,\nu)$ is ``For every set $Y$ of $n$ elements sets there is a function $f$ such that $\forall X\in Y,\,f(X)$ is a two element subset of X.''

Necessary and sufficient conditions are given for
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(A)] $\mathrm{ZF}\vdash C(\infty,\,Z_{1})\wedge C(\mathrm{LO},\,Z_{2})\wedge C(WO,\,Z_{3})\rightarrow C(\infty,\,\nu)$
\item[(B)] $\mathrm{ZF}\vdash C(\infty,\,Z_{1})\wedge C(LO,\,Z_{2})\wedge C(WO,\,Z_{3})\rightarrow C(LO,\,\nu)$ and
\item[(C)] $\mathrm{ZF}\vdash C(\infty,\,Z_{1})\wedge C(LO,\,Z_{2})\wedge C(WO,\,Z_{3})\rightarrow C(WO,\,\nu)$.
\end{enumerate}

They are

$A(Z,\nu)$. If $\nu\in V(m,\,n)$ and $G$ is a group of permutations of $n$ which moves every member of $\nu$ then there is an $X\in e(k,\,n)$ for some $k$ such that there is and a $w\in Z$ such that $w\in V(n^{\prime},\,|X|)$ for some $n^{\prime}$ and for each $\zeta \in w(X)$, $H(X) \cap G$ is not a subset of $H(\zeta)$. $(\mathrm{If}\,\zeta\,\in e(n,\,X)$ then $H(\zeta)=\{\sigma\in S(X):\sigma(\zeta)=\zeta\}$.)

\begin{theorem*}
$A(Z_{1},\,\nu)$ is equivalent to ($A$).
\end{theorem*}

$B(Z_{1},\,Z_{2},\,\nu)$. If $G$ is a group of permutations of $n$ (where
$\nu\in V(j,\,n)$ for some $j$) which moves every member of $\nu$, there is an $X$ such that either
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] $X\in e(k,\,n)$ for some $k$, and there is some $w\in Z_{1}$ a such that $w\in V(k,\,|X|)$ for some $k$ and for each $\zeta \in w(X)$, $H(X) \cap G$ is not a subset of $H(\zeta)$ or
\item[] $X\in e(k,\,n\cdot m)$ for some $k$ and $m\in \omega$ and there is a $w\in Z_{2}$ such that $w\in V(j,\,|X|)$ for some $j\in \omega$ and for each $\zeta\in w(X),\, G^{m}$ is not a subset of $H(\zeta)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{theorem*}
$B(Z_{1},\,Z_{2},\,\nu)$ is equivalent to ($B$).
\end{theorem*}

$C(Z_{1},\,Z_{2},\,\nu)$. If $G$ is a group of permutations of $n$ (where
$\nu\in V(j,\,n)$ for some $j\in \omega)$ which moves every member of $\nu$, then there is an $X\in e(j,\,n\cdot m)$ for some $j,\,m\in\omega$ such that either
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] for some $w\in Z_{1},\,w\in V(j,\,|X|)$ for some $j\in \omega$ and for each $\zeta \in w(X)$, $G^{m}\cap H(X)$ is not a subset of $H(\zeta)$
or
\item[] for some $w\in Z_{2},\,w\in V(j,\,|X|)$ for some $j\in \omega$ and $H(X)=G^{m}$ and for each $\zeta \in w(X)$, $G^{m}$ is not a subset of $H(\zeta)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{theorem*}
$C(Z_{1},\,Z_{2}\cup Z_{3},\,\nu)$ is equivalent to ($C$).
\end{theorem*}

\noindent See note 73 for adding dependent choice to the independence results above.

The finite axioms of choice have been generalized in Conway\index{Author}{Conway} \cite{bib:1971} as follows:

\begin{definition*}
Let $k$ be a natural number.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] An ordered $k$-tuple $(A,\,B,\,C,\,\ldots)$ of disjoint finite sets of cardinalities $a,\,b,\,\ldots$ respectively is called an $(a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots)$ set.
\item[2.] $[a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots]$ is the axiom: For every collection of $(a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots)$ sets there is a function $f$ defined on the collection such that $f(A,\,B,\,C,\,\ldots) \in A\cup B \cup C \cup\cdots$
\item[3.] $\langle a,\, b,\,c,\,\ldots\rangle$ is the additive semi-group generated by $a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots$ (I. e., the closure of $\{a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots\}$ under addition.)
\item[4.] If $S=\langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots\rangle$ then $[S]$ denotes the axiom $[a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots]$. (by result I below, if $\langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots\rangle$ and $\langle\alpha,\,\beta,\,\gamma\ldots\rangle$ are equal then $[a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots]$ and $[\alpha,\,\beta,\,\gamma,\,\ldots]$ are equivalent.)

\item[5.] If $G$ is any finite group, $\langle G\rangle\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is the semi-group generated by the indices in $G$ of all proper subgroups of $G$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
(Some parts due to Mostowski)
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{I.}] If $\langle\alpha,\,\beta,\,\gamma,\,\ldots\rangle\subseteq\langle a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots\rangle$ then $[\alpha,\, \beta,\,\gamma,\,\ldots]\Rightarrow[a,\,b,\,c,\,\ldots]$.
\item[\emph{II.}] Let $S_{1},\,\ldots,\,S_{N},\,S$ be semi-groups ($\subseteq \mathbb{N}$), then for the implication
\begin{equation*}\tag{$^{\ast}$}
[S_{1}]\wedge[S_{2}]\wedge\cdots\wedge[S_{N}]\Rightarrow[S]
\end{equation*}
to hold it suffices that every group $G$ with $S\subseteq\langle G\rangle$ has some subgroup $H$ for which $S_{i}\subseteq\langle H\rangle$ for some $i,\,1\leq i\leq N$.
\item[\emph{III.}] (Mostowski) For ($\ast$) to hold it is necessary that every Abelian group $G$ with $S\subseteq\langle G\rangle$ have some subgroup $H$ with $S_{i}\subseteq\langle H\rangle$ for some $i,\,1\leq i\leq N$.
\item[IV.] The condition of II is necessary and sufficient for effective implication, that is, for the existence of a formula $F(f_{1},\,\ldots,\,f_{N})=f$ which defines a choice function $f$ for the class of all $S$ sets whenever we substitute such choice functions for the classes of all $S_{1}$ sets, $S_{2}$ sets, $\ldots$, $S_{N}$ sets for $f_{1},\,f_{2},\ldots,f_{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

The following are proved in Wi\'{s}niewski\index{Author}{Wi\'{s}niewski} \cite{bib:1972}:

\begin{theorem*}
Let $P$ be the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by a set $Z$ of prime numbers ($P$ consists of sums of the form $p_{1}+p_{2}+\cdots+p_{k}$ where $p_{i},\, i=1,\,\ldots,\,k$ are in $Z$.) Then there is a model $\mathcal{N}$ of $ZF^{0}$ in which $C(\infty,\,n)$ is true for all $n\not\in P$ and $C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$ is false for all $n\in P$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
Let $G$ be a finite group, $Q(G)$ the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by the indices of proper subgroups of $G$ in $G$ and $R(G)$ the additive semi-group of positive integers generated by the orders of non-identity elements of G. Then there is a model $\mathcal{N}$ of $ZF^{0}$ in which $C(LO,\,n)$ is true for all $n\not\in Q(G)$, $C(\infty,\, n)$ is false for all $n\not\in R(G)$ and $C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$ is false for all $n\in Q(G)$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
 Let $p$ and $q$ be primes such that $p_{1}=(p^{q}-1)/(p-1)$ is prime. Then there is a model $\mathcal{N}$ of $ZF^{0}$ in which
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{1.}] $C(LO,\,n)$ is true for $n$ of the form $kp_{1}+rp^{q}$
\item[\emph{2.}] $C(\infty,\,n)$ is false for $n$ of the form $kp+rq$
\item[\emph{3.}] $C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$ is false for $n$ of the form $kp_{1}+rp^{q}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
If for every prime $p$ there are infinitely many primes of the form $(p^{q}-1)/(p-1)$ then there is a model $\mathcal{N}$ of $ZF^{0}$ where $C(\aleph_{0},\,n)$ is true for every $n$ and $C(\infty,\,n)$ is false for every $n>1$.
\end{theorem*}

\textsc{Note.} The Mersenne Prime conjecture\index{Subject}{Mersenne prime conjecture} (there are infinitely many primes of the form $2^{n}-1$) is a special case of the hypotheses of this theorem.

Along the same lines Zuckerman\index{Author}{Zuckerman} \cite{bib:1971} proves

\begin{theorem*}
Let $Z$ be any set of primes and $P$ the additive semigroup of positive integers generated by Z. Then there is a model $\mathcal{N}$ of $ZF^{0}$ in which form 67 (the axiom of multiple choice, $MC(\infty,\,\infty)$) is true and for every $n\in \omega,\,n>1,\,C(\infty,\,n)$ is true if and only if $n\in P$.
\end{theorem*}

\section*{NOTE 16}

This note contains the definitions necessary to understand the forms in Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1984d}, that is, form 126.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A $B$-\emph{lattice}\index{Subject}{$B$-lattice} is a vector lattice\index{Subject}{vector lattice} (see below for the definition of vector lattice) together with a Frechet-complete (Cauchy sequences are convergent) Riez-norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ (i.e., (i) $-y\leq x\leq y\rightarrow\Vert x\Vert\leq\Vert y\Vert$ (ii) if $\Vert x\Vert\leq 1$ there is a $y\geq 0$ such that $-y\leq x\leq y$ and $\Vert y\Vert\leq 1.)$
\item[2.] A \emph{positive linear functional} on $X$ is a linear mapping $f: X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)\geq 0$ when $x\geq 0$.
\item[3.] A \emph{wedge}\index{Subject}{wedge}\index{Subject}{wedge in a linear space} $W$ in a real linear space $L$ is a convex set such that $t\subseteq W$ for every $t\geq 0\ (t\in \mathbb{R})$. A \emph{cone}\index{Subject}{cone in a linear space} is a wedge which contains no line through 0.
\item[4.] An \emph{ordered linear space}\index{Subject}{ordered linear space} (OSL) is a linear space $L$ in which some wedge $W$, called the positive wedge has been, specified. The partial ordering $\leq$ on $L$ is defined by $y\leq x$ iff $x-y\in W$. (Note that this differs from the definition of \emph{ordered vector space} in note 31.)

\item[ ] (Facts: (a) $\leq$ is reflexive \& transitive (b) translation and multiplication by positive numbers preserves order, multiplication by negative numbers reverses order, (c) ($x\geq y$ and $y\geq x$ implies $y=x$) if and only if the wedge is a cone. (d) $x\geq 0$ iff $x\in W$. If a relation satisfies (a) and (b) then (d) defines a wedge.)
\item[5.] Let $V$ be a partially ordered linear space with a positive wedge (defined). $V$ is a \emph{vector lattice} if the positive wedge in $V$ is a cone and if each set $\{x,\,x^{\prime}\}$ of two elements has a least upper bound $x\vee x^{\prime}$. These definitions are taken primarily from Day\index{Author}{Day} \cite{bib:1973}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 17}

\begin{definition*}
An $\epsilon$ lattice\index{Subject}{$\epsilon$ lattice} in a metric space ($X$,dist) is a maximal subset $L$ of $X$ which satisfies $(\forall x,\,y\in L)(\mathrm{dist}(x,\,y)\geq\epsilon$ for $x\neq y)$. From Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1984e}. See [1 I].
\end{definition*}
