\section*{NOTE 19}

It is clear that K\"{o}nig's lemma\index{Subject}{K\"{o}nig's lemma}, [10 F] implies [10 K] and using the usual proof that the Completeness Theorem implies the Compactness Theorem, it follows that [10 K] implies [10 L]. To show that [10 L] implies 10, $C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$, let $X=\{x_{i}: i\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable set of finite sets, where each $x_{i}=\{x_{i,0},\,x_{i,1},\,\cdots x_{i,n_{i}}\}$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a first order language with a single function symbol $f$ and constant symbols for each $x_{i}\in X$ and each element $x_{i,j}$ of $\bigcup X$. Let $S$ be the following set of sentence in $\mathcal{L}$: For each $i\in\omega$, the conjunction of

$\wedge (\{x_{i,j}\neq x_{i,k}:j,\,k\leq n_{i}$ and $j\neq k\})$ and

$\vee\,(\{f(x_{i})=x_{i,0},\,\ldots,\,f(x_{i})=x_{i,n_{i}}\})$.

Each finite subset of $S$ has a model, so [10 L] implies that the denumerable set of sentences has a model. In that model, $f$ is a choice function on $X$.

\section*{NOTE 20}

We give some definitions and properties of inaccessible cardinals\index{Subject}{inaccessible cardinal}. (Proofs of the results given below can be found in Drake\index{Author}{Drake} \cite{bib:1974}.)

\begin{definition*}
A cardinal $\kappa$ is \emph{(strongly) inaccessible} if $\kappa$ is regular and for all $\mu<\kappa,\, 2^{\mu}<\kappa$. (An inaccessible cardinal is also called a \emph{strong limit cardinal}.)
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
No successor cardinal, $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$, is inaccessible. (This is form [0 AJ].)
\end{lemma*}

\begin{definition*}
$\mu$ is called a 2-\emph{valued}, $\kappa$-\emph{additive (complete) measure on} $x$ if $\mu$ is a function from $x$ to $\{0,1\}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\mu(x)=1$;
\item[(b)] If $y=\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}x_{\alpha}\subseteq x$ is a disjoint union, then $\mu(y)=\sum\nolimits_{\alpha\in \kappa}\mu(x_{\alpha})$.
\end{enumerate}
(The measure is called \emph{non-trivial} if the measure of a one-element set is 0.)
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
A cardinal $\kappa$ is said to be \emph{measurable} if $\kappa >\aleph_{0}$ and $\kappa$ has a 2-valued $\kappa$-additive non-trivial measure.
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
($ZFC$) Every measurable cardinal\index{Subject}{measurable cardinal} is inaccessible. (Form 319.)
\end{theorem*}

\begin{definition*}
A filter is $\kappa$-\emph{additive (complete)} if the intersection of $<\kappa$ members of the filter is in the filter.
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
A cardinal $\kappa$ is measurable iff there is a non-principal ultrafilter on $\kappa$ which is $\kappa$-additive.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{definition*}
A measure $\mu$ on $\kappa$ is \emph{normal} if $\mu$ is a non-trivial $\kappa$-additive measure on $\kappa$ such that for any function $f:\kappa \rightarrow\kappa$ that is regressive (i.e., such that $f(\alpha)<\alpha$ for all $\alpha<\kappa,\,\alpha\neq 0$) there is a $\beta<\kappa$ such that $\mu(\{\alpha<\kappa:f(\alpha)=\beta\})=1$ (i.e., every regressive function on $\kappa$ is constant on a set of measure
1).
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If $X=\langle X_{\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\rangle$ is $\kappa$-sequence of subsets of $\kappa$, the \emph{diagonal intersection}\index{Subject}{diagonal intersection}, $D(X)=\bigcap_{\alpha<\kappa}(X_{\alpha}\cup
\alpha+1)=\{\beta<\kappa:\forall\alpha<\beta(\beta\in X_{\alpha}\}$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
$\mu$ is normal iff the diagonal intersection of any $\kappa$-sequence of sets of measure 1 is also of measure 1.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{theorem*}
(ZFC) If $\kappa$ is measurable then $\kappa$ has a normal measure.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{definition*}
If $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ are cardinals, $\mathcal{L}_{\kappa,\lambda}$ is the language obtained by adding infinite conjunctions and disjunctions of cardinality less than $\kappa$ and infinite quantifications of blocks of variables of cardinal less than $\lambda$. (The ordinary first-order language is equivalent to $\mathcal{L}_{\omega,\omega}.$)
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A cardinal $\kappa >\aleph_{0}$ is \emph{weakly compact}\index{Subject}{weakly compact cardinal} if the language $\mathcal{L}_{\kappa,\kappa}$ is $(\kappa,\,\kappa)$-compact, i.e., if $\Gamma$ is a set of sentences of $\mathcal{L}_{\kappa,\kappa}$ with cardinality $\leq\kappa$ and every subset of $\Gamma$ of cardinality $<\kappa$ has a model, then $\Gamma$ has a model.
\item[(b)] A cardinal $\kappa >\aleph_{0}$ is \emph{strongly compact} if $\mathcal{L}_{\kappa,\kappa}$ is compact, i.e., if $\Gamma$ is any set of formulas of $\mathcal{L}_{\kappa,\kappa}$ such that every subset of $\Gamma$ of cardinality $<\kappa$ has a model, then $\Gamma$ has a model.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For $n\in \omega,\,[X]^{n}$ is the set of all $n$-element subsets of $X$, and $[X]^{<\omega}$, is the set of all finite subsets of $X$.
\item[(b)] The partition relation\index{Subject}{partition relation} $\kappa \rightarrow(\kappa)^{n}$ holds iff for every function $f:[\kappa]^{n}\rightarrow 2$ there is an unbounded subset $X$ of $\kappa$ such that $f/[X]^{2}$ is constant. (The set $X$ is called \emph{homogeneous for} $f$.)
\item[(c)] The partition relation $\kappa \rightarrow(\kappa)^{<\omega}$ holds iff for every function $f:[\kappa]^{<\omega}\rightarrow 2$ there is an unbounded subset $X$ of $\kappa$ such that $f$ is constant on $[X]^{n}$ for every $n\in \omega$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
(ZFC) If $\kappa$ is inaccessible, then $\kappa$ is weakly compact iff $\kappa \rightarrow(\kappa)^{2}$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{lemma*}
(ZFC) Every measurable cardinal is weakly compact.
\end{lemma*}

\noindent(Bull\index{Author}{Bull} \cite{bib:1978} defines a measurable cardinal as a cardinal that has a normal measure. With this definition, ZF $\vdash$ Every measurable cardinal is weakly compact.)

\begin{theorem*}
(ZFC) If $\kappa$ is a regular infinite cardinal, $\kappa$ is strongly compact iff for any $\kappa$-complete filter $J$ on a set $X,\,J$ can be extended to a $\kappa$-complete ultrafilter on $X$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{lemma*}
(ZFC) Every strongly compact cardinal\index{Subject}{strongly compact cardinal} is measurable.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\lambda)$ is the set of all subsets of $\lambda$ of cardinality $<\kappa$.
\item[(b)] Let $X=\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\lambda)$,
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For each $\xi <\lambda$, let $C_{\xi}=\{x\in X:\xi\,\in x\}$. An ultrafilter extending the filter $\{C_{\xi}:\xi\,<\lambda\}$ is called a \emph{regular} ultrafilter\index{Subject}{regular ultrafilter}. (The measure corresponding to the regular ultrafilter is called a \emph{regular} measure\index{Subject}{regular measure}.)
\item[(ii)] A measure $\mu$ on $X$ is called \emph{normal} if it is $\kappa$-additive, regular and such that if $f(x)\in x$ for each $x\in X$, then for some $\xi <\lambda,\,\mu(\{x\in X:f(x)=\xi\})=1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ are cardinals such that $\aleph_{0}<\kappa \leq\lambda,\,\kappa$ is $\lambda$-\emph{supercompact} if there is a normal measure\index{Subject}{normal measure} on $\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\lambda)$.
\item[(b)] If $\kappa >\aleph_{0},\,\kappa$ is \emph{supercompact} if $\kappa$ is $\lambda$-supercompact for every $\lambda\geq\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
(ZFC) Every supercompact cardinal\index{Subject}{supercompact cardinal} is strongly compact.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{lemma*}
Form 319 implies form 320. (Use [0 AJ].)
\end{lemma*}

\begin{definition*}
$\kappa$ is a \emph{Ramsey cardinal}\index{Subject}{Ramsey cardinal} iff $\kappa \rightarrow(\kappa)^{<\omega}$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
Every measurable cardinal is a Ramsey cardinal.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{definition*} A cardinal $\kappa$ is called a \emph{Rowbottom cardinal}\index{Subject}{Rowbottom cardinal} iff, whenever $\mathfrak{A} = \langle A,\,U,\,\cdots\rangle$ is a structure of countable length, where $|A|=\kappa,\,U\subset A$, and $|U|<\kappa$, then
$\mathfrak{A}$ has an elementary substructure $\mathfrak{B} =\langle B,\,U^{\prime},\cdots\rangle$ with $|\mathfrak{B}|=\kappa$ and $|U^{\prime}|\leq\aleph_{0}$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
Every Ramsey cardinal is a Rowbottom cardinal.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{definition*} A cardinal $\kappa$ is said to be \emph{almost huge} iff there is an $n\in \omega$ and a cardinal $\lambda>\kappa$, a $\kappa$-additive normal ultrafilter $U$ on $2^{\lambda}$, and a sequence $\kappa =\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}<\cdots<\lambda_{n}=\lambda$ such that for each $i<n,\,\{x\subseteq\lambda:x\cap\, \lambda_{i+1}=\lambda_{i}\}\in U$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{lemma*}
Every almost huge cardinal\index{Subject}{almost huge cardinal} is supercompact.
\end{lemma*}

In a series of papers (Apter\index{Author}{Apter} \cite{bib:1985b}, \cite{bib:1988}, \cite{bib:1990}, \cite{bib:1992} and Apter/Henle\index{Author}{Apter/Henle} \cite{bib:1991}) various consistency results about large cardinals are obtained. We give some examples below.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] Con(ZFC + There exists cardinals $\kappa <\lambda$ such $\kappa$ is $\lambda$-supercompact and $\lambda$ is measurable) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF + $\mathrm{cof}(\kappa)=\omega+\kappa$ is a Rowbottom cardinal $+\ \kappa^{+}$ is a measurable cardinal).
\item[2.] Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF
+ $\aleph_{1}$ is measurable + All uncountable cardinals are singular).
\item[3.] Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF
+ $\neg C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)\ +$ An uncountable cardinal is measurable iff it is the successor of a singular cardinal).
\item[4.] Con(ZFC + There exists an almost huge cardinal) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF $+\neg C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)+ \forall\alpha\,\aleph_{\alpha}$ or $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is measurable).
\item[] In Bull\index{Author}{Bull} \cite{bib:1978}, besides form 321, there are the following consistency results. Let $S$ be the following statement:
\end{enumerate}

$S$. There are cardinals $\aleph_{\alpha}<\aleph_{\beta}<\aleph_{\gamma}$ such that $\aleph_{\alpha}$ is $\aleph_{\gamma}$-supercompact; $\aleph_{\beta}$ is the first measurable cardinal greater than $\aleph_{\alpha}$; and $\aleph_{\gamma}=|2^{\aleph_{\beta}}|$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] Con(ZFC + $S$) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF + form 43 + $\aleph_{1}$ is weakly compact + $\aleph_{2}$ is measurable).
\end{enumerate}

$S^{\prime}$.: There\index{Subject}{ramification system} are cardinals $\aleph_{\alpha}<\aleph_{\beta}$ such that $\aleph_{\beta}$ is the first weakly compact cardinal greater than $\aleph_{\alpha}$ and $\aleph_{\alpha}$ is $\aleph_{\beta}$-supercompact.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[2.] Con(ZFC + $S^{\prime}$) $\rightarrow$ Con(ZF + $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)+\aleph_{\alpha}$ and $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ are both weakly compact. (In fact, 2 may be extended to a finite sequence of weakly compact cardinals.)
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 21}

Definitions for forms [10 F], [14 M], [14 N], [43 H], [106 A], 216, and 249.

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{tree}\index{Subject}{tree} is a connected undirected graph without circuits one of whose vertices is designated as the origin.
\item[] Note that a tree may also be defined as a partially ordered set $(P,\,\leq)$ with a least element and with the property that for any element $x\in P$ the set of predecessors of $x$ is a finite set which is linearly ordered by $\leq$. Every tree in this sense is also a tree in the sense of definition 1 (under the obvious translation) and vice versa. Note also that the definition of \emph{tree} for form [86 A($\alpha$)] in note 119 differs from the definition given above.

\item[2.] The number of vertices on the unique path connecting a vertex $v$ with the origin is the \emph{level}\index{Subject}{level in a tree} of $v,\,l(v)$. (Thus the set of vertices of a tree can be decomposed into an at most denumerable set of levels.)
\item[3.] A vertex $v^{\prime}$ is a \emph{successor} of a vertex $v$ if $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ are connected by an edge and $l(v^{\prime})=l(v)+1$.

\item[4.] A tree is \emph{finite} if its set of vertices is finite and \emph{locally finite} if each vertex has only finitely many successors.
\item[5.] A \emph{branch} in a tree\index{Subject}{branch in a tree} is a maximal path beginning at the origin. If $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ are on the same branch, then $v^{\prime}$ \emph{dominates} $v$ if $l(v^{\prime})\geq l(v)$.
\item[] Konig's lemma states that any infinite locally finite tree\index{Subject}{locally finite tree} has an infinite branch.
\item[6.] An $\omega$-\emph{tree}\index{Subject}{$\omega$-tree} is a locally finite tree with at least one vertex of level $n$ for each $n\in \omega$.
\item[7.] A \emph{subtree}\index{Subject}{subtree} of a tree $(P,\,\leq)$ is a subset of $P$ which is a tree under the induced ordering and which is closed under predecessor.
\item[8.] An \emph{antichain} in a tree\index{Subject}{antichain in a tree} $(P,\,\leq)$ is a subset of $P$ whose elements are pairwise incomparable. (Note that this differs from the definition of \emph{antichain} used in form [86 A($\alpha$)] and given in note 119.)
\item[9.] Let $T$ be a collection of locally finite trees (not necessarily pairwise disjoint).
\item[] By a \emph{vertex} or a \emph{level} of $T$, we mean a vertex or a level of some tree in $T$.
\item[10.] If $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ are vertices of $T$, then $v^{\prime}$ \emph{dominates} $v$ in $T$ if $v^{\prime}$ dominates $v$ in some tree in T.
\item[11.] Let $S$ be a set of vertices of $T$. $S$ \emph{pierces} a level $l$ of $T$ if $|S\cap l|=1$.
\item[12.] $S$ is \emph{consistent} if for every $v,\,v^{\prime}$ in $S$ there is a $v^{\prime\prime}$ which dominates them both in T.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 22}

Definitions for forms [1 L], [1 M], [1 N], [10 C] and [132 A]. A \emph{set mapping}\index{Subject}{set mapping} $f$ is a function $f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that for all $x\in X,\,x\not\in f(x)$. A \emph{free subset}\index{Subject}{free subset} of $X$ (relative to $f$) is a subset $H$ of $X$ such that for all $x,\,y\in H,\,x\not\in f(y)$. A \emph{ramification system} is a triple $\langle X,\,E,\,S\rangle$ where $X$ and
$E$ are sets and $S\,:\,X^{\leq\theta}\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E)$ (where $\theta$ is an ordinal and $X^{\leq\theta}$ denotes all functions $t:\alpha\rightarrow X$ where $\alpha\leq\theta$) satisfies (i) $S(\emptyset)=E$ (ii) If $f,\, g\in\mathrm{dom}(S)$ and $f\subseteq g$, then $S(g)\subseteq S(f)$ and (iii) If $f\in\mathrm{dom}(S)$ and $\eta=\mathrm{dom}(f)$ is a limit ordinal then $S(f)=\bigcap_{\alpha<\eta}S(f/\alpha)$.

\section*{NOTE 23}

Definitions for forms [14 Q] and [52 E]: If $E$ is a Banach space\index{Subject}{Banach space} (complete, normed, linear space) then $E^{\ast}$ (the \emph{dual} of $E$) is the space of all bounded linear functionals on $E$. (That is, all $f:E\rightarrow\,\mathbb{R}$
such that $(\exists M)(\forall x\in E)(|f(x)|\leq\Vert x\Vert M)$. $E^{\ast}$ is a Banach space if we define $\Vert f\Vert=\sup_{x\neq 0}\Big(\frac{|f(x)|}{\Vert x\Vert}\Big)$. Each $x\in E$ can be thought of as a linear functional on $E^{\ast}$ if we define $x(f)=f(x)$ for all $f$ in $E^{\ast}$. The \emph{weak}$^{\ast}$ \emph{topology}\index{Subject}{weak$^{\ast}$ topology} on $E^{\ast}$ is the weakest topology that makes all these linear functionals continuous. Sets of the form $w_{x,\epsilon}=\{f\in E^{\ast}:|f(x)|<\epsilon\}$ form a basis for this topology. If $X\subseteq E,\,X$ is \emph{convex-compact}\index{Subject}{convex-compact subset of a topological
vector space} if whenever $F_{i}$, for $i\in I$, are closed convex subsets of $X$ and $\{X\,\cap\,F_{i}:i\in I\}$ has the finite intersection property, then $\bigcap_{i\in I}(X\cap\,F_{i})\neq\emptyset$. Note that the definition of \emph{convex-compact} may be given in any topological vector space.

\section*{NOTE 24}

This note contains some definitions from group theory that are used in $\mathcal{M}22$, and forms [62 C], [62 D], [67 D], 180, and 308.

\begin{definition*}
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The \emph{Frattini subgroup of}\index{Subject}{Frattini subgroup} $G,\,\Phi(G)$, is the intersection of all maximal subgroups of $G$.
\item[(b)] Let $Z(G)$ be the center of $G$ and $G^{\prime}$, the commutator subgroup of $G$.
\item[(c)] $G$ is said to be a $p$-\emph{group}\index{Subject}{$p$-group} if for all $x\in G$ there is an $n\in \omega$ such that $x^{p^{n}}=1$. $G$ is said to have \emph{exponent} $p$ if for every $x\in G,\,x^{p}=1$. An Abelian group is said to be \emph{elementary} if there is a prime $p$ such that every non-identity element has order $p$.
$\qquad G$ is said to be \emph{divisible}\index{Subject}{divisible group} if for each $a\in G$ and for each integer $m\neq 0$ the equation $x^{m}=a$ has a solution in $G$ and $G$ is called $n$-\emph{divisible}\index{Subject}{$n$-divisible group} if the equation $x^{m}=a$ has a solution for all $m<n$.
\item[(d)] A factor $H/K$ of a series of $G$ is said to be a \emph{central factor}\index{Subject}{central factor of a group} of $G$ if $K$ is normal in $G$ and $H/K$ is a subgroup of $Z(G/K)$.
\item[(e)] $G$ is said to be \emph{nilpotent}\index{Subject}{nilpotent group} if it has a series all of whose factors are central factors of $G$.
\item[(f)] $Z_{n}(G)$ is defined as follows: $Z_{0}(G)=1$ and for each integer $n>0$,
\begin{equation*}
Z_{n}(G)/Z_{n-1}(G)=Z(G/Z_{n-1}(G)).
\end{equation*}
The \emph{class} of $G$ is the least integer $n$ such that $Z_{n}(G)=G$.
\item[(g)] $G$ is a \emph{special} $p$-\emph{group} if $G$ is a $p$-group, $G^{\prime}=Z(H)=\Phi(H)$, and $G$ is either elementary Abelian\index{Subject}{elementary Abelian group} or nilpotent of class 2.
\item[(h)] $G$ is an \emph{extra-special} $p$-\emph{group}\index{Subject}{special $p$-group} if $G$ is special and $G^{\prime}$ is cyclic of order $p$.
\item[(i)] A group is \emph{divisible} if each element is divisible by each positive integer.
\item[(j)] A group is \emph{torsion free}\index{Subject}{torsion free group} if the only element of finite order is the identity element.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

For forms 144 and 179: Let $W(0)$ be the class of well orderable sets and let $W(\alpha+1)=\{\bigcup Q:Q\subseteq W(\alpha)$ and $Q\in W(0)\}$ and $W(\lambda)=\bigcup\{W(\beta):\beta<\lambda\}$ for limit ordinals $\lambda$. Then $W$ (the class of almost well orderable sets\index{Subject}{almost well orderable sets}) is defined to be $\bigcup\{W(\alpha):\alpha\in\, On\}$. See Keisler\index{Author}{Keisler} \cite{bib:1970}. Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1977b} has shown that If $P\subseteq W$ and $P\in W$, then $\bigcup P\in W$. Regarding the form(s) 179 $(\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha))$, R. David\index{Author}{David} \cite{bib:1980} shows that for ordinals $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $0<\alpha<\beta$, the statement $\forall x,\,x\in W(\beta)$ does not imply $\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha)$. (Clearly,
$\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha)$ implies $\forall x,\,x\in W(\beta).)$ It is clear that 30 + 294 (every linearly ordered $W$-set\index{Subject}{$W$-set} can be well ordered) implies that every $W$-set can be well ordered. Thus, 30 + 294 + 144 (every set is a $W$-set) implies AC.

\section*{NOTE 26}

A summary of the definitions and results from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1983d}. Brunner considers 16 properties a topological space $(X,\,\underline{X})$ may have:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[W1] : $\underline{X}$ is w.o. (well ordered);
\item[W2] : $X$ is w.o.;
\item[D1] : $X$ is covered by a w.o. family of closed, discrete sets.
\item[D2] : $X$ is covered by a w.o. family of discrete sets;
\item[B1] : $X$ has a w.o. base
\item[B2] : $\exists f:X\times W\rightarrow\underline{X}$ such that $W$ is w.o. and $f^{\prime}\{x\}\times W)$ is a neighborhood base at $x$ for each $x\in X$.
\item[B3] : $\exists f:X\times W\rightarrow\underline{X}$ such that $W$ is w.o. and $\forall x\in X,\,\{x\}=\bigcap f^{\prime}\{x\}\times W)$
\item[L1] : Each open cover of $X$ has a w.o. subcover;
\item[L2] : Each open cover of $X$ has a w.o. refinement;
\item[S] : $X$ has a dense, w.o. subset;
\item[C] : Each family $O\subseteq\underline{X}$ of pairwise disjoint sets is w.o.
\item[A1] : If $O\subseteq\underline{X}$ covers $X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow O$ such that $\forall x\in X,\, x\in f(x)$;
\item[A2] : If $O\subseteq\underline{X}$ covers $X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow\underline{X}$ s.t. $\forall x\in X,\,x\in f(x)$ and $f^{\prime}X$ refines $O$;
\item[H1] : $X$ is hereditarily $A1$;
\item[H2] : $X$ is hereditarily $A2$;
\item[F] : $X$ is a continuous finite to one image of an $A1$ space.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{definition*}
If $P$ is one of the above then $A(P)$ is the statement: ``Every topological space $(X,\, \underline{X})$ is P.'' $A(P,\,Q)$ is the statement: ``If a topological space satisfies $P$ then it satisfies $Q$.''
\end{definition*}

All of the $A(P)$'s occur in the list of forms, but not all the $A(P,\,Q)$'s occur.

The table below, taken from Brunner \cite{bib:1983d}, summarizes the results. In the table, $0$ means that $A(P,\, Q)$ ($P$ the row heading and $Q$ the column heading) is provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. $N$ means $A(P,\,Q)$ is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. $AC$ (form 1), $MC$ (form 67) and $PW$ (form 91) mean respectively that $A(P,\,Q)$ is equivalent to $AC,\,MC$ or $PW$ in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. And $IMC$ or $IPW$ mean that $A(P,\,Q)$ implies $MC$ or $PW$ respectively in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

\section*{NOTE 28}

In this note we give definitions for the various versions of the Baire category theorem and summarize the results from Brunner \cite{bib:1983c}.

\begin{definition*}
Let $(X,\,T)$ be a topological space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A set $Y\subseteq X$ is \emph{nowhere dense} if the closure of $Y$ has empty interior.
\item[2.] A set $Y\subseteq X$ is \emph{meager}\index{Subject}{meager set} or \emph{of the first category}\index{Subject}{first category set} if $Y$ is a countable union of nowhere dense sets\index{Subject}{nowhere dense set}.
\item[3.] A set $Y\subseteq X$ is \emph{perfect}\index{Subject}{perfect set} if $Y$ is closed, non-empty and has no isolated points.
\item[4.] A set $Y\subseteq X$ has the \emph{Baire property}\index{Subject}{Baire property} if $(Y\backslash U)\cup(U\backslash Y)$ is meager for some open set $U$.
\item[5.] $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{Baire} or is a \emph{Baire space}\index{Subject}{Baire space} if the intersection of each countable sequence of dense, open sets in $X$ is dense in $X$.
\item[6.] $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{sequentially complete} if every sequence has a convergent subsequence.
\item[7.] $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{\v{Cech complete}}-$I$ if it satisfies
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(X,\,T)$ is regular (every neighborhood of a point $x\in S$ contains a closed neighborhood of $x$) and
\item[(ii)] there is a denumerable collection $\{\mathcal{C}_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ of open covers of $X$ such that for any collection $F$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection property, if for each $n,\,F$ contains a subset of diameter less than $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ (that is, $(\exists u\in F)(\exists c\in \mathcal{C}_{n})(u\subseteq c))$, then $F$ has a non-empty intersection.
\end{enumerate}
(This is the definition of \v{C}ech complete used in form [43 E].)
\item[8.] $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{\v{C}ech complete-II} if ($X,\, T)$ is homeomorphic to a $G_{\delta}$ set in a compact, $T_{2}$ space. ($ G_{\delta}\equiv$ countable intersection of open sets.)
\item[] (This is the definition of \v{C}ech complete used in $K9$ below. $K9$ is equivalent to form 106.)
\item[9.] ($X,\, T)$ is \emph{co-compact}\index{Subject}{co-compact space} if $\exists$ a family $F$ of closed sets such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If $G\subseteq F$ and $G$ has the finite intersection property, then $\bigcap G\neq\emptyset$ and
\item[(ii)] If $x\in \mathcal{O}$, with $\mathcal{O}$ open, then $\exists A\in F$ with $x\in A^{\circ}$ (the interior of $A$) and $A\subseteq$ closure $(\mathcal{O}).)$
\end{enumerate}
\item[10.] $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{scattered}\index{Subject}{scattered space} or \emph{Boolean}\index{Subject}{Boolean space} if it is Hausdorff and has a basis of clopen sets.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
Let ($X, d$) be a metric space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] ($X, d$) is \emph{complete} or \emph{Frechet complete}\index{Subject}{Frechet complete space} if Cauchy sequences converge.
\item[2.] ($X, d$) is \emph{Cantor complete} if $\bigcap_{n\in\omega}A(n)\neq\emptyset$ for every sequence $(A(n))_{n\in\omega}$ of non-empty closed sets satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(\forall n\in \omega)(A(n+1)\subseteq A(n))$ and
\item[(ii)] $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}$ diameter$(A(n))=0$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[3.] ($X, d$) is \emph{Kuratowski complete} if $\bigcap_{n\in\omega}A(n)\neq\emptyset$ for each nested sequence $(A(n))_{n\in\omega}$ of non-empty closed sets for which $a(A(n))\rightarrow 0$ where for $A\subseteq X,\, a(A)=\inf\{\max\{\mathrm{diameter}(B):B\in Y\}:Y$ is a finite covering of $A$\}.
\item[4.] ($X, d$) is \emph{filter complete}\index{Subject}{filter complete space} if every Cauchy filter converges.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$K1$] : Every Frechet Complete metric space is Baire. (This is what is usually known as the Baire Category Theorem and is [43 F] in the list of forms.)
\item[$K2$] : Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. ([43 J])
\item[$K3$] : Every metric Kuratowski complete space\index{Subject}{Kuratowski complete space} is Baire.
\item[$K4$] : Every sequentially compact metric space is Baire.
\item[$K5$] : Every countably compact (Every countable open cover has a finite subcover.) metric space is Baire.
\item[$K6$] : Banach spaces (complete, normed, linear spaces) are Baire.
\item[$K7$] : Countably compact, regular spaces are Baire.
\item[$K8$] : Compact $T_{2}$-spaces are Baire. (This is form 106)
\item[$K9$] : \v{C}ech complete\index{Subject}{\v{C}ech complete space}-II spaces are Baire.
\item[$K10$] : Co-compact, $T_{2}$ spaces are Baire.
\item[K11] : Separable, Frechet complete, metric spaces are Baire.
\item[$K12$] : Separable, countably compact, regular spaces are Baire.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

The following results are proved in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}:K1$ and $K2$ are equivalent to $DC$. $DC$ (form 43) implies $K9$ and $K10$. $K1$ implies $K6$. $DMC$ (Dependent Multiple choice, Form [106 A]) implies $K3$ implies $K5$. $K4$ for Cantor complete spaces\index{Subject}{Cantor complete space} implies $DF=F$ (form 9). $K11$ is provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. $DMC$ (form [106 A]) implies $K7$ implies $K8$. $DMC$ implies $K9$ implies $K8$. $DMC$ implies $K10$ implies $K8$. $PW$ (form 91) implies $K12$.

The following independences are shown to hold in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}:MC\not\rightarrow K4,\, MC\not\rightarrow K6$, BPI (Form 14) $\not\rightarrow K8$ (Form 106), $MC_{\mathrm{LO}}$ (form 112) $\not\rightarrow K7,\,C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty) \not\rightarrow K8$ and none of the following are provable in ZF: $Ki,\,i=1,2,4,6,7,8,9,10$.

The following questions are asked:

Are the following provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$?: $K3,\,K5,\,K12$.

Are $Ki,\,7\leq i\leq 10$, equivalent to $DMC$ (form [106 A]).

In Fossy/Morillon\index{Author}{Fossy/Morillon} \cite{bib:1995} it is shown that $K8$ implies $DMC$ from which it follows that $Ki,\,7\leq i\leq 10$ are all equivalent to $DMC$.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 29}

Definitions for forms [14 R] through [14 U], [14 BH] through [14 BL], and [86 B]. See Banaschewski\index{Author}{Banaschewski} \cite{bib:1981}, \cite{bib:1983}, \cite{bib:1997}, Paseka\index{Author}{Paseka} \cite{bib:1989}, and Vickers\index{Author}{Vickers} \cite{bib:1989}.

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{local lattice}\index{Subject}{local lattice} (or \emph{frame}\index{Subject}{frame} or \emph{complete Heyting algebra}\index{Subject}{Heyting algebra}) is a complete lattice $L$ satisfying the distribution law: $x\bigvee_{i\in I}x_{i}=\bigvee_{i\in I}(x\wedge x_{i})$, for all $x,\,x_{i}\in L$ and $\{x_{i}:i\in I\}\subseteq L$. (Example: $\mathcal{D}X$ - the open sets of a topological
space)
\item[2.] A lattice $L$ is \emph{spatial}\index{Subject}{spatial lattice} if for some topological space $X,\,L$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{D}X$. (Theorem. Every complete Boolean algebra is a local lattice. A complete Boolean algebra is a spatial iff it is atomic.)
\item[3.] $c\in L$ ($L$ a local lattice) is \emph{compact}\index{Subject}{compact local lattice} if and only if $c\leq \bigvee_{i\in I}x_{i}$ implies $c\leq x_{i_{1}}\vee\ldots\vee x_{i_{n}}$, for some indices $i_{1},\,\ldots,\,i_{n}$.
\item[4.] $L$ is \emph{compact} iff its top element $e$ is compact.
\item[5.] $L$ is \emph{coherent}\index{Subject}{coherent local lattice} iff (i) Each element of $L$ is the join of compact elements and (ii) the meet of any finite set, including the empty set, of compact elements is compact.
\item[6.] $L$ is \emph{regular}\index{Subject}{regular local lattice} iff for each $x\in L,\,x$ is the join of all $y\ll x$, where $y\ll x$ means $(\exists z\in L)(y\wedge z=0$ and $x\vee z=e)$.
\item[7.] $L$ is 0 \emph{dimensional} iff for each $x\in L,\,x=\bigvee\{y\in L:y^{\ast}\vee y=e$ and $y\leq x\}$. $(y^{\ast}$ is the pseudo-complement
of $y,\,y^{\ast}=\bigvee\{c\in L\,:\,c\wedge a=0\}.)$
\item[8.] $L$ is \emph{conjunctive}\index{Subject}{conjunctive local lattice} iff $\forall a,\,b\in L$, such that $a<b,\,\exists c\in L$ such that $a\vee c<e$ and $b\vee c=e$.
\item[9.] A closed set $F$ of a topological space $X$ is \emph{irreducible}\index{Subject}{irreducible set in a topological space} iff whenever $G_{i},\,1\leq i\leq n$, are closed sets with $F\subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}$, then $F\subseteq G_{i}$ for some $i$.
\item[10.] If $F$ is a closed set in a topological space $X$, then $x\in X$ is a \emph{generic point for} $F$ iff $F$ is the closure of $\{x\}$.
\item[11.] A topological space is \emph{sober}\index{Subject}{sober topological space} iff every irreducible closed set has a unique generic point\index{Subject}{generic point}.
\item[12.] The \emph{sum of two frames} $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is the lattice whose set is the Cartesian product of the two frames with operations done componentwise.
\item[13.] A ring $R$ is \emph{regular} iff $(\forall a)(\exists b)(aba=a)$. (It is known that every prime ideal in a commutative regular ring\index{Subject}{regular ring} is maximal.)
\item[14.] A \emph{Gelfand algebra}\index{Subject}{Gelfand algebra} is a commutative Banach algebra $A$ with unit 1 over the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\Vert a^{2}\Vert=\Vert a\Vert^{2}$ and $1+a^{2}$ is invertible for all $a\in A$.
\item[15.] A $\aleph_{\alpha}$-\emph{frame} is a partially ordered set $A$ with zero (0) and unit (e) in which every pair of elements has a meet and every subset of cardinality $\leq\aleph_{\alpha}$ has a join and which satisfies the distributive law: $a\wedge \bigvee S=\bigvee\{a\wedge t:t\in S\}$ for any $a\in A$ and subset $S$ of $A$ of cardinality $\leq\aleph_{\alpha}$.
\item[16.] A \emph{cover} of a lattice $L$ is a subset $S$ of $L$ such that $\bigvee S=e$ where $e$ is the unit in the lattice. A \emph{subcover} of $S$ is a subset of $S$ which is still a cover.
\item[17.] A lattice $L$ is $\aleph_{\alpha}$-\emph{Lindel\"{o}f} if every cover of $L$ has a subcover of cardinality $\leq\aleph_{\alpha}$.
\item[18.] For any $\aleph_{\alpha}$-frame $A$ and ideal $J$ of $A$, let $k_{0}(A)=\{\bigvee S:S\subseteq A\wedge|S|\leq\aleph_{\alpha}\}$. Then \{$J:J$ is an ideal in $A$ and $k_{0}(J)=J$\} ordered by $\subseteq$ is a frame and is called \emph{the frame envelope of}\index{Subject}{frame envelope} $A$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 30}

This note contains the proof that forms 14 (The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem), [14 BM], [14 BN], and [14 BO] are equivalent. ([14 BM]: A system of equations over a finite ring $R$ has a solution in $R$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $R$. [14 BN]: A system of equations over a finite field $F$ has a solution in $F$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $F$. [14 BO]: A system of equations over a finite structure $(A,\,+,\,\cdot)$ has a solution in $A$, if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $A$.) First, it is clear that [14 BO] implies [14 BM] implies [14 BN]. We shall show that [14 J] implies [14 BO] and that [14 BN] implies 14.

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm1}
[14 J] implies [14 BO].
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $A$ be a finite set with two operations + and $\cdot$ defined on it. Suppose $\Sigma$ is a set of equations over $A$ such that every finite subset of $\Sigma$ has a solution. Let $V$ be the set of variables which occur in $\Sigma$. Since $A$ is finite the discrete topology on $A$ is compact. By [14 J], the product $P=\prod_{i\in V} A$ is compact. For each finite subset $\sigma$ of $\Sigma$, let $x_{\sigma}=\{f\in P:f$ is a solution for $\sigma$\}. Let $B=\{x_{\sigma}:\sigma$ is a finite subset of $\Sigma$\}. The set $B$ is a set of closed subsets of $P$ with the finite intersection property. Since $P$ is compact, the intersection of $B$ is non-empty. Any element of the intersection is a solution of the system $\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm2}
[14 BN] implies 14.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra and for each $b\in B$, let $x_{b}$ be a variable. For $b\in B$, let $b^{\prime}$ be the complement of $b$. For each $b,\,c\in B$, consider the following set of equations $\Sigma$ over the two element field $\{0,1\}$:
\begin{equation*}
x_{b}+x_{b}^{\prime}=1,\qquad\quad x_{b\cap c}=x_{b}\cdot x_{c}.
\end{equation*}
It is easy to see that each finite subset of $\Sigma$ has a solution. [14 BN] implies that $\Sigma$ has a solution. Therefore, the set $\{b\in B:x_{b}=1\}$ is an ultrafilter.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 31}

Definitions for forms [14 W], [70 A], [52 H] through [52 L], 372 and [372
A] through [372 D]. These are modifications of definitions from Schechter\index{Author}{Schechter} \cite{bib:1996a} and \cite{bib:1996b}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{pre-order}\index{Subject}{pre-order} is a reflexive, transitive relation.
\item[2.] A \emph{directed set}\index{Subject}{directed set} $(\mathbb{D},\,\leq)$ is a non-empty, preordered set in which each finite subset has an upper bound.
\item[3.] A \emph{net}\index{Subject}{net} in a set $X$ is any function from a directed set into $X$. $(x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X$, usually denoted $(x(\delta):\delta\in \mathbb{D})$ or $(x_{\delta}))$.
\item[4.] If $x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X$ is a net and $S$ is any set we say $x$ is \emph{eventually in} $S$ if $(\exists\delta_{o}\in \mathbb{D})(\forall\delta\in \mathbb{D})(\delta\geq\delta_{o}\rightarrow x(\delta)\in S)$ and we say $x$ is \emph{frequently in} $S$ if $(\forall\delta\in \mathbb{D})(\exists\delta^{\prime}\in \mathbb{D})(\delta^{\prime}\geq\delta$ and $x(\delta^{\prime})\in S)$
\item[5.] $x$ is \emph{frequently constant} if for some $c,\,x$ is frequently in $\{c\}$.
\item[6.] Assume $(x(\alpha):\alpha\in \mathbb{A})$ and $(y(\beta):\beta\in \mathbb{B})$ are two nets in $X$, then $(y(\beta))$ is a \emph{subnet}\index{Subject}{subnet} of $(x(\alpha))$ (in the sense of Aarnes and Andenees - (This is not the usual definition of subnet.)) if $(\forall S\subseteq X)$(If ($x(\alpha))$ is eventually in $S$, then $(y(\beta))$ is eventually in $S$). (Which is equivalent to $(\forall S\subseteq X)($ If $(y(\beta))$ is frequently in $S$ then $(x(\alpha))$ is frequently in $S$). )
\item[7.] A \emph{universal net}\index{Subject}{universal net} (or \emph{ultranet})\index{Subject}{ultranet} on a set $X$ is a net $(x(\delta):\delta\in \mathbb{D})$ with the property that $(\forall S\subseteq X)$ ($x$ is eventually in $S$ or $x$ is eventually in $X\backslash S$).
\item[8.] A partially ordered set is \emph{Dedekind complete}\index{Subject}{Dedekind complete partially ordered set} if each subset that has an upper bound has a least upper bound. (Equivalently, if each subset that has a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.)
\item[9.] An \emph{ordered vector space}\index{Subject}{ordered vector space} is a real vector space $Z$ equipped with a partial ordering $\preccurlyeq$ which also satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[ ] $x\preccurlyeq y$ implies $x+z\preccurlyeq y+z$
\item[ ] $x\succcurlyeq 0$ and $r\geq 0$ imply $rx\succcurlyeq 0$.
\end{enumerate}

(Note: This differs from the definition of \emph{ordered linear space} in note 16.)

\noindent In definitions 10 through 13, $X$ is a vector space, $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$ is an ordered vector space and $p:X\rightarrow Z$.
\item[10.] $p$ is \emph{sublinear}\index{Subject}{sublinear function} if $p(x+y)\preccurlyeq p(x)+p(y)$ and for all $c\in[0,\,+\infty)$, $p(cx)=cp(x)$.
\item[11.] $p$ is \emph{convex}\index{Subject}{convex function} if $p(cx+(1-c)y)\preccurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in[0,1]$.
\item[12.] $p$ is \emph{concave}\index{Subject}{concave function} if $p(cx+(1-c)y)\succcurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in[0,1]$.
\item[13.] $p$ is \emph{affine}\index{Subject}{affine function} if $p(cx+(1-c)y)=cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in[0,1]$.
\item[14.] Let $(\Delta,\,\sqsubseteq)$ be a directed set and $(Z,\preccurlyeq)$ be a Dedekind complete ordered vector space. Let $B(\Delta,\,Z)$ be the set of functions $f$ from $\Delta$ to $Z$ such that the range of $f$ has both an upper bound and a lower bound. For $f\in B(\Delta,\,Z)$ let
\begin{enumerate}
\item[]$\liminf(f)=\sup_{\alpha\in\Delta}\inf_{\alpha\sqsubseteq\beta}f(\beta)$ and
\item[] $\limsup(f)=\inf_{\alpha\in\Delta}\sup_{\alpha\sqsubseteq\beta}f(\beta)$
\end{enumerate}
(Since $Z$ is Dedekind complete both $\liminf(f)$ and $\limsup(f)$ exist in $Z$ and $\lim\inf(f)\preccurlyeq \limsup(f).)$ We define a $Z$-\emph{valued Banach limit on}\index{Subject}{$Z$-valued Banach limit on} $\Delta$ to be a linear map LIM: $B(\Delta,\,Z)\rightarrow Z$ which satisfies
\begin{equation*}
(\forall f\in B(\Delta,\,Z)) (\liminf(f)\preccurlyeq \mathrm{LIM}\ (f)\preccurlyeq \limsup(f)
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 32}

Notes for forms [159 A] and [159 B] from Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1983b}.

A \emph{similarity type}\index{Subject}{similarity type} $\tau$ is a set $J$ of operation symbols and for each $j\in J$, an arity $I_{j}$ ($I_{j}$ indexes the argument places of $j$). An \emph{algebra of type} $\tau$\index{Subject}{algebra of type $\tau$} is a set $A$ and for each $j\in J$, an operation $j_{A}$ from $A^{I_{j}}$ into $A$. The following is a theorem of ZF. (See Blass \cite{bib:1983b}.)

\begin{theorem*}
For any similarity type $\tau$ and set $V$ there is an algebra $F(V)$ of type $\tau$ (called the $\tau$ free algebra generated by $V$) with the property that $V\subseteq F(V)$ and for any $A$ of type $\tau$ and any $\eta:V\rightarrow A$ there is a unique homomorphism $\alpha:F(V)\rightarrow A$ with $\alpha(v)=v$ for all $v\in V$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{definition*}
A $\tau$ \emph{identity} is a triple $(V,\,w,\,w^{\prime})$ where $V$ is a set (of variables) and $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ are words in the free $\tau$ algebra $F(V)$.

Given a similarity type $\tau$ and a set of identities $E$, the \emph{variety}\index{Subject}{variety} determined by $\tau$ and $E$ is the class of all algebras of type $\tau$ where all the identities in $E$ are true. $((V,\,w,\,w^{\prime})$ is true in $A$ if for every function $\eta:V\rightarrow A,\,\alpha(w)=\alpha(w^{\prime})$ where $\alpha$ is the unique homomorphism extending $\eta$.)

If $V$ is a variety and $X$ is a set then a \emph{free algebra}\index{Subject}{free algebra in a variety} in the variety on $X$ is an algebra $A$ and a function $\eta:X\rightarrow A$ such that for any $A^{\prime}$ in the variety, and $\eta^{\prime}:X\rightarrow A^{\prime}$, there is a unique homomorphism $\alpha:A\rightarrow A^{\prime}$ with $\eta^{\prime}=\alpha\eta$.

If $X=\emptyset$ then $A$ is called an \emph{initial algebra} in the variety.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 33}

The following proof that form 99 (Rado's selection lemma) and form 62 $(C(\infty, < \aleph_{0}))$ imply the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is due to A. Blass.

Assume Rado's lemma and $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ and let $B$ be a Boolean algebra. Let $X=\{\{x,\overline{x}\}:x\in B\}$ where $\overline{x}$ denotes the complement of $x$ in B. For each finite subset $A$ of $X$, let $f_{A}$ be a choice function on $A$ chosen so that $\{f_{A}(Y):Y\in A\}$ can be extended to a proper ideal in the subalgebra of $B$ generated by $\bigcup A$. (Choosing $f_{A}$ for each finite $A\subseteq X$ uses $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}).)$ By Rado's lemma there is a choice function $f$ for $X$ such that for each finite $A\subseteq X$ there is a finite $B\subseteq X$ such that $A\subseteq B$ and $f_{B}$ agrees with $f$ on $A$. Let $I=\{f(Y):Y\in X\}$. It is reasonably easy to show that $I$ is a maximal proper ideal in $B$.

\section*{NOTE 34}

A proof that Alexander's subbase lemma\index{Subject}{Alexander's subbase lemma} [14 AA] (A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase $S$ for the topology such that every cover by elements of $S$ has a finite subcover.) implies [14 Z] (Tychonoff's Compactness Theorem for families of finite spaces.)

Let $\{X_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of non-empty finite sets and let $X=\prod_{i\in I}X_{i}$. If $X$ is empty we are done otherwise let $g\in X$ and for each $j\in I$ and $a\in X_{j}$ let $B_{j,a}=\{f\in X:f(j)\in X_{j}\backslash \{a\}\}$.
$\mathcal{B} =\{B_{a,j}:j\in I$ and $a\in X_{j}\}$ is a subbase for the topology on X. We show every cover of $X$ by elements of $\mathcal{B}$ has a finite subcover. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be such a cover. If for some $j\in I,\,B_{a,j}$ and $B_{a^{\prime},j}$ are in $\mathcal{C}$ with $a\neq a^{\prime}$, then these two sets are the required finite subcover. If not then we can define an element of $X$ that is not covered by $\mathcal{C}$ as follows: $f(j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
a, & \mathrm{if}\ B_{j,a}\in C\\ g(j), & \mathrm{otherwise}
\end{array}\right. . $

F] (Every $\omega$-tree has an infinite chain.) The proof that 10 implies [10 F] uses the fact that form 10 is equivalent to $UT(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ which implies an $\omega$-tree is denumerable. For the argument that [10

\section*{NOTE 36}

In this note we prove that form 284 (Every finitely solvable system of linear equations over a field has a solution in the field.) implies $\forall n\in \omega,\,n\geq 2,\,C(\infty,\,n)$ (form 61). The proof is by mathematical induction on $n$, starting with the case $n=1$ which is clear. Assume that $C(\infty,\,k)$ is true for every $k<n$ and let $X$ be a collection of pairwise disjoint $n$ element sets. By the induction hypothesis there is a choice function $h$ for the set $Y=\{z:(\exists x\in X)(z\subseteq x)\wedge 1\leq|z|<n\}$. Let $p$ be the smallest prime that divides $n$, say $n=r\cdot p$. We define a system of linear equations over the field $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ (the integers $\mod\,p$) as follows: We have one variable $t_{a}$ for each $a\in\bigcup X$ and for each $x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}\in X$ we include the equation $t_{a_{1}}+\cdots+t_{a_{n}}=1$. This system of equations is clearly finitely satisfiable hence by form 284 it has a solution $S:\{t_{a}:a\in\bigcup\,X\}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{p}$. We now define a choice function $f$ on $X$. Let $x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}$ be an element of $X$. The solution $S$ determines a partition of $x$ into the sets $z_{m}=\{a\in x:S(t_{a})=m\},\,0\leq m\leq p-1$, some of which may be empty. However, there is no $m,\,0\leq m\leq p-1$, for which $x=z_{m}$ because the existence of such an $m$ would mean that $S(t_{a_{1}})=\cdots=S(t_{a_{n}})=m$. Hence $S(t_{a_{1}})+\cdots+S(t_{a_{n}})=m\cdot n=m\cdot(r\cdot p)=0$, which is a contradiction since $S$ is a solution to the equation $t_{a_{1}}+\cdots+t_{a_{n}}=1$.

Let $m_{0}$ be the least element of $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ for which $z_{m_{0}}\neq\emptyset$. Since $z_{m_{0}}\neq x,\, |z_{m_{0}}|<n$ and we may therefore define $f(x)=h(z_{m_{0}})$.

\section*{NOTE 37}

Definitions for form [14 AB] (Tychonoff theorem for sober spaces).

\begin{definition*}
A topological space is \emph{sober}\index{Subject}{sober topological space} if every closed set $C\neq\emptyset$ that is not the union of two proper closed (not necessarily disjoint) subsets (such a $C$ is called \emph{irreducible}) is the closure of a unique singleton.
\end{definition*}

In Hausdorff spaces, irreducible closed sets are singletons and therefore

\begin{theorem*}
Hausdorff implies sober implies $T_{0}$.
\end{theorem*}

See Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1986} and Johnstone\index{Author}{Johnstone} \cite{bib:1984}.

\section*{NOTE 38}

Definitions from Manka\index{Author}{Manka} \cite{bib:1988a} and \cite{bib:1988b}.

\begin{definition*}
Suppose that $(X,\,\leq)$ is a partial ordering
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A set $\mathcal{A}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is \emph{supremal in}\index{Subject}{supremal set} $(X,\,\leq)$ if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\forall S\in \mathcal{A}$ and for every upper bound $y$ of $S,\,S\cup\{y\}\in \mathcal{A}$ and
\item[(b)] $\forall S\in \mathcal{A}$ every initial segment of $S$ is in $\mathcal{L}$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[2.] If $\mathcal{A}$ is supremal in $(X,\,\leq)$ and $\sigma:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow X$ then $\sigma$ is a \emph{sup function}\index{Subject}{sup function} iff
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\forall S\in \mathcal{A},\,\sigma(S)$ is an upper bound for $S$ and
\item[(b)] $\forall S\in \mathcal{A},\,\sigma(S)$ is the greatest element of $S$ if there is one.
\end{enumerate}
\item[3.] $(X,\,\leq)$ is \emph{directed} if each two element subset of $X$ has an upper bound.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If ($X, \rho$) is a metric space and $\phi:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, then $\phi$ is \emph{upper semi-continuous}\index{Subject}{upper semi-continuous} iff for every convergent sequence $\{x_{n}\}$ in $(X,\,\rho)$ and for all $r\in \mathbb{R}$, the inequality $\phi(x_{n})\geq r$ for all $n\in\omega$ implies $\phi(\lim x_{n})\geq r$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If $(X,\,\leq)$ is a directed, partially ordered set and $\tau$ is a topology on $X$, then $(X,\,\leq)$ is \emph{upper-semi continuous with respect to} $\tau$ if for every $x_{0}$ in $X,\,\{y\in X:x_{0}\leq y\}$ is closed.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 39}

In this note the results of Harper/Rubin\index{Author}{Harper/Rubin} \cite{bib:1976} are summarized.

\begin{definition*}
Suppose that $R$ is a relation on $X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $R$ is \emph{connected} on $X$ if $(\forall u,\,v\in X)(u\neq v\rightarrow uRv$ or $vRu)$.
\item[2.] An element $u\in X$ is $R$-\emph{maximal} in $X$ if $(\forall v\in X)(uRv\rightarrow vRu)$. $R$-\emph{minimal} is defined similarly.
\item[3.] If $Y\subseteq X,\,u\in X$ is an $(R)$ \emph{upper bound} for $Y$ if $(\forall v\in Y)(v\neq u\rightarrow vRu)$. \emph{Lower bound} is defined similarly.
\item[4.] $X$ is \emph{directed (upwards)} by $R$ iff $R$ partially orders $X$ and every finite subset of $X$ has an upper bound.
\item[5.] If $y\in X$, the \emph{initial segment generated by} $y$ is $y^{\ast}=\{u\in X:uRy\}$.
\item[6.] $X$ is \emph{ramified}\index{Subject}{ramified set} by $R$ if $R$ partially orders $X$ and for every $y\in X,\,y^{\ast}$ is linearly ordered by $R$.
\item[7.] $(X,\,R)$ is a \emph{forest}\index{Subject}{forest} if $R$ is a partial ordering and $y^{\ast}$ is well ordered by $R$ for every $y\in X$.
\item[8.] $(X,\,R)$ is a \emph{tree} if $(X,\,R)$ is a forest and is directed downward by $R$.
\item[9.] $Q\subseteq X$ is \emph{quasi-cofinal}\index{Subject}{quasi-cofinal} in $X$ if $Q$ has no strict upper bound in $S$. (``Strict'' $=$ ``not in $Q$''.)
\item[10.] $Q\subseteq X$ is \emph{cofinal} in $X$ if $Q$ is linearly ordered by $R$ and $(\forall y\in X)(\exists z\in Q)(y\,R\,z)$.
\item[11.] $A\subseteq X$ is an \emph{antichain}\index{Subject}{antichain} if $\forall x,\,y\in A$, neither $xRy$ nor $yRx$ holds.
\item[] In Harper/Rubin \cite{bib:1976}, the following weak forms of $AC$ are studied:
\item[]$Z(Q,\,U)$: Every non-empty $Q$-ordered set in which every $U$-ordered subset has an upper bound, has a maximal element.
\item[]$C(Q,\,U)$: Every $Q$-ordered set contains a quasi-cofinal $U$-ordered subset.
\item[]$H(Q,\,U)$: Every $Q$-ordered set contains a $\subseteq$-maximal, $U$-ordered subset.
\item[]$H^{\prime}(Q,\,U)$: Every $Q$-ordered set has the property that each $U$-ordered subset can be extended to a $\subseteq$-maximal $U$-ordered subset.
\end{enumerate}
where $Q$ and $U$ range over the following properties: $A$: arbitrary (binary) relation, $TR$: transitive, $AS$: antisymmetric, $C$: connected, $P$: partially ordered, $W$: well ordered, $L$: linearly ordered, $D$: directed, $R$: ramified, $F$: forest, $T$: tree\index{Subject}{tree}, $AS$ \& $C$ and, $TR$ \& $C$.

In particular:

\noindent Form 51 is equivalent to $Z(L,\,U)$ where $U=W,\,F$ or $T$ and to $Z(R,\,F)$ and to $Z(R,\,T)$.

\noindent Form 143 is equivalent to $H(C,\,TR)$ and $H(C,\,TR$\&$C$),

\noindent Form 202 ([202 A]) is equivalent to $H(TR\& C,\,U)$ where $U=AS,\,AS$\&$C,\,P,\,L,\,D$, or $R$.

\noindent Form 255 is equivalent to $Z(P,\,R)$

\noindent Form 256 is equivalent to $Z(Q,\,U)$ where $Q\in\{P,\,D\}$ and $U\in\{F,\,T\}$.

\noindent Form 257 is equivalent to $Z(TR,\,AS)$ and $Z(TR,\,P)$.

\noindent Form 258 is equivalent to $Z(D,\,U)$ where $U\in\{C,\,AS\& C,\,TR\& C,\,L\}$.

\noindent Form 259 is equivalent to $Z(TR\& C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{W,\,F,\,T\}$.

\noindent Form 260 is equivalent to $Z(TR\& C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{AS,\,AS\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 261 is equivalent to $Z(TR,\,F)$ and $Z(TR,\,T)$.

\noindent Form 263 is equivalent to $H(AS\& C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{TR,\,TR\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 264 is equivalent to $H(C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 266 is equivalent to $H(AS,\,TR)$ and $H(AS,\,P)$ and $\{AS,\,AS\&
C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 261 is equivalent to $Z(TR,\,F)$ and $Z(TR,\,T)$.

\noindent Form 263 is equivalent to $H(AS\& C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{TR,\,TR\& C,\,P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 264 is equivalent to $H(C,\,U)$ where $U\in\{P,\,L,\,D,\,R\}$.

\noindent Form 202 ([202 A]) is equivalent to $H(TR\& C,U)$ where $U=AS,\,AS\&
C,\,P,\,L,\,D$, or $R$.

\noindent Form 266 is equivalent to $H(AS,\,TR)$ and $H(AS,\,P)$.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 40}

Notes on [94 A] and [94 B]. Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982d} proves that [94 B] implies form 13 (lemma 6, p. 164) by showing that the negation of form 13 implies the negation of [94 A] which implies the negation of [94 B]. Since [94 A] clearly implies [94 B], it only remains to prove that [94 A] implies 94 (to complete the argument for the equivalence of 94, [94 A] and [94 B]). (Form
94: $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty,\, \mathbb{R})$; [94 A]: The discrete topology on $\omega$ is Lindel\"{o}f; and [94 B]: There is a Lindel\"{o}f space with a closed, discrete infinite subset.)

Assume [94 A] and let $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable family where for all $i\in \omega,\, A_{i}\neq\emptyset$ and $A_{i}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\omega)$. It suffices to find a choice function for the family $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ (identifying reals with sets of natural numbers).

Now using the family $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ we define a second family of sets of sets of natural numbers $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ so that
\begin{equation*}\tag{$\ast$}
\forall i\in \omega,\, 2^{i}\in\bigcup B_{i}\ \text{and for}\ j\in \omega,\,j\neq i\ \text{implies}\ 2^{i}\not\in\bigcup B_{j}.
\end{equation*}
More specifically, for each $i\in\omega$, let $m(i)$ be the least element of $\bigcup A_{i}$. Define $f_{i}:\{k\in \omega:k\geq m(i)\}\rightarrow \omega$ by $f_{i}(k)=[2(k-m(i))+1]2^{i}$ and let $B_{i}=\{f_{i}^{\prime\prime}x:x\in A_{i}\}$. It is clear that $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ satisfies $(\ast)$ and that it suffices to find a choice function for $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega\}$. Further $\bigcup_{i\in\omega}B_{i}\cup\big\{\{k\in \omega:k\not\in\bigcup_{i\in\omega}(\bigcup\,B_{i})\}\big\}$ is an open cover for $\omega$ (using the discrete topology). Since the topology is Lindel\"{o}f there is a countable subcover $\{x_{j}:j\in \omega\}$. Defining, for each $i\in \omega,\,F(B_{i})=x_{j}$ where $j$ is the least element of $\omega$ such that $2^{i}\in x_{j}$ provides a choice function for $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega\}$.

\section*{NOTE 41}

The following proof that form 233 is true in $\mathcal{N}1$ is due to David Pincus. Form 233 is ``Algebraic closures of fields, if they exist, are unique.''

\begin{lemma*}
If $K$ is an algebraically closed field, if $\pi$ is a non-trivial automorphism of $K$ satisfying $\pi^{2}=1_{K}$ (the identity on $K$), and if $i\in K$ is a square root of $-1$, then $\pi(i)=-i\neq i$.
\end{lemma*}

(H. L\"{a}uchli has given a proof of this lemma with the additional hypothesis that the characteristic of $K$ is not equal to 2. See Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, p. 147.)

\begin{proof}
Let $L=\{x\in K:\pi(x)=x\}$. The order of the group of automorphisms generated by $\pi$ is 2. Therefore by Artin's theorem (theorem 1.8 on page 264 of Lang \cite{bib:1993}) the index of $L$ in $K$ is 2. By corollary 9.3, page 299 of Lang \cite{bib:1993} (If $L$ is a field and $K$ is the algebraic closure of $L$ and is of finite degree over $L$, then $K=L(i)$ where $i^{2}=-1$ and L has characteristic $0$.) $K=L(i)$, where $i^{2}=-1$ and $L$ has characteristic $0$, and hence $K$ has characteristic $0$.

Choose $x\in K$\index{Author}{Lang} such that $\pi(x)\neq x$. Let $y=\pi(x)-x$ so that $y\neq 0$ and $\pi(y)=-y$. Let $z$ be a square root of $y$. Then $\pi(z)$ is a square root of $\pi(y)=-y$ hence $\pi(z)=iz$ for some square root $i$ of --1. Since $y\neq 0,\,z\neq 0$. We can therefore compute
\begin{equation*}
\pi(i)=\pi\Big(\frac{\pi(z)}{z}\Big)=\frac{z}{\pi(z)}=\frac{1}{i}=-i\neq i.
\end{equation*}
The last inequality is a consequence of the fact that the characteristic of $K$ is not 2. Since $\pi$ has order 2, and $\pi(-i)=i$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

Now let $(K,\,+,\,\cdot,\,0,1)$ be a field in $\mathcal{N}1$ with finite support $E\subseteq A$ where $A$ is the set of atoms. Assume that $K$ is algebraically closed. We will show that every element of $K$ has support $E$. This implies that all algebraically closed fields are well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$ and therefore the standard proof of the uniqueness of algebraic closures (using AC) is valid in $\mathcal{N}1$.

The proof is by contradiction. Assume that $x\in K$ does not have support $E$. We will arrive at a contradiction in two steps. The first is to show that for some permutation $\pi$ of $A$ which fixes $E$ pointwise, $\pi(x)\neq x$ and $\pi^{2}$ is the identity. The permutation $\pi$ induces an automorphism of $(K,\,+,\cdot,\,0,1)$ and we can therefore apply the lemma to conclude that $\pi(i)=-i\neq i$ for some square root $i$ of -1 in $K$. The second step is to show that for every permutation $\pi$ of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, $\pi(i)=i$ for every square root $i$ of -1 in $K$.

For step one, suppose that $x$ has support $E\cup F$ where $E\cap F=\emptyset$. Let $F^{\prime}$ be a subset of $A$ for which $|F^{\prime}|=|F|$ and $F^{\prime}\cap(E\cup
F)=\emptyset$. Let $\pi$ be a permutation of $A$ which interchanges the elements of $F$ and $F^{\prime}$, that is, $\pi$ is a product of cycles of length 2, $\pi=(a_{1},\,b_{1})(a_{2},\, b_{2})\cdots(a_{n},\,b_{n})$ where $F=\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}$ and $F^{\prime}=\{b_{1},\,\ldots,\,b_{n}\}$. Clearly $\pi^{2}$ is the identity and $\pi$ fixes $E$ pointwise. The proof that $\pi(x)\neq x$ is a standard permutation model argument and depends on the fact that $x$ does not have support $E$.

For step two, we note that if $i$ is a square root of --1 in K, then $i$ is a solution to the equation $x^{2}+1=0$ all of whose coefficients are fixed by any permutation that fixes $E$ pointwise. Therefore if $\eta$ is a permutation of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, $\eta(i)$ is also a solution to $x^{2}+1=0$. Suppose that $i$ does not have support $E$. Let $E\cup F$ be a support of $i$ where $E\cap F=\emptyset$. By a standard permutation model argument, we can show that if $\pi$ and $\pi^{\prime}$ are any two permutations of $A$ that fix $E$ pointwise and $\pi(F) \cap \pi^{\prime}(F)=\emptyset$ then $\pi(x)\neq\pi^{\prime}(x)$. It follows that the equation $x^{2}+1=0$ has infinitely many solutions in $K$ which is a contradiction and the proof is complete.

\section*{NOTE 42}

In Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} is a study, in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ without $AC$, of conditions under which a topological space is well orderable. These conditions are summarized below.

\begin{theorem*}
(2.4 from Brunner \emph{\cite{bib:1982a}}) Assume $X$ is a $T_{2}$ topological space
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(1)}] Assuming form 163, $X$ is well orderable if (a) $X$ is hereditarily separable or (b) $X$ is hereditarily Lindel\"{o}f and linearly orderable.
\item[(2)] Assuming form 164, $X$ is well orderable if (a) $X$ is hereditarily Lindel\"{o}f or (b) $X$ is first countable\index{Subject}{first countable} and Lindel\"{o}f or (c) $X$ is first countable and hereditarily Souslin\index{Subject}{Souslin space} or (d) $X$ is second countable\index{Subject}{second countable} or (e) $X$ is separable.

\item[(3)] Assuming form 133, $X$ is well orderable if (a) $X$ is hereditarily Souslin or (b) $X$ is linearly orderable. (Note: $X$ is linearly orderable means that the topology on $X$ is the order topology of some linear order, $X$ is well orderable means that the set $X$ is well orderable but the topology need not be the order topology of the well ordering.)
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $X$ is \emph{first countable} if every point has a countable neighborhood base.
\item[(2)] $X$ is \emph{second countable} is $X$ has a countable basis.
\item[(3)] $X$ is \emph{Souslin} if every family of disjoint open sets is countable.
\item[(4)] $X$ is \emph{metacompact}\index{Subject}{metacompact} if every open cover has a point finite refinement. (See form 135 for a definition of point finite.)
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{corollary*}
(2.5 in Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \emph{\cite{bib:1982a})} Assuming form 164, the following are equivalent for a metric space $X$: (1) $X$ is separable, (2) $X$ is second countable, (3) $X$ is Souslin and (4) $X$ is Lindel\"{o}f.
\end{corollary*}

\begin{theorem*}
(2.6) Under the assumption of form 133 and form 17 (Ramsey' s Theorem) a regular, Lindel\"{o}f, Souslin and hereditarily metacompact space is well orderable.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
(2.7) Assuming form 133, a $T_{2}$ topological space $X$ is well orderable if $X^{2}$ is hereditarily normal and $X$ is Lindel\"{o}f.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
(2.8) Assuming form 164, a $T_{2}$ space is well orderable if $X^{2}$ is hereditarily locally Lindel\"{o}f and $X$ is hereditarily Souslin.
\end{theorem*}

Finally some counter examples: In the model $\mathcal{M}1$ (The basic Cohen model) $X=[0,1]$ (the closed interval in $\mathbb{R}$) with the order topology is compact, metric, separable, second countable, hereditarily Souslin and linearly ordered, but $X$ is not well orderable.

In the model $\mathcal{N}3$ (The ordered Mostowski model of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$): Let $X=[a,\,b]$ be an interval in the set of atoms with the order topology. $X$ is compact, hereditarily normal (that is $T_{5}$) and $T_{2}$. Further, each finite power of $X$ is compact, $T_{4}$ and hereditarily Souslin, but $X$ is not well orderable.

In the model $\mathcal{N}1$ (The basic Fraenkel model with a denumerable set of atoms, using the group of all permutations of the atoms and finite supports): Let $X= [A]^{<\omega}$ (all finite subsets of the set of atoms) with a basis for the topology all set of the form $\{x:E\subseteq x$ and $x\cap F=\emptyset\}$ where $E$ and $F$ range over the finite subsets of U. The space $X$ is Souslin, perfectly regular and not well orderable.

\section*{NOTE 43}

These are definitions from Brunner \cite{bib:1982b} and results similar to the equivalence of [8 C] and [8 D] to form 8 and [10 H] to form 10. We also include some results from Brunner \cite{bib:1987b}.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A topological space is $\sigma$-\emph{compact}\index{Subject}{$\sigma$-compact} if it can be covered by a countable set of compact sets.
\item[2.] A space is \emph{weakly Lindel\"{o}f}\index{Subject}{weakly Lindel\"{o}f} if every open cover has a countable refinement. If $C$ is an open cover of a space $X$ a \emph{refinement} of $C$ is an open cover $C^{\prime}$ of $X$ such that for all $y\in C^{\prime}$, there is a $z$ in $C$ such that $y\subseteq z$.
\item[3.] A space $X$ is \emph{paracompact}\index{Subject}{paracompact} if $X$ is Hausdorff and every open covering of $X$ has an open, locally finite refinement. (An open covering $C$ of $X$ is \emph{locally finite} if for all $x\in X$, there is an open set containing $x$ that intersects only finitely many elements of $C$. In general, a family of subsets $S$ of $X$ is called locally finite if each point in $X$ has a neighborhood meeting a finite number of sets in $S.)$
\item[4.] An \emph{ultra metric group}\index{Subject}{ultra metric group} is a topological group with a metrizable topology using a metric $d$ that satisfies for all $x,\,y$, and $z$ in the group,
\begin{equation*}
d(x,\,y)\leq\max(d(x,\,z),\,d(y,\,z)).
\end{equation*}
The results from Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982b} are:
\item[a.] It is not possible to prove, without $AC$, that every weakly Lindel\"{o}f space is Lindel\"{o}f since in the basic Cohen model $\mathcal{M}1,\,\mathbb{R}$ is weakly Lindel\"{o}f but not Lindel\"{o}f.
\item[b.] The assertion that every $\sigma$-compact, locally compact space with countable neighborhood bases is Lindel\"{o}f implies form 32 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0}))$.
\item[c.] In the basic Cohen model, $\mathcal{M}1,\,C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ holds and there is a $\sigma$-compact locally compact space with countable neighborhood bases which is not Lindel\"{o}f.
\item[d.] $C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0})$ is implied by ``Every $\sigma$-compact, ultra metric group without isolated points is Lindel\"{o}f.''
\item[e.] The assertion ``Every $\sigma$-compact, regular space without isolated points is Lindel\"{o}f'' implies form 9 (Dedekind finite = Finite).

\noindent The results from Brunner \cite{bib:1987b} are:
\item[a.] In $\mathcal{N}3,\,L$ is a paracompact and weakly Lindel\"{o}f topological space which is not Lindel\"{o}f. (In $\mathcal{N}3,\,L=(A\times \mathbb{Z})\cup \mathbb{Z}$, where the ordering on $L$ is defined as follows: for $a,\, b\in A$ and $m,\,n\in \mathbb{Z},\,(a,\,n)<(b,\,n)$ if $a<b$ and $(a,\,n)<m<(b,\,m)$ if $n<m$. The topology on $L$ is the order topology.)
\item[b.] In $\mathcal{M}1$, every $T_{1}$ Lindel\"{o}f space is compact.
\item[c.] In $\mathcal{M}17$, every countably compact space is compact.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 47}

Definitions from Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1990}.

\begin{definition*}
Assume that $(P,\,\leq)$ is a quasi-order\index{Subject}{quasi-order} (reflexive and transitive).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $x$ and $y$ in $P$ are \emph{compatible}\index{Subject}{compatible} if $\exists z\in P$ such that $z\leq x$ and $z\leq \mathrm{y}$.
\item[2.] \emph{Incompatible} means not compatible.
\item[3.] $I\subseteq P$ is an \emph{antichain}\index{Subject}{antichain} if each pair of elements of $I$ are incompatible.
\item[4.] $D\subseteq P$ is \emph{dense}\index{Subject}{dense subset of a quasi-order} if $\forall x\in P,\,\exists y\in D$ such that $y\leq x$.
\item[5.] $F\subseteq P$ is a \emph{filter}\index{Subject}{filter in a quasi-order} if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a)] $\forall x,\,y\in F\,\exists z\in F$ such that $z\leq x$ and $z\leq y$ and
\item[b)] $\forall x\in F\, \forall y\in P,\,x\leq y$ implies $y\in F$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[6.] If $\mathcal{D}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(P)$, a filter $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$ \emph{generic}\index{Subject}{generic filter} if $F\cap D\neq\emptyset$ for all $D$ in $\mathcal{D}$. $F$ is $P$ \emph{generic} if $F\cap D\neq\emptyset$ for all dense subsets $D$ of $P$.
\item[7.] A chain $C$ of $(P,\,\leq)$ is a \emph{covering chain}\index{Subject}{covering chain} iff for all $x\in C$, if $x$ is not maximal in $C$, then $\exists y\in C$ such that $y$ covers $x$ in $P$ (i.e., $y>x$ and there is no $z\in P$ such that $y>z>x$).
\item[8.] If $Q\subseteq P$ and $x\in P$, the \emph{depth} of $x$ (relative to $Q$) is the order type of the smallest well ordered (under the quasi-order) covering chain $C$ which begins at $x$ and ends at an element of $Q$. (The depth of $x$ is only defined if such a chain exists.)
\item[9.] Two elements $x$ and $y$ of $P$ are $Q$ \emph{strongly incompatible}\index{Subject}{strongly incompatible} if $x$ and $y$ are incompatible and the depth of $x$ is different from the depth of $y$.
\item[10.] $I\subseteq P$ is a $Q$ \emph{strong antichain}\index{Subject}{strong antichain} if any two elements are $Q$ strongly incompatible.
\end{enumerate}

Shannon\index{Author}{Shannon} \cite{bib:1990} proves that the following are equivalent for each ordinal $\alpha$:

(i) $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\, <\aleph_{0})$

(ii) If $(P,\,\leq)$ is a quasi-order such that $P\neq\emptyset$ and $P$ is a union of $\aleph_{\alpha}$ finite sets and every antichain is finite, then there is a well orderable, $P$ generic filter.

(iii) For some ordinal $\beta\geq\alpha$, for every quasi-order $(P,\,\leq)$ such that $P\neq\emptyset$ and such that $P$ is the union of $\aleph_{\alpha}$ finite sets and such that every antichain is finite then for every family $\mathcal{D}$ of $\aleph_{\beta}$ dense sets there is a well orderable $\mathcal{D}$ generic filter.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 49}

In von Rimscha\index{Author}{Rimscha} \cite{bib:1982} three transitivity conditions are considered:

$Tr.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $f$ is a function from $f$ one to one and onto $u$. This is form 175.

$Tr^{\prime}.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $u\subseteq TC(x)$ and $f$ is a one to one function from $x$ onto $u$.

$Tr^{\prime\prime}.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $f$ is a one to one function from $x$ onto $u$ and $\forall s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s)$.

It is shown that in ZF, AC implies $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ and that $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ implies $Tr^{\prime}$ implies $Tr$. All proofs can be done in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ with minor modifications. It is also shown that $\mathrm{ZF} \vdash Tr\rightarrow$ form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite). This could be reformulated as $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash Tr\rightarrow$ all pure Dedekind finite sets are finite. We can therefore conclude that $Tr$ (form 175) implies Dedekind finite sets of reals are finite (form 13).

It is however possible to prove in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ that $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ (form 174) implies Dedekind finite $=$ finite (form 9). We proceed as follows: Assume $Tr^{\prime\prime}$. We first show that every infinite subset of the atoms $A$ is Dedekind infinite. Assume $B\subseteq A$ and that $B$ is infinite. We will use $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ to get a choice function for $\mathcal{P}(B)$ from which it follows that $B$ has a denumerable subset. Let $\kappa$ be the least well ordered cardinal which is not $\leq|\mathcal{P}(B)|$. For each $a\in B$ and ordinal $\alpha$, define $a_{\alpha}$ by induction: $a_{0}=a,\,a_{\lambda}=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}a_{\alpha}$ for limit ordinals $\lambda$ and $a_{\alpha+1}=a_{\alpha}\cup\{a_{\alpha}\}$.
$(a_{\alpha}$ is the ordinal $\alpha$ with every occurrence of $\emptyset$ replaced by $a$.) Then for each $\alpha,\, |a_{\alpha}|=|\alpha|$. Let $B^{\prime}=\{a_{\kappa}:a\in B\}$ and let $x=\mathcal{P}(B^{\prime})$. By $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ there is a transitive set $u$ and a function $f:x\rightarrow u$ which is one to one and onto and such that for each $s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s)$. Suppose that $C\subseteq B$ and let $s=\{a_{\kappa}:a\in C\}\in x$. Then
\begin{equation*}
TC(s)=\{s\}\cup s\cup \bigg(\bigcup_{a\in C}a_{\kappa}\bigg)
\end{equation*}
since $|TC(s)|\geq\kappa,\,s\not\in u$. $(|u|=|\mathcal{P}(B)|$ which is not $\geq\kappa.)$. So $f(s)\in\bigcup_{a\in C}a_{\kappa}$. Since $a\neq b$ implies $a_{\kappa}\cap b_{\kappa}=\emptyset,\, f(s)$ determines a unique element of $C$.

Now let $x$ be any infinite set. By $Tr^{\prime\prime}$ there is a transitive $u$ and a one to one function $f$ from $x$ onto $u$. If $u$ contains only finitely many atoms, then the von Rimscha\index{Author}{Rimscha} proof can be modified to show that $x$ has a denumerable subset. If $u$ contains an infinite set of atoms $B$, then by the first argument $B$ and therefore $x$ contains a denumerable subset.

\textsc{Problem}
(from von Rimscha \cite{bib:1982}): Are any of the implications $Tr\rightarrow Tr^{\prime}\rightarrow Tr^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow AC$ provable in ZF?

\section*{NOTE 50}

Definitions from Andreka/Nemeti\index{Author}{Andreka/Nemeti} \cite{bib:1981} and H\"{o}ft/Howard\index{Author}{H\"{o}ft/Howard} \cite{bib:1981}.

An \emph{algebra} is a pair $(A,\,F)$ where $A$ is a set and $F$ is a function from an index set $I$ such that for each $i\in I$, there is a $k_{i}\in \omega$ such that $F(i)$ is a function from $A^{k_{i}}$ into $A$. The function $\Delta$ with domain $I$ defined by $\Delta(i)=k_{i}$ is called the \emph{type of the algebra}\index{Subject}{type of an algebra} $(A,\,F)$. Two algebras of the same type are \emph{similar}.

\begin{definition*}
Let $K$ be any class of similar algebras
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $S(K)=$ the class of subalgebras of algebras in $K$
\item[2.] $H(K)=$ homomorphic images of algebras in $K$
\item[3.] $P(K)=$ direct products of non-empty families of algebras in $K$
\item[4.] $HSP\ K=H(S(P(K)))$.
\item[5.] $Mod\,Eq\,K=$ the class of all algebras which are models of the set of equations which hold in every member of $K$.
\end{enumerate}

The fact that [0 U] is equivalent to form $0$ answers problem 31 in Gr\"{a}tzer\index{Author}{Gr\"{a}tzer}
\cite{bib:1979}.

A \emph{multi-algebra}\index{Subject}{multi-algebra} is a pair $(A,\,F)$ where $A$ is a set and $F$ is a function from an index set $I$ such that for each $i\in I$, there is a $k_{i}\in \omega$ such that $F(i)$ is a function from $A^{k_{i}}$ into $\mathcal{P}(A)-\{\emptyset\}$. We will denote $F(i)$ by $f_{i}$. The function $\Delta$ with domain $I$ defined by $\Delta(i)=k_{i}$ is called the \emph{type of the algebra}. Note that this doesn't require that constants, i. e., 0-ary operations, have to be singleton sets.

If $(A,\,F)$ and $(B,\,G)$ are algebras or multi-algebras of the same type then a function $\phi:A\rightarrow B$ is a \emph{homomorphism} if for every $i\in I$ and $\mathbf{a}= (a_{1},\,\ldots a_{k_{i}})\in A^{k_{i}},\,\phi(f_{i}(a_{1},\,\ldots a_{k_{i}}))=g_{i}(\phi(a_{1}),\,\ldots\phi(a_{k_{i}}))$. The function $\phi$ is an \emph{isomorphism} between multi-algebras if $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ are bijective homomorphisms.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
Suppose that $(A,\,F)$ is a multi-algebra of type $\Delta$ and $(B,\,G)$ is an algebra of type $\Delta$. Let $E$ be an equivalence relation on $B$ and let $C/E$ be the set of equivalence classes, $(C/E,\,G/E)$ is the multi-algebra of type $\Delta$ defined by
\begin{equation*}
(G/E)(i)([a_{1}],\ldots[a_{k_{i}}])=\{[b]:b=g_{i}(c_{1},\,\ldots\,c_{k_{i}})\wedge[c_{j}]=[a_{j}]\ \mathrm{for}\ j=1,\,\ldots,\,k_{i}\}.
\end{equation*}
Here we have used $[a]$ to denote the $E$ equivalence class of $a\in C$.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 51}

In Drake\index{Author}{Drake} \cite{bib:1974}, p.203 there is a proof of Ramsey's theorem (form 17) which uses K\"{o}nig's lemma (form [10 F]). However this proof also uses the well ordering theorem and hence does not show that [10 F] implies form 17. (Which is in fact false. See Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1977a}.) Therefore the proof in Lolli\index{Author}{Lolli} \cite{bib:1977} that Ramsey's theorem implies form 10 is invalid because it uses ``[10 F] implies 17''

In Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1981a} it is shown that there is a model of ZF in which $\mathbb{R}^{A}$ is metrizable and connected, where A is a suitably chosen set and the box topology is used on the product. (If for each $i\in I,\,X_{i}$ is a topological space, then the \emph{box product}\index{Subject}{box product} is the topological space whose underlying set is the Cartesian product $\prod_{i\in I}X_{i}$ and whose topology has as a basis, sets of the form $\prod_{i\in I}U_{i}$, where $U_{i}$ is open in $X_{i}$.)

In Zuckerman\index{Author}{Zuckerman} \cite{bib:1969a} and \cite{bib:1981} the relationship between versions of form $178(n,\,N)$ are considered. (Form $178(n,\,N)$: If $n\in \omega,\,n\geq 2$ and $N\subseteq\{1,2,\,\ldots,\,n-1\},\, N\neq\emptyset,\, MC(\infty,\,n,\,N)$: If $X$ is any set of $n$-element sets then there is a function $f$ with domain $X$ such that $\forall A\in X,\,f(A)\subseteq A$ and $|f(A)|\in N.)$ A sample of the results follows. Using the notation of Zuckerman \cite{bib:1981}, $S(n,\,\ell)$ is $MC(\infty,\,n,\,\{\ell\})$ and $T(n,\,\ell)$ is $MC(\infty,\, n,\,\{1,2,\,\ldots,\,\ell\})$.

\begin{theorem*}
If $m\leq n$ and $n-\ell<m$ then $S(n,\,\ell)\rightarrow T(m,\,\ell)$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
If $l<n$ and $k\geq 0$, then $S(n,\,\ell)\wedge S(kn+\ell,\,1)$ imply $S(n,\,1)$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
Assume $K\geq 1$

a) $\ell<n,\,T(kn,\,\ell)\rightarrow T(n,\,\ell)$.

b) for $\ell$ not of the form $jn$ for any $j\leq k,\,S(kn,\,\ell)\rightarrow T(n,\,l)$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
If $l<n$ and $k\geq 0$, then $S(n,\,\ell)\wedge S(kn+\ell,\,1)$ imply $S(n,\,1)$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{theorem*}
Assume $K\geq 1$

a) $\ell<n,\,T(kn,\,\ell)\rightarrow T(n,\ell)$.

b) for $\ell$ not of the form $jn$ for any $j\leq k,\,S(kn,\,\ell)\rightarrow T(n,\, l)$.
\end{theorem*}
