\section*{NOTE 55}

The following results are from Gitik\index{Author}{Gitik} \cite{bib:1980}. Let $\Omega=\{\alpha\in$ On: $(\forall\beta\leq\alpha)(\beta= 0\vee(\exists\gamma)(\beta=\gamma+1)\vee(\forall n\in \omega)(\exists\gamma_{n}\leq\beta)(\beta=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}\gamma_{n})\}$. Gitik shows, by making small changes in $\mathcal{M}17$, that each of the following are consistent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] ZF + $\Omega=$ On.
\item[2.] ZF + $\Omega=\omega_{\Omega}$.
\item[3.] ZF + $\Omega=\omega_{\alpha+1}$, for any $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
In fact, item 1 holds in $\mathcal{M}17$ itself. It is clear that ZFC $\vdash\Omega=\omega_{1}$ (form 315).

In Gitik \cite{bib:1985}, the following theorem is given: Suppose $M$ is a countable model of ZFC and $\kappa$ is an almost huge cardinal in $M$. (See note 20 for the definition of various types of inaccessible cardinals.) If $S$ is any subset of $\kappa$ consisting of nonlimit cardinals, then there is a model $\mathcal{M}(S)$ of ZF such that the regular cardinals are exactly $\{\aleph_{\alpha}:\alpha\in S\cup\{0\}\}$. In the case that $S=\emptyset$, then all uncountable $\aleph_{\alpha}$'s are singular. Note, however, that in $\mathcal{M}17$ all uncountable $\aleph_{\alpha}$'s are singular. Further, the construction of $\mathcal{M}17$ requires only the existence of a strongly compact cardinal which is weaker than the existence of an almost huge cardinal.

\section*{NOTE 56}

Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1980b}\index{Subject}{amorphous set} generalizes the notion of amorphous as follows:

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $X$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ \emph{set} if $|X|$ is incomparable with $\aleph_{\alpha}$ and for all $\beta<\alpha,\,\aleph_{\beta}<|X|$.
\item[2.] $X$ is $\aleph_{\alpha}$ \emph{minimal} if $X$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ set and for all $Y\subseteq X$, either $|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$ or $|X-Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$, (abbreviated $X$ is $\alpha$-m).
\item[3.] $X$ is \emph{weakly} $\aleph_{\alpha}$ \emph{minimal}\index{Subject}{weakly $\aleph_{\alpha}$, minimal} if $X$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ set and for all $Y\subseteq X$ at most one of $Y$ and $X-Y$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ set, ($X$ is $\alpha$-wm).
\item[4.] $X$ is \emph{pseudo} $\aleph_{\alpha}$ \emph{minimal}\index{Subject}{pseudo $\aleph_{\alpha}$ minimal} if $X$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ set and for all $Y\subseteq X$, exactly one of $Y$ and $Y-X$ is an $\aleph_{\alpha}$ set, ($X$ is $\alpha$-pm).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

The following are proved:

\setcounter{theorem}{0}
\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm1a}
$X$ is $0$-m iff $X$ is $0$-wm iff $X$ is 0-pm.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm2a}
(a) For all $\alpha,\,X$ is $(\alpha+1)$-pm implies $X$ is $(\alpha+1)$-wm and (b) $X$ is $(\alpha+1)$-wm iff $X$ is $(\alpha+1)$-m.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm3}
If $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal $(\alpha\neq 0)$, then

\noindent (a) $X$ is $\alpha$-m implies $X$ is $\alpha$-wm.

\noindent (b) $X$ is $\alpha$-wm iff $X$ is $\alpha$-pm.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm4}
For all ordinals $\alpha,\,Con(ZF+\exists X(X$ is $\alpha$-m$))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm5}
(a) For all ordinals $\alpha$, the following is not theorem of $ZF$:
\begin{equation*}
\forall X(X\,is\,(\alpha+1)\text{-m}\rightarrow X\ is\ (\alpha+1)\text{-mp})
\end{equation*}
(b) For all limit ordinals $\alpha$, it is not a theorem of $ZF$ that
\begin{equation*}
\forall X(X\ is\ \alpha\text{-mp}\rightarrow X\ is\ \alpha\text{-m}).
\end{equation*}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm6}
If $\aleph_{\alpha}$ is regular, then Con(ZF + there is a linearly ordered $(\alpha+1)$-pm set).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm7}
For any $\alpha$, Con(ZF + there is a linearly ordered $(\alpha+1)$-m set).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm8}
If $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal there are no linearly ordered $\alpha$-wm sets.
\end{theorem}

\textsc{Open Problem.}
The consistency of the existence of linearly ordered $(\alpha+1)$-pm set where $\aleph_{\alpha}$ is not regular.

\section*{NOTE 57}
Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1995} studies the various structures an amorphous set\index{Subject}{amorphous set} can carry. (A set is \emph{amorphous} if it is infinite but is not the disjoint union of two infinite sets.) If $\pi$ is a partition of an amorphous set $U$ into infinitely many parts, then each part must be finite. (Otherwise,
if $X$ were an infinite part, then $U=X\cup (U-X)$, contradicting the fact that $U$ is amorphous.) Define a map $f$ from $U$ into $\omega$ such that for each $x\in U,\,f(x)=n$ where $x\in\xi \in\pi$ and $|\xi|=n$. Since $U$ is amorphous, the range of $f$ must be finite. Since $U=\bigcup\{f^{-1}(n): n\in$ range of $f$\}, there is a unique $n$ such that $f^{-1}(n)$ is infinite. Let $n(\pi)$ be this unique $n$, then $\{\xi\in\pi:|\xi|=n(\pi)\}$ is infinite.

Let $\Pi(U)$ be the set of finitary partitions of $U$ and let $n(U)= \sup\{n(\pi):\pi\in\Pi(U)\}$. If $n(U)$ is finite, $U$ is called \emph{bounded}, and if $n(U)$ infinite, $U$ is called \emph{unbounded}.

Two interesting results that Truss obtains are:

\begin{theorem*}
The following are consistent with $ZF$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] There is an amorphous set and all amorphous sets are bounded.
\item[2.] There is an amorphous set and all amorphous sets are unbounded.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

See Truss \cite{bib:1995} for additional results.

\section*{NOTE 59}

Form 191 is the statement: There is a set $S$ such that for every set $a$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function from $S\times\alpha$ onto $a$ and form 182 is: There is an aleph whose cofinality is greater than $\aleph_{0}$. In Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979} it is proved, assuming form 191, that $\forall A$ there is a limit ordinal $\alpha$ such that $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\alpha$. If $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\alpha$, then $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\aleph_{\alpha}$. Therefore form 191 implies form 182.

Blass also shows that if 191 holds with a set $S$ then form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) holds if and only if there is an ultrafilter $U$ on $S^{<\omega}$ that is regular in the sense that $\{p\in S^{<\omega}: s\in$ range $p\}$ is in $U$ for every $s\in S$.

With regard to $(191,n)$, Blass shows that 191 holds in most known models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ or ZF. In particular,
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] Every permutation model whose class of atoms forms a set satisfies 191.
\item[2.] Every symmetric model satisfies 191. (A symmetric model is a model constructed from a ground model $M$ of ZFC by taking a complete Boolean algebra $B$ in $M$, an $M$ generic filter $G$ in $B$, a group $\mathcal{G}$ of automorphisms of $B$ and a normal filter of subgroups of $\mathcal{G}$. The model consists of members of $M[G]$ that have hereditarily symmetric names.)
\item[3.] If $V$ is any model of ZFC and $A\in V$, then the submodel $HOD(A)$ of sets hereditarily ordinal definable over A satisfies 191.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 60}

Definitions from category theory, in particular for forms 188, 189, 190, 192 and 193 from Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1979}.

\begin{definition*}
Assume $\mathbf{C}$ is a category
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] An object $p$ in $\mathbf{C}$ is \emph{projective}\index{Subject}{projective object in a category} (in $\mathbf{C}$) if for all objects $a$ and $b$ in $\mathbf{C}$, if $f\in \mathrm{hom}(a,\, b)$ is an epimorphism and $g\in \mathrm{hom}(p,\,b)$, then there is an $h\in \mathrm{hom}(p,\,a)$ such that $f\circ h=g$.
\item[2.] $p$ is \emph{injective}\index{Subject}{injective object in a category} if for all objects $a$ and $b$ in $\mathbf{C}$, if $f\in \mathrm{hom}(b,\,a)$ is a monomorphism and $g\in \mathrm{hom}(b,p)$ then there is an $h\in \mathrm{hom}(a,p)$ such that $h\circ f=g$.
\item[3.] An Abelian group $G$ is \emph{projective}\index{Subject}{projective Abelian group} if for all Abelian groups $A$ and $B$ if $f:A\rightarrow B$ is a homomorphism from $A$ onto $B$ and $g:G\rightarrow B$ is a homomorphism then there is a homomorphism $h:G\rightarrow A$ such that $f\circ h=g$.
\item[4.] An Abelian group $G$ is \emph{injective}\index{Subject}{injective Abelian group} if for all Abelian groups $A$ and $B$, if $f:B\rightarrow A$ is a one to one homomorphism and $g:B\rightarrow G$ is a homomorphism then there is a homomorphism $h:A\rightarrow G$ such that $h\circ f=g$.
\item[5.] A set $X$ is \emph{projective}\index{Subject}{projective set} if for all sets $A$ and $B$, for all $f$ from $A$ onto $B$ and for all $g$ from $X$ into $B$ there is a function $h$ from $X$ into $A$ such that $f\circ h=g$, (i.e., For any $X$-indexed family $\{y_{t}:t\in X\}$ of non-empty sets there is a choice function.)
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 61}

Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} \cite{bib:1979} studies the relationships between $AC(K)$ and $DC(K)$ where $K$ is either in the analytic or projective hierarchy\index{Subject}{projective hierarchy}. We give definitions and summarize some of the results from Kanovei \cite{bib:1979}. $AC(K)$ is: For any $P\subseteq \omega\times {^{\omega}}\omega$ with domain $\omega$, if $P\in K$, then there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega\rangle$ of elements of ${^{\omega}}\omega$ with $\langle k,\,x_{k}\rangle\in P$ for all $k\in\omega$. And

\noindent $DC(K)$ is: For every $P\subseteq {^{\omega}}\omega\times {^{\omega}}\omega$ with domain $^{\omega}\omega$, if $P\in K$ then for any $y\in{^{\omega}}\omega$ there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in\omega\rangle$ with $x_{0}=y$ and for all $k\in\omega, \langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle\in P$. The sets in the analytic hierarchy\index{Subject}{analytic hierarchy} $(\varSigma_{n}^{1},\, \varPi_{n}^{1}$ and
$\varDelta_{n}^{1}$ for $n\in \omega)$ and the sets in the projective hierarchy $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n}^{1},\, \boldsymbol{\Pi}_{n}^{1}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{n}^{1}$
for $n\in\omega)$ are defined as follows: For purposes of these definitions $^{k,\ell}\omega$ is ${^{k}}\omega\times{^{\ell}}(^{\omega}\omega)$ and a relation $R\subseteq {^{k,\ell}}\omega$ is of rank $(k,\,\ell)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell)$ is \emph{arithmetic} if for all $\mathbf{m}\in {^{k}} \omega$ and all $\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in{^{\ell}}(^{\omega}\omega)$, $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ iff $Q_{1}x_{1}\ldots Q_{r}x_{r}P(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha},)$ where $P\subseteq^{r+k,\ell}\omega$ is recursive, and each $Q_{i}$ is either
$\exists$ or $\forall$.
\item[2.] $R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell)$ is \emph{analytic} if $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ iff $Q_{1}\beta_{1}\ldots Q_{r}\beta_{r}P(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha},\,\beta_{1},\,\ldots,\,\beta_{r})$ where $P$ is of rank $(k,\,\ell+r)$ and is arithmetic.
\item[3.] (The analytic hierarchy)
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\varSigma_{0}^{1}=\varPi_{0}^{1}=$ the arithmetic relations.
\item[(ii)] $\varSigma_{r+1}^{1}=\{\exists\beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}):P\in\varSigma_{r}^{1}\wedge P$ has rank $(k,\, \ell+1)\}$
\item[(ii)] $\varPi_{n+1}^{1}=\{\forall\beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}):P\in\varSigma_{r}^{1}\wedge P$ has rank $(k,\, \ell+1)\}$
\item[(iv)] $\varDelta_{r}^{1}=\varSigma_{r}^{1}\cap \varPi_{r}^{1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[4.] $R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell)$ is \emph{recursive} in $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ iff the characteristic function $K_{R}(\mathbf{m},\, \boldsymbol{\alpha})$ of $R$ is $G(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha},\,\boldsymbol{\beta})$ for some partial recursive $G$.
\item[5.] Assume $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ has rank $(0,\,\ell)$ then $\varSigma_{r}^{1}[\beta]$ and $\varPi_{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]$ are defined by $R\in\varSigma_{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]$ iff $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha})\leftrightarrow S(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha},\,\boldsymbol{\beta})$ for some $S\in\varSigma_{r}^{1}$. $\varPi_{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]$ is defined similarly.
\item[6.] (The projective hierarchy)
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{r}^{1}=\bigcup\{\varSigma_{r}^{1}[\beta]:b\in
{^{\omega}}\omega\}$
\item[(ii)] $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{r}^{1}=\bigcup\{\varPi_{r}^{1}[\beta]:b\in {^{\omega}}\omega\}$
\item[(iii)] $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{r}^{1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{r}^{1}\cap\boldsymbol{\Pi} 1_{r}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
In Kanovei\index{Author}{Kanovei} \cite{bib:1979}, it is shown for any $n\geq 2$ that, $AC(\varPi_{n+1}^{1})$ does not follow, in ZF from $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{n}^{1})$, that $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{n}^{1})$ implies $AC(\varPi_{n}^{1})$ and that $AC(\varPi_{n}^{1})$ does not imply $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{n}^{1})$. Kanovei \cite{bib:1976} has further results on $AC$ and the projective hierarchy. See forms [0 X], 194 and 199.

\section*{NOTE 62}

The following definitions for form 195 are from Harazisville (see Kharazishvili\index{Author}{Kharazishvili}
\cite{bib:1979}.)

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] If $X$ and $Y$ are vector spaces over a field $K$ then a \emph{general linear system}\index{Subject}{general linear system} is a relation $S\subseteq X\times Y$ which has domain $X$ and is a subspace of $X\times Y$.
\item[2.] If $S$ is as in 1. then a \emph{linear global reaction of}\index{Subject}{linear global retraction} $S$ is a function $\Phi:C\times X\rightarrow Y$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $C$ is a vector space over $K$
\item[(ii)] $\Phi$ is a global reaction of $S$ (i.e., $(x,\,y)\in S$ iff $x\in X$ and $(\exists c)(c\in C$ and $y=\Phi(c,\,x)).)$
\item[(iii)] There are linear functions $\Phi_{1}:C\rightarrow Y$ and $\Phi_{2}:X\rightarrow Y$ such that $\Phi(c,\,x)=\Phi_{1}(c)+\Phi_{2}(x)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

Form 200 is studied in Dawson/Howard\index{Author}{Dawson/Howard} \cite{bib:1976} where it is shown that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] Each of
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\exists$ infinite $x$ such that $2^{x}<x!$
\item[(b)] $\exists$ infinite $x$ such that $2^{x}>x!$ and
\item[(c)] $\exists$ infinite $x$ such that $2^{x}$ and $x!$ are incomparable

are consistent with ZF. ($x!$ is the cardinality of the set of all one to one functions from $x$ onto $x$.).

In Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1978} a model of ZF is constructed in which AC (form 1) is false, $\forall$ infinite $x,\, 2x=x$ (form 3) is false and $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=x!$ is true. Also true in this mod
el are $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}|$ and $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}-x!|$.

Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1978} shows that in Feferman's\index{Author}{Feferman} model, $\mathcal{M}2$ (Feferman \cite{bib:1965}), the following hold:

\item[2.] For all $X$, if $[X]^{2}$ has a choice function, then $\exists\alpha$ such that $|X|\leq 2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$.
\item[3.] Form 40 $(C(WO,\,\infty))$.
\item[4.] $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ has no non-principal prime ideal, (the negation of form 70).
\item[5.] $\neg C(\infty,\,2)$, (the negation of form 88).
\item[6.] There is a partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ into non-empty subsets without a choice function, (the negation of form 203).
\item[7.] Form 204, For every infinite $X$ there is a function from $X$ onto $2\times X$.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 66}

In this note we prove that form 322 $(KW(WO,\,\infty))$ is true in $\mathcal{N}1$. (Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a}, (Proposition~ 4.5) also has a proof of this result.)

Assume that $X$ is a well ordered set in $\mathcal{N}1$ and that $\forall y\in X,\,|y|\geq 2$. Let $E$ be a (finite) support of a well ordering of $X$ and let fix$(E)$ be the group of permutations of $A$ (the set of atoms) which fix $E$ pointwise. Then for all $\phi\in$ fix$(E)$, $\phi$ fixes $X$ pointwise. Choose an atom $a\in A-E$. We will show that for every $y\in X,\,E\cup\{a\}$ is a support of a non-empty proper subset $y^{\prime}$ of $y$. This will suffice since it follows that the function $y\mapsto y^{\prime}$ is in $\mathcal{N}1$.

Choose an element $y\in X$. If every element of $y$ has support $E$ then any nonempty proper subset of $y$ has support $E$ and therefore has support $E\cup\{a\}$. So we may assume that $y$ has some element $t$ such that $E$ is not a support of $t$. Choose a finite non-empty subset $F$ of $A$ such that $E\cap F=\emptyset$ and $E\cup F$ is a support of $t$ and such that $F$ is minimal in the sense that for no proper subset $F^{\prime}$ of $F$ is $E\cup F^{\prime}$ a support of $t$. We may assume without loss of generality that $a\in F$. (If $a\not\in F$ then we replace $t$ by $\psi(t)$ and $F$ by $\psi(F)$ where $\psi$ is a permutation of $A$ chosen so that $\psi\in$ fix$(E)$ and $a\in\psi(F).)$ Let $y'=\{\phi(t):\phi \in$ fix$(E\cup\{a\})\}$. Clearly $y^{\prime}$ has support $E\cup\{a\},\,y^{\prime}\subseteq y$ and $y^{\prime}\neq\emptyset$ (since $t\in y^{\prime}$). It only remains to show that $y^{\prime}\neq y$.

\begin{lemma*}
If $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are in fix$(E)$ and $\beta(F)\neq\gamma(F)$ then $\beta(t)\neq\gamma(t)$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
Assume $b\in\beta(F)-\gamma(F)$. Since $F$ is minimal, there is no proper subset $B$ of $\beta(F)$ for which $E\cup B$ is a support of $\beta(t)$. Hence there is a $\psi\in$ fix$((E\cup \beta(F))-\{b\})$ such that $\psi(\beta(t))\neq\beta(t)$. We can find such a $\psi$ for which $\psi(b)\not\in\gamma(F)$. (If $\psi(b)\in\gamma(F)$ then we choose $d\in A-(\gamma(F)\cup\beta(F)\cup E)$. Since $\psi(\beta)\not\in\beta(F)$ the cycle $\rho=(d,\,\psi(b))$ of length two fixes $E\cup\beta(F)$ pointwise so that $\rho(\beta(t))=\beta(t)$. If we let $\psi^{\prime}=\rho \circ\psi$ then $\psi^{\prime}$ fixes $(E\cup \beta(F))-\{b\}$ pointwise. Further, since $\rho(\beta(t))=\beta(t)$ and $\psi(\beta(t))\neq\beta(t)$, we conclude that $\psi^{\prime}(\beta(t))=\rho(\psi(\beta(t)))\neq\beta(t)$. We can therefore replace $\psi$ by $\psi^{\prime}$.)

Let $\sigma$ be the cycle $(b,\,\psi(b))$. Since $\sigma$ agrees with $\psi$ on a support of $\beta(t)$, $\sigma(\beta(t))=\psi(\beta(t))\neq\beta(t)$. Since $\sigma$ fixes $\gamma(F)$ pointwise, $\sigma(\gamma(t))=\gamma(t)$. Therefore $\beta(t)\neq\gamma(t)$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

Choose an $\eta\in$ fix$(E)$ so that $\eta(F) \cap F=\emptyset$. Then for every $\phi\in$ fix$(E\cup\{a\})$, $\eta(F)\neq\phi(F)$. It follows from the lemma that for all such $\phi,\,\eta(t)\neq\phi(t)$. Therefore $\eta(t)\in(y-y^{\prime})$.

\section*{NOTE 67}

\begin{theorem*} Form 203 (Every partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ into non-empty subsets has a choice function) implies form 94 ($C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty,\,\mathbb{R})$).
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Form 203 implies that every partition of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)\times \omega$ into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Assume $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ is a denumerable set of sets of reals. (We identify $\mathbb{R}$ with $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$.) For each $i\in \omega$, let $B_{i}=A_{i}\times\{i\}$. Then the family $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ is a disjoint family from $\mathcal{P}(\omega)\times \omega$ and therefore, by 203, has a choice function. This induces a choice function on $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 68}

\begin{theorem*}
form 3 ($2m =m$ for infinite cardinals $m$) implies form 53 ($m^{2}\leq 2^{m}$ for infinite cardinals $m$).
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Assume that for all infinite cardinals $m,\,2m=m$ and that $X$ is an infinite set. Then $f(x,\, y)=\{(0,\,x),\,(1,\,y)\}$ is a 1-1 function from $X\times X$ into $\mathcal{P}(2\times X)$.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 69}

\begin{definition*}
$|x|\leq^{\ast}|y|$\index{Subject}{$\leq^{\ast}$} (or $x\precsim^{\ast} y)$\index{Subject}{$\precsim^{\ast}$} if $y$ can be mapped onto $x$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
Form [40 B] implies form 208.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}

[40 B] is ``For all ordinals $\alpha$ and all sets $x$ if $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq^{\ast}|x|$, then $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq|x|$.'' and 208 is ``$2^{\aleph_{\alpha}}\geq\aleph_{\alpha+1}$'' (Form 208 depends on the ordinal $\alpha$).) Assume [40 B]. As is shown in Kunen\index{Author}{Kunen} \cite{bib:1980}, chapter 1, $|\aleph_{\alpha}\times\aleph_{\alpha}|=\aleph_{\alpha}$ and therefore, $|\mathcal{P}(\aleph_{\alpha}\times\aleph_{\alpha})|= |\mathcal{P}(\aleph_{\alpha})|$. The function $f$ from $\mathcal{P}(\aleph_{\alpha}\times\aleph_{\alpha})$ defined by $f(R)=$ the order type of $R$, if $R$ is a well ordering and $f(R)=0$ otherwise is onto $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$. It follows that $\aleph_{\alpha+1}\leq^{\ast}|\mathcal{P}(\aleph_{\alpha})|$ and therefore by [40 B], $\aleph_{\alpha+1}\leq|\mathcal{P}(\aleph_{\alpha})|$.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 70}

We give a proof that form [62 E] $(KW(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ implies form 62 $(C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$. Let $x$ be a set of finite sets and let $y=\{u:(\exists v\in x)u\subseteq v\}$. By [62 E], there is a Kinna-Wagner selection function, $f$, on $y$. We define a choice function $g$ on $x$ as follows: Let $u\in x$ be such that $|u|=n$. There exists an $m\in \omega,\,m<n$, such that $f^{m}(u)$ is a singleton. Define $g(u)$ to be the single element of $f^{m}(u)$. (Form 323, $KW(WO,\,\infty)$, clearly implies [62 E].)

\section*{NOTE 71}

In this note we give definitions from Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1988} for forms [14 L], [14 BP] through [14 BX], [14 CC] through [14 CH], [118 I] through [118 T], 331, 332, 343, 344, and [345 C] through [345 E].

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $E=\{(A,\,B):A$ and $B$ are closed in $X$ and $A \cap B=\emptyset\}$ and let $F=\{(U,\,V):U$ and $V$ are open in $X$ and $U\cap V=\emptyset$\}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $f:E\rightarrow F$ is a \emph{normality operator}\index{Subject}{normality operator} on $X$ if $\forall(A,\,B)\in E,\,f(A,\, B)=(U,\,V)$ where $A\subseteq U$ and $B\subseteq V$.
\item[2.] $X$ is \emph{effectively normal}\index{Subject}{effectively normal} if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and there is a normality operator on $X$.
\item[3.] $X$ is \emph{hereditarily normal}\index{Subject}{hereditarily normal} (or \emph{completely normal})\index{Subject}{completely normal} if all subspaces of $X$ are normal.
\item[4.] $X$ is \emph{hereditarily effectively normal} if all subspaces of $X$ are effectively normal.
\item[5.] A set $I\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is \emph{discrete} if $\forall x\in X,\,\exists$ a neighborhood $N$ of $x$ such that $N\cap A\neq\emptyset$ for at most one element $A\in I$.
\item[6.] $X$ is\index{Subject}{hereditarily effectively normal} \emph{collectionwise normal}\index{Subject}{collectionwise normal} if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and for every discrete $I\subseteq\{U:U$ is closed in $S\}$ there is a set $J$ of pairwise disjoint open subsets of $X$ such that for every $F\in I,\,\exists U\in J$ such that $F\subseteq U$.
\item[7.] Let $D=$\{ $I:I$ is a discrete collection of closed subsets of $X$\} and $O=\{J:J$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint open subsets of $X$\}. Then $f:D\rightarrow O$ is a \emph{collectionwise normality operator}\index{Subject}{collectionwise normality operator} on $X$ if $\forall I\in D$, if $f(I)=J$ then $\forall F\in I,\,\exists U\in J$ such that $F\subseteq U$. $N_{c}(X)$ denotes the set of collectionwise normality operators on $X$.
\item[8.] $X$ is \emph{effectively collectionwise normal}\index{Subject}{effectively collectionwise normal} if X is $T_{2}$ and $N_{c}(X)\neq\emptyset$.
\item[9.] $X$ is \emph{highly separated}\index{Subject}{highly separated} if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and $\{N_{c}(F):F\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.
\item[10.] $X$ is \emph{functionally separated}\index{Subject}{functionally separated} if for all pairs $(A,\,B)$ of closed disjoint subsets of $X$ there is a function $f:X\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ such that $A\subseteq f^{-1}(0)$ and $B\subseteq f^{-1}(1)$.
\item[11.] $X$ is \emph{Tietze-Urysohn}\index{Subject}{Tietze-Urysohn space} if for every closed $F\subseteq X$ and every continuous function $f:F\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ there is a continuous function $g:X\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ which extends $f$.
\item[12.] Let $C=$\{ $g:g:X\rightarrow[0, 1]$ and $g$ is continuous\}. A function $f:E\rightarrow C$ is a \emph{Urysohn operator}\index{Subject}{Urysohn operator} on $X$ if $\forall(A,\,B)\in E$, if $U=f(A,\,B)$ then $A\subseteq U^{-1}(0)$ and $B\subseteq U^{-1}(1)$. $U(X)$ denotes the set of Urysohn operators on $X$.
\item[13.] Let $B=\{(F,\,U):F$ is a closed subset of $X$ and $U:F\rightarrow[0, 1]$ is continuous\}. A function $f:B\rightarrow C$ is a \emph{Tietze-Urysohn operator}\index{Subject}{Tietze-Urysohn operator} if $\forall(F,\,U)\in B$, if $f(F,\, U)=V$ then $V$ extends $U$.
\item[14.] $X$ is \emph{effectively functionally separated}\index{Subject}{effectively functionally separated} if $U(X)\neq\emptyset$.
$X$ is \emph{effectively Tietze-Urysohn}\index{Subject}{effectively Tietze-Urysohn} if T-U$(X$) $\neq\emptyset$. (Where T-U($X$) is the set of all Tietze-Urysohn operators on $X$.)
\item[15.] $X$ is \emph{highly functionally separated}\index{Subject}{highly functionally separated} if $\{U(A):A\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.
\item[16.] $X$ is \emph{highly Tietze-Urysohn}\index{Subject}{highly Tietze-Urysohn} if \{T-U$(A):A\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.
\item[17.] $X$ is \emph{collectionwise separated}\index{Subject}{collectionwise separated} (or \emph{collectionwise Hausdorff})\index{Subject}{collectionwise Hausdorff} if it is $T_{2}$ and for every discrete set $I$ of singletons from $X$ there is a set $J$ of open subsets of $X$ such that for every $F\in I$, there is a unique $O\in J$ containing (the singleton) $F$.

\noindent Assume that $(X,\,\leq)$ is a linear order.
\item[18.] $A\subseteq X$ is \emph{convex} if $\forall(x,\,y)\in A^{2},\,\forall u\in X$, if $x<u<y$ then $u\in A$.
\item[19.] $(X, \leq)$ is \emph{conditionally complete} if each non-empty subset with an upper bound has a least upper bound and each non-empty subset with a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.
\item[20.] $(X,\,\leq)$ is \emph{complete} if $X=\emptyset$ or every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.
\item[21.] Let $X$ be a topological space, let $E$ be defined as above and let $\Omega(X)$ be the set of open subsets of $X$. A function $f:E\rightarrow\Omega(X)$ is a \emph{monotone normality operator}\index{Subject}{monotone normality operator} on $X$ if for every $(F,\,G)\in E$ the following conditions hold
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $F\subseteq f(F,\,G)\subseteq \overline{f(F,\,G)}\subseteq X-G$.
\item[(ii)] If $(F^{\prime},\,G^{\prime})\in E,\,F\subseteq F^{\prime}$ and $G^{\prime}\subseteq G$ then $f(F,\,G)\subseteq f(F^{\prime},\,G^{\prime})$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[22.] A topological space $X$ is \emph{monotonely normal} if it is $T_{1}$ and there is a monotone normality operator on $X$.
\item[23.] Let $(X,\,\leq)$ be a complete linear order and let $E$ be the set of non-empty open intervals of $X$. An \emph{increasing choice function} on $(X,\,\leq)$ is a function $\ast:E\rightarrow X$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\forall I\in E,\,\ast(I)\in I$.
\item[(ii)] If $(a,\,b)\in E$ and $(b,\,c)\in E$ then $\ast((a,\,b))\leq\ast((a,\,c))\leq\ast((b,\,c))$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[24.] A topological\index{Subject}{increasing choice function} space $X$ is \emph{completely regular}\index{Subject}{completely regular} if for all open $U\subseteq X$ and all $p\in U$, there is a continuous $f:X\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ such that $f(p)=0$ and $\forall x\in X-U,\,f(x)=1$.
\item[25.] An ordered set $(T,\,\leq)$ is a \emph{lattice} if any two elements have a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. A lattice is \emph{bounded} is it has a smallest and largest element.
\item[26.] An ideal $I$ in a lattice $(T,\,\leq)$ is \emph{prime} if $\forall x,\,y\in T$, if $x\wedge y\in I$ then either $x\in I$ or $y\in I$.
\item[27.] If $T$ is a bounded distributive lattice a function $f$ is a \emph{prime ideal choice function} on $T$ if for each proper ideal $I$ of $T,\,f(I)$ is a prime ideal containing $I$.
\item[28.] Assume that $T$ is a bounded distributive lattice in which every subset has a least upper bound then $T$ is $\vee$-\emph{compact}\index{Subject}{$\vee$-compact} if for all $F\subseteq T$ such that $\bigvee F=1$, there is a finite $F^{\prime}\subseteq F$ such that $\bigvee F^{\prime}=1.$ (If $(\Omega,\,\subseteq)$ is the lattice of open sets of a topological space $X$ then $X$ is compact if and only if $(\Omega,\,\subseteq)$ is $\vee$-compact.)
\item[29.] Let $E$ be a set. An \emph{ultra filter choice function}\index{Subject}{ultrafilter choice function} $f$ on $E$ is a function such that for all proper filters $I$ in $\mathcal{P}(E)$, $f(I)$ is an ultra filter containing $I$.
\item[30.] Let $E$ be a set and $U$ an ultra filter on a set $I$. $U$ is $E$-\emph{adequate} if for every filter $F$ in $\mathcal{P}(E)$ there is a function $g:I\rightarrow E$ such that $g(U)$ contains $F$.
\item[31.] A topological space is \emph{irreducible} if it is not empty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets.
\item[32.] A topological space $X$ is \emph{sober}\index{Subject}{sober topological space} if every closed irreducible subset of $X$ is the closure of a unique singleton.
\item[33.] A \emph{Banach algebra}\index{Subject}{Banach algebra} is a normed algebra in which every Cauchy filter converges.
\item[34.] Let $(I,\,\leq)$ be a preorder (reflexive and transitive), let $(E_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I}$ be a family of sets and for each $(\alpha,\,\beta)\in I\times I$ let $f_{\alpha,\beta}$ be a function from $E_{\beta}$ to $E_{\alpha}$. Assume that the $f_{\alpha,\beta}$ satisfy the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] $(LP_{I})\ \alpha\leq\beta\leq\gamma\Rightarrow f_{\alpha,\gamma}=f_{\alpha,\beta}\circ f_{\beta,\gamma}$.
\item[] $(LP_{II})$ For all $\alpha\in I,\,f_{\alpha,\alpha}$ is the identity on $E_{\alpha}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $((E_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I},\,(f_{\alpha,\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I\times I})$ is called a \emph{projective system relative to the preorder}\index{Subject}{projective system} $(I,\,\leq)$. Let $E=\prod_{\alpha\in I}E_{\alpha}$ and for each pair $(\alpha,\,\beta)\in I\times I$ such that $\alpha\leq\beta$, let $E_{\alpha,\beta}=\{x\in E:f_{\alpha,\beta}(x_{\beta})=x_{\alpha}\}$. Then the set $Y=\bigcap_{\alpha<\beta}E_{\alpha,\beta}$ is called the \emph{projective limit}\index{Subject}{projective limit} of the projective system $((E_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I},\,(f_{\alpha,\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I\times I})$. $Y$ is denoted $\lim_{\leftarrow}(E_{\alpha},\,f_{\alpha,\beta})$. In case the preorder $(I,\,\leq)$ is directed to the right (that is, $\forall(\alpha,\,\beta)\in I^{2},\,\exists\gamma\in I$ such that $\alpha\leq\gamma$ and $\beta\leq\gamma$.) we say that the projective system $((E_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I},\, (f_{\alpha,\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I\times I})$ is directed.
\item[35.] If $((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I},\,(f_{\alpha,\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I\times I})$ is a projective system relative to the preorder $(I, \leq)$ and if each $X_{\alpha}$ has a topology $C_{\alpha}$ such that $f_{\alpha,\beta}$ is continuous relative to the topologies $C_{\alpha}$ and $C_{\beta}$ then the system $((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in I},\,(f_{\alpha,\beta})_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I\times I})$ is called $a$ \emph{projective system of topological spaces}. In this case the projective limit of the system with the topology induced by the product topology on $\prod_{\alpha\in I}X_{\alpha}$ is called the \emph{the projective limit of the projective system of topological spaces}.
\item[36.] If $(A,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a bounded, distributive lattice, $X$ is a subset of $A$ and $F$ is a filter in $A$, then $F$ \emph{respects} $X$ if $X\subseteq F$ and $\bigwedge X$ exists implies $\bigwedge X\in F$.
\item[37.] If $(A,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a bounded, distributive lattice, $X$ is a subset of $A$ and $F$ is a filter in $A$, then $F$ \emph{strongly respects} $X$ if $X\subseteq F$ implies $\exists y\in F$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,y\leq x$.
\item[38.] If $X$ is a subset of a bounded, distributive lattice $(A,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ then $X$ \emph{is of Boolean type} if for all $b\in A,\,[(\forall x\in X,\,b\vee x=1)$ and $(\forall y\leq X,\,y\leq b)]$ implies $b=1$. $(y\leq X$ means $(\forall x\in X)(y\leq x).)$
\item[39.] If $(A,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a bounded, distributive lattice we say that \emph{A has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property}\index{Subject}{Rasiowa-Sikorski property} (respectively \emph{the strong Rasiowa-Sikorski property}) if for all $a,\,b\in A$ such that $a\not\leq b$ and all sequences $(X_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ of subsets of $A$ of Boolean type there is a prime filter containing $a$, not containing $b$ and respecting (respectively strongly respecting) each $X_{n}$.
\item[40.] If $(A,\,\wedge,\,\vee)$ is a bounded distributive lattice then an element $a\in A$ is $\vee$-\emph{compact} if for every subset $I\subseteq A,\,\bigvee I=a$ implies $(\exists J\subseteq I)$ ($J$ finite and $\bigvee J=a$).
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 72}

We prove that form $207(\beta)$ implies 209 for any ordinal $\beta$. (form $207(\beta)$ is $UT(\aleph_{\beta},\,\aleph_{\beta},\,<2^{\aleph_{\beta}})$ and 209 is ($\exists$ an ordinal $\alpha$) $(\forall X)$ (If $X$ is a denumerable union of denumerable sets then $\mathcal{P}(X)$ cannot be partitioned into $\aleph_{\alpha}$ non-empty sets.)) Assume form $207(\beta)$ is true. Then for any set $X$, if $X$ is a denumerable union of denumerable sets, then $|X|<2^{\aleph_{\beta}}$. Choose an ordinal $\alpha$ so that $\neg(\aleph_{\alpha}\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph_{\beta}}))|)$. For any $X$ which is the denumerable union of denumerable sets we have $|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|\leq|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph_{\beta}}))|$.
A partition of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ into $\aleph_{\alpha}$ non-empty sets would give $\aleph_{\alpha}\leq|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|$.

Similarly, form 26 implies form 209 and form 31 implies form 209.

\section*{NOTE 73}

In Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1977a} a general method for adding Dependent Choice (43) to models of ZF is described and the following models of ZF are constructed with the properties indicated:

\textsc{Model A} ($\mathcal{M}43$). Form 62 $(C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ and form 43 (DC) are true and form 30 (OP) is false.

\textsc{Model B} ($\mathcal{M}44$). Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 15 (Kinna-Wagner Principle) is false.

\textsc{Model C} $(\mathcal{M}45)$. Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 49 (the order extension principle) is false.

\textsc{Model D} $(\mathcal{M}46(n,\,M))$. For each finite set $Z$ of positive natural numbers and natural number $n>1$, for which the following is false
\begin{enumerate}
\item[]$S(Z,\,n)$: For every decomposition $n=p_{1}+\ldots+p_{s}$ of $n$ into a sum of primes at least one $p_{i}$ divides and element of $Z$, (See Mostowski\index{Author}{Mostowski} \cite{bib:1945}. Also see note 15. Condition $S$ implies condition $D$ of note 15.)
\end{enumerate}

there is a model in which form 46 $(C(\infty,\,Z))$ and form 43 are true and form 45 $(C(\infty,\,n))$ is false.

\textsc{Model E} $(\mathcal{M}47(n,\,M))$. For every finite set $Z$ of positive integers and integer $n>1$, for which the following condition is false
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] $M(Z,\,n)$: For any decomposition $n=p_{1}+\ldots+p_{s}$ of $n$ into a sum of primes there are non-negative $q_{1},\,\ldots$, $q_{s}$ such that $q_{1}p_{1}+\ldots+q_{s}p_{s}\in Z$.
\end{enumerate}

There is a model in which form 46 $(C(\infty,\,Z))$ and form 43 are true and form 47 $(C(WO,\,n))$ is false. (See Mostowski \cite{bib:1945}. Also, condition $K$ of note 15 implies condition $M$.)

\section*{NOTE 74}

In Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1977a} it is shown that $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{\alpha})\rightarrow C(\infty,\,\aleph_{\alpha})$ is not a theorem of ZF for regular $\aleph_{\alpha}$. For singular $\aleph_{\alpha}$ the question is open.

\section*{NOTE 75}

Several weak\index{Author}{Felgner/Jech}\index{Author}{Mostowski} forms of AC are known to be equivalent to AC in ZF\index{Subject}{forms equivalent to AC in ZF}. These include:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] MC: The Axiom of Multiple Choice, form 67;
\item[2.] LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered, form 90;
\item[3.] PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered, form 91;
\item[4.] VB: Every vector space has a basis, form 66;
\item[5.] A: The Antichain Principle, form 89; and
\item[6.] $C(LO,\,\infty)$: Every linearly ordered family of non-empty sets has a choice function, form 202.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently everything that implies one of these six forms is equivalent to AC in ZF. That is, 95, 109, 112, 114, 133, 147, 149, 164, 218, 264, 292, 333, 334, and $335(n)$ for $n\geq 2$, also imply AC in ZF. In fact in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ the following two chains of implications are provable: AC $\rightarrow$ VB $\rightarrow$ MC $\rightarrow$ A $\rightarrow$ LW $\rightarrow$ PW, and AC $\rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty)\rightarrow$ LW. With regard to the reverse implications, VB $\rightarrow$ AC, MC $\rightarrow$ VB and LW $\rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty)$ are open questions. The other reverse implications are known to be unprovable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. (See Jech\index{Author}{Jech} \cite{bib:1973b}, page 134, Felgner/Jech
\cite{bib:1973}, Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1984a}, H. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin} \cite{bib:1960}, H. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{H. Rubin/ J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1985}, Part I, 5, Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1983d},\cite{bib:1984b},\cite{bib:1985a}, Howard/Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/Rubin} \cite{bib:1977}, Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1978}, Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996a},\cite{bib:1996c}, and note 18.) It follows from the two chains of implications that each of the twenty forms mentioned above implies PW, form 91, in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

In Pincus \cite{bib:1972a}, page 740, it is shown that if $\neg\Phi$ is boundable (see Pincus \cite{bib:1972a}, p. 722 for the definition of boundable) and $\Phi\rightarrow AC$ is a theorem of ZF, then $\Phi\rightarrow$ form 91 (PW) is a theorem of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

\section*{NOTE 76}

In this note we prove that form 126 $(MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty))$ implies forms 82 (If a set is infinite then its power set is Dedekind infinite.) and 185 (Every Dedekind finite, linearly ordered set is finite.)

\begin{lemma*}
$MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ implies that for every infinite set $X$ there is a sequence $(Y_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ of finite subsets of $X$ such that $\forall n\in \omega,\,Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1}$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be an infinite set and for each $n\in\omega$, let $X_{n}=\{Y\subseteq X:|Y|=n\}$. By $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ there is a function $f$ such that $\forall n\in\omega,\,f(X_{n})$ is a finite non-empty subset of $X_{n}$. We define the sequence $(Y_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ by induction as follows: $Y_{0}=\emptyset$. Assume that $Y_{n}$ is defined and let $k$ be the least natural number such that $|Y_{n}|<k$. We let $Y_{n+1}=(\bigcup f(X_{k}))\cup Y_{n}$. Since $\mathrm{f}(X_{k})$ is a set of $k$ element sets $|Y_{n}|<k\leq |\bigcup f(X_{k})|\leq|Y_{n+1}|$.
\end{proof}

It is clear from the lemma that $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ implies that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite. To show that $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ implies form 185, let $X$ be a Dedekind finite set which is linearly ordered by $\leq$. The assumption that $X$ is infinite leads to a contradiction as follows: By the lemma we get a sequence $(Y_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ of finite subsets of $X$ such that $Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1}$ for all $n\in \omega$. If we define $t_{n}$ to be the $\leq$-least element of $Y_{n+1}-Y_{n}$ then $(t_{n})_{n\in \omega}$ is an infinite sequence of distinct elements of $X$ and therefore $X$ is Dedekind infinite.

\section*{NOTE 77}

In this note we include definitions from Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis} \cite{bib:1996b} for forms [1 BL] through [1 BR], [1CB], and [67 G].

In what follows $(X,\,T)$ is a topological space and $P\subset \mathcal{P}(X)$.

\begin{definition*}
A non-empty set $\mathcal{F}\subseteq P-\{\emptyset\}$ is called a $P$-\emph{filter} iff
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $F_{1},\,F_{2}\in \mathcal{F}$ implies $F_{1}\cap F_{2}\in \mathcal{F}$.
\item[(2)] $F\in \mathcal{F},\,F\subset F^{\prime}$ and $F^{\prime}\in P$ implies $F^{\prime}\in \mathcal{F}$.
\end{enumerate}
A $T$-filter is called an \emph{open filter}. $\mathcal{F}$ is called a \emph{filter base} if it just satisfies (1) above.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
A non-empty set $\mathcal{I}\subseteq P-\{X\}$ is called a $P$-\emph{ideal} iff
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $I_{1},\,I_{2}\in \mathcal{I}$ implies $I_{1}\cup I_{2}\in \mathcal{I}$.
\item[(2)] $I\in \mathcal{I},\,I^{\prime}\subset I$ and $I^{\prime}\in P$ implies $I^{\prime}\in \mathcal{I}$.
\end{enumerate}
If $F$ is the set of closed subsets of $X$, then a $F$-ideal is called a \emph{closed ideal}. $\mathcal{I}$ is called \emph{complete} if $\bigcup C\in \mathcal{I}$ for every $C\subseteq \mathcal{I}$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
A disjoint set $C\subseteq T-\{\emptyset\}$ is called a \emph{cellular family
of} $X$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
A \emph{nest} of $(X,\,T)$ is a maximal linearly ordered subset of the partially ordered set $(T-\{\emptyset\},\,\subseteq)$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
A \emph{tower} $\mathcal{T}$ of $(X,\,T)$ is a linearly ordered subset of the partially ordered set $(T-\{\emptyset\},\,\subseteq)$ such that either the interior of $\bigcap \mathcal{T}$ is empty or the interior of $\bigcap \mathcal{T}$ does not properly contain any non-empty open set.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If $\{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\}$ is a family of topological spaces, then the \emph{box topology} on $\prod_{i\in k}X_{i}$ is the topology having a base of all sets of the form $\prod_{i\in k}O_{i}$ where $O_{i}\in T_{i}$ for all $i\in k$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
If $\{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\}$ is a family of disjoint topological spaces, then the \emph{free union} is the set $X=\bigcup\{X_{i}:i\in k\}$ together with the topology $T$ containing all sets $O\subseteq X$ such that $O\cap X_{i}\in T_{i}$ for all $i\in k$.
\end{definition*}

In Rav\index{Author}{Rav} \cite{bib:1977}, it is shown that under the assumption of $RL$ (form 99) and certain conditions on a set $X$ and filter $\mathcal{F}$ in $\mathcal{P}(X)$, $\mathcal{F}$ can be extended to an ultrafilter. Either of the following conditions suffices:

\item[2.] $\mathcal{F}$ has a choice function.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 79}

Definitions for forms 227 and 228.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{partially ordered group} is a triple $(G,\,\circ,\,\leq)$ such that $(G,\,\circ)$ is a group and $(G,\,\leq)$ is a partially ordered set satisfying for all $x,\,y,\,a$ and $b$ in $G$ if $x\leq y$, then $axb\leq ayb$.
\item[2.] $P=\{a\in G:a\geq e\}$ is the \emph{positive cone}\index{Subject}{positive cone} (where $e$ is the identity in $G$).
\item[3.] If $P\cup P^{-1}=G$\index{Subject}{partially ordered group} then $G$ is \emph{fully ordered}\index{Subject}{fully ordered group}. (This is equivalent to saying that $\leq$ is a linear ordering.)
\item[4.] A group is \emph{torsion free}\index{Subject}{torsion free group} if the only element of finite order is the identity element.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 80}

In Rav\index{Author}{Rav} \cite{bib:1977} forms [14 AL], [14 AM], [14 AO] and [14 AP] are shown to follow from form 14 (BPI). The arguments that they imply form 14 are fairly straightforward. ([14 AL]: The radical of a proper ideal $A$ in a commutative ring $R$ with identity (The radical of $A=\{x\in R$: for some $m\in \omega,\,x^{m}\in A\}.)$ is the intersection of all prime ideals in $R$ containing A; [14 AM]: Let $A$ be a subring of a commutative ring $R$ and $p$ a prime ideal in $A$ such that $p=Rp\cap A$. Then there is a prime ideal $J$ in $R$ such that $p=J\cap A;$ [14 AO]: Suppose $R$ is a commutative ring, $A$ is a proper ideal in $R$, and $S$ is a multiplicative semigroup in $R$ not meeting $A$. Then there is a prime ideal $p$ in $R$ such that $A\subseteq p$ and $p\cap S=\emptyset$; and [14 AP]: Suppose to each finite subset $F$ of a set I there corresponds a set $\Phi(F)$ of functions whose domains are subsets of $I$ including $F$ and such that (a) $F_{1}\subseteq F_{2}$ implies $\Phi(F_{2})\subseteq\Phi(F_{2})$ and (b) $\forall i\in I,\,\{\phi(i):\phi \in\bigcup$\{ $\Phi(F):F$ finite and $F\subseteq I\}\}$ is finite. Then there is a function $f$ with domain $I$ such that for all finite $F\subseteq I,\,\exists\phi\in\Phi(F)$ such that $\phi$ and $f$ coincide on F.)

\begin{theorem*}\quad
[14 AL] implies BPI.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $B$ is a Boolean algebra with more than two elements. Choose $b\in B$ with $b\neq 0$ and $b\neq 1$. Let $A$ be the ideal generated by $b$ and apply [14 AL] to get a prime ideal in $B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}\quad

[14 AM] implies BPI.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra and let $r$ be a proper ideal in B. Let $A=\{x:x\in r$ or $\overline{x}\in r\}$. $A,\,B$ and $r$ satisfy the hypotheses of [14 AM]. The conclusion of [14 AM] gives a prime ideal $J$ in $B$ containing $r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}\quad

[14 AO] implies BPI.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
If $B$ is a Boolean algebra and $A$ is a proper ideal in $B$ let $S=\{1\}\subseteq B$. $S$ is a multiplicative sub-semi-group of $B$ and therefore the hypotheses of [14 AO] are satisfied. The conclusion of [14 AO] gives a prime ideal in $B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}\quad

[14 AP] implies BPI.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Since it is shown in Cowen \cite{bib:1973} (see Rav \cite{bib:1977}, Corollary~ 2.3) that [14 AP] implies Rado's lemma (form 99) and it is known that Rado's lemma together with $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ (form 62) imply BPI (see form [14
Y]), it suffices to prove that [14 AP] implies $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$. Let $\{x_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of pairwise disjoint finite sets. For each finite subset $F$ of $I$, let
\begin{equation*}
\Phi(F)=\{\phi: \mathrm{dom}\ \phi\ \text{is finite}\ \wedge F\subseteq \text{dom}\ \phi \subseteq I\wedge(\forall i\in \text{dom}\ \phi)(\phi(i)\in x_{i})\}
\end{equation*}
$\Phi$ and $I$ satisfy the hypotheses of [14 AP] and therefore by [14 AP] there is a function $f$ with domain $I$ such that $\forall$ finite $F\subseteq I,\,\exists\phi$ in $\Phi(F)$ such that $\phi$ and $f$ agree on $F$. Therefore, for all $i\in I,\,f(i)\in x_{i}$ and we have a choice function for $\{x_{i}:i\in I\}$.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 81}

We argue that form 30 (the ordering principle) implies form 83 (If every subset of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ has a maximum element then $X$ is finite.)

Assume $X$\index{Author}{Cowen}\index{Author}{Rav} is infinite and let $\leq$ be a linear ordering of $X$. There must be either a non-empty subset $Y$ of $X$ with no least element (under $\leq$) or a non-empty subset with no greatest element. (If every non-empty subset of $X$ has a least element then let $x_{1}$ be the least element of $X,\,x_{2}$ be the least element of $X-\{x_{1}\}$, etc. This produces a subset $\{x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots\}$ with no greatest element.) If $Y$ is an infinite subset of $X$ with no greatest element, we get a linearly ordered subset $A$ of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ with no maximum by letting $A=\{\{x:x\in Y\wedge x\leq y\}:y\in Y\}$. We can proceed similarly if $Y$ is an infinite subset of $X$ with no smallest element.

\section*{NOTE 82}

We give the definitions for form 230 $(L^{1}=HOD)$\index{Subject}{$L^{1}$} from Myhill/Scott\index{Author}{Myhill/Scott} \cite{bib:1971}.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $DF^{0}(A)$ is the set of all subsets of $A$ definable by first order formulas in $\langle A, \in_{A}\rangle$ using parameters from $A$, i.e., $DF^{0}(A)$ is all sets of the form $\{x\in A:\Phi^{(A)} (x,\,a_{0},\,\ldots a_{n-1})\}$ where $\Phi$ is a formula of the type described above, $a_{0},\,\ldots,\, a_{n-1}$ are in $A$ and $\Phi^{(A)}$ means all variables range over $A$.
\item[2.] G\"{o}del's constructible sets are defined by $L_{\alpha}^{0}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}DF^{0}(L_{\beta}^{0})$ and $L^{0}= \bigcup_{\alpha\in \mathrm{On}}L_{\alpha}^{0}$.
\item[3.] $DF^{1}(A)$ consists of all sets of the form $\{x\in A:\Phi(x,\,a_{0},\,\ldots,\,a_{n-1})\}$ where $a_{0},\,\ldots,\,a_{n-1}$ are in $A$ and the quantifiers are restricted to $A$ or $\mathcal{P}(A)$.
\item[4.] $L_{\alpha}^{1}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}DF^{1}(L_{\beta}^{1})$ and $L^{1}=\bigcup_{\alpha\in \mathrm{On}}L_{\alpha}^{1}$.
\item[5.] $HOD$\index{Subject}{$HOD$} is the class of hereditarily ordinal definable sets.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 84}

This note contains (standard) algebraic definitions for forms 241 through 244.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] If $F$ is a subfield of $E,\,\alpha\in E$ is \emph{algebraic over} $F$ if $\exists a_{0},\,a_{1},\, \ldots,\,a_{n}\in F$ not all zero such that $a_{0}+a_{1}\alpha\ldots+a_{n}\alpha^{n}=0$.
\item[(2)] $E$ is \emph{algebraic over} $F$ if every element of $E$ is algebraic over $F$.
\item[(3)] A field $L$ is \emph{algebraically closed} if every polynomial of degree $\geq 1$ with coefficients in $L$ has a root in $L$.
\item[(4)] If $K$ is a field, an \emph{algebraic closure} of $K$ is an algebraically closed algebraic extension of $K$.
\item[(5)] A field $K$ is \emph{real} if --1 is not the sum of squares in $K$.
\item[(6)] A field is \emph{real closed} if it is real and any real, algebraic extension of $K$ equals $K$.
\item[(7)] A \emph{principal ideal domain} is an integral domain (commutative ring with identity and no zero divisors) in which every ideal is principal.
\item[(8)] A \emph{unique factorization domain}\index{Subject}{unique factorization domain} is an integral domain in which
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] every non-zero,\index{Subject}{principal ideal domain}\index{Subject}{real closed field} non-unit element (unit $\equiv$ invertible) can be written $a= c_{1}c_{2}\ldots c_{n}$ with $c_{1},\,c_{2},\,\ldots,\,c_{n}$ irreducible. (That is, each $c_{i}$ is non-zero and non-unit and if $c_{i}=ab$ then either $a$ or $b$ is a unit.)
\item[(ii)] If\index{Subject}{algebraic closure}\index{Subject}{algebraic over a field} $a=c_{1}c_{2}\ldots c_{n}=d_{1}d_{2}\ldots d_{m}$ where $c_{i}$ and $d_{i}$ are irreducible then $n=m$ and there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{$1, 2, $\ldots,\,n\}$ such that $c_{i}=r_{i}d_{\sigma(i)}$ where $r_{i}$ is a unit, $i=1,\,\ldots,\,n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

The monadic theory $MT(\omega_{1},\,<)$ mentioned in form 246 is defined as follows: The language has a countable set $x,\,y,\,\ldots$ of variables ranging over $\omega_{1}$, a countable set of variables $X,\,Y,\, \ldots$ ranging over subsets of $\omega_{1}$, a relation $<$ on $\omega_{1}$ and a relation $\in$ between individual variables and set variables. The formulas are built up with the usual logical connectives and quantifiers $\forall$ and $\exists$ on both types of variables. $MT(\omega_{1},\,<)$ is the set of all sentences true in $(\omega_{1},\,<)$

\section*{NOTE 88}

Either $\mathcal{N}1$ or $\mathcal{N}3$ may be used to prove that form 31 $(UT(\aleph^{0},\,\aleph^{0},\,\aleph^{0}))$ does not imply form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite). Form 9 is known to be false in these models and a proof that form 31 holds is given below. The result is transferable to ZF by Pincus \cite{bib:1972a}.

Let $\mathcal{N}$ be either $\mathcal{N}1$ or $\mathcal{N}3$ with set of atoms $A$ and $\mathcal{G}$ the group of permutations used in defining the model. Assume that in $\mathcal{N},\,B$ is a denumerable set of denumerable sets. Let $e\subseteq A$ be a finite support for every $b\in B$. Such an $e$ exists since $B$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}$. Assume $b\in B$ and $x\in b$. The proof will be completed by showing that $e$ is a support of $x$. We argue by contradiction. Assume that $e$ is not a support of $x$. We will show that under this assumption $b$ has a subset of the same cardinality as an infinite subset of $A$ which contradicts the countability of $b$.

Let $e^{\prime}\supseteq e$ be a support of $x$. Then there is a $t\in e^{\prime}\backslash e$ and a $\phi\in \mathcal{G}$ which fixes $e^{\prime}\backslash \{t\}$ pointwise and such that $\phi(x)\neq x$. (It follows that $\phi(t)\neq t$.) It can be verified that
\begin{equation*}
\{\langle\psi(t),\psi(x)\rangle:\psi\in \mathcal{G}\ \text{and}\ \psi\ \text{fixes}\ e^{\prime}\backslash \{t\}\ \text{pointwise}\}
\end{equation*}
is a\index{Author}{Pincus} one to one function from an infinite subset of $A$ into $b$ which is in $\mathcal{N}$.

\section*{NOTE 91}

In this note we argue that form 269 is false in the first Fraenkel model $\mathcal{N}1$ of ZF$^{0}$. Form 269 is: ``For every cardinal $m$, there is a set $A$ such that $2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m$ and there is a choice function on the collection of 2 element subsets of $A$.'' It suffices to show that for any set $A$ in $\mathcal{N}1$ if the set $[A]^{2}$ of two element subset of $A$ has a choice function, then $A$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$. Assume that $A$ is such a set and assume that $E$ is a (finite) support of $A$ and a choice function $f$ on $[A]^{2}$. Assume $x\in A$. We show by contradiction that $E$ must be a support of $x$. Suppose not and let $F$ be a support of $x$ containing $E$. We claim there is a permutation $\psi$ in $\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$ and an element $y\in A$ such that $x\neq y,\,\psi(x)=y$ and $\psi(y)=x$. This would contradict our choice of $E$ as a support for a choice function on $[A]^{2}$ since $\psi$ fixes $\{x,\,y\}$ but moves both of its elements. To get such a $\psi$, let $\phi\in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$ satisfy $\phi(x)\neq x$ and $\phi$ moves only finitely many atoms. Assume $F-E=\{t_{1},\,\ldots,\,t_{n}\}$ and choose a set of atoms $\{s_{1},\,\ldots,\, s_{n}\}$ disjoint from $F\cup\{t\in U:\phi(t)\neq t\}$. Let $\psi$ be the product of transpositions $\prod_{i=1}^{n}(t_{i},\,s_{i})$. The element $\psi(x)$ is different from $x$ since $\phi(x)\neq x$ and $\phi(\psi(x))=\psi(x)$. It is also clear that if $y=\psi(x)$, then $\psi(y)=x$.

\section*{NOTE 93}

We give\index{Subject}{compactness theorem}\index{Author}{Kolany/Wojtylak} proofs due to A. Rubin\index{Author}{A. Rubin} that $MC(\infty,\,\infty$, even) (334) is true in $\mathcal{N}2$ and $MC(\infty,\, \infty$, odd) (333) is true in $\mathcal{N}2^{\ast}(3)$.

\setcounter{theorem}{0}
\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm1b}
$MC(\infty,\,\infty,\,even)$ is true in $\mathcal{N}2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $M$ be a non-empty set in $\mathcal{N}2$, each of whose elements has at least two elements. The group $\mathcal{G}$ in $\mathcal{N}2$ is Abelian and each of its elements has order two. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the filter determined by $S$, the set of finite subsets of the set of atoms, $A$. $(\mathcal{F}$ is generated by the set of all subgroups $H$ of $\mathcal{G}$ such that there is an $E\in S$ such that $H$ fixes $E$ pointwise.) The filter $\mathcal{F}$ is in the model because each element in $\mathcal{G}$ has order two so $\mathcal{F}$ has null support. In fact,
\begin{equation}
\label{part04:eqn1} (\forall H\in \mathcal{F})(\forall\sigma\in H)\sigma(H)=H.
\end{equation}
Define a linear ordering $\leq$ on $\mathcal{F}$ which extends $\supseteq$, that is, if $H_{1},\,H_{2}\in \mathcal{F}$ and $H_{1}\supseteq H_{2}$, then $H_{1}\leq H_{2}$. The relation $\leq$ is in the model because of (\ref{part04:eqn1}). (In fact, $\leq$ is a well ordering, but we do not need this.) Let $W$ be the set of all sets in the model that have null support. Every permutation in $\mathcal{G}$ leaves $W$ pointwise fixed so $W$ can be well ordered by a relation $R$.

Suppose $X\in M$. We shall give an algorithm to construct a subset of $X$ whose cardinality is a power of two. Let $Y=\{\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}\{x\}:x\in X\}$. Each element of $Y$ has null support so $Y$ can be well ordered by $R$. Moreover, each element of $Y$ is finite. (In fact, the cardinality of each element of $Y$ is a power of two because $|\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}\{x\}|=|\mathcal{G}/\mathrm{sym}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)|$, where $\mathrm{sym}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)=\{\sigma\in \mathcal{G}:\sigma(x)=x\}.)$ Let $y$ be the $R$-first element of $Y$ and let $x=y\cap X$. Let $\mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)$ be the group of all $\sigma \in \mathcal{G}$ that fixes $x$ pointwise and let
\begin{equation*}
J=\{H\in \mathcal{F}:\mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}} (x) \subseteq H\ \&\ (\exists z\in x)H^{\prime\prime}\{z\}\subseteq x\}
\end{equation*}
Since $\mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(x)\in J,\, J\neq\emptyset$. Moreover, $J$ is finite and is linearly ordered by $\leq$. Let $H_{0}$ be the $\leq$-first element of $J$. We claim that if $z,\,w\in x$ and, $H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{z\}$ and $H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{w\}$ are both subsets of $x$, then $H^{\prime\prime}_{0}\{z\}=H^{\prime\prime}_{0}\{w\}$. The reason for this is as follows. By the definition of $y(x\subseteq y)$, there is a $\sigma \in \mathcal{G}$ such that $\sigma(z)=w$. Let $K=H_{0}\cup
H_{0}\sigma$. Then $K^{\prime\prime}\{z\}=H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{z\}\cup H^{\prime\prime}_{0}\{w\}\subseteq x$. We have $\mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}} (x)\subseteq H_{0}\subseteq K$ so $K\in J$, and $K\leq H_{0}$. However, $H_{0}$ is the $\leq$-first element of $J$, so $K=H_{0}$. Consequently, $H^{\prime\prime}_{0}\{z\}=H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{w\}$.

Then, for each $X\in M$, we choose the unique $H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{z\}$ which is a subset of $x\subseteq X$. $H_{0}^{\prime\prime}\{z\}$ has the same cardinality as the factor group, $H_{0}/\mathrm{sym}_{H_{0}}(z)$, which is a power of two.

Let $Z=\{u\subseteq X:X\in M\}$ and let $f$ be a multiple choice function on $Z$ such that for each $u\in Z,\,|f(u)|$ is a power of 2. We define a multiple choice function $g$ on $M$ satisfying $MC(\infty,\, \infty$, even) as follows. Suppose $X\in M$. If $|f(X)|>1$, then $g(X)=f(X)$. If $|f(X)|=1$, consider $u=f(X-\{f(X)\})$. If $|u|=1$, then define $g(X)=\{f(X),\,u\}$; and if $|u|>1$, define $g(X)=u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm2b}
$MC(\infty,\,\infty,\,odd)$ is true in $\mathcal{N}2^{\ast}(3)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In this model the group $\mathcal{G}$ is Abelian and each element has order three. Let $M$ be a set of non-empty sets. We shall show that there is a multiple choice function $f$ on $M$ such that for each $X\in M,\,|f(X)|$ is a power of three. The proof is the same as the proof of $MC(\infty,\,\infty$,
even) in Theorem~\ref{part04:thm1b} above up to and including the definition of $x=y\cap X$. Then we proceed as follows. For each $u\in x$, let $Q(u)=\{\sigma\in \mathcal{G}:\sigma(u)\in x\}$. Each $Q(u)$ has null support and is therefore in $W$. Let $Q_{0}$ be the $R$-first element of $\{Q(u):u\in x\}$ and let $z=\{u\in x:Q(u)=Q_{0}\}$. We claim that the cardinality of $z$ is a power of three. Fix $u\in z$ and let $K=\{\sigma\in \mathcal{G}:\sigma(u)\in z\}.\,K$ is a subgroup of $\mathcal{G}$ because $K=\{\sigma\in \mathcal{G}:(\sigma^{-1})^{\prime\prime}Q_{0}=Q_{0}\}$. Therefore, $|z|=|\mathcal{G}/$fix$_\mathcal{G}(u)|$ which is a power of three.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 94}

In this note we summarize what is known about the relationships between possible definitions of ``finite''\index{Subject}{definitions of finite}.

Several authors have studied this topic they include Diel\index{Author}{Diel} \cite{bib:1974}, Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989}, Levy\index{Author}{Levy} \cite{bib:1958}, Spi\u{s}iak\index{Author}{Spi\u{s}iak} \cite{bib:1993}, Spi\u{s}iak/Vojt\'{a}\u{s}\index{Author}{Spi\u{s}iak/Vojt\'{a}\u{s}} \cite{bib:1988}, Tarski\index{Author}{Tarski} \cite{bib:1938b} and \cite{bib:1954a}, Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1974a} and Hickman\index{Author}{Hickman} \cite{bib:1972}. The first eight definitions and their names are due to Tarski \cite{bib:1954a}

\begin{definition*}. A set $A$ is said to be
\begin{enumerate}
\item[] \emph{decomposable} if there are two pairwise disjoint non-empty sets $x$ and $y$ such that $x\prec A,\, y\prec A$, and $A=x\cup
y$. (Similarly, a cardinal number $m$ is said to be \emph{decomposable}, if there exist two non-zero cardinal number $p$ and $q$ such that $p<m,\,q<m$, and $m=p+q$.)

\item[]\emph{Dedekind finite}\index{Subject}{Dedekind finite} if it is not equivalent to a proper subset of itself. Otherwise, $A$ is \emph{Dedekind infinite}.

\item[] $T$-\emph{finite}\index{Subject}{$T$-finite} if every non-empty, monotone $X\subseteq \mathcal{P}(A)$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element.
\item[] $I$-\emph{finite} if every non-void family of subsets of $A$ has an $\subseteq$-maximal element. (This is (equivalent to) the usual definition of finite.)
\item[] $Ia$-\emph{finite} if it is not the union of two disjoint sets neither of which is I-finite.
\item[] \emph{II-finite} if every non-empty $\subseteq$-monotone family of subsets of $A$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element.
\item[] \emph{III-finite} if the power set of $A$ is Dedekind finite.
\item[] \emph{IV-finite} if $A$ is Dedekind finite.
\item[] \emph{V-finite} if $|A|=0$ or 2 $\cdot|A|>|A|$.

\item[] $VI$-\emph{finite} if $|A|=0$ or $|A|=1$ or $|A|^{2}>|A|$.
\item[] \emph{VII-finite} if $A$ is I-finite or not well orderable.
\end{enumerate}

In Tarski \cite{bib:1954a} and Levy \cite{bib:1958} it is shown that if a set is finite according to any definition in the above list then it is finite according to any following definition and none of the reverse implications hold.

In Tarski \cite{bib:1938b} the following definitions are considered:
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
For each $n\in \omega$, A set $A$ is $T(n)$-finite if for every $S\subseteq \mathcal{P}(A)$, if every collection of $n$ non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets of $A$ contains an element of $S$, then there are $2n+1$ elements $x(i)$, $1\leq i\leq 2n+1$ of $S$ such that $A\subseteq\bigcup\{x(i):1 \leq i\leq 2n+1\}$.
\end{definition*}

In Howard/Yorke \cite{bib:1989} the following definition is introduced:

\begin{definition*}
A set $A$ is $D$ finite if $|A|=0$ or $|A|=1$ or $A=C\cup D$ with $|C|<|A|$ and $|D|<|A|$. (Note that $A$ is $D$ finite if and only if $|A|=0$ or $|A|=1$ or $A$ is decomposable.
\end{definition*}

It is\index{Author}{Levy}\index{Author}{Tarski} shown there that IV $\rightarrow D$ and $D\rightarrow$ VII. Further, $V \not\rightarrow D$ and $D\not\rightarrow$ VI.

In Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1974a} the following classes of Dedekind finite cardinals are considered:

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[]$\Delta_{1}=\{x:x=y+z\rightarrow y$ or $z$ is finite\}. (We will say $A$ is $\Delta_{1}$ finite if $|A|\in\Delta_{1}$.
\item[] $\Delta_{1}$-finite is equivalent to Ia-finite.)
\item[] $\Delta_{2}=\{|A|$: any linearly ordered partition of $A$ is finite\}. $(\Delta_{2}$-finite is equivalent to II-finite.)
\item[] $\Delta_{3}=\{|A|$: any linearly ordered subset of $A$ is finite\}.
\item[] $\Delta_{4}=\{x:\neg(\aleph_{0}\leq^{\ast}x)\}$. ($\Delta_{4}$-finite is equivalent to III-finite.)
\item[] $\Delta_{5}=\{x:\neg(x+1\leq^{\ast}x)\}$.
\end{enumerate}

It is shown that I-finite $\rightarrow\Delta_{1}\rightarrow\Delta_{2}\rightarrow\Delta_{4}\rightarrow\Delta_{5}\rightarrow$ IV-finite and $\Delta_{2}\rightarrow\Delta_{3}\rightarrow$ IV-finite and that none of the implications are reversible. It is also shown that various combinations of equality and inequality between these classes are consistent. For example, it is shown that
\begin{equation*}
\text{ZF}+\omega=\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{4}\neq\Delta_{5}\neq\ \text{IV-finite}\ +\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{3}\neq\ \text{IV-finite}
\end{equation*}
is consistent.

In Diel\index{Author}{Diel} \cite{bib:1974} two definitions are finite are considered: ``Almost finite''\index{Subject}{almost finite}  which is equivalent to III-finite and ``strongly Dedekind finite''\index{Subject}{strongly Dedekind finite} which is equivalent to $\Delta_{5}$-finite.

Finally in Howard/Spi\u{s}iak\index{Author}{Howard/Spi\u{s}iak}\index{Author}{Spi\u{s}iak} \cite{bib:1994}, Spi\u{s}iak \cite{bib:1993} and Spi\u{s}iak/Vojt\'{a}\u{s}\index{Author}{Spi\u{s}iak/Vojt\'{a}\u{s}} \cite{bib:1988} the following forms are considered:
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
Let $F$ be one of I, Ia, II, III, IV, V, VI or VII. Then a set $A$ is $F^{\prime\prime}$-finite if $\mathcal{P}(A)$ is $F$-finite.
\end{definition*}

It is shown that each of $\mathrm{I}^{\prime\prime}, \mathrm{Ia}^{\prime\prime}, \mathrm{II}^{\prime\prime}$ and $\mathrm{III}^{\prime\prime}$ are equivalent to I and that the following implications hold: III $\rightarrow \mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow \mathrm{IV},\mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime} \rightarrow \mathrm{V}$, and $\mathrm{VII}\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime}$. Further it is consistent (with $\mathrm{ZF}$) that there exists a set with any combination of the properties $\mathrm{III},\mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime},\mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime}, \mathrm{IV}$ and $\mathrm{V}$ not excluded by the known implications described so far in this note. Finally, it is shown that form 88 $(C(\infty,\,2))$ implies that $\mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime}$ and III are equivalent.

In addition, in Howard/Yorke\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} \cite{bib:1989}, if $J$ and $K$ are two possible definitions of finite then the assertion that $J$ and $K$ are equivalent is denoted by $E(J,\,K)$ and the strength of these weak forms of $AC$ is investigated. Several of these appear in the list of forms: $E(I,\,IV)$ is form 9, $E(I,\,Ia)$ is form 64, $E(I,\,III)$ is form 82, $E(I,\,II)$ is form 83, $E(II,\,III)$ is form 84, $E(II,\,IV)$ is form [9 B], $E(IV,\,V)$ is form [3 E], $E(V,\,VI)$ is form [1 AH], $E(VI,\,VII)$ is form [1 AI], $E(V^{\prime\prime},\,III)$ is form 276 and $E(D,\,VII)$ is form 277.

We note that $E(I,\,D)$ which is equivalent to ``\emph{every infinite set is decomposable}'' is equivalent to the axiom of choice since it is form CN 4F in H. Rubin/J. Rubin \cite{bib:1985}, p. 139.

The known relationships between the various definitions of finite are summarized in the following diagram:

\begin{figure}[h]
\includegraphics{part04-vend-scan-01.eps}
\end{figure}

\noindent(In addition\index{Author}{H. Rubin/ J. Rubin} $\mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime}\not\rightarrow \mathrm{IV}, \mathrm{IV} \not\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime},\, \mathrm{V}\not\rightarrow D,\, D\not\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}$, and none of the arrows are reversible.)

This leaves\index{Author}{Howard/Yorke} several problems open. For example, what is the relationship between $\Delta_{3}$ and III or between $\Delta_{5}$ and $\mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime}$?

(In addition $\mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime}\not\rightarrow \mathrm{IV}, \mathrm{IV} \not\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime\prime},\,\mathrm{V} \not\rightarrow D,\, D\not\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}$, and none of the arrows are reversible.)

This leaves several problems open. For example, what is the relationship between $\Delta_{3}$ and III or between $\Delta_{5}$ and $\mathrm{V}^{\prime\prime}$?

A] is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. In Brunner \cite{bib:1983c} (p 437 Satz 2.2 (5)), the result $(tych_{2}(\omega)$ + form 106) $\Leftrightarrow DC$ appears, that is,

\section*{NOTE 96}

In Wright \cite{bib:1973} it is shown that form $0\not\Rightarrow$ form 281 by showing that every linear operator on a Hilbert space is bounded in Solovay's model $\mathcal{M}5$. In this note we give the definitions for forms 279 and 281 and related results from Wright \cite{bib:1973}.

\begin{definition*}
Suppose $X$ is a topological vector space
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $X$ is\index{Author}{Brunner} \emph{locally convex}\index{Subject}{locally convex} if there is a neighborhood base at $\overset{\rightarrow}{0}$ consisting of convex sets.
\item[2.] A metric $d$ on $X$ is \emph{invariant} if for all $x,\,y$ and $z$ in $X,\,d(x+z,\,y+z)=d(x,\,y)$.
\item[3.] $X$ is a \emph{Fr\'{e}chet space}\index{Subject}{Fr\'{e}chet space} if $X$ is locally convex and the topology on $X$ is induced by a complete, invariant metric\index{Subject}{invariant metric}.
\end{enumerate}

In the model $\mathcal{M}5$ (Solovay\index{Author}{Solovay}\cite{bib:1970}) form 43 (DC) and the negation of form 280 hold (the negation of 280 is ``Every subset of a complete, separable metric space has the Baire property.''). Wright\index{Author}{Wright} \cite{bib:1973} shows that the following are consistent by showing that they are theorems of $\mathrm{ZF}+DC+\neg \mathrm{form}\,280$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[A.] If $X$ and $Y$ are separable, metrizable topological groups and $X$ is complete and $H:X\rightarrow Y$ is a group homomorphism, then $H$ is continuous.
\item[B.] If $X$ is a Fr\'{e}chet space and $Y$ is a separable, metrizable topological vector space and $T:X\rightarrow Y$ is linear, then $T$ is continuous.
\item[C.] Every linear functional on a Fr\'{e}chet space is continuous.
\item[D.] If $X$ and $Y$ are Fr\'{e}chet spaces, $T:X\rightarrow Y$ is linear and there are enough linear functionals on $Y$ to separate the points of $Y$ then $T$ is continuous.
\item[E.] If $H$ is a Hilbert space and $T:H\rightarrow H$ is linear, then $T$ is bounded.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 97}

Definitions for forms 282 and [0 AD] and related results from Kleinberg/Seiferas\index{Author}{Kleinberg/Seiferas}
\cite{bib:1973}.

\begin{definition*}
Assume $\kappa \geq\omega$ and $\gamma\geq 1$ are well ordered cardinals and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are ordinals. Then $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$\index{Subject}{$\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$} denotes the partition relation ``For every function $F$ mapping the set of $\alpha$-sequences from $\kappa$ into $\gamma$ there exists a subset $X$ of $\kappa$ of order type $\beta$ such that the range of $F$ on the set of $\alpha$ sequences from $X$ has cardinality 1.'' If $\gamma=2$ we write $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)^{\alpha}$. (An $\alpha$-sequence from $Y\subseteq On$ is an order preserving map from $\alpha$ to $Y$.) $\kappa\not\rightarrow (\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$ denotes the negation of $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$.
\end{definition*}

Form [0 AD] is: For any finite $n$, for all ordinals $\beta$ and well ordered cardinals $\gamma$, there is a well ordered cardinal $\kappa$ such that $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{n}$ and form 282 is $\omega\not\rightarrow(\omega)^{\omega}$. The axiom of choice implies for any $\alpha\geq \omega$, given any well ordered cardinal $\gamma>1$ and ordinal $\beta$ there is no $\kappa \geq \omega$ for which $\kappa \rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$. Also proved in Kleinberg/Seiferas \cite{bib:1973} are the following:

\begin{theorem*}
Assume $\gamma>1$ is a well ordered cardinals and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are ordinals with $\alpha\leq\beta$ then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{1.}] $C(WO,\,\infty)$ (which is form 40) implies $\neg\exists\kappa(\kappa\rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha})$ provided
\begin{equation*}\tag{$\ast$}
\alpha\geq \omega+\omega\ \text{(ordinal addition) or}\ \beta\geq\lfloor\alpha\rfloor+\omega+\lceil\alpha\rceil\ \mathrm{or}\ \gamma\geq \omega
\end{equation*}
\item[\emph{2.}] If ($\ast$) fails then $\exists \kappa(\kappa\rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha})\Leftrightarrow \omega\rightarrow(\omega)^{\omega}$.
\item[\emph{3.}] Assume $C(WO,\,\infty)$ and ``$\mathbb{R}$ can be well ordered'' then for all $\alpha,\,\beta$ and $\gamma,\,\neg\exists \kappa(\kappa\rightarrow(\beta)_{\gamma}^{\alpha})$
\item[\emph{4.}] $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)$ (which is form 86) implies $\aleph_{\alpha}\not\rightarrow(\omega+\omega)^{\omega+\omega}$.
\item[\emph{5.}] $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)\Rightarrow\aleph_{\alpha}\not\rightarrow(\omega+\omega)^{\omega}$.
\item[\emph{6.}] $C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)\Rightarrow\aleph_{\alpha}\not\rightarrow (\omega)_{\omega}^{\omega}$. (So form 8 ($C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$) implies form 282.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

\section*{NOTE 98}

Definitions for\index{Author}{Kleinberg/Seiferas} forms [1 AK], [1 AL] and [1 AM] from Truss\index{Author}{Truss} \cite{bib:1973a}.

\begin{definition*}
Assume $x$ and $y$ are cardinal numbers
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $\aleph(x)$ is the least well ordered cardinal $\aleph$ such that $\aleph\not\leq x$.
\item[2.] $\alpha(x,\,y)$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ such that whenever $\{z_{\gamma}:\gamma<\beta\}$ is a sequence of cardinals satisfying $x<z_{\gamma}<y$ for all $\gamma<\beta$ and $\gamma<\delta\rightarrow z_{\gamma}<z_{\delta}$ then $\beta<\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
