Form 65 (Krein-Milman Theorem)\index{Subject}{Krein-Milman theorem} does not imply form 14 (BPI) in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. The argument is as follows: By results of Bell/Jellett\index{Author}{Bell/Jellett} \cite{bib:1971}, form 14 + form 65 implies form 1 (AC). By Pincus \cite{bib:1972b} and \cite{bib:1972c}, 65 is true and 1 is false in $\mathcal{N}2$ hence form 14 is false in $\mathcal{N}2$. Similarly, form 52 does not imply form 286 in ZF since form 52 + form 286 implies form 1 (Bell/Jellett \cite{bib:1971}) and by Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972b}, form 52 does not imply form 14 in ZF.

\section*{NOTE 100}

In this note we show that in $\mathcal{N}23\,C(\infty,\,2)$ (form 88) is false and $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 126) is true. The proof that $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ is true is due to A. Rubin.

First we shall show that $C(\infty,\,2)$ is false. Let $B$ be the set of subsets $x$ of $A$ such that the order type of $x$ with respect to $<$ is $\omega$. Let $D$ be the set of equivalence classes of elements of $B$ under the relation $xRy$ iff the symmetric difference, $(x-y) \cup(y-x)$ is finite. (Denote the equivalence class of $x$ by $[x]$.) Let $P$ be the set of pairs of elements of $D$. $P$ has no choice function in the model because if $f$ is such a choice function and $E\subseteq A$ is a support of $f$ it follows that for all order preserving permutations $\phi$ of $A$ such that $\phi$ fixes $E$ pointwise and for all $[x],\, [y]$ in $D$, if $\phi$ fixes $\{[x],\,[y]\}$ then $\phi$ fixes both $[x]$ and $[y]$. We can construct a $\phi,\,x$ and $y$ for which this is false as follows: Since $E$ is well ordered there are elements $a,\,b\in A$ such that the interval $(a,\,b)$ contains no points of $E$. Let $\phi$ be an order preserving permutation of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, fixes $a$ and $b$ but moves at least one element $t$ of $(a,\,b)$. We may assume (by replacing $\phi$ with $\phi^{-1}$ if necessary) that $t<\phi(t)$. Let $x=\{\phi^{2n}(t):n\in \omega\}$ and $y=\{\phi^{2n+1}(t):n\in\omega\}$. Then $\phi([x])=[y]$ and $\phi([y])=[x] ($and $[x]\neq[y])$.

Next, we shall show that $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ is true in $\mathcal{N}23$. Let $X=\{Y_{i}:i\in\omega\}$ be a denumerable set of non-empty sets in the model. Let $B$ be a common support for $X$ and the $Y_{i}$'s, $i\in \omega$. Let the open intervals of $A-B$ be denoted by $I_{\beta}$, for $\beta<\alpha$. For each $i\in\omega$, choose (in the outer model) $z_{i}\in Y_{i}$ and let $B_{i}$ be a support of $z_{i}$. Let $J_{\beta i}=I_{\beta}\cap B_{i}$. (Note: Whenever we choose a sequence of elements in $A$, we choose them in increasing order. Also, $\beta$ will range over $\alpha$, and $i$ and $j$ will range over $\omega$.)

We then define $K_{\beta ji}$ as follows: For each $\beta$ and $i$, choose $E_{\beta i}=\{e_{\beta ji}:j\in \omega\}$ cofinal in $I_{\beta}$ such that each $e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}$ and $E_{\beta i}\cap \mathrm{cl}(B_{i})=\emptyset$. Then define $K_{\beta ji}= B_{i}\cap (e_{\beta ji},\,e_{\beta j+1i})$. (If $J_{\beta i}$ is not cofinal in $I_{\beta}$, choose $E_{\beta i}$ such that $e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}<e_{\beta 1i}$ so there is only one non-empty $K_{\beta ji}$.)

For each $\beta$, choose $\{c_{\beta i}:i\in \omega\}$ cofinal in $I_{\beta}$ and choose $\{d_{\beta ji}:i\in \omega\}$ in the interval $(c_{\beta j},\,c_{\beta j+1})$. For each $\beta,\,j$, and $i$, let $f_{\beta ji}$ be a function mapping $K_{\beta ji}$ into the interval $(d_{\beta ji},\,d_{\beta ji+1})$ and let $L_{\beta ji}$ be the range of $f_{\beta ji}$. Next, let $f_{i}$ be an extension of $\bigcup_{\beta,j}f_{\beta ji}$ to a complete isomorphism of $A$ fixing $B$. We claim that $F=\{<Y_{i},\,f_{i}(z_{i})>:i\in \omega\}$ is a choice function for $X$ that is in the model. Since $f_{i}$ preserves $B$, we must have that $f_{i}(z_{i})\in f(Y_{i})=Y_{i}$. A support of $F$ is $\bigcup_{\beta,j,i}L_{\beta ji}$ which is a well ordered union of the well ordered sets $L_{\beta ji}$ and, therefore, can be well ordered.

\section*{NOTE 101}

The argument that form 43 (DC) implies [43 S] (If $S$ is a relation on $A$ such that $(\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(x\,S\,y)$ and $x_{0}$ is any element of A, then there is a sequence $a(1),a(2),\ldots$ of elements of $A$ such that $a(n)\,S\,a(n+1)$ for all $n\in \omega$ and such that $a(0)=x_{0}.)$ is as follows: Let $S$ be a relation on a set $A$ satisfying the hypotheses of [43 S] and assume that $x_{0}\in A$. Let $B$ be the set of finite sequences $y=\langle y(i)\rangle_{i=0}^{n}$ of distinct elements of $A$ such that $y(0)=x_{0}$ and $y(i)\,S\,y(i+1)$ for $i=0$ to $n-1$. Define $R$ on $B$ by $y\,R\,z\Leftrightarrow y$ is a proper initial segment of $z$. Then the relation $R$ on $B$ satisfies the hypotheses of form 43. The conclusion of form 43 gives a sequence $y_{0}\,R\,y_{1}\,R\,y_{2}\,\ldots$ which gives an infinite sequence of elements of $A$ satisfying the conclusion of [43 S].

\section*{NOTE 102}

Form 289 (If $S$ is a set of subsets of a countable set and $S$ is closed under chain unions, then $S$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element.) is false in $\mathcal{M}1$. Let $b$ be the generic set of generic reals in $\mathcal{M}1$, let $E(b)$ be the set of all finite subsets of $b$, and let $S=\{\cup x:x\in E(b)\}$. Since $b$ is generic, for any finite subset $\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}$ of $b,\,a_{0}\not\subseteq \cup\{a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}\}$ It follows that if $x,\,y\in E(b)$, then $\cup x\subseteq \cup y$ iff $x\subseteq y$. Hence, any chain in $S$ corresponds to a chain in $E(b)$ and a $\subseteq$-maximal element of $S$ corresponds to a $\subseteq$-maximal element of $E(b)$. We claim that there is no infinite chain in $E(b)$. For suppose $x_{0}\subset x_{1}\subset x_{2}\cdots$ is an infinite chain in $E(b)$. Let $a_{n}$ be the smallest element in $x_{n+1}-x_{n}$ for $n\in \omega$. Then $\{a_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ is a denumerable subset of $b$, which is impossible because $b$ is Dedekind finite. Thus, all chains in $E(b)$ are finite so $E(b)$ is closed under chain unions. Consequently, $S$ is closed under chain unions. Since $b$ is infinite, $E(b)$ has no $\subseteq$-maximal element and, therefore, $S$ has no $\subseteq$-maximal element.

\section*{NOTE 103}

The results of Jech/Sochor \cite{bib:1966a} and \cite{bib:1966b} and Pincus \cite{bib:1971}, \cite{bib:1972a}, and \cite{bib:1977a} show that many independence results in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ will transfer automatically to ZF. These transfer theorems are given in this note. We use the notation of Pincus.

\begin{definition*}
Assume $x$ is a set, $A$ is a class and $\Phi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is a
formula in the language of $\mathrm{ZF}$ with variables among $x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $|x|$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ such that there is a one to one function from $x$ onto $\alpha$. (Note that this definition of $|x|$ is for this note only and differs from the definition of $|x|$ used elsewhere in this document. Also note that $|x|$ is defined only for well ordered sets $x$.)
\item[(2)] $|x|^{-}=\sup\{|y|$ : there is a surjection from $x$ onto $y$\}.
\item[(3)] $|x|_{-}=\sup\{|y|$ : there is an injection from $y$ to $x$\}.
\item[(4)] $R_{\beta}(x)$ is defined for ordinals $\beta$ by induction: $R_{0}(x)=x,\, R_{\alpha+1}(x)=R_{\alpha}(x)\cup \mathcal{P}(R_{\alpha}(x))$ and for limit ordinals $\lambda,\, R_{\lambda}(x)=\bigcup_{\gamma<\lambda}R_{\gamma}(x)$.
\item[(5)] $\Phi^{A}(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is $\Phi$ with quantifiers restricted to $A$. Similarly, if $\sigma$ is a term in $\mathrm{ZF}$ then $\sigma^{A}$ is the term defined by the same formula that defines $\sigma$ but with its quantifiers restricted to $A$.
\item[(6)] Assume that $V$ is a model of $\mathrm{ZF}$ and $V_{0}\subseteq V$ is a substructure of $V$ which is a model of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ such that every element of a $V_{0}$ \emph{set} is an element of $V_{0}$. (But elements of $V_{0}$ atoms are not in $V_{0}$.) Assume also that $V$ and $V_{0}$ have the same ordinals, the same cofinality function, the same surjective cardinal function $|x|^{-}$ (on $V_{0}$ sets), the same injective cardinal function $|x|_{-}$ (on $V_{0}$ sets) and the same cardinality function $|x|$ (on $V_{0}$ sets.) Then the formula $\Phi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is \emph{absolute} if for all $x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n}$ in $V_{0},\, \Phi^{V_{0}} (x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})\leftrightarrow\Phi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$. (This is sometimes called absolute for $V_{0},\,V$.)
\item[(7)] A term $\sigma(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is \emph{ordinal valued} if $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash\sigma(x_{1},\, \ldots,\,x_{n})\in On$.
\item[(8)] A formula $\Phi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is \emph{boundable} if for some absolute ordinal valued term $r,\,\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash\Phi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})\leftrightarrow\Phi^{R_{r}(x_{1}\cup\cdots\cup
x_{n})}(x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{n})$. Similarly, the term $\sigma(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is \emph{boundable} if
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash\sigma(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})=\sigma^{R_{r}(x_{1}\cup\cdots \cup x_{n})}(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n}).
\end{equation*}
\item[(9)] A sentence is \emph{boundable} if it is the existential closure of a boundable formula\index{Subject}{boundable formula}.
\end{enumerate}

The theorem of Jech/Sochor\index{Author}{Jech/Sochor} \cite{bib:1966b} is
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
A boundable sentence is transferable\index{Subject}{transfer theorems}.
\end{theorem*}

Many applications of the theorem use the following corollary:

\begin{corollary*}
If $\Phi$ is a sentence such that there is an ordinal $\alpha$ such that $ZF^{0}\vdash \Phi\leftrightarrow\Phi^{R_{\alpha}(A)}$ where $A$ is the set of atoms, then $\Phi$ is transferable. (Note that $\alpha$ must be a constant absolute ordinal valued term.)
\end{corollary*}

For example, form 5, $C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0},\,\mathbb{R})$ is the statement ``If $D$ is a denumerable collection of denumerable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ then $\exists f: D\rightarrow\bigcup D$ such that $\forall d\in D,\,f(d)\in D$. This is equivalent to $(C(\aleph_{0},\, \aleph_{0)}\mathbb{R}))^{R_{\omega_{2}}(A)}$. Similarly, the following forms are boundable and therefore transferable: 6, 11, 12, 13, 35, 36, 37, 38, 70, 73, 74, 79, 92, 93, 94, 130, 142, 169, 170, 194, 197, 199, 203, 206, 211, 212, 222, 223, 251, 252, 272, 273, 280, 289, 305, 306, 307, 309, 313, 361, 362, 363, 364, 366, 367, 368, and 369. In addition all of these forms are true in all Fraenkel-Mostowski models since they make assertions about the standard part of the model only.

Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} has strengthened the theorem of Jech/Sochor by the following:

\begin{definition*}
A formula $\Phi(y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{k})$ is \emph{surjectively boundable} if it is a con junction of formulas of the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Phi_{i}=\forall x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{n}[(|\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}|^{-}\leq\sigma_{i}(y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{k})\wedge&
\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}\cap TCL( \bigcup_{m=1}^{k}y_{m})=\emptyset)\\
&\rightarrow\Psi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n},\,y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{k})],
\end{split}\tag{$\ast$}
\end{equation*}
where $\sigma(y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{k})$ and $\Psi(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n},\,y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{k})$ are boundable. A sentence is \emph{surjectively boundable}\index{Subject}{surjectively boundable} if it is the existential closure of a surjectively boundable formula.

A formula is \emph{injectively boundable}\index{Subject}{injectively boundable} if it is a conjunction of formulas of the form $(\ast)$ but with $\bigcup_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}|^{-}$ replaced by $\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}|_{-}$ and a sentence is \emph{injectively boundable} if it is the existential closure of an injectively boundable formula.
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
An injectively boundable statement is transferable.
\end{theorem*}

Note that boundable statements are surjectively boundable and surjectively boundable statements are injectively boundable.

In many cases the following corollary suffices:

\begin{corollary*}
A formula $\Phi$ is transferable if $\Phi$ is a conjunction of sentences of the form
\begin{equation*}
\forall x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n}(|\bigcup_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}|_{-}\leq\sigma_{i}\rightarrow\Psi_{i}(x_{1},\,\ldots,\, x_{n}))
\end{equation*}
where $\sigma_{i}$ is a boundable constant term and $\Psi$ is boundable.
\end{corollary*}

For example, form 9, Dedekind finite $\cong$ finite, is injectively boundable since it is equivalent to $\forall x$ ($|x|_{-}\leq \omega\rightarrow x$ is finite). Similarly, 18 and 128 are injectively boundable. Form 166 $(PC(\infty,\,2,\,\infty))$ is injectively boundable since it is equivalent to $(\forall x)(|x|_{-}\leq\omega\rightarrow$ every infinite family of pairs whose union is $x$ has an infinite subfamily with a choice function). Similarly, 132, 336, 342, 376, 377, and 378 are injectively boundable. Other injectively boundable forms are 10, 31, 32, 80, 119, 350, 357, 358, 373, and 374 (all using Howard/Solski\index{Author}{Howard/Solski} \cite{bib:1993}, lemma 3.5), 17 (Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1977a}), 64 (Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972a}, 2B3), 71, 82, 83 (Pincus \cite{bib:1972a}, 2B4), 98, 163, 216, (Pincus \cite{bib:1972a},
2B5), 217 (Pincus \cite{bib:1972a} 2B6), and 325 (note 46).

In Pincus \cite{bib:1972a} the following transfer theorem also appears.

\begin{definition*}
A formula $\Psi(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})$ is an \emph{onto property} if it is provable that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If there is a function $f$ from $x$ onto $y$ and $\Psi(x, w_{1},\,\ldots,\, w_{n})$ then $\Psi(y, w_{1},\,\ldots w_{n})$.
\item[(b)] $x\in V_{0}\rightarrow(\Psi(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})\leftrightarrow\Psi^{V_{0}}(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\, w_{n}))$.
\item[] A term $\sigma(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots w_{n})$ is \emph{invariant} if
\item[(a)] $\sigma(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})=\{z\in R_{\alpha}(x):\Phi^{R_{\alpha}(x)}(z,\,x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\, w_{n})\}$ for some $\Phi$.
\item[(b)] $\sigma(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})\neq\emptyset$ if $x$ is infinite
\item[(c)] There is a definable operator $\hat{\ }$ such that if $f:y\rightarrow x$ is one to one then $\hat{f}:\sigma(y,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})\rightarrow\sigma(x,\,w_{1},\,\ldots,\,w_{n})$ is one to one.
\end{enumerate}

A formula $Z(\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})$ with ordinal parameters $\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta}$ is a \emph{term-choice formula} if it is equivalent to a formula in the form
\begin{align*}
(\forall y)&[(\Psi(y,\,\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})\wedge(\forall x\in y)[x\text{is well orderable}])\\
&\rightarrow(\{\sigma(x,\,\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta}):x\in y\wedge\sigma(x,\,\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})\neq\emptyset\}\ \text{has a choice function})]
\end{align*}
where $\Psi(y,\,\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})$ is onto and $\sigma(y,\,\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})$ is invariant.

A sentence is a \emph{term-choice sentence} if it is equivalent to a statement in the form $\forall\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta}[\Omega(\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})\wedge Z(\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})]$ where $Z(\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})$ is term choice and $\Omega(\overset{\rightarrow}{\beta})$ is absolute.
\end{definition*}

\begin{theorem*}
Class 2 statements are transferable where a class 2 statement is a finite conjunction of

(a) surjectively\index{Subject}{onto property} boundable statements,

(b) ``every set can be linearly ordered'',

(c) term-choice\index{Subject}{term-choice sentence} statements.
\end{theorem*}

The following forms are class 2 statements: forms 30, 45, 46, 47, 48, 60 and 165 (all from Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972a}, pp 736--737), 61, 85, 88, 122, 178, 185, 213, 250, and 295.

Another transfer theorem from Pincus \cite{bib:1972a}:

\begin{theorem*}
If $\Phi$ is a class 2 statement which is true in the Mostowski linear order model $(\mathcal{N}3)$ then $\Phi$ is $ZF$ consistent with the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14).
\end{theorem*}

Finally a transfer theorem from Pincus \cite{bib:1977a}.

\begin{theorem*}
If $\Phi$ is a conjunction of any of the following seven kinds of statements and $\Phi$ has a Fraenkel-Mostowski model, then $\Phi$ has a $ZF$ model:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{1.}] Injectively boundable statements.
\item[\emph{2.}] For any ordinal number $\alpha,\,C(<\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)$. (This includes, for any ordinal $\alpha,\,C(\aleph_{\alpha},\,\infty)$ which is equivalent to $C(<\aleph_{\alpha+1},\, \infty)$.)
\item[\emph{3.}] For every ordinal $\eta,\, DC^{<\eta}$. See the note below for definitions.
\item[\emph{4.}] The ordering principle, $OP$ (form 30)
\item[\emph{5.}] Term choice statements
\item[\emph{6.}] The Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14).
\item[\emph{7.}] The Hahn-Banach theorem (form 52).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem*}

\textsc{Note.} $DC^{<\eta}$ is the statement $\forall\lambda<\eta,\,DC^{\lambda}$ and $DC^{\lambda}$ is ``If for every $\alpha<\lambda$ every $R$-admissible $\alpha$ sequence extends to an $R$-admissible $\alpha+1$ sequence then there is an $R$-admissible $\lambda$ sequence.'' (An $\alpha$ sequence is a function with domain $\alpha$ and an $\alpha$ sequence $\sigma$ is $R$-admissible if for all $\beta<\alpha,\,\sigma|\beta\, R\,\sigma(\beta)$.

Note also that $DC^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$ is equivalent to form 87 $(DC(\aleph_{\alpha}))$.

\begin{proof}
We show that $DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$ implies $DC^{\aleph_{\alpha}}$. The proof of the other impli cation is easier. Assume $R$ is a binary relation such that for every $\beta<\aleph_{\alpha}$ every $R$-admissible $\beta$ sequence of elements of $X$ extends to an $R$-admissible $\beta+1$ sequence of elements of $X$. Define the relation $R^{\prime}$ by $\sigma\, R^{\prime}\,t$ iff $(\sigma$ is an $R$-admissible $\beta$ sequence for some $\beta<\aleph_{\alpha}$ and the $\beta+1$ sequence $\sigma^{\prime}$ which extends $\sigma$ for which $\sigma^{\prime}(\beta)=t$ is $R$-admissible) or ($\sigma$ is not $R$-admissible). $R^{\prime}$ satisfies the hypotheses of $DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$ and therefore there is an $R^{\prime}$-admissible $\aleph_{\alpha}$ sequence $f$. $f$ is $R$-admissible for if not let $\beta$ be the least ordinal $<\aleph_{\alpha}$ for which $\neg(f|\beta\, R\,f(\beta))$. Since $f|\beta\, R^{\prime}\, f(\beta)$ it must be the case that $f|\beta$ is not $R$-admissible. Hence for some $\gamma<\beta,\,\neg((f|\beta)|\gamma\, R\,f(\gamma))$. Since $(f|\beta)|\gamma=f|\gamma$, this contradicts the definition of $\beta$.
\end{proof}

Forms that can be transferred using this theorem and which have not been mentioned in this note include 8, 14, 39, 40, 43, 44, 52, 86, and 87,

In Pincus \cite{bib:1974c}, Postscript 3, it is shown that 123 is transferable and according to Pincus \cite{bib:1976}, 120 and 121 are transferable.

\section*{NOTE 104}

If $N=N(A,\,\mathcal{G},\,S)$ is a permutation model, then the $2m=m$ principle (form 3) is false in $N$ if the following holds in $N$:
\begin{equation*}\tag{$\ast$}
\begin{split}
(\forall E\in S)&[A-E\neq\emptyset\\
&\wedge(\forall a\in A-E)(\forall b\in A-\{a\})(\exists\sigma\in \mathcal{G})(\forall c\in E)(\sigma(c)=c\\
&\wedge(\sigma(a)\neq a\wedge\sigma(b)=b)\\
&\vee(\sigma(a)=b\wedge\sigma(b)=a\wedge(\forall c\in A-\{a,\,b\})\sigma(c)=c))].
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\begin{proof}
Suppose there is a $1-1$ function $f$ in $N$ mapping $2\times A$ into $A$. Let $E$ be a support of $f$ and let $a\in A-E$. Then, since $f$ is $1-1$, $f(i,\,a)\neq a$ for $i=0$ or $i=1$. Suppose that $f(i,\, a)=b\neq a$. It follows from $(\ast)$ that there is a $\sigma\in \mathcal{G}$ that leaves $E$ pointwise fixed (so $\sigma(f)=f)$ and $\sigma(a)=c\neq a$. If $\sigma(b)=b$, then $f(i,\,a)=b$ and $f(i,\,c)=b$, contradicting the fact that $f$ is $1- 1$. If $\sigma(a)=b$ and $\sigma(b)=a$, then $f(i,\,a)=b$ and $f(i,\, b)=a$. If $j\in\{0,1\}$ and $j\neq i$, then $f(j,\,a)=c$, where $c\neq a$ and $c\neq b$. Consequently, $f(j,\,b)=c$ again contradicting the fact that $f$ is $1-1$.
\end{proof}

Examples of models that satisfy $(\ast)$ are $\mathcal{N}1,\,\mathcal{N}2,\,\mathcal{N}2(\aleph_{\alpha})$, and $\mathcal{N}12(\aleph_{\alpha})$.

\section*{NOTE 105}

Proofs for the models given in 2B3--2B6 of Pincus\index{Author}{Pincus} \cite{bib:1972a}.

\setcounter{theorem}{0}
\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm1c}
$\mathcal{N}4\models$ 64, but 83 is false (2B3)
\end{theorem}

(Form 64 is ``There are no amorphous sets. (Every infinite set is the union of two disjoint infinite sets.)'' and form 83 is ``$T$-finite is equivalent to finite.'' (A set $S$ is $T$-finite if every non-empty, monotone $X\subseteq \mathcal{P}(S)$ has a $\subseteq$-maximal element.).)

\begin{proof}
First we shall show that in $\mathcal{N}4$ there is no infinite $\subseteq$-chain in $\mathcal{P}(A)$. Suppose $C=\{S_{i}:i\in I\}$ is such a chain with support E. Then for all $\phi\in \mathrm{fix}(E)(=\{\psi\in \mathcal{G}:(\forall a\in A)\psi(a)=a\})$, for all $i\in I,\,\phi(S_{i})\in C$, and for all $i,\,j\in I,\,S_{i}\subseteq S_{j}$ iff $\phi(S_{i})\subseteq\phi(S_{j})$. There must be an $S_{j}\in C$ and a $\phi\in$ fix$(E)$ such that $\phi(S_{j})\neq S_{j}$. Otherwise, $C$ can be well ordered, which contradicts the fact that in $\mathcal{N}4,\, \mathcal{P}(A)$ is Dedekind finite. Suppose $\phi(S_{j})=S_{k}$. We may assume without loss of generality that $S_{j}\subset S_{k}$. It follows that $S_{k}$ is Dedekind infinite, contradicting the fact that $A$ is Dedekind finite.

Next, we shall show that every infinite set is the union of two disjoint infinite sets (64 is true). Let $x$ be an infinite set with support $E$. Suppose there is a $t\in x$ and a $\phi\in$ fix$(E)$ such that $\phi(t)\neq t$. (If no such $t$ exists, $x$ can be well ordered and is therefore the union of two disjoint infinite sets.) Let $F$ be a support of $t$, then $\phi(F)$ is a support of $\phi(t)$ and $F-E\neq\emptyset$. Let $a\in F-E$. Since $\precsim$ is a homogeneous universal partial ordering there are infinitely many elements $b\in A-(E\cup F)$ such that $a\prec b$ and infinitely many $c\in A-(E\cup
F)$ such that $c\prec a$. Let $B=\{b\in A-(E\cup F):a\prec b\}$ and $C=\{c\in A-(E\cup F):c\prec a\}$. Since $a\in F-E$, for each $b\in B$ and $c\in C$ there are $\phi,\,\psi\in \mathrm{fix}(E)$ such that $\phi(a)=b$ and $\psi(a)=c$. It follows that both of the following subsets of $x$ are infinite: $\{\phi(t):\phi\in$ fix$(E)\wedge(\exists b\in B)(\phi(a)=b)\}$ and $\{\psi(t):\psi\in$ fix$(E)\wedge(\exists c\in C)(\psi(a)=c)\}$. Thus, $x$ can be partitioned into two infinite sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm2c}
$\mathcal{N}2\models$ 83, but 215 is false (2B4).
\end{theorem}

(Form 83 is given in theorem 1 and form 215 is ``If $(\forall y\subseteq X)(y$ can be linearly ordered implies $y$ is finite), then $X$ is finite.'')

\begin{proof}
First we note that the set of atoms, $A$, has the property that no infinite $x\subseteq A$ can be linearly ordered so 215 is false. We shall show that for all infinite $x$ in $\mathcal{N}2,\,\mathcal{P}(x)$ has an infinite $\subseteq$-chain. Suppose $x$ is an infinite set with support $E$. Suppose $t\in x$ with support $F$, then $y=\{\phi(F):\phi\in$ fix$(E)\}$ is finite. Consequently, $z_{t}=\{\phi(t):\phi\in$ fix$(E)\}$ is finite. Hence, since $x$ is infinite, $Z=\{z_{t}:t\in x\}$ is infinite and it can be well ordered because each element has support $E$. Let $u_{0},\,u_{1},\,u_{2},\,\cdots$ be an infinite sequence of elements of $Z$. We can construct an infinite $\subseteq$-chain $\{U_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ in $\mathcal{P}(x)$ as follows: $U_{0}=u_{0}$ and $U_{n+1}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{n}u_{i}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm3a}
$\mathcal{N}34\models$ 216, but 217 is false (2B5).
\end{theorem}

(Form 216 is ``Every infinite tree has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.'' and form 217 is ``Every infinite partially ordered set has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.''.)

\begin{proof}
First we note that the relation $R$ on the atoms defined by $c\, R\, d$ if and only if $(\exists q,\,r\in \mathbb{Q})(q<r\wedge c\in C_{q}\wedge d\in C_{r})\vee c=d$ is a partial ordering in the model with no infinite chain and no infinite antichain in the model (217 is false). We shall prove that Every infinite tree $(X,\,\precsim)$ in the model has either an infinite chain (in the model) or an infinite antichain (in the model).

If $H$ is a subgroup of $\mathcal{G}$ and $E\subset A$, we will use the notation $\mathrm{fix}_{H}(E)$ to denote the subgroup $\{\phi\in H:(\forall x\in E)(\phi(x)=x)\}$ of $H$. $H$ will usually be $\mathcal{G}$ or $G_{1}$. One useful fact is that if $\phi\in G_{1}$ and $\psi\in G_{2}$ then there is a $\psi^{\prime}\in G_{2}$ such that $\phi\circ\psi=\psi^{\prime}\circ\phi$.

We will call a finite subset $D$ of $\mathcal{C}$ a $\ast$-support of $x$ if $\bigcup D$ is a support of $x$. The following lemma about dense linear orderings and their automorphisms will be useful.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{part04:lemA}
Assume $a,\,b\in \mathbb{Q},\,a<b$ and that $E$ and $F$ are finite subsets of the interval $(a,\,b)$. Also assume that $\phi$ is an order automorphism of $(a,\,b)$ which fixes $E$ pointwise. Then there is a finite set $\{\phi_{1},\,\ldots,\,\phi_{n}\}$ of automorphisms of $(a,\,b)$ each of which fixes $E$ pointwise and such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(1)}] For $i=1,\,\ldots,\,n,\,\phi_{i}$ moves at most one element of $F$ and
\item[\emph{(2)}] $(\forall z\in F)(\phi_{1}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_{n}(z)=\phi(z))$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

(Although we won't prove this lemma, the first step would be the case where $E=\emptyset,\,F=\{y,\,z\}$ with $y<z$ and $z<\phi(y)$. In this case we would choose $\phi_{2}$ so that $\phi_{2}(z)=z$ and $y<\phi_{2}(y)<z$. Then $\phi_{1}$ could be chosen so that $\phi_{1}(y)=y,\, \phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2}(y)=\phi(y)$ and $\phi_{1}(z)=\phi(z).)$

Assume $(X,\,\precsim)$ is a tree in $\mathcal{N}34$ with $\ast$-support $E$. If every element of $X$ has $\ast$-support $E$ then $X$ is well ordered in the model and therefore applying the axiom of choice in the ground model will give either an infinite chain or infinite antichain in the model. We therefore may assume that $(\exists t\in X)(\exists\eta\in \mathrm{fix}_{\mathcal{G}}(\bigcup E))(\eta(t)\neq t)$. Assume that $t$ has $\ast$-support $E\cup F$ where $E\cap F=\emptyset$. By a previous remark $\eta$ can be written $\psi \circ \phi$ where $\phi\in G_{1}$ and $\psi\in G_{2}$ and by Lemma~\ref{part04:lemA} there are permutations $\phi_{1},\,\ldots,\,\phi_{n}$ in $\mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(E)$ such that each $\phi_{i}$ moves at most one element of $F$ and $\forall z\in F,\, \phi_{1}\circ\cdots \circ\phi_{n}(z)=\phi(z)$.

\begin{claim*}
There is a $\gamma$ in $\mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(E)$ that moves at most one element of $F$ such that $\gamma(t)\neq t$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}If $\phi(t)\neq t$ then for at least one $i,\,1\leq i\leq n,\,\phi_{i}(t)\neq t$ and the proof is finished by letting $\gamma=\phi_{i}$. Otherwise $\phi(t)=t$ and therefore $\psi(t)=\psi\circ\phi(t)=\eta(t)\neq t$. The permutation $\psi$ is a product of transpositions one of which, say $\tau_{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q})$ moves $t$. Further $C_{q}=\{a_{q},\,b_{q}\}\in F$ otherwise $\tau_{q}$ fixes $\bigcup F$ pointwise and hence $\tau_{q}(t)=t$. Choose $\gamma\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(\bigcup[(E\cup
F)-\{C_{q}\}])$ so that $\gamma(C_{q})\neq C_{q}$. Then $\gamma(t)$ has $\ast$-support $[(E\cup F)-\{C_{q}\}]\cup \{\gamma(C_{q})\}$ hence $\tau_{q}(\gamma(t))=\gamma(t)$ since $\tau_{q}$ fixes a support of $\gamma(t)$ pointwise. But $\tau_{q}(t)\neq t$ therefore $\gamma(t)\neq t$. This completes the proof of the claim.
\end{proof}

Using the notation of the claim, let $D=(E\cup F)-\{C_{q}\}$. And assume, as in the claim, that $\gamma\in G_{1}$ fixes $D$ pointwise and that $\gamma(t)\neq t$. We will show that the set $W=\{\beta(t):\beta\in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(\bigcup
D)\}$ (which is clearly in the model) is an infinite antichain in $(X,\,\precsim)$.

The first step is to argue by contradiction that $\{t,\,\gamma(t)\}$ is not a (two element) chain in $(X,\,\precsim)$. Assume $\{t,\,\gamma(t)\}$ is a chain and assume that $\gamma(t)\prec t$. (The argument is similar is $t\prec\gamma(t).)$ We also assume that $\gamma(C_{q})\prec C_{q}$ in the ordered set $(\mathcal{C},\, \preceq)$ (Again, an argument similar to the one we will give here will work if $C_{q}\prec\gamma(C_{q}).)$ The set $S=$\{ $\phi(C_{q}):\phi\in G_{1}$ and $\phi$ fixes $D$ pointwise\} is an interval in $(\mathcal{C},\, \preceq)$. We will argue that, under the above assumptions, that $T=\{\phi(t):\phi\in G_{1}$ and $\phi$ fixes $D$ pointwise\} under the ordering $\precsim$ is order isomorphic to $S$. The isomorphism $f$ is defined by $f(\phi(t))=\phi(C_{q})$. (The details of the proof that $f$ is an isomorphism will be left to the reader.) This is a contradiction since a tree cannot have dense linearly ordered subset.

Therefore $\{t,\,\gamma(t)\}$ is an antichain. There is only one element of $\mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}}(\bigcup D)$ that could move $t$, namely the transposition $\tau_{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q})$. If $\tau_{q}(t)\neq t$ then $\{t,\, \tau_{q}(t)\}$ is also an antichain since $\tau_{q}^{2}$ is the identity permutation. In addition $\{\tau_{q}(t),\,\gamma(t)\}= \tau(\{t,\,\gamma(t)\}$ is an antichain because $\tau$ fixes $\precsim$. Similarly $\{t,\,\gamma(\tau_{q}(t))\}$ is an antichain.

Now assume $\beta_{1}(t)$ and $\beta_{2}(t)$ are in $W$. We first argue that if $\beta_{1}(t)\neq\beta_{2}(t)$ then $\{\beta_{1}(t),\,\beta_{2}(t)\}$ is an antichain. Since $\beta_{1}\in G,\,\beta_{1}=\phi_{1}\circ\psi_{1}$ where $\phi_{1}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(\bigcup D)$ and $\psi_{1}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}}(\bigcup D)$. Since the only transposition in $\mathrm{fix}_{G_{2}}$ that can possibly move $t$ is the transposition $\tau_{q}=(a_{q},\,b_{q})$ we can assume that $\psi_{1}$ is either $\tau_{q}$ or the identity. Therefore $\beta_{1}(t)=\phi_{1}(t)\circ\psi_{1}(t)$ where $\phi_{1}\in G_{1}$ and fixes $\bigcup D$ pointwise and $\psi_{1}$ is either $\tau_{q}$ or the identity. Similarly $\beta_{2}(t)=\phi_{2}(t)\circ\psi_{2}(t)$ where $\phi_{2}\in G_{1}$ and fixes $\bigcup D$ pointwise and $\psi_{2}$ is either $\tau_{q}$ or the identity. The proof now proceeds by cases.

\textsc{Case 1.} $\beta_{1}(t)=\phi_{1}(t)$ and $\beta_{2}(t)=\phi_{2}(t)$.

Since $\beta_{1}(t)\neq\beta_{2}(t)$ we have $\phi_{1}(C_{q})\neq\phi_{2}(C_{q})$. Therefore there is an $\alpha\in G_{1}$ which fixes $D$ pointwise and for which $\alpha(\{C_{q},\, \gamma(C_{q})\})=\{\phi_{1}(C_{q}),\,\phi_{2}(C_{q})\}$. Hence $\alpha(\{t,\,\gamma(t)\})=\{\phi_{1}(t),\, \phi_{2}(t)\}$ and therefore, since $\alpha$ fixes $\precsim,\,\{\beta_{1}(t),\,\beta_{2}(t)\}$ is an antichain.

\textsc{Case 2.} $\beta_{1}(t)=\phi_{1}\circ\tau_{q}(t)$ and $\beta_{2}(t)=\phi_{2}(t)$ where $\tau_{q}(t)\neq t$.

Assume that $\phi_{1}(C_{q})\prec\phi_{2}(C_{q})$ and that $C_{q}\prec\gamma(C_{q})$. (The arguments in the other possible cases are similar.) Then there is an $\alpha\in G_{1}$ which fixes $D$ pointwise and for which $\alpha(C_{q})=\phi_{1}(C_{q})$ and $\alpha(\gamma(C_{q}))=\phi_{2}(C_{q})$. Hence $\alpha(\tau_{q}(t))= \phi_{1}(\tau_{q}(t)$ and $\alpha(\gamma(t))=\phi_{2}(t)$. Therefore $\alpha(\{\tau_{q}(t), \gamma(t)\})=\{\beta_{1}(t),\,\beta_{2}(t)\}$. which must therefore be an antichain.

The other cases are similar. Since every two element subset of $W$ is an antichain, $W$ is an antichain.

It remains to show that $W$ is infinite. This can be done by showing that for all $\phi_{1},\,\phi_{2}\in \mathrm{fix}_{G_{1}}(\bigcup D)$, $\phi_{1}(t)=\phi_{2}(t)\leftrightarrow\phi_{1}(C_{q})=\phi_{2}(C_{q})$

\begin{theorem}\label{part04:thm4a}
$\mathcal{N}1\models$ 217, but 9 is false (2B6).
\end{theorem}

(Form 217 is given in theorem 3 and form 9 is ``Every Dedekind finite set is finite.''.)

\begin{proof}
The set of atoms is an infinite Dedekind finite set so 9 is false. We shall show that every infinite partially ordered set (poset) in $\mathcal{N}1$ either has an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Let $(X,\, \leq)$ be a poset with support $E$. If every element of $X$ has support $E$, then $X$ can be well ordered and we are done. Assume there is a $t\in X$ and a $\psi\in \mathrm{fix}(E)$ such that $\psi(t)\neq t$. We may assume that $\psi$ moves only finitely many atoms. Let $F=E\cup K$ be a support of $t$, where $E\cap K=\emptyset$.
\end{proof}

We first argue that there is a $k\in K$ and $\phi\in \mathcal{G}$ which fixes $F-\{k\}$ pointwise and $\phi(t)\neq t$. Choose $\eta \in \mathrm{fix}(E)$ such that $\eta(K)$ is disjoint from $K\cup \{a\in A:\psi(a)\neq a\}$. We have that $\eta(t)\neq t$ because $\psi(t)\neq t$ but $\psi(\eta(t))=t$. Assume $K=\{k_{1},\,k_{2},\,\cdots,\,k_{n}\}$ and for $i=1,2,\,\cdots,\,n$, let $f_{i}$ be the permutation of $A$ that interchanges $k_{i}$ and $\eta(k_{i})$. Then $\prod_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}$ agrees with $\eta$ on a support of $t$, so $\gamma(t)= \eta(t)\neq t$. Therefore, for at least one of the $f_{i}$'s, $f_{i}(t)\neq t$.

Now, for $\gamma,\,\sigma\in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\})$, $\gamma(t)=\sigma(t)$ iff $\gamma(k)=\sigma(k)$. It follows that $y=\{\gamma(t):\gamma\in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\})\}$ is an infinite subset of $x$ that is in $\mathcal{N}1$. Moreover, $y$ is an antichain, for suppose $\gamma(t)<\sigma(t)$, where $\gamma(t),\sigma(t)\in y$. Let $\rho \in \mathrm{fix}(F-\{k\})$ be a permutation that interchanges $\gamma(t)$ and $\sigma(t)$. Then $\sigma(t)<\gamma(t)$ which is a contradiction.

\section*{NOTE 106}

This note contains results from McCarten\index{Author}{McCarten} \cite{bib:1988} and Schnare\index{Author}{Schnare} \cite{bib:1968} relating to forms [1 BF] (D$T_{0})$, [1 BG] (C$T_{0})$, [1 BH] (T$T_{0})$, and [1 BI] (M$T_{0})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[][1 BF] (D$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is dense in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{dense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open subset $O\subseteq X$ such that $O\cap Y=\emptyset.)$
\item[] [1 BG] (C$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is codense in $X$. ($Y$ is \emph{codense in} $X$ if there is no non-empty closed subset $C\subseteq X$ such that $C\cap Y=\emptyset.)$
\item[] [1 BH] (T$T_{0}$): Every topological space $X$ has a $T_{0}$ subspace that is thick in $X$. $(Y$ is \emph{thick in} $X$ if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset $H\subseteq X$ such that $H\cap Y=\emptyset$.)
\item[][1 BI] (M$T_{0}$): Every topological space has a maximal $T_{0}$ subspace.
\item[1.] Forms $\mathrm{D}T_{0}$ and $\mathrm{C}T_{0}$ are false if ``$T_{0}$'' is replaced by ``$T_{1}$''. (A counter example is the topological space $(\mathbb{R},\,\tau)$, where $\tau =\{G\subseteq \mathbb{R}:G=(a,\,\infty)$, $a\in \mathbb{R} \vee G= \emptyset \vee G=\mathbb{R}\}.)$ McCarten \cite{bib:1988}.
\item[2.] Form $\mathrm{T}T_{0}$ remains equivalent to $\mathrm{AC}$ if $T_{0}$ is replaced by $T_{n}$, for any $n$ such that $T_{n}$ implies $T_{0}$. McCarten \cite{bib:1988}.
\item[3.] $\mathrm{M}T_{0}$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{M}T_{1}$. Schnare \cite{bib:1968}.
\item[4.] Schnare\index{Author}{Schnare} \cite{bib:1968} shows that the statement $\mathrm{MP}$ is false if $\mathrm{P}=T_{2},\,T_{3},\,T_{4}$, regular, completely regular, normal, paracompact, metrizable, linearly disconnected or discrete. (It follows from the lemma that if P is a property that is possessed by every finite discrete space, but not by a countably infinite minimal $T_{1}$ space, then MP is false.)
\end{enumerate}

\section*{NOTE 107}

Good/Tree\index{Author}{Good/Tree}\index{Author}{McCarten} \cite{bib:1995} proves that each of [34 B] through [34 E] implies 34. In this note we supply the details of the converses.

In Kelley\index{Author}{Kelley} \cite{bib:1955}, pages 173--2 there is an outline of a proof that form [34 B] ($\omega_{1}$ with the order topology is not paracompact.) follows from $\mathrm{AC}$. We note that the proof requires only form 34 ($\omega_{1}$ is regular.) and therefore 34 implies [34 B].

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the open cover of $\omega_{1}$ from Kelley's hint. That is, $\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta:\beta<\alpha\}:\alpha<\omega_{1}\}$. We show that $\mathcal{C}$ has no open, locally finite refinement by contradiction. Assume that $\mathcal{A}$ is an open, locally finite refinement of $\mathcal{C}$. We define an increasing function $f:\omega\rightarrow \omega_{1}$ by induction: $f(0)=0$. Assume that $f(n)$ is defined. For each $\beta\leq f(n)$, the set $D_{\beta}=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:\beta\in x\}$ is finite since $\mathcal{A}$ is locally finite. It's also true that for each $x\in D_{\beta},\, \sup\{\gamma:\gamma\in x\}$ is less that $\omega_{1}$ since $x$ is a subset of one of the elements of $\mathcal{C}$. Let $g(\beta)$ be the maximum of $\{\sup(x):x\in D_{\beta}\}$.
$g(\beta)$ is also less than $\omega_{1}$. Now apply form 34 to the set $W=\{g(\beta):\beta\leq f(n)\}$. This is a countable set of ordinals each $<\omega_{1}$ and therefore $\sup W<\omega_{1}$. Let $f(n+1)$ be the least ordinal greater than $\sup W$. The important property of the function $f$ is that
\begin{equation*}\tag{$\ast$}
(\forall n\in \omega)(\forall j<n)(\forall x\in \mathcal{A})(f(j)\in x\rightarrow f(n)\not\in x)
\end{equation*}
The sequence $\langle f(n)\rangle_{n\in \omega}$ is strictly increasing so its $\sup$ (call the $\sup\, \beta$) is a limit ordinal. Further, by form 34, $\beta<\omega_{1}$. Since $\mathcal{A}$ is locally finite, there is an (open) neighborhood $y$ of $\beta$ such that $\{x\in \mathcal{A}:x\cap\,y\neq\emptyset\}$ is finite. Since $y$ is open and $\beta$ is a limit ordinal, there is an ordinal $\gamma<\beta$ such that the interval $(\gamma,\,\beta+1)\subseteq y$. For some natural number $k$, this interval must contain $f(n)$ for all $n\geq k$. For each $n\geq k$ we consider the sets $D_{f(n)}=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:f(n)\in x\}$. These sets are pairwise disjoint (by $(\ast)$), each is non-empty and for each element $x\in D_{f(n)},\, x\cap (\gamma,\, \beta+1)\neq\emptyset$. Therefore $\{x\in \mathcal{C}:x\cap\,y\neq\emptyset\}$ is infinite, a contradiction.

To show that 34 implies [34 C] $(\omega_{1}$ with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in $\omega_{1}$.), let $X$ be an infinite subset of $\omega_{1}$. Since $X$ is well ordered and infinite, it must have an initial segment of order type $\omega$. Form 34 implies that each such initial segment must be bounded, so the least upper bound of this set is a limit point of $X$ in $\omega_{1}$.

If $\omega_{1}$ is regular and contains a denumerable discrete family of open sets, then the set of smallest elements in each set would be an infinite set with no limit point, contradicting [34 C]. Thus, 34 implies [34 D] $(\omega_{1}$ with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets.).

The uncountable open cover of $\omega,\,\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta:\beta<\alpha\}:\alpha<\omega_{1} \}$, described above does not contain a countable subcover. If it did we could construct a countable cofinal sequence in $\omega_{1}$, contradicting 34. Therefore, 34 implies [34 E] $(\omega_{1}$ with the order topology is not Lindel\"{o}f.).

\section*{NOTE 108}

We give the proof that each pair of cardinal numbers has a greatest lower bound (glb) (form 187) is true in $\mathcal{N}12(\aleph_{1})$. (The proof is due to A. Rubin.)\index{Author}{A. Rubin}

\begin{theorem*}
$\mathcal{N}12(\aleph_{1})\models$ every pair of cardinals has a greatest lower bound (187).
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Let $A^{[\omega]}$ be the set of all 1-1 functions from $\omega$ to $A$, the set of atoms. Let $Q_{0}$ be the set of all partitions of $A^{[\omega]}$ that have the empty set as a support. (Thus, for all $q\in Q_{0}$ if $u,\,v\in q$, then $|u|=|v|.)$ Since $Q_{0}$ can be well ordered, we can construct a subset $Q\subseteq Q_{0}$ such that for each $q\in Q_{0}$ there is exactly one $q^{\prime}\in Q$ such that $|q'|=|q|$. Let $D:Q_{0}\longrightarrow Q$ be such that for each $q\in Q_{0},\,D(q)$ is the unique member $q^{\prime}\in Q$ such that $|q'|=|q|$. Then, define $J$ on $Q_{0}$ such that for each $q\in Q_{0},\, J(q):q\approx D(q)$. Both $D$ and $J$ are in the model. (Clearly $D$ has empty support. The set $F=$\{ $\{f:f$ is a 1--1 function from $q$ onto $D(q)\}:q\in Q_{0}$\} is a well ordered family of sets and, therefore, has a choice function in $\mathcal{N}12(\aleph_{1})$. The function $J$ is a choice function on $F$.)

Suppose $X$ is a set with support $E$. Let $B$ and $C$ be pairwise disjoint denumerable sets of atoms that are disjoint from $E$. Let $H= \mathrm{fix}(E\cup
B)$ and let $T_{X}=\{\{\sigma(x):\sigma\in H\}:x\in X\}$. $T_{X}$ can be well ordered because $H$ leaves $T_{X}$ pointwise fixed. Since the axiom of choice for a well ordered family of sets is true in this model, we can construct a choice function $ch$ for $T_{X}$ with support $E\cup B\cup C$. Define functions $g$ and $h$ such that $g:\omega\approx C$ and $h:A\approx A-E\cup B$. Let $t\in T_{X}$ and $s\in A^{[\omega]}$. Let $\sigma_{s}$ be a permutation in $H$ such that for all $c\in C,\, \sigma_{s}(c)=h\circ s
\circ g^{-1}(c)$. For each $x\in t\in T$, define $j_{t}^{\prime}(x)=\{s\in A^{[\omega]}:x=\sigma_{s}(ch(t))\}$, then $\{j_{t}^{\prime}(x):x\in t\in T\}=q^{\prime}\in Q_{0}$ and $j_{t}^{\prime}:t\approx q^{\prime}$. Define the function $j_{t}$ so that $j_{t}=J(q^{\prime})\circ j_{t}^{\prime}$, then $j_{t}(t)=D(q^{\prime})\in Q$. Suppose $F: T\approx\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is an ordinal. For each $x\in X$, where $x\in t\in T$, define $f(x)=\langle F(t)$, $j_{t}(x)\rangle$, then $f:X  \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}A_{q}\times q$, where $A_{q}$ is a set of ordinal numbers. Suppose for each $q\in Q,\,|A_{q}|=\alpha_{q}$, then $X \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}\alpha_{q}\times q$. This construction is independent of the choice of $E,\,B$ and $C$. Now that we have this representation for each set in the model, we are ready to prove that form 187 is true.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma*}
Suppose, using the construction above, $X \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}\alpha_{q}\times q$ and $Y\approx  \bigcup_{q\in Q}\beta_{q}\times q$. Then, $X\precsim Y$ iff for all $q,\,\alpha_{q}\leq\beta_{q}$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $f:X\precsim Y$. Let $E$ be a support for $X$ and choose $B\subseteq A$ disjoint from $E$ such that $E\cup B$ is a support for $X,\,Y$, and $f$. It follows that for each $t_{X}\in T_{X},\, f(t_{X})=t_{Y}\in T_{Y}$ and $f:t_{X}\approx t_{Y}$. Thus, for each $q\in Q,\,f$ induces a 1-1 map from $\alpha_{q}$ into $\beta_{q}$. The converse is clear.
\end{proof}

Finally, if $X \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}\alpha_{q}\times q$ and $Y \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}\beta_{q}\times q$ are the representations of $X$ and $Y$, we claim that $Z= \bigcup_{q\in Q}\min(\alpha_{q},\,\beta_{q})\,\times\, q$ has the property that $|Z|= \mathrm{glb}(|X|,\,|Y|)$. Clearly, $|Z|\leq|X|$ and $|Z|\leq|Y|$. Suppose, $|Z_{0}|\leq|X|$ and $|Z_{0}|\leq|Y|$. Also, suppose $Z_{0} \approx\bigcup_{q\in Q}\gamma_{q}\times q$ is the representation of $Z_{0}$. By the lemma, $\gamma_{q}\leq\alpha_{q}$ and $\gamma_{q}\leq\beta_{q}$ for all $q$. Thus, $\gamma_{q}\leq\min(\alpha_{q},\,\beta_{q})$ for all $q$ so it follows that $|Z_{0}|\leq|Z|$.

\section*{NOTE 109}

Below are some definitions for forms involving conditional choice and variations of Rado's lemma.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $M$ is a \emph{binary mess on a set}\index{Subject}{binary mess} $S$ if $M$ is a set of functions from finite subsets of $S$ to $\{0,1\}$ such that for all finite $P\subseteq S$, there is a $t\in M$ with domain $P$ and for all $t\in M$, and for all finite $P\subseteq S,\,t|P\in M$.
\item[2.] If $M$ is a binary mess on $S$, a function $f:S\rightarrow\{0,\,1\}$ is \emph{consistent with} $M$ if $f|P\in M$ for all finite $P\subseteq S$.
\item[3.] If $f$ is a function and $R$ a symmetric binary relation, $f$ is $R$-\emph{consistent} if for all $x$ and $y$ in the domain of $f,\,f(x)Rf(y)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 110}

In this note we prove the result from G. Moore\index{Author}{G. Moore} \cite{bib:1982} that form 36 (If $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $A \bigcap B$ is countable for every bounded $B$ then $A$ is countable.) implies form 38 ($\mathbb{R}$ is not the union of a countable family of countable sets.)

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that form 38 is false and therefore that $\mathbb{R} = \bigcup_{n\in\omega}A_{n}$ where each $A_{n}$ is countable. Let $f$ be any bijection between $\mathbb{R}$ and the interval $(0,1)$. For each $n\in \omega$ let $A_{n}^{\prime}=f^{\prime\prime}A_{n}+n$ (where for any set $X$ of reals and any real $t,\,X+t=\{x+t:x\in X\})$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $A_{n}^{\prime}\subseteq(n,\,n+1)$
\item[(b)] $|A_{n}^{\prime}|=|A_{n}|$ and therefore each $A_{n}$ is countable.
\item[(c)] There is an injection from $\mathbb{R}= \bigcup_{n\in \omega}A_{n}$ to $\bigcup_{n\in\omega}A_{n}^{\prime}(x\mapsto f(x)+n$ where $n$ is the least natural number such that $x\in A_{n}$).
\end{enumerate}

Let $A= \bigcup_{n\in\omega}A_{n}^{\prime}$. It follows from (a) that every bounded subset of $A$ is contained in some finite union $\bigcup_{n<N}A_{n}^{\prime}$. Hence, by (b), every bounded subset of $A$ is countable. By (c), $A$ is uncountable hence form 36 is false.

\section*{NOTE 112}

In this note we prove that in $\mathcal{N}41$, form 9 (Dedekind finite and finite are equivalent) is true and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ is true.

\begin{lemma*}
Assume that $\psi$ is an order automorphism of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ with the property that $\forall a\in \mathbb{Q},\, \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\psi^{n}(a)=\infty$.
 (That is, $(\forall a\in \mathbb{Q})(\forall b\in \mathbb{Q})(\exists n\in \omega)(\psi^{n}(a)\geq b)$.) Then there is an order automorphism $\eta$ of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ such that for all $a\in \mathbb{Q},\,\eta\psi\eta^{-1}(a)=a+1$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
It follows from the hypotheses that $\psi^{n}(0)<\psi^{n+1}(0)$ for each $n\in\omega$ and that $\mathbb{Q}$ is the disjoint union $\mathbb{Q} = \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}[\psi^{n}(0),\, \psi^{n+1}(0))$. Let $\sigma$ be an order isomorphism from the interval $[0,\,\psi(0))$ onto the interval $[0,1)$. We define the function $\eta$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ as follows: Assume $a\in[\psi^{n}(0),\,\psi^{n+1}(0))$, then $\eta(a)=\sigma(\psi^{-n}(a))+ n$.

A straightforward argument shows that $\eta\ |\ [\psi^{n}(0),\,\psi^{n+1}(0))$ is an order automorphism from $[\psi^{n}(0),\,\psi^{n+1}(0))$ onto $[n,\,n+1)$ for all $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ and that for $b\in[n,\,n+1)$, $\eta^{-1}(b)=\psi^{n}\sigma^{-1}(b-n)$. It follows from the first assertion that $\eta$ is an order automorphism of $\mathbb{Q}$ and from the second we can calculate for $b\in[n,\,n+1)$:
\begin{align*}
\eta\psi\eta^{-1}(b)&=\eta\psi(\psi^{n}\sigma^{-1}(b-n))=\eta(\psi^{n+1}\sigma^{-1}(b-n))\\
&=\sigma(\psi^{-(n+1)}(\psi^{n+1}\sigma^{-1}(b-n)))+(n+1)\\
&\qquad(\mathrm{since}\ \psi^{n+1}(\sigma^{-1}(b-n))\in[\psi^{n+1}(0), \psi^{n+2}(0)))\\
&=b+1
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary*}
Any order automorphism $\psi$ of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ satisfying
\begin{equation*}
(\forall a\in \mathbb{Q})(\forall b\in \mathbb{Q})(\exists n\in \omega)(b\leq\psi^{n}(a))
\end{equation*}
has an $n^{th}$ root for every $n\in \omega-\{0\}$. That is, there is an order automorphism $\psi^{\prime}$ of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ such that $(\psi^{\prime})^{n}=\psi$.
\end{corollary*}

\begin{proof}
With $\eta$ as in the lemma, $\psi=\eta^{-1}\pi\eta$ where $\pi(a)=a+1$. Assume $n\in \omega-\{0\}$ and let $\pi_{n}(a)=a+\frac{1}{n}$. If we let $\psi^{\prime}=\eta^{-1}\pi_{n}\eta$, then $(\psi^{\prime})^{n}=\psi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary*}
Any order automorphism $\psi$ of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ which satisfies $(\forall a\in \mathbb{Q})(\forall b\in \mathbb{Q})(\exists n\in \omega)(\psi^{n}(a)\leq b)$ has an $n^{th}$ root for all $n\in \omega-\{0\}$.
\end{corollary*}

\begin{corollary*}
Every order automorphism of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ has an $n^{th}$ root for all $n\in \omega-\{0\}$.
\end{corollary*}

\begin{proof}
Let $\phi$ be an order automorphism of $(\mathbb{Q},\,\leq)$ and for each $a\in \mathbb{Q}$ let $[a]=$\{ $b\in \mathbb{Q}:\exists n\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $b$ is between $a$ and $\phi^{n}(a)$ \}. If $a$ is a fixed point of $\phi$ then $[a]=\{a\}$ otherwise $[a]$ is an open interval in the sense that if $c<d<e$ and $c$ and $e$ are in $[a]$, then $d\in[a]$ and $[a]$ has no first or last element. Further the set $\{[a]:a\in \mathbb{Q}\}$ is a partition of $\mathbb{Q}$. If $a$ is not a fixed point of $\phi$, then it is also the case that $\phi|[a]$ is an order automorphism of $[a]$ and either $(\forall b\in[a])(\forall c\in [a])(\exists n\in \omega)(c\leq\phi^{n}(b))$ (if $\phi(a)>a)$ or $(\forall b\in[a])(\forall c\in[a])(\exists n\in\omega)(\phi^{n}(b)\leq c)$ (if $\phi(a)<a)$. Therefore, by the previous two corollaries $\phi\ |\
[a]$ has an $n^{th}$ root which we denote by $(\phi|[a])^{\frac{1}{n}}$. Then $\psi^{\prime}$ defined by $\psi^{\prime}(a)=(\phi\ |\ [a])^{\frac{1}{n}}(a)$ is an $n^{th}$ root of $\psi$.
\end{proof}

It will follow from the lemma below that form 9 $(DF=F)$ and form 122 $(C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0}))$ are true in $\mathcal{N}41$.

\begin{lemma*}
If $x\in \mathcal{N}41$ has support $E=B_{0}\cup\cdots \cup B_{k}$ and there is some $\phi\in G$ which fixes $E$ pointwise but does not fix $x$ pointwise, then $x$ has a well orderable, infinite subset.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
Assume the hypotheses. Then there is some $y\in x$ and $\phi\in G$ such that $\phi$ fixes $E$ pointwise and $\phi(y)\neq y$. If we assume that $y$ has support $E^{\prime}= (B_{0}\cup\cdots B_{k})\cup(B_{k+1}\cup\cdots \cup B_{r})$ then we may also assume without loss of generality that for some $i$ with $k+1\leq i\leq r,\,\phi$ fixes $A-B_{i}$ pointwise.

We note that if $z$ is any element of $\mathcal{N}41$ of the form $z=\psi(y)$ where $\psi\in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $A-B_{i}$ pointwise, then $z$ has support $E^{\prime}$ (because $\psi(E^{\prime})=E^{\prime}$) and $z\in X$ (since $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise). We intend to show that there are infinitely many such elements $z$. Assume not. Let $W$ be the set of all such $z$ and assume $|W|=q\in \omega$. By the last corollary, the permutation $\phi$ has an $n^{th}$ root for every positive integer $n$ and we choose an $n$ which is divisible by all of the integers $1,2,\ldots ,q+1$. Let $\eta \in G$ satisfy $\eta^{n}=\phi$ (and we may assume that $\eta$ fixes $A-B_{i}$ pointwise). Clearly, for any $j,\,1\leq j\leq q+1,\,\eta^{j}(y)\neq y$ (otherwise $\eta^{n}(y)=\phi(y)=y$). It follows that for $1\leq j<m\leq q+1,\,\eta^{j}(y)\neq\eta^{m}(y)$ because equality would imply that $y=\eta^{m-j}(y)$. Therefore, $|W|\geq q+1$ a contradiction and $W$ is infinite. Since each $z\in W$ has support $E^{\prime},\,W$ can be well ordered. This complete the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

To show that $C(WO,\,<\aleph_{0})$ is true in $\mathcal{N}41$ let $Y$ be a well ordered set of finite sets in $\mathcal{N}41$. Suppose that $E$ is a support of a well ordering of $Y$. Then for each $x$ in $Y,\,E$ is a support of $x$. By the lemma, since $x$ is finite, $E$ is a support of every element of $x$. It follows that if $f$ is any choice function for $Y$ (in the ground model) then $E$ is a support of $f$.

\section*{NOTE 113}

\begin{theorem*}
$C(\infty,\,2)$ (form 88) is false in $\mathcal{N}10$.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be the set of all order preserving functions $f:\omega\rightarrow A$ such that rng$(f)$ has an upper bound in $A$ but no least upper bound in $A$. This means that rng$(f)$ is a support and therefore $f$ is in $\mathcal{N}10$.
$C$ is in $\mathcal{N}10$ since it has empty support. Now define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $C$ by $f\sim g\leftrightarrow(\exists n\in \omega)(f(k)= g(k+n)$ for all $k\in\omega$ or $g(k)=f(k+n)$ for all $k\in \omega$. Let $[f]_{\sim}$ denote the $\sim$ equivalence class of $f$ and let $X$ be the set of all pairs of elements of $\{[f]_{\sim}:f\in C\}$. The set $X$ has no choice function in $\mathcal{N}10$ for suppose that $E$ is a support of such a choice function. Choose a sequence $\langle a_{n}\rangle_{n\in \omega}$ which has order type $\omega$ in the ordering on $A$ and which lies in one of the intervals determined by $E$ in the ordering on $A$. There is a permutation $\psi\in \mathcal{G}$ which fixes $E$ pointwise and which satisfies $(\forall n\in\omega)(\psi(a_{n})=a_{n+1})$. Therefore, if we define $f:\omega\rightarrow A$ by $f(n)=a_{2n}$ and $g:\omega\rightarrow A$ by $g(n)=a_{2n+1}$, then $\psi([f]_{\sim})=[g]_{\sim}$ and $\psi([g]_{\sim})=[f]_{\sim}$. Therefore, no choice function with support $E$ for a set containing $\{[f]_{\sim},\,[g]_{\sim}\}$ exists.
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 114}

Definitions from Bell \cite{bib:1988}.

\begin{definition*}
Assume that $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] If $f$ is a continuous surjection from $X$ onto $Y,\,f$ is \emph{irreducible} if the image of a proper closed subset of $X$ is a proper subset of $Y$.
\item[2.] $X$ is \emph{0-dimensional} if $X$ has a base of clopen sets.
\item[3.] $X$ is \emph{Boolean} if $X$ is compact, Hausdorff and $0$-dimensional.
\item[4.] $X$ is \emph{extremally disconnected} if the closure of any open set is open.
\item[5.] $X$ is $\sigma$-\emph{extremally disconnected}\index{Subject}{extremally disconnected}\index{Subject}{$\sigma$-extremally disconnected} if $X$ is $0$-dimensional and the algebra of clopen subsets of $X$ is $\sigma$-complete (that is, countably complete). (From Morillon\index{Author}{Morillon} \cite{bib:1993})
\item[6.] If $X$\index{Subject}{Boolean topological space}\index{Author}{Bell} is compact Hausdorff, a \emph{Gleason cover}\index{Subject}{Gleason cover} of $X$ is a pair $(E,\,\pi)$ where $E$ is an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space and $\pi$ is an irreducible\index{Subject}{irreducible function} continuous surjection $\pi:E\rightarrow X$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 115}

Definitions from Diener\index{Author}{Diener} \cite{bib:1989}.

\begin{definition*}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{type} $\tau$ is a function $\tau =(K_{i})_{i\in I}$ where for each $i\in I,\,K_{i}$ is a set (not necessarily finite). If $I=\{i\}$ and $K_{i}=M$ we write $\tau =(M)$.
\item[2.] An \emph{algebra of type} $\tau$\index{Subject}{algebra of type $\tau$} is an ordered pair $\mathbf{A}=(A,\,(f_{i})_{i\in I})$ such that $(\forall i\in I)(f_{i}:A^{K_{i}}\rightarrow A)$.
\item[3.] A \emph{homomorphism} from an algebra \textbf{A} of type $\tau$ to an algebra \textbf{B} of type $\tau$ is closed if the image of every subalgebra of \textbf{A} is a subalgebra of \textbf{B}.
\item[4.] An algebra is a \emph{Peano algebra}\index{Subject}{Peano algebra} if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a.] The ranges of the operations are pairwise disjoint.
\item[b.] All of the operations are injective.
\item[c.] The elements which are not values of any operation form a generating set.
\end{enumerate}
\item[5.] $\mathfrak{P}(\tau;Z)$ is the Peano algebra of type $\tau$ with generating set $Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

In Diener \cite{bib:1989} it is shown that for any set $M$, if $\tau =(M)$, then the axiom of choice for families of cardinality $|M|$ (that is, $C(|M|,\,\infty)$) is equivalent to the the statement ``Every homomorphism of $\tau$ algebras is closed.'' See also forms [1 AP], [1 AQ], [1 AR], [67 E] and [67 F].

\section*{NOTE 116}

A proof that form 304 (There does not exist a $T_{2}$ topological space $X$ such that every infinite subset of $X$ contains an infinite compact subset.) is true in $\mathcal{N}1$.

\noindent Let $X$ be an infinite $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ topological space in $\mathcal{N}1$. We need to show that there is an infinite $Y\subseteq X\ (Y\in \mathcal{N}1)$ such that $Y$ has no infinite compact subsets (in $\mathcal{N}1)$. If $X$ is well orderable then it is clear that such a $Y$ exists. Assume that $X$ is not well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$.

Choose an $x\in X$, a support $E$, an element $a\in A$, and a permutation $\phi\in G$ which fixes $E$ pointwise so that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $E$ is a support of $X$ and its topology.
\item[(b)] $E\cup \{a\}$ is a support of $x$ and
\item[(c)] $\phi(x)\neq x$. (And therefore by (b) $\phi(a)\neq a$.)
\end{enumerate}

\begin{lemma*} For all $\psi,\,\eta \in G$ such that $\psi$ and $\eta$ fix $E$ pointwise, $\psi(x)=\eta(x)$ if and only if $\psi(a)=\eta(a)$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
If $\psi(a)=\eta(a)$, then $\psi$ and $\eta$ agree on a support of $x$ and therefore $\psi(x)=\eta(x)$. Conversely, if $\psi(a)\neq\eta(a)$, then the permutation $\beta$, defined to be the product of the two transpositions $\beta=(a,\,\psi(a))(\phi(a),\,\eta(a))\in G$, fixes $E$ pointwise, agrees with $\psi$ on a support of $x$, and agrees with $\eta\phi^{-1}$ on a support of $\phi(x)$. It follows that $\beta(x)=\psi(x)$ and that $\beta(\phi(x))=\eta\phi^{-1}(\phi(x))=\eta(x)$. Since $x\neq\phi(x)$ we conclude that $\beta(x)\neq\beta(\phi(x))$, that is $\psi(x)\neq\eta(x)$.
\end{proof}

By the lemma, the set of pairs $F=\{(\psi(x),\,\psi(a)):\psi\in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise\} is a one to one function (in the model $\mathcal{N}1$) from $Y=_{\mathrm{def}}\{\psi(x):\psi\in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise\} onto $A-E$.

Since the topology on $X$ is $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ we can choose open sets $C$ and $D$ so that $x\in C,\,\phi(x)\in D$ and $C\cap D=\emptyset$. Since $Y$ can be put in a one to one correspondence with a subset of the atoms in the model, every subset of $Y$ in the model must be finite or cofinite. This means that at least one of $Y\cap C$ or $Y\cap D$ is finite. We may assume that $Y\cap C$ is finite by replacing $C$ by $C\cap\phi^{-1}(D)$ if necessary. Under this assumption we can conclude that $\mathcal{C}=\{\psi(C):\psi\in G$ and $\psi$ fixes $E$ pointwise\} is an open cover for $Y$. Further each element of $\mathcal{C}$ is finite. It follows that for any infinite subset $Z$ of $Y,\,\mathcal{C}$ is an open cover for $Z$ without a finite subcover.

\section*{NOTE 117}

Definitions from Cowen\index{Author}{Cowen} \cite{bib:1990} for forms [14 BD] through [14 BG]. A \emph{hypergraph}\index{Subject}{hypergraph} is a pair $H=\langle V,\, E\rangle$ where $V$ is a set (of vertices) and $E$ is a set of non-empty finite subsets of $V$. $E$ is called the set of edges. $H$ is finite if $V$ is finite. $K=\langle W,\, F\rangle$ is a \emph{subhypergraph}\index{Subject}{subhypergraph} of $H=\langle V,\, E\rangle$ if $W\subseteq V$ and $F\subseteq E$. $W\subseteq V$ is \emph{independent} in $H=\langle V,\, E\rangle$ if no two elements of $W$ belong to the same edge of $H$.
 $W\subseteq V$ is a \emph{vertex cover}\index{Subject}{vertex cover} of $H=\langle V,\, E\rangle$ if each element of $\mathrm{E}$ contains at least one element of $W$. An $n$-\emph{coloring} of $H=\langle V,\, E\rangle$ is a function $f:V\rightarrow\{0,\,1,\,\ldots,\,n-1\}$ such that $|f^{\prime\prime}e|>1$ for all $e\in E$ with $|e|>1$.

\section*{NOTE 118}

Definitions from Galvin/Komj\'{a}th\index{Author}{Galvin/Komj\'{a}th} \cite{bib:1991} for forms [1 AT] through [1 AW].

\begin{definition*}
Assume that $G=(V,\,E)$ is a graph.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $S\subseteq V$ is \emph{dependent} if $\{x,\,y\}\in S$ for some $\{x,\,y\}\in E$. Otherwise $S$ is \emph{independent}.
\item[2.] $f:V\rightarrow C$ is a \emph{good coloring} if $f^{-1}(c)$ is independent for each $c\in C$.
\item[3.] Let $\kappa=|C|$, then $G$ is $\kappa$ \emph{colorable} if there is a good coloring $f:V\rightarrow C$. ($C$ need not be well orderable.)
\item[4.] The least $\kappa$ for which $G$ is $\kappa$ colorable (if it exists) is the \emph{chromatic number} of $G$.
\item[5.] A good coloring $f:G\rightarrow C$ is \emph{irreducible} if $f^{-1}(c_{1})\cup
f^{-1}(c_{2})$ is dependent whenever $c_{1},\,c_{2}\in C$ and $c_{1}\neq c_{2}$.

\noindent (So a graph admits an irreducible good coloring just in case its vertex set can be partitioned into independent sets such that the union of any two is dependent.)
\item[6.] For any two sets $A$ and $B$ define the graph $G(A,\,B)$ with vertex set $A\times B$ by $(a_{1},\,b_{1})\neq(a_{2},\,b_{2})$ are adjacent if $a_{1}=a_{2}$ or $b_{1}=b_{2}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 119}

Definitions from Shannon \cite{bib:1992} for form [86($\alpha$) A].

\begin{definition*}
Assume $(P,\,\leq)$ is a quasi-order (i.e., reflexive and transitive).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $x,\,y\in P$ are \emph{incompatible} if there is no $z\in P$ such that $z\leq x$ and $z\leq y$.
\item[2.] $I\subseteq P$ is an \emph{antichain} if any two different elements of $I$ are incompatible.
\item[3.] A partially ordered set $(P,\,\leq)$ is a \emph{tree} iff $\forall x\in P,\,\{y\in P:y\leq x\}$ is well ordered by $\leq$ and $(P,\,\leq)$ has a unique minimal element.
\end{enumerate}
Assume $(P,\,\leq)$ is a tree\index{Subject}{tree}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[4.] If\index{Subject}{chromatic number}\index{Subject}{incompatible elements}\index{Subject}{$\kappa$ colorable graph}\index{Author}{Shannon} $x\in P$ then $ht(x)$ (the \emph{height} of $x$) is the order type of $\{y\in P:y<x\}$.
\item[5.] $\mathrm{lev}_{\alpha}(P)=\{x\in P:ht(x)=\alpha\}$.
\item[6.] The \emph{height}\index{Subject}{height of a tree} of $P$ is the least $\alpha$ such that $\mathrm{lev}_{\alpha}(P)=\emptyset$.
\item[7.] A \emph{branch}\index{Subject}{branch in a tree} in $(P,\,\leq)$ is a maximal chain.
\item[8.] If $(P,\,\geq)$ is an upside down tree then a \emph{strong antichain in}\index{Subject}{antichain}\index{Subject}{strong antichain} $(P,\,\geq)$ is an antichain that has at most one element from each level of $(P,\,\leq)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}
