\section*{NOTE 121}

This note contains an argument that the order extension principle (form 49) together with ``Every linear ordering has a cofinal well ordered subset.'' (form 51) implies AC (form 1). This result was announced in Morris\index{Author}{Morris} \cite{bib:1969}.

Assume that $Y$ is a set of non-empty sets. Let $P$ be the set of choice functions $f$ such that the domain of $f$ is a subset of $Y$. We define the following partial ordering on $P$:
\begin{equation*}
f\preceq_{0} g\Leftrightarrow \mathrm{dom}(f)\subsetneq \mathrm{dom}(g)\vee f=g.
\end{equation*}
Extend $\preceq_{0}$ to a linear ordering $\preceq$ on $P$. Let $\{f_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\beta\}$ be a cofinal subset of the linear ordering $(P,\,\preceq)$ where $f_{\alpha}\prec f_{\gamma}\leftrightarrow\alpha\in\gamma$. ($\in$ is the usual well ordering on the ordinals.) The set $W= \bigcup_{\alpha\in\beta} \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha})$ has a choice function $F$ defined by $F(x)=f_{\alpha}(x)$ where $\alpha$ is the least ordinal for which $x\in \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha})$. We complete the proof by showing that $W=Y$. If not, then there is some $x\in Y-W$. Let $t$ be any element of $x$, then $G=F\cup \{(x,\,t)\}$ is in $P$ and has the property that $\forall\alpha\in\beta,\,f_{\alpha}\prec_{0}G$ and hence, since $\preceq$ extends $\preceq_{0},\,f_{\alpha}\prec G$. This contradicts the cofinality of $\{f_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\beta\}$.

\section*{NOTE 122}

In $\mathcal{N}43$, both $C(\aleph_{0},2)$ (form 80) and the Multiple Choice Axiom $(MC(\infty,\,\infty)$, form 67) are false.

\noindent $C(\aleph_{0},2)$ is false in $\mathcal{N}43$: For each $n\in \omega$, let $w_{n}=(a_{0}^{n},\,a_{1}^{n},\,\ldots,\, a_{n}^{n})$ be a fixed well ordering of $P_{n}$. (The function choosing these well orderings will not be in the model.) Let $C_{0}^{n}=$\{$\phi(w_{n}):\phi$ is an even permutation of $P_{n}$\} and $C_{1}^{n}=\{\phi(w_{n}):\phi$ is an odd permutation of $P_{n}$\}. Then for every $n\in \omega$, $\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}$ is in $\mathcal{N}43$ and has empty support. In fact if $\psi|P_{n}$ is even then $\psi$ fixes $\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}$ pointwise and if $\psi|P_{n}$ is odd then $\psi$ interchanges $C_{0}^{n}$ and $C_{1}^{n}$.

If $E$ is any support, then there is a $\psi\in G$ that fixes $E$ pointwise and an $n\in\omega$ such that $\psi|P_{n}$ is odd. Since such a $\psi$ fixes $\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}$ but moves both its elements, $E$ is not a support of a choice function on $\{\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}:n\in \omega\}$.

\noindent $MC(\infty,\,\infty)$ is false in $\mathcal{N}43$: Let $F$ be the set of all choice functions $f:\omega\rightarrow A$ such that $\forall n\in\omega,\,f(n)\in P_{n}$. Suppose that $E$ is a support of a multiple choice function $H$ on $\mathcal{P}(F)-\{\emptyset\}$ in $\mathcal{N}43$. Let $k= \sup\{|E\cap P_{n}|:n\in \omega\}$ and define $T\subseteq F$ by $T=\{f\in F:(\forall i>k)(f(i)\in P_{n}-E)\}$. Since $E$ is a support of $T$ and of $H,\, E$ is a support of $H(T)$ which must be a finite, non-empty subset of $T$. Fix $f$ in $H(T)$ then for every $g\in T$ for which $g(i)=f(i)$ for $i\leq k$, there is a $\phi\in G$ which fixes $E$ pointwise such that $\phi(f)=g$. Therefore $g\in H(T)$. Since there are infinitely many such $g$'s, $H(T)$ is infinite. This is a contradiction.

\section*{NOTE 123}

We shall prove that form 10 $(C(\aleph_{0},\,<\aleph_{0}))\ +$ form 163 (Every non-well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) implies form 231 $(UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO))$ and also that form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous set.) implies form 231. (It is shown in Brunner\index{Author}{Brunner} \cite{bib:1982a} that 10 + 163 implies 165 $(C(WO,\,WO)).)$

Suppose $X$ is a well ordered set of pairwise disjoint well orderable sets. Assume $Y=\bigcup X$ cannot be well ordered. Form 163 implies that $Y$ has an infinite Dedekind finite set $Z$. Let $T=\{w\cap\,z:w\in X\wedge w\cap z\neq\emptyset\}$ For each $w\in Z,\,w\cap Z$ is a well ordered Dedekind finite set so it must be finite. If $T$ is finite, then $Z$ is a finite union of finite sets and is therefore finite. This contradicts the definition of $Z$. If $T$ is infinite, then $T$ is well ordered because $X$ is well ordered. Therefore $T$ must have a denumerable subset, $U$. $U$ is a denumerable set of finite sets, so by 10, $U$ has a choice set. This choice set is a denumerable subset of $Z$. This contradicts the definition of $Z$. Thus, the union of $X$ can be well ordered.

Since form 133 (every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset) implies form 10 (Brunner \cite{bib:1984b}) and 133 implies 163 (clear), it follows that 133 implies 231.

\section*{NOTE 124}

A proof that form 314 (Every permutation on a non-empty set can be expressed as a product of two reflections.) implies form 119 ($C(\aleph_{0}$,uniformly orderable with order type of the integers)).

Assume that $B=\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ is a denumerable set of denumerable sets and $f$ is a function defined on $\omega$ such that $\forall i\in \omega,\,f(i)$ is an ordering of $A_{i}$ with order type that of the integers. We want to construct a choice function $g$ for $B$ so we may assume that the elements of $B$ are pairwise disjoint.

Let $\eta$ be the permutation of $\bigcup B$ defined by $\eta(a)=$ the immediate successor of $a$ under the ordering $f(A_{i})$ where $A_{i}$ is the unique element of $B$ such that $a\in A_{i}$. By form 314, $\eta$ is the product of two reflections: $\eta =\phi\circ\psi$.

Fix an $i\in \omega$ and for each permutation $\beta$ of $\bigcup B$, let $\beta^{\prime}=\beta\ |\ A_{i}$. Then $\eta^{\prime}=\phi^{\prime}\circ\psi^{\prime}$ and $\phi^{\prime}$ and $\psi^{\prime}$ are reflections. We complete the proof by showing that exactly one of $\phi^{\prime}$ or $\psi^{\prime}$ has exactly one fixed point. (This fixed point will be $g(A_{i})$.)

Since $\phi^{\prime}$ and $\psi^{\prime}$ are both reflections, $\phi^{\prime}$ and $\psi^{\prime}$ can both be written as a product of disjoint cycles, $\phi'=\prod_{i\in I}(s_{i},\,t_{i})$ and $\psi^{\prime}=\prod_{j\in J}(c_{j},\,d_{j})$. Assume that $A_{i}=\{\ldots,\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots\}$ where the elements are listed in the order determined by the ordering $f(A_{i})$. Then $\eta^{\prime}$ is the infinite cycle $\eta^{\prime}= (\ldots,\,a_{-1},\, a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots)$. Let $r$ be the smallest positive integer such that for some integer $k$ the transposition $(a_{k},\,a_{k+r})$ is one of the $(s_{i},\,t_{i})$ or one of the $(c_{j},\,d_{j})$

We first show that $r=1$. Assume that $r>1$ and that $(a_{k},\,a_{k+r})$ is one of the $(c_{j},\,b_{j})$. (The argument is similar if $(a_{k},\,a_{k+r})$ is one of the $(s_{i},\,t_{i})$.) This means that $\psi^{\prime}(a_{k})=a_{k+r}$. Since $\eta^{\prime}(a_{k})=a_{k+1}$ (and $r\neq 1)$, $\phi^{\prime}(a_{k+r})$ must be $a_{k+1}$, hence the transposition $(a_{k+1},\,a_{k+r})$ must be one of the $(s_{i},\,t_{i})$. This contradicts the definition of $r$.

Assume that $(a_{k},\,a_{k+1})$ is one of the $(c_{j},\,d_{j})$. (The argument is similar if $(a_{k},\, a_{k+1})$ is one of the $(s_{i},\,t_{i}).)$ This means that $\psi^{\prime}(a_{k})=a_{k+1}$. Since $\eta^{\prime}(a_{k})= a_{k+1}$ we conclude that $a_{k+1}$ must be a fixed point of $\phi^{\prime}$. Further, since $\psi^{\prime}(a_{k+1})=a_{k}$ and $\eta^{\prime}(a_{k+1})=a_{k+2}$ we conclude that $\phi^{\prime}(a_{k})=a_{k+2}$, that is, $(a_{k},\,a_{k+2})$ is one of the $(s_{i},\,t_{i})$. By this last conclusion, $\psi^{\prime}(a_{k+2})=a_{k}$. It follows that $\psi^{\prime}(a_{k-1})=a_{k+2}$, that is $(a_{k-1},\, a_{k+2})$ is one of the $(c_{j},\,d_{j})$. Continuing in this way, we see that for every natural number $j,\,\psi^{\prime}$ interchanges $a_{k-j}$ and $a_{k+j+1}$ and $\phi^{\prime}$ interchanges $a_{k-j}$ and $a_{k+j+2}$. Therefore, $\psi^{\prime}$ has no fixed points and $\phi^{\prime}$ has exactly one fixed point.

\section*{NOTE 125}

In this note we survey forms of the Hahn-Banach Theorem\index{Subject}{Hahn-Banach theorem} discussed in Buskes\index{Author}{Buskes}
\cite{bib:1993}.

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def1}
Let $E$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, and let $p$ be a mapping from $E$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $p$ is called \emph{sublinear}\index{Subject}{sublinear function} if $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$, for all $x,\,y\in E$, and $p(rx)=rp(x)$, for all $x\in E$ and all $r\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.
\item[(b)] $p$ is called a \emph{seminorm} if $p$ is sublinear and $p(rx)=|r|p(x)$, for all $x\in E$ and all $r\in \mathbb{R}$.
\item[(c)] $p$ is called a \emph{norm} if $p$ is a seminorm and $p(x)=0$ iff $x=0$, for all $x\in E$.
\item[(d)] $p$ is called \emph{superlinear} if $p(x)+p(y)\leq p(x+y)$ for
all $x,\,y\in E$, and $p(rx)=rp(x)$, for all $x\in E$ and all $r\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se1}
(Form 52) Assume $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a sublinear function. Suppose $E_{0}$ is a subspace of $E$ and $f_{0}$ is a linear function from $E_{0}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that $f_{0}(x)\leq p(x)$, for all $x\in E_{0}$. Then there is a linear function $f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that extends $f_{0}$ and $f(x)\leq p(x)$, for all $x\in E$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se2}
Assume $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $p$ is a norm on E. Suppose $E_{0}$ is a subspace of $E$ and $f_{0}$ is a continuous linear function from $E_{0}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Then there is a continuous linear function $f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that extends $f_{0}$ and $\Vert f_{0}\Vert=\Vert f\Vert$. (For any subspace $E_{0}\subseteq E$ and any linear function $f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation*}
\Vert f_{0}\Vert=sup\{|f_{0}(x)|:x\in E_{0}\wedge p(x)\leq 1\}.\text{)}
\end{equation*}
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se3}
Assume $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{R},\,p$ a sublinear function on $E$, and $q$ a superlinear function on E. If $q(x)\leq p(x)$ for all $x\in E$, then there exists a linear function $f: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $q(x)\leq f(x)\leq p(x)$ for all $x\in E$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se4}
(Complex form of $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 1}$) Assume $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{C}$ and $p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ a seminorm (a sublinear function for which $p(\alpha x)=|\alpha|p(x)$ for all $x\in E$ and all $\alpha\in \mathbb{C}$). Let $E_{0}$ be a subspace of $E$ and $f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be linear such that $|f_{0}(x)|\leq p(x)$ for all $x\in E$. Then there is a linear function $f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $|f(x)|\leq p(x)$ for all $x\in E$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se5}
(Complex form of $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 2}$)\index{Subject}{seminorm}\index{Subject}{superlinear function} (Change ``$\mathbb{R}$'' in $\mathbf{H}\text{-}\mathbf{B\ 2}$ to ``$\mathbb{C}$''. $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 5}$ is equivalent to $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 2}$. Let $f_{0}=f_{1}+if_{2}$, where $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ are real continuous function from $E_{0}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Let $f_{1}^{\ast}$ be an extension of $f_{1}$ to $E$ so that $\Vert f_{1}^{\ast}\Vert\leq\Vert f_{0}\Vert$. Then the desired extension $f$ of $f_{0}$ can be defined as $f(x)=f_{1}^{\ast}(x)-if_{1}^{\ast}(x)$ for all $x\in E$.)
\end{unsec}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def2}
A metric space $E$ is \emph{spherically complete} if the set of its closed
balls has the binary intersection property (if the intersection of each pair of balls is non-empty, the intersection of the whole set is non-empty).
\end{definition}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se6}
(Ingleton' s Theorem) Assume $K$ is a spherically complete, non-Archimedean valued field. Let $E$ be a normed vector space over $K$ and let $E_{0}$ be a subspace of $E$.

\noindent Let $f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow K$ be a continuous linear function. Then there exists a continuous linear function $f:E\rightarrow K$ that extends $f_{0}$ and for which $\Vert f\Vert=\Vert f_{0}\Vert$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def3}
Let $(E,\,\Vert\ \Vert)$ be a normed vector space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The norm\index{Subject}{norm} is said to be \emph{Gateaux differentiable}\index{Subject}{Gateaux differentiable} at $x\in E$ if for all $y\in E$,
\begin{equation*}
\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Vert x+ty\Vert-\Vert x\Vert}{t}
\end{equation*}
exists.
\item[(b)] $(E,\,\Vert\ \Vert)$ is said to be \emph{uniformly convex}\index{Subject}{uniformly convex} if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that for all $x,\,y\in E$ with $\Vert x\Vert=\Vert y\Vert=1,\,\Vert x-y\Vert\geq\epsilon$ implies $\frac{1}{2}\Vert x+y\Vert\leq 1-\delta$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se7}
(Ishihara's Theorem) Let $E_{0}$ be a subspace of a uniformly convex Banach space $E$ with a Gateaux differentiable norm. Let $f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-zero continuous linear function. Then there is a unique linear continuous extension $f$ from $E$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\Vert f\Vert=\Vert f_{0}\Vert$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se8}
Suppose $E$ is a normed vector space in which the unit ball is weakly compact and the norm in $E$ is Gateaux differentiable. Let $E_{0}$ be a subspace of $E$. Then every continuous linear function $f_{0}:E_{0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be uniquely extended to a continuous linear function $f: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\Vert f\Vert=\Vert f_{0}\Vert$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se9}
(Mazur-Orlicz Theorem) Assume $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a sublinear function. Let $T$ be a set and let $\phi$ and $\alpha$ be functions such that $\phi:T\rightarrow E$ and $\alpha:T\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Then the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(1)}] There exists a linear $f:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(i)}] $f\leq p$ and
\item[\emph{(ii)}] $\alpha(t)\leq f(\phi(t))$ for all $t\in T$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(2)}] For all $k\in \mathbb{N}$, for all $r_{1},\,r_{2},\cdots,\,r_{k}\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$, and for all $t_{1},\,t_{2},\,\cdots,\,t_{k}\in T$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\sum\limits_{n=1}^{k}r_{n}\alpha(t_{n})\leq p\bigg(\sum\limits_{n=1}^{k}r_{n}\phi(t_{n})\bigg).
\end{equation*}
$(\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 9}$ \emph{implies} $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 1}$ \emph{and} $\mathbf{H\text{-}B\ 3}.)$
\end{enumerate}
\end{unsec}

The last three forms are examples of Hahn-Banach theorems in which the range of the function that is to be extended may not be commutative.

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se10}
(Kantorovich) Suppose $E$ is an ordered vector space and $E_{0}$ a cofinal subspace. Let $F$ be an order complete vector space. Then each positive linear map from $E_{0}$ to $F$ can be extended to a positive linear map from $E$ to $F$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se11} (Lipecki-Plachky-Thomsen, Luxemburg-Schep) Suppose $E$ is a vector lattice and $E_{0}$ is a cofinal vector sublattice. Let $F$ be an order complete vector lattice. Then each vector lattice homomorphism from $E_{0}$ to $F$ can be extended to a vector lattice homomorphism from $E$ to $F$.
\end{unsec}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def4}\
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A \emph{Banach algebra}\index{Subject}{Banach algebra} is a complex algebra together with a complete norm satisfying the condition $\Vert xy\Vert\leq\Vert x\Vert\Vert y\Vert$, for all $x$ and $y$. If the algebra contains an identity element $e,\,\Vert e\Vert=1$.
\item[(b)] A $C^{\ast}$-\emph{algebra}\index{Subject}{$C^{\ast}$-algebra} is a Banach algebra with an involution $x\mapsto x^{\ast}$ on it satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $x^{\ast\ast}=x$ for all vectors $x$.
\item[(ii)] $(ax+bx)^{\ast}=\overline{a}x^{\ast}+\overline{b}y^{\ast}$ for all vectors $x$ and $y$ and all complex numbers $a$ and $b$.
\item[(iii)] $(xy)^{\ast}=y^{\ast}x^{\ast}$ for all vectors $x$ and $y$.
\item[(iv)] $\Vert x^{\ast}x\Vert=\Vert x\Vert^{2}$ for all vectors $x$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{unsec}\label{part04:se12}
(Arveson) Suppose $E$ is a $C^{\ast}$-algebra and $E_{0}$ is a cofinal $\ast$-invariant subspace of E. Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $B(H)$ the space of all bounded operators on H. Then each completely positive linear map from $E_{0}$ to $B(H)$ extends to a completely positive linear map from $E$ to $B(H)$.
\end{unsec}

For additional results see Buskes\index{Author}{Buskes} \cite{bib:1993} and his references.

\section*{NOTE 126}

We give definitions for form [43 B] from Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985}.

Let $\Phi$ be a class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus and suppose the deducibility relation, $\vdash$, satisfies the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[D1.] $\emptyset \vdash\phi$, for every tautology $\phi$.
\item[D2.] $\Gamma \cup\{\phi\}\vdash\psi$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\phi\rightarrow\psi$, where $\Gamma\subseteq\Phi$.
\item[D3.] If $\Gamma\vdash\phi$ and $\Gamma\subseteq\Delta$, then $\Delta\vdash\phi$, where $\Gamma,\, \Delta\subseteq\Phi$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def1a}
$\Gamma\subseteq\Phi$ is \emph{finitely consistent} if every finite subset of $\Gamma$ is consistent.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def2a}
An ordered pair $(\Pi,\,\psi)$ is called an \emph{inference} if $\Pi\subseteq\Phi$ and $\psi\in\Phi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def3a}
If $\Gamma\subseteq\Phi,\,\Gamma$ \emph{respects} the inference $(\Pi,\,\psi)$ if
\begin{equation*}
(\Gamma\vdash\phi,\,\forall\phi\in\Pi)\ \text{implies}\ \Gamma\vdash\psi.
\end{equation*}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{part04:def4a}
If $\Gamma\subseteq\Phi,\,\Gamma$ \emph{decides} the inference $(\Pi,\,\psi)$ if
\begin{equation*}
\text{either}\ \Gamma\vdash\psi\ \text{or}\ \exists\phi\in\Pi\ \text{such that}\ \Gamma\vdash\neg\phi.
\end{equation*}
(We say $\Gamma$ respects (decides) a set of inferences $I$ if $\Gamma$ respects (decides) each inference in $I$.)
\begin{enumerate}
\item[[43 B{]}] Countable Henkin Principle: Let $\Phi$ be the class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus. Let $I$ be a countable set of inferences, and $\Gamma$ a consistent subset of $\Phi$ such that $\Gamma \cup\{\psi\}$ respects $I$ for each $\psi\in\Phi$. Then for any $\phi\in\Phi$, if $\phi$ is consistent with $\Gamma$ then $\Gamma$ has a finitely consistent extension that contains $\phi$ and decides $I$.
\end{enumerate}

Goldblatt\index{Author}{Goldblatt} \cite{bib:1985} proves that [43 B] is equivalent to the principle of dependent choices (form 43) and Goldblatt \cite{bib:1984} shows how [43
B] may be used to prove completeness and omitting-types theorems for countable first-order languages.
\end{definition}

\section*{NOTE 127}

Forms [1 BZ] (Vector space multiple choice) and 346 (Vector space Kinna-Wagner principle) were suggested by K. Keremedis. It is clear that [1 BZ] implies 346. In this note we prove that 346 implies the Kinna-Wagner principle $KW(\infty, < \aleph_{0})$ (form [62 E]). Since the axiom of choice is implied by the conjunction of forms 62 and 67, we obtain a proof that $346+67$ implies the axiom of choice. (Form 62 is $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ and 67 is the axiom of multiple choice.) Similarly, since [1 BZ] implies form 67, we obtain the result: [1 BZ] implies the axiom of choice.

Let $X=\{y_{i}:i\in K\}$ be a family of finite sets. For each $y_{i}$ let $U_{i}$ be the real vector space $\mathbb{R}^{y_{i}}$ with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. (If $y_{i}= \{a_{1},\,\ldots,\, a_{n}\}$ we could think of $U_{i}$ as being the set of all formal sums $k_{1}a_{1}+\cdots+k_{n}a_{n}$ where the $k_{i}$'s are real.) Let $S_{i}$ be the subspace \{ $g\in U_{i}:g$ is constant\}. (Or in terms of formal sums, $S_{i}$ is all formal sums $ka_{1}+\cdots+ka_{n}$.) Let $V_{i}$ be the quotient space $V_{i}=U_{i}/S_{i}$. That is, $V_{i}$ consists of all equivalence classes $[g]$ of elements of $U_{i}$ under the relation $g\sim f\Leftrightarrow g-f\in S_{i}$. By form 346 there is a family $\{F_{i}:i\in K\}$ such that for each $i\in K,\,F_{i}$ is an independent subset of $V_{i}$. Since $U_{i}$ is finite dimensional $F_{i}$ must be finite. Say $F_{i}=\{b_{1},\,\ldots,\,b_{r}\}$ then since $F_{i}$ is independent, the element $w_{i}=b_{1}+\cdots+b_{r}$ is not zero. The vector $w_{i}=[g]$ for some $g\in U_{i}$. Assume $f\in[g]$. Then if $a,\,a^{\prime}\in y_{i}$ and $g(a)\leq g(a^{\prime})$ it follows from the fact that $f-g$ is constant that $f(a)\leq f(a^{\prime})$. Therefore the set $K_{i}=\{a\in y_{i}:g(a)$ is minimum among the numbers $g(a^{\prime})$ for $a^{\prime}\in y_{i}$\} is independent of the choice of $g\in w_{i}$. It is also true that $K_{i}\neq y_{i}$. This follows from the fact that $w_{i}\neq 0$ which implies that $g$ is not constant. The family $\{K_{i}:i\in K\}$ is therefore a Kinna-Wagner function for X.

\section*{NOTE 128}

In this note we prove that in $\mathcal{N}51$, form 64 (There are no amorphous sets.) and form 90 (Every linearly orderable set is well orderable.) are true and form 221 (Every infinite set has a non-principal measure.) is false. The Hahn-Banach Theorem (form 52) implies 221, so it is also false. (See Brunner/Howard/Rubin \cite{bib:1996}.)

We first note that for each finite ordered partition $P= (B_{1},\,\ldots,\,B_{n})$ of $A,\,G_{P}\in \mathcal{F}$, where $G_{P}=\{\psi\in G:\psi(P)=P\}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is the filter of subgroups which determine $\mathcal{N}51$. Further, if $H\in \mathcal{F}$ then there is a finite ordered partition $P$ of $A$ such that $G_{P}\subseteq H$. Therefore for each $x\in \mathcal{N}51$, there is a finite ordered partition $P$ of $A$ such that $(\forall\psi\in G_{P})(\psi(x)=x)$. We will refer to such a partition $P$ as a support of $x$.

In order to prove that form 221 is false we shall give a proof that in $\mathcal{N}51$ there is no non-principal measure on $A$, the set of atoms.

Suppose, $m$ is a non-principal measure on $A$ supported by the partition $P= (B_{1},\,\ldots,\,B_{n})$ of $A$. Since $m$ is finitely additive on disjoint sets, $m(A)=1$, and $m(\{a\})=0$, for all $a\in A$. It follows that there must be an $i\leq n$ such that $B_{i}$ is infinite and $m(B_{i})\neq 0$. There exist pairwise disjoint infinite subsets, $S_{1},\,S_{2}$, and $S_{3}$, of $B_{i}$ such that $B_{i}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cup S_{3}$. Suppose $\sigma_{1},\,\sigma_{2}\in G_{P}$ are such that
\setcounter{equation}{0}
\begin{equation}\label{part04:eqn1a}
\sigma_{1}(S_{1})=S_{2}\cup S_{3}\ \mathrm{and}\ \sigma(S_{2}\cup S_{3})=S_{1}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{part04:eqn2} \sigma_{2}(S_{1})=S_{2},\,\sigma_{2}(S_{2})=S_{3},\ \text{and}\
\sigma_{2}(S_{3})=S_{1}
\end{equation}
Then,\index{Author}{Brunner/Howard/Rubin} we would have
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $m(S_{1})=m(S_{2}\cup S_{3})=m(S_{2})+m(S_{3})$, by (\ref{part04:eqn1a}).
\item[(b)] $m(S_{1})=m(S_{2})=m(S_{3})$, by (\ref{part04:eqn2}).
\end{enumerate}

Consequently, $m(S_{1})=2m(S_{1})$, which implies that $m(S_{1})=0$. Thus, by (b), $m(B_{i})=0$, which is a contradiction.

In order to prove that forms 90 and 64 are true, we need the following lemma which is a slight strengthening of form 314 (from Degen\index{Author}{Degen} \cite{bib:1988}). The proof requires the axiom of choice but we intend to use the lemma in the ground model where AC holds.

\begin{lemma*}
If $\psi$ is a permutation of a non-empty set $A$ then there are two reflections $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ (a reflection on a set $A$ is a permutation $\rho$ for which $\rho^{2}=1_{A}$.) satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(i)}] $\psi=\rho_{2}\circ\rho_{1}$ and
\item[\emph{(ii)}] For all $B\subseteq A$, if $\psi(B)=B$ then $\rho_{1}(B)=B$ and $\rho_{2}(B)=B$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
Assume $\psi$ is a permutation of $A$. Write $\psi=\prod_{i\in K}c_{i}$ as a product of disjoint cycles. Each $c_{i}$ can be written as a product of reflections $c_{i}=\rho_{2,i}\circ\rho_{1,i}$ as follows. If $c_{i}= (a_{-n},\,a_{-(n-1)},\,\ldots,\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n})$ has odd length then
\begin{gather*}
\rho_{1,i}=(a_{-1},\,a_{1})(a_{-2},\,a_{2})\cdots(a_{-n},\,a_{n})\ \mathrm{and}\\
\rho_{2,i}=(a_{0},\,a_{1})(a_{-1},\,a_{2})\cdots(a_{-(n-1)},\,a_{n}).
\end{gather*}
If $c_{i}= (a_{-(n-1)},\,a_{-(n-2)},\,\ldots,\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n})$ has even length then
\begin{gather*}
\rho_{1,i}=(a_{-1},\,a_{1})(a_{-2},\,a_{2})\cdots(a_{-(n-1)},\,a_{(n-1)})\ \mathrm{and}\\
\rho_{2,i}=(a_{0},\,a_{1})(a_{-1},\,a_{2})\cdots(a_{-(n-1)},\,a_{n}).
\end{gather*}
If $c_{i}= (\ldots,\,a_{-2},\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots)$ is infinite then
\begin{equation*}
\rho_{1,i}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_{-n},\,a_{n})\ \mathrm{and}\ \rho_{2,i}=\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}(a_{-n},\, a_{n+1}).
\end{equation*}
Then if $\rho_{1}=\prod_{i\in K}\rho_{1,i}$ and $\rho_{2}=\prod_{i\in K}\rho_{2,i}$ we have $\rho_{1}^{2}=1_{A},\,\rho_{2}^{2}=1_{A}$ and $\psi=\rho_{2}\circ\rho_{1}$. For the argument that (ii) holds we first note that if $\eta$ is a permutation whose expression as a product of disjoint cycles is $\eta =\prod_{j\in J}\sigma_{j}$ and $B\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(\eta)$ then
\begin{equation*}\tag{$\ast$}
\eta(B)=B\Leftrightarrow(\forall j\in J)(\{x:\sigma_{j}(x)\neq x\}\subseteq B\ \mathrm{or}\ \{x:\sigma_{j}(x)\neq x\}\cap\,B=\emptyset).
\end{equation*}
Now assume that $B\subseteq A$ and that $\psi(B)=B$. By $(\ast)$ for each $i\in K$, either $\{a\in A:c_{i}(a)\neq a\}\subseteq B$ or $\{a\in A:c_{i}(a)\neq a\}\cap B=\emptyset$. When $\rho_{1}$ is written as a product of disjoint cycles each cycle is a transposition $(a,\,b)$ which is a cycle of $\rho_{1,i}$ for some $i\in K$. Hence by the definition of $\rho_{1,i},\,\{a,\,b\}\subseteq\{a\in A:c_{i}(a)\neq a\}$. Therefore $\{a,\,b\}\subseteq B$ (if $\{a\in A:c_{i}(a)\neq a\}\subseteq B)$ or $\{a,\,b\}\cap B=\emptyset$ (if $\{a\in A: c_{i}(a)\neq a\}\cap B=\emptyset)$. It follows from $(\ast)$ that $\rho_{1}(B)=B$. Similarly, $\rho_{2}(B)=B$. 
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}
In $\mathcal{N}51$ every linearly orderable set is well orderable.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be linearly orderable in $\mathcal{N}51$ and assume that the ordered partition $P= (B_{1},\,\ldots,\, B_{k})$ is a support of a linear ordering $<$ on $X$. We shall show that if $\psi\in G_{P}$, then $\psi$ fixes $X$ pointwise and hence $P$ is a support of a well ordering of $X$. Assume $\psi\in G_{P}$. By the lemma, $\psi=\rho_{2}\circ\rho_{1}$ where $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ are reflections and (by part (ii)) $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ are in $G_{P}$. The permutations $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ are therefore order automorphisms of $(X,\,<)$. Since no order automorphism of a linearly ordered set can have a finite cycle of length greater than 1, we conclude that for all $x\in X,\,\rho_{1}(x)=x$ and $\rho_{2}(x)=x$ hence $\forall x\in X,\,\psi(x)=x$. 
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem*}
In $\mathcal{N}51$ there are no infinite amorphous sets.
\end{theorem*}

\begin{proof}
Assume that $X\in \mathcal{N}51$ is infinite and that the ordered partition $P= (B_{1},\,\ldots,\,B_{k})$ of $A$ is a support of $X$. We will show that there is an infinite set $R\in \mathcal{N}51$ such that $R\subset X$ and $X-R$ is infinite.

If every element of $X$ has support $P$ then $X$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}51$ and the proof is easy. We therefore assume that $y\in X$ and there is a $\phi\in G_{P}$ such that $\phi(y)\neq y$.

\textsc{Step 1.}
We show that we may assume that $y$ has a support
\begin{equation*}
Q=(C_{1},\,C_{2},\,C_{3},\,\ldots,\,C_{n_{0}},\,C_{n_{0}+1},\,\ldots,\,C_{n})
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a.] $n_{0}\geq 3$ and $C_{3}$ is infinite.
\item[b.] For $1\leq j\leq n_{0},\,C_{j}\subseteq B_{1}$ and for $n_{0}<j\leq n,\, C_{j}\cap B_{1}=\emptyset$.
\item[c.] $\phi(C_{1})=C_{2},\,\phi(C_{2})=C_{1}$, and for every $a\in A-(C_{1}\cup
C_{2})$, $\phi(a)=a$.
\end{enumerate}

First, we may assume (by refining $P$ if necessary) that each $B_{i}$ is either infinite or a singleton. Secondly, by writing $\phi=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\phi_{i}$ where $\phi_{i}(a)=a$ for $a\in A-B_{i}$ and replacing $\phi$ by one of the $\phi_{i}$, we may assume that there is an $i\leq k$ such that $\phi(a)=a$ for $a\in A-B_{i}$. (If $\prod_{i=1}^{k}\phi_{i}(y)\neq y$ then for some $i,\,\phi_{i}(y)\neq y$.) Further it is no loss of generality to assume that $i=1$.

Let $Q= (C_{1},\,\ldots,\,C_{n})$ be a support of $y$. By replacing each $C_{j}$ with the two sets $C_{j}\cap B_{1}$ and $C_{j}-B_{1}$ (if necessary) and reordering the $C_{j}$'s we may assume that there is an $n_{0}\leq n$ such that $C_{j}\subseteq B_{1}$ for $j\leq n_{0}$ and $C_{j}\cap B_{1}=\emptyset$ for $j>n_{0}$. As in the proof of the previous theorem (using the lemma) we may assume that $\phi$ is a reflection. By replacing $Q$ by a partition whose cells are $\{C_{i}\cap \phi(C_{j}):1\leq i,\, j\leq n\}-\{\emptyset\}$ we may assume (since $\phi$ is a reflection) that $\forall i,\,1\leq i\leq n,\,\exists j,\,1\leq j\leq n$ such that $\phi(C_{i})=C_{j}$ and $\phi(C_{j})=C_{i}$. (By our simplifying assumptions so far, $\phi(C_{j})=C_{j}$ for $j>n_{0}$.) By decomposing $\phi$ into a product $\phi=\prod_{r=1}^{m}\gamma_{r}$ where for each $r,\,1\leq r\leq m$ there are $i$ and $j$ such that $\gamma_{r}(a)=a$ for $a\in A-(C_{i}\cup C_{j})$, $\gamma_{r}(C_{i})=C_{j}$ and $\gamma)r(C_{j})=C_{i}$ and replacing $\phi$ by one of the $\gamma_{r}$, we may assume that $\phi(a)=a$ for $a\in A-(C_{i}\cup C_{j})$, $\phi(C_{i})=C_{j}$ and $\phi(C_{j})=C_{i}$. It is no loss of generality to assume that $i=1$ and $j=2$.

Finally, we may assume that for some $i,\,3\leq i\leq n_{0},\,C_{i}$ is infinite. Assuming that this is not the case and using the facts that $C_{1}\cup C_{2}\subseteq B_{1}$ and that $B_{1}$ is infinite we conclude that $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are infinite. Let $C^{\prime}$ be any infinite subset of $C_{1}$ whose complement in $C_{1}$ is infinite. Note that $C_{2}$ is the disjoint union $C_{2}= \phi(C^{\prime})\cup\phi(C_{1}-C^{\prime})$. Therefore, $Q^{\prime}=(C^{\prime},\,\phi(C^{\prime}),\,C_{1}-C^{\prime},\,\phi(C_{1}-C^{\prime}),\,C_{3},\,\ldots,\,C_{n})$ is a partition of $Q$ which supports $y$. Define $\phi^{\prime}$ and $\phi^{\prime\prime}$ (both in $G_{P}$) as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\phi^{\prime}(a)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\phi(a) & a\in C^{\prime}\cup\phi(C^{\prime})\\
a & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
\phi^{\prime\prime}(a)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\phi(a) & a\in(C_{1}-C^{\prime})\cup\phi(C_{1}-C^{\prime})\\
a & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.\ .
\end{equation*}
Clearly $\phi=\phi^{\prime}\circ\phi^{\prime\prime}$ and therefore one of $\phi^{\prime}$ or $\phi^{\prime\prime}$ moves $y$. Assume without loss of generality that $\phi^{\prime}(y)\neq y$ then replace $Q$ with $Q^{\prime}$ and $\phi$ by $\phi^{\prime}$.

This completes step 1.

\textsc{Step 2.} We use $y$ to obtain an infinite subset $R$ of $X$ whose complement in $X$ is infinite. Our primary tool will be the following lemma.

\begin{lemma*}
Assume that $\delta,\,\lambda\in G_{P}$, that $\lambda(a)=a$ for all $a\in A-(\delta(C_{1})\cup\delta(C_{2}))$, that $\lambda(\delta(C_{1}))=\delta(C_{2})$, and that $\lambda(\delta(C_{2}))=\delta(C_{1})$. Then $\lambda(\delta(y))\neq\delta(y)$.
\end{lemma*}

\begin{proof}
By the hypotheses, $\delta^{-1}\lambda\delta(C_{1})=C_{2}$ and $\delta^{-1}\lambda\delta(C_{2})=C_{1}$ and for all $a\in A-(C_{1}\cup C_{2})$, $\delta^{-1}\lambda\delta(a)=a$. This means that $\delta^{-1}\lambda\delta(Q)=\phi(Q)$ and since $Q$ is a support of $y,\,\delta^{-1}\lambda\delta(y)=\phi(y)\neq y$. It follows that $\lambda(\delta(y))\neq\delta(y)$. 
\end{proof}

Now by using permutations in $G_{P}$ which move $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ we can obtain infinitely many ``copies'' of $y$ all of which are in $X$.

Partition $C_{3}$ into sets $\{S_{j},\,T_{j},\,U_{j},\,V_{j}:j\in \omega\}$ so that $|S_{j}|=|T_{j}|=|U_{j}|=|V_{j}|= |C_{1}|(=|C_{2}|)$. Let $C_{3}^{\prime}$ and $C_{3}^{\prime\prime}$ denote the sets $\bigcup_{j\in\omega}(S_{j}\cup T_{j})$ and $\bigcup_{j\in\omega}(U_{j}\cup V_{j})$ respectively. Let $\tau \in G_{P}$ satisfy $\tau(a)=a$ for all $a\in A-(C_{1}\cup C_{2}\cup S_{0}\cup
T_{0}),\tau(C_{1})=S_{0},\,\tau(S_{0})=C_{1},\,\tau(C_{2})=T_{0}$ and $\tau(T_{0})=C_{2}$. Let $\nu\in G_{P}$ satisfy $\nu(a) =a$ for all $a \in A -(C_{1}\cup C_{2}\cup U_{0}\cup V_{0})$, $\nu(C_{1})=U_{0},\,\tau(U_{0})=C_{1},\,\tau(C_{2})=V_{0}$ and $\tau(V_{0})=C_{2}$. For $j\in \omega,\,j\geq 1$, let $\sigma_{j}\in G_{P}$ satisfy $\sigma_{j}(a)=a$ for $a\in A-(S_{0}\cup T_{0}\cup S_{j}\cup
T_{j})$, $\sigma_{j}(S_{0})=S_{j},\,\sigma_{j}(S_{j})=S_{0},\,\sigma_{j}(T_{0})=T_{j}$ and $\sigma_{j}(T_{j})=T_{0}$. Similarly, for $j\geq 1$, let $\gamma_{j}\in G_{P}$ satisfy $\gamma_{j}(a)=a$ for all $a\in A-(U_{0}\cup V_{0}\cup U_{j}\cup
V_{j})$, $\gamma_{j}(U_{0})=U_{j},\,\gamma_{j}(U_{j})=U_{0},\, \gamma_{j}(V_{0})=V_{j}$, and $\gamma_{j}(V_{j})=V_{0}$. The partition $P^{\prime}= (C_{1},\,C_{2},\,C_{3}^{\prime},\, C_{3}^{\prime\prime},\,\ldots,\,C_{n_{0}},\,B_{2},\,\ldots,\,B_{k})$ is a refinement of $P$ and therefore is a support of $X$. Hence the two sets $R_{1}=\{\psi(\tau(y)):\psi\in G_{P^{\prime}}\}$ and $R_{2}=\{\psi(\nu(y)):\psi\in G_{P^{\prime}}\}$ are subsets of $X$. Further, $P^{\prime}$ is a support of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ so $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are in $\mathcal{N}51$. We shall also prove the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(\forall j\in \omega,\,j\geq 1)(\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))\in R_{1}\wedge\gamma_{j}(\nu(y))\in R_{2})$.
\item[(ii)] $(\forall j\in \omega,j\geq 1)(\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))\not\in R_{2}\wedge\gamma_{j}(\nu(y))\not\in R_{1})$.
\item[(iii)] $(\forall j,\,r\in \omega,j,\,r\geq 1)(j\neq r\rightarrow[\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))\neq\sigma_{r}(\tau(y))\wedge(\gamma_{j}(\nu(y))\neq\gamma_{r}(\nu(y))])$.
\end{enumerate}

It will follow that $R=R_{1}$ is an infinite subset of $X$ with infinite complement in $X$ and the proof will be complete. To prove (i) we observe that since $\sigma_{j}$ and $\gamma_{j}$ agree with the identity permutation outside of $C_{3}^{\prime}$ and $C_{3}^{\prime\prime}$ respectively for $j\geq 1$, they are both in $G_{P^{\prime}}$.

For (ii) we first note that since $Q$ is a support of $y$, a support of $\nu(y)$ is given by
\begin{align*}
\nu(Q)&=(\nu(C_{1}),\,\nu\,(C_{2}),\,\nu(C_{3}),\,\ldots,\,\nu(C_{n}))\\
&=(U_{0},\,V_{0},\,[C_{3}-(U_{0}\cup V_{0})]\cup(C_{1}\cup C_{2}),\,C_{4},\,\ldots,\,C_{n}).
\end{align*}
Therefore if $\psi$ fixes $P^{\prime}$ then $\psi(\nu(y))$ has support $\psi(\nu(Q))=(\psi(U_{0}), \psi(V_{0})$, $[\psi(C_{3})-\psi(U_{0}\cup V_{0})]\cup\psi(C_{1}\cup C_{2})$, $\psi(C_{4}),\,\ldots,\, \psi(C_{n}))=(\psi(U_{0})$, $\psi(V_{0})$, $[C_{3}-\psi(U_{0}\cup
V_{0})]\cup(C_{1}\cup C_{2})$, $\psi(C_{4})$, $\ldots,\,\psi(C_{n}))$. Since $C_{3}^{\prime}\subseteq C_{3}-\psi(U_{0}\cup V_{0})$ we may conclude that for any $\lambda \in G_{P}$, if $\lambda(a) =a$ for all $a \in A -C_{3}^{\prime}$ then $\lambda(\psi(\nu(Q)) =\psi(\nu(Q))$ and therefore $\lambda(\psi(\nu(y)))=\psi(\nu(y))$. Hence such an $\lambda$ fixes $R_{2}$ pointwise. In particular, if we choose $\lambda$ so that $\lambda(a)=a$ for all $a\in A-(S_{j}\cup T_{j})$, $\lambda(S_{j})=T_{j}$ and $\lambda(T_{j})=S_{j}$ then $\lambda$ fixes $R_{2}$ pointwise and by the lemma (with $\delta=\sigma_{j}\circ\tau)\lambda(\sigma_{j}(\tau(y)))\neq\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))$. It follows that $\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))\not\in R_{2}$. A similar argument shows that $\gamma_{j}(\nu(y))\not\in R_{1}$.

The argument for (iii) is similar. We shall show
\begin{equation*}
(\forall j,\,r\in \omega,\,j,\,r\geq 1)(j\neq r\rightarrow\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))\neq\sigma_{r}(\tau(y)))
\end{equation*}
and leave the similar argument that $\gamma_{j}(\nu(y))\neq\gamma_{r}(\nu(y))$ to the reader. First note that $\sigma_{r}(\tau(y))$ has support
\begin{equation*}
\sigma_{r}(\tau(Q))=(S_{r},\,T_{r},\,[C_{3}-(S_{r}\cup T_{r})]\cup (C_{1}\cup
C_{2}),\,C_{4},\,\ldots,\,C_{n}).
\end{equation*}
Call this support $Q^{\prime}$. Since $S_{j}\cup T_{j}\subseteq C_{3}-(S_{r}\cup
T_{r})$ any $\lambda$ satisfying $\lambda(a)=a$ for all $a\in A-(S_{j}\cup
T_{j})$ fixes $Q^{\prime}$ and therefore fixes $\sigma_{r}(\tau(y))$. In particular if we choose such a $\lambda$ for which $\lambda(S_{j})=T_{j}$ and $\lambda(T_{j})=S_{j}$ then $\lambda$ fixes $\sigma_{r}(\tau(y))$ and by the lemma (with $\delta=\sigma_{j}\circ \tau)\lambda(\sigma_{j}(\tau(y)))\neq\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))$. We can therefore conclude that $\sigma_{r}(\tau(y))\neq\sigma_{j}(\tau(y))$. This completes the proof of the theorem. 
\end{proof}

\section*{NOTE 129}

In this note we give definitions concerning free groups for forms [1 BB], [1 CA], 68 and 348.

\begin{definition*}
Assume that $(G,\,\circ)$ is a group freely generated by $X$, that $A\subseteq G$, and that $a,\,b$ and $c$ are in $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] The subgroup of $G$ generated by $A$ is denoted $\langle A\rangle$.
\item[2.] The \emph{length of a with respect to} $X$ (denoted by $L_{X}(a)$ or $L(a)$) is the unique natural number $n$ such that there are elements $a_{1},\,\ldots,\,a_{n}$ of $X\cup X^{-1}$ such that $a_{j}\neq a_{j+1}^{-1}$ and $a=a_{1}\circ\cdots \circ a_{n}$.
\item[3.] The subset $A$ is \emph{level} with respect to $X$ if $\langle A\rangle$ is freely generated by $A$ and for each $b\in\langle A\rangle,\,b\in\langle\{a:a\in A\wedge L(a)\leq L(b)\}$.
\item[4.] A subset $A$ of $G$ has the \emph{Nielsen property} with respect to $X$ if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a.] $A\cap A^{-1}=\emptyset$.
\item[b.] If $a,\,b\in A\cup A^{-1}$ and $L(a\circ b)<L(a)$ then $b=a^{-1}$, and
\item[c.] If $a,\,b$ and $c\in A\cup A^{-1}$ and $L(abc)\leq L(a)-L(b)+L(c)$ then either $b=a^{-1}$ or $c=b^{-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

In Federer/Jonsson \cite{bib:1950} it is shown that a set with the Nielsen property is level.
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 130}

In this note we prove that form [30 G] (Every $\subseteq$-chain in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is contained in a maximal $\subseteq$-chain) is equivalent to form 30 (The ordering principle). Form [30 G] was suggested by Adam Kolany.

Assume [30 G].\index{Subject}{level set}\index{Subject}{Nielsen property}\index{Author}{Federer/Jonsson} Let $X$ be a set and let $Y$ be a maximal $\subseteq$-chain in $\mathcal{P}(X)$. Define $\leq$ on $X$ by $a\leq b$ iff $(\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b\not\in A)$. $\leq$ is linear because if not there are $a,\,b\in X$ such that $a\not\leq b$ and $b\not\leq a$. If this happens then $Y\cup\{A_{0}\}$ (where $A_{0}=(\bigcup\{A\in Y:a\not\in A\})\cup\{b\})$ is a chain in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ which properly extends $Y$.

Assume form 30. Let $X$ be a set and $Y$ a $\subseteq$-chain in $\mathcal{P}(X)$. Let $\leq$ be a linear ordering of $X$. Define another linear ordering $R$ on $X$ by $a\, R\,b$ iff $[(\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b\not\in A)]$ or $[(\forall A\in Y)(a\in A\leftrightarrow b\in A)\wedge a\leq b]$. Then $Y^{\prime}=\{A\subseteq X:(\forall a\in A)(\forall x\,R\,a)(x\in A)\}$ is a maximal $\subseteq$-chain containing $Y$.

\section*{NOTE 131}

In this note we give a proof of form [ $0$ AL] (For every set $A$, there is an $\aleph$ which cannot be covered by fewer than $|A|$ sets each of cardinality $<|A|.)$ in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. Form [0 AL] was suggested by K. Keremedis.

Let $A$ be a set and suppose that $K$ is an aleph which is covered by fewer than $|A|$ sets of cardinality $<|A|$. Let $\leq$ be the usual ordering on $K$ and let $\bigcup_{b\in B}C_{b}=K$ where $|B|<|A|$ and for each $b\in B,\,|C_{b}|<|A|$. Since each $C_{b}$ is well orderable, $|C_{b}|<H(A)$. (The
function $H$ is Hartogs' aleph function, $H(A)$ is the least aleph that is not $\leq|A|.)$ Therefore the ordering $(C_{b},\,\leq)$ has order type that of an ordinal $\alpha_{b}<H(A)$. Let $f_{b}$ be the unique order automorphism from $\alpha_{b}$ onto $C_{b}$. Let $\gamma$ be a fixed element of $K$ and define $F:A\times H(A)\rightarrow K$ by $F(b,\,\beta)=f_{b}(\beta)$ if $b\in B$ and $\beta\in\alpha_{b}$ and $F(b,\,\beta)=\gamma$ otherwise. $F$ is onto and $|K|=|\mathcal{E}|$ where $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of equivalence classes $\subseteq A\times H(A)$ under the relation $q\sim r\Leftrightarrow F(q)=F(r)$. Therefore $|K|=\aleph_{\sigma}$ where $A\times H(A)$ has a partition of cardinality $\aleph_{\sigma}$. Therefore, if we let $\aleph_{\rho}$ be the smallest well ordered cardinal greater than every cardinal in the set $\{\aleph_{\sigma}:A\times H(A)$ has a partition of cardinality $\aleph_{\sigma}$\}, then $\aleph_{\rho}$ cannot be covered by fewer than $|A|$ sets each of cardinality $|A|$.

\section*{NOTE 132}

The following definitions and results for forms [8 M], [8 N], [43 Q], [126
B] through [126 F] are from Keremedis \cite{bib:1996d}.

\begin{definition*}
Let $(X,\,T)$ be a topological space. $B\subseteq T-\{\emptyset\}$ is said to be a $\pi$-\emph{base for} $X$ if every non-empty element of $T$ includes an element of $B$.
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
Let $(P,\,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set (poset).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A subset $D\subseteq P$ is set to be \emph{dense} if every element of $P$ has a lower bound in $D$. $D$ is said to be \emph{open} if it is open in the order topology.
\item[(b)] An element $a\in P$ is said to be an \emph{atom} if every pair of lower bounds of $a$ are compatible (have a common lower bound).
\item[(c)] If $P$ has no atoms it is called \emph{atomless}. A pairwise incompatible subset of $P$ is called an \emph{antichain}.
\item[(d)] Let $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable family of dense open sets in $P$. $C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega\},\,\bigcup C=\omega$ is called a \emph{matrix} for $D$ if the following three conditions are satisfied:
\end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\forall i\in \omega\, C_{i}$ is a countable antichain in $P$.
\item[(ii)] $\forall i\in \omega,\,\forall j>i,\,\forall c\in C_{i}$ there exist infinitely many $t\in C_{j}$ such that $t\leq c$.
\item[(iii)] $\forall i\in \omega,\,\forall j\in \omega$, all but finitely many element of $C_{j}$ belong to $D_{i}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\begin{definition*}
Let $A=\{A_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of non-empty sets.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $A$ has the \emph{strong finite intersection property, sfip}\index{Subject}{strong finite intersection property
(sfip)} if for each finite $Q\subseteq A,\,|\bigcap Q|\geq \omega $.
\item[(b)] An infinite subset $S$ of $A$ is a \emph{pseudo-intersection}\index{Subject}{pseudo-intersection} if $|S-A_{i}|<\omega$ for all $i\in I$.
\end{enumerate}

The following statements are considered:

\noindent $MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$: For every denumerable family $A$ of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets, there exists a set $C$ such that for all $a\in A,\,0<|C\cap a|\leq \omega$.

\noindent \emph{pseudo}$(w)([126\ \mathrm{F}])$: Every denumerable family of sets having the sfip also has a pseudo-intersection.

\noindent $DP$: If $(X,\,T)$ is a topological space having a countable $\pi$-base\index{Subject}{$\pi$-base}, then for every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$, there is a countable dense set $S\subseteq X$ such that for all $i\in \omega$ and for all but finitely many $s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}$. ($DP$ is form [8 N]).

\noindent$DP^{\ast}\ ([126\ \mathrm{E}])$: If $(X,\,T)$ is a topological space, then for every family $D=\{D_{i}: i\in \omega\}$ of dense open sets of $X$, there is a countable dense set $S\subseteq X$ such that for all $i\in \omega$ and for all but finitely many $s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}$.

\noindent $WCMC\ ([126\ \mathrm{D}])$: For every denumerable family $A$ of disjoint non-empty sets there is a set $C\subset\bigcup A$ such that for every $a\in A,\, 0\leq|C\cap a|<\omega$.

\noindent $FSCB$: Every separable first countable space $(X,\,T)$ has a countable $\pi$-base.

\noindent $Matrix(\omega)$: For every atomless poset\index{Subject}{atomless poset} $(P,\,\leq)$ and every family $D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ of dense open subsets of $P$, there exists a matrix $C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega\},\, |\bigcup C|=\omega$ of $P$ for $D$. ($Matrix(\omega)$ is form [43 Q].)

Results:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 126) $\leftrightarrow MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)+MC(\aleph_{0},\, \aleph_{0})$ (form 350). (The conjunction $MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)+MC(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ is form [126 B].)
\item[2.] $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 8) $\leftrightarrow MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)+C(\aleph_{0},\, \aleph_{0})$ (form 32). (The conjunction $MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)+C(\aleph_{0},\,\aleph_{0})$ is form [8 M].)
\item[3.] $C(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 8) $\leftrightarrow DP$ (form [8
N]).
\item[4.] $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 126) $\leftrightarrow WCMC$ ([126
D]).

\noindent (Clearly, $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)\rightarrow WCMC$. Let $X=\{A_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable set of pairwise disjoint non-empty sets. For each $n\in \omega$, let $B_{n}=A_{0}\times A_{1}\times\cdots\times A_{n}$ and let $B=\{B_{n}:n\in \omega\}$. Let $C=\{B_{n_{i}}:n_{i}\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable subset of $B$ which has a multiple choice function $f$. The function $f$ can be used to construct a choice function on $A$. This result was noted by K. Keremedis\index{Author}{Keremedis}.)
\item[5.] $WCMC$ ([126 D])$\leftrightarrow DP^{\ast}$ ([126 E]) $\leftrightarrow pseudo(\omega)$ ([126 F]).
\item[6.] $MC(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ (form 126) $\leftrightarrow FSCB\, +\, MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$. (The conjunction $FSCB+ MC_{\omega}(\aleph_{0},\,\infty)$ is form [126 C].)
\item[7.] $DC(\omega)$ (the Principle of Dependent Choices (43)) $\leftrightarrow Matrix(\omega)$ (form [43 Q]).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 133}

In this note we prove that forms [1 F] and [1 CC] are equivalent to form 1.

Form [1 F] is ``For all ordinals $\alpha,\,DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$: Given a relation $R$ such that for every subset $Y$ of a set $X$ with $|Y|<\aleph_{\alpha}$, there is and $x\in X$ with $Y\,R\,x$, then there is a function $f:\aleph_{\alpha}\rightarrow X$ such that $\forall\beta<\aleph_{\alpha},\, \{f(\gamma):\gamma<\beta\}\
R\ f(\beta).)$''. It is clear that form 1 implies [1 F]. To prove the converse, well order $X$ by using $Y\,R\,x\Leftrightarrow x\not\in Y$ and use $DC(\aleph_{\alpha})$ for sufficiently large $\aleph_{\alpha}$.

The question of the equivalence of [1 CC] and 1 was first raised by K. Keremedis. Form [1 CC] is the conjunction of $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty)$: ``Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.'' and $MC_{\omega^{+}}$: ``For every natural number $n\geq 1$ and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function $f$ such that for each $u\in x,\,f(u)$ is a non-empty finite subset of $u$ such that $|f(u)|$ and $n$ are relatively prime.'' We first prove that $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty)$ implies ``every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function''. Let $X=\{x_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ be a denumerable family of odd sized sets. For each $n\in \omega$, let $y_{n}=\{f:f$ is a choice function for $\{x_{i}:i\leq n\}$\}. $|y_{n}|=|x_{1}|\cdots|x_{n}|$ and is therefore odd. Applying $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty)$ to $Y=\{y_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ gives an infinite subset $Y^{\prime}$ of $Y$ with a choice function $F$. Then defining $G$ by $G(x_{n})=F(y_{k})(x_{n})$ where $k$ is the least natural number $\geq n$ for which $y_{k}\in\mathrm{dom}(F)$ gives a choice function for $X$.

To prove that $PC(\aleph_{0}, \mathrm{odd},\infty)$ and $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ imply $AC$. It suffices to show that $\forall n\in \omega,\,C(\infty,\,n)(form
61)+MC(form 67)+MC_{\omega^{+}}+$ ``Every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function'' implies $AC$. This is because $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ is equivalent to $\forall n\in \omega,\, C(\infty,\,n)+MC$ (by lemma 3  of Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin\index{Author}{Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin} \cite{bib:1997}) and because $PC(\aleph_{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\, \infty)$ is equivalent to ``Every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice
function''

Let $X$ be a set of pairwise disjoint, non-empty sets. By $MC$ there is an $f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\bigcup X)$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,\emptyset \neq f(x)\subseteq x$ and $|f(x)|$ is finite. For each $n\in \omega$, let $Y_{n}=\{x\in X:|f(x)|=n\}$. By $C(\infty,\,n)$, $Y_{n}$ has a choice function (even if $Y_{n}$ happens to be empty, but it might be clearer to exclude $n$ for which $Y_{n}$ is empty). Therefore the set $C_{n}=\{g:g$ is a choice function for $Y_{n}$\} is non-empty. By $MC_{\omega^{+}}$ there is a function $F$ defined on $\omega$ such that $F(n)$ is an odd sized subset of $C_{n}$ for each $n\in \omega$. Since every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice function, there is a function $G$ defined on $\omega$ such that for every $n\in \omega,\,G(n)\in F(n)$. We can now define a choice function $Ch$ for $X$ by $Ch(x)=G(n)(x)$ where $|f(x)|=n$.

\section*{NOTE 134}

In this note we prove the result from Luzin/Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{bib:1917} that form 100 (If $n$ and $m$ are cardinal numbers, then $m\leq^{\ast}n\rightarrow\neg(n<m).)$ implies form 369 (If $\mathbb{R}$ is partitioned into two sets, at least one has cardinality $2^{\aleph_{0}}$.). We give a proof here because Luzin/Sierpi\'{n}ski \cite{bib:1917} is not readily available.

Since $2^{\aleph_{0}}=|\mathcal{P}(\omega)|=|2^{\omega}|$ it suffices to show that for any partition $\{A,\,B\}$ of $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$, either $|A|=|2^{\omega}|$ or $|B|=|2^{\omega}|$. Since $|A|\leq|2^{\omega}|$ and $|B|\leq|2^{\omega}|$, by 100 it suffices to show that there is either a function from $A$ onto $2^{\omega}$ or a function from $B$ onto $2^{\omega}$. Define $f:\mathcal{P}(\omega)\rightarrow 2^{\omega}$ by the following: Assume $X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots\}\in \mathcal{P}(\omega)$ where $a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots$. Then
\begin{equation*}
(f(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
0 &\mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\ \text{is even or}\ |X|\leq n+1\\
1 & \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\ \text{is odd}
\end{array}\right. .
\end{equation*}
Assume that $f|B$ is not onto $2^{\omega}$. Then for some $\gamma$ in $2^{\omega}$, the non-empty set $C= \{X\in \mathcal{P}(\omega):f(X)=\gamma\}\subseteq A$. Then we can define a function $g$ from $C$ onto $2^{\omega}$ as follows: Assume $X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots\} \in C$ where $a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots$ and assume $n\in \omega$. If $\gamma(n)=0$, then $a_{n+1}-a_{n}$ is even or $|X|\leq n+1$, and we define
\begin{equation*}
(g(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
0 &\mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 0\mod4\ \text{or}\ |X|\leq n+1\\
1& \text{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 2\mod4
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
If $\gamma(n)=1$,\index{Author}{Luzin/Sierpi\'{n}ski} then $a_{n+1}-a_{n}$ is odd and we define
\begin{equation*}
(g(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
0& \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 1\mod4\\
1& \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 3\mod4.
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
The proof that $g$ is onto $2^{\omega}$ could be done by induction, that is, given any $\beta\in 2^{\omega}$ we could define by induction a sequence $\langle a_{n}\rangle_{n\in\omega}$ so that $X=\{a_{1},\,a_{2},\, \ldots\}\in C$ and $g(X)=\beta$.

\section*{NOTE 135}

In this note we prove that form 18 $(PUT(\aleph_{0},2,\,\aleph_{0}))$ and [18 B] (The union of a denumerable family of pairs has a denumerable subset.) are equivalent. It suffices to show that [18 A] $(PC(\aleph_{0},2,\,\infty))$ implies [18 B].

Let $X$ be a denumerable family of pairs. By [18 A] there is a denumerable subset $Y\subseteq X$ and a choice function $f$ for $Y$. If the range of $f$ is infinite then it is a denumerable subset of $\bigcup X$. If the range of $f$ is finite, then for some $t\in\bigcup X$ there are infinitely many elements $y\in Y$ such that $f(y)=t$. Each such $y$ has the form $y=\{a_{y},\,t\}$. In this case the set $\{a_{y}:f(y)=t\}$ is a denumerable subset of $\bigcup X$.

\section*{NOTE 136}

In this note we prove that the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is true in $\mathcal{N}19$. We shall use Blass' theorem (Blass\index{Author}{Blass} \cite{bib:1986}, Theorem~\ref{part04:thm2c}) which characterizes Fraenkel-Mostowski models in which BPI is true. According to this theorem BPI holds in a Fraenkel-Mostowski model if and only if the model is determined by a filter of subgroups $\Gamma$ with the Ramsey property described below.

\begin{definition*}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is a \emph{Ramsey subgroup} if for every finite $F\subseteq G/H$ (the set of left cosets of $H$ in $G$) there is a finite $Y\subseteq G/H$ such that whenever $Y$ is partitioned into two pieces there is a $g\in G$ such that $gF$ is included in one of the pieces.
\item[2.] A filter $\Gamma$ of subgroups of $G$ has the \emph{Ramsey property} if it has a basis consisting of Ramsey subgroups of $G$.
\end{enumerate}

Let $E$ be a support. By Blass' theorem it suffices to show that $\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$ is a Ramsey subgroup of $G$. We shall argue that this follows from Rado's corollary which is given in Halpern \cite{bib:1964}, page 61. Rado's corollary is
\end{definition*}

\textsc{Rado's Corollary.}
\emph{Assume that} $n,p\in \omega$ \emph{and that} $\langle m_{i}\rangle_{i\in n}\in\omega^{n}$. \emph{Then there is a} $q\in \omega$ \emph{such that for all sequences} $\langle X_{i}\rangle_{i\in n}$ \emph{of disjoint sets such that} $|X_{i}|\geq q$ \emph{for every} $i\in n$, \emph{if} $\Delta$ \emph{is a partition of} $\{Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap\,X_{i}|=m_{i})\}$ \emph{into two pieces there then is a sequence} $\langle Y_{i}\rangle_{i\in n}$ \emph{such that for all} $i\in n,\,Y_{i}\subset X_{i}$ \emph{and} $|Y_{i}|=p$ \emph{and} $\{Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap\,Y_{i}|=m_{i})\}$\
\emph{is a subset of one of the pieces}.

Let $F=\{\phi_{1}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E),\ldots,\,\phi_{k}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\}$ be a finite subset of $G/\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$. We will find a $Y$ satisfying the condition from definition 1 above. We first note that it is easy to verify that
\setcounter{equation}{0}
\begin{equation}
\label{part04:eqn1b} (\forall\phi,\,\psi\in G)(\phi\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)=\psi\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\Leftrightarrow\phi(E)=\psi(E))
\end{equation}
Let $E^{\prime}=\phi_{1}(E)\cup\cdots \cup\phi_{k}(E)$.\index{Author}{Halpern} $E$ and $E^{\prime}$ are finite and therefore there are natural numbers $j_{0},\,\ldots,\,j_{n-1}$ such that $E\cup E^{\prime}\subseteq B_{j_{0}}\cup\cdots \cup B_{j_{n-1}}$. For $i\in n$, define $E_{i}=B_{j_{i}}\cap E,\,E_{i}^{\prime}=B_{j_{i}}\cap E^{\prime},\,m_{i}=|E_{i}|$ and let $p= \max\{|E_{i}^{\prime}|:i\in n\}$. The integers $n,\,p$ and the sequence $\langle m_{i}\rangle_{i\in n}\in \omega^{n}$ satisfy the hypothesis of Rado's corollary. Therefore there is a $q\in \omega$ satisfying the conclusion. For $i\in n$, choose a set $X_{i}\subseteq B_{j_{i}}$ so that $|X_{i}|=q$. Let $Y= \{\phi\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E):\phi(E)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}X_{i}\}$. We now show that this $Y$ satisfies the condition of definition~\ref{part04:def1}.

Let $\Delta=\{\Delta_{1},\,\Delta_{2}\}$ be a partition of $Y$ into two pieces. Let $\Gamma_{1}=\{\phi(E):\phi\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in\Delta_{1}\}$ and $\Gamma_{2}=\{\phi(E):\phi\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in\Delta_{2}\}$. By (\ref{part04:eqn1b}), $\Gamma=\{\Gamma_{1},\,\Gamma_{2}\}$ is a partition of $\{Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)\,|Z\cap\,X_{i}|=m_{i}\}$. By Rado's corollary, there is a sequence $\langle Y_{i}\rangle_{i\in n}$ such that $|Y_{i}|=p$ for $i\in n$ and $W= \{Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap Y_{i}| =m_{i}\}$ is either a subset of $\Gamma_{1}$ or a subset of $\Gamma_{2}$. We assume without loss of generality that $W\subseteq\Gamma_{1}$. Let $\eta \in G$ be a permutation such that $\eta(E_{i}^{\prime})\subseteq Y_{i}$ for $i\in n$. (This is possible since $|Y_{i}|=p\geq|E_{i}^{\prime}|$.) Then (since $\phi_{t}(E_{i})\subseteq E_{i}^{\prime}$ for $1\leq t\leq k) \eta\phi_{t}(E_{i})\subseteq Y_{i}$ for $i\in n$ and $1\leq t\leq k$. Therefore, for $1\leq t\leq k,\, \eta\phi_{t}(E)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in n}Y_{i}$. Using this and the fact that $|\eta\phi_{t}(E)\cap Y_{i}|=|\eta\phi_{t}(E_{i})|=|E_{i}|=m_{i}$ for $1\leq t\leq k$ and $i\in n$ we conclude that $\eta\phi_{t}(E)\in\Gamma_{1}$. Hence $\eta\phi_{t}\circ\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in\Delta_{1}$.

\section*{NOTE 137}

We shall give a proof that [1 BU] (In every vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, every generating set includes a basis.) implies 1, AC. Bleicher\index{Author}{Bleicher} \cite{bib:1964} has shown that

\noindent [1 BU]implies $C(\infty,\,<\aleph_{0})$ (62), so it is sufficient to prove that [1 BU] implies MC (67). (The proof is due to K. Keremedis.)

Let $X=\{x_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a set of pairwise disjoint infinite sets. For each $i\in I$, let $V_{i}$ be the set of all functions from $x_{i}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ such that for all $f\in V_{i},\,\exists r\in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $\{u\in x_{i}:f(u)\neq r\}$ is finite. Then $V_{i}$ is a vector space. Let $V$ be the weak direct product of the $V_{i}$'s. For each $i\in I$, define
\begin{gather*}
G_{i}=\{F\in V\,:\,(\forall j)[(\forall u\in x_{j})(j\neq i\rightarrow F_{j}(u)=0)\wedge\\
(j=i\rightarrow(\exists u\in x_{j})(F_{j}(u)=1\wedge(\forall v\in x_{j})(v\neq u\rightarrow F_{j}(v)=0)\vee\\
(F_{j}(u)=0\wedge(\forall v\in x_{j})(v\neq u\rightarrow F_{j}(v)=1)))]\}
\end{gather*}
Let $G=\bigcup\{G_{i}:i\in I\}$. Then $G$ is a generating set for $V$. Let $B\subseteq G$ be a basis for $V$. For each $i\in I$, let $H^{i}$ be the function in $V$ such that $\forall u\in x_{j}$,
\begin{equation*}
H^{i}(u)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
0,\,j\neq i\\
1,\,j=i
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
For each $i\in I,\,H^{i}$ can be uniquely represented as a linear combination of a finite number of basis elements. It follows from the definition of $G_{i}$ that each basis element uniquely specifies an element in $x_{i}$. Thus, each $H^{i}$ uniquely specifies a finite subset of $x_{i}$.

\section*{NOTE 138}

In this note we include a proof due to K. Keremedis that form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem) implies form 119 ($C(\aleph_{0}$,uniformly orderable with order type of the integers).

Fix $\mathcal{A}=\{A_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ as in form 19, where the $A_{i}$ are pairwise disjoint. Let $\bar{A}_{i}=\{a_{i}\}\cup A_{i}\cup \{b_{i}\}$, where $a_{i},\,b_{i}$ are chosen so that $a_{i},\, b_{i}\not\in A_{i}$ and the $\bar{A}_{i}$ are pairwise disjoint. Declare $a_{i}$ to be less than every member of $A_{i}$ and $b_{i}$ to be greater than every member of $A_{i}$. Put $X=\cup\{\bar{A}_{i}:i\in \omega \}$. Order $X$ by requiring: elements of $\bar{A}_{i}$ are ordered in $X$ the way they are ordered in $\bar{A}_{i}$, otherwise if $x\in\bar{A}_{i}$ and $y\in\bar{A}_{j}$ then $x$ is less than $y$ iff $i<j$. Put $\bar{X}=X\cup \{a\},\,a\not\in X$ and declare $a$ to be greater than every member of $X$. Clearly $\bar{X}$ with the order topology is a compact $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ space and consequently a $\mathrm{T}_{4}$ space. Furthermore, $G=A(=\{a_{i}: i\in \omega \})\cup B(=\{b_{i}:i\in \omega \})\cup
\{a\}$ is a closed subset of $\bar{X}$ and the function $f:G\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ given by $f(a)=0$ and for $i\in \omega\  f(a_{i})=1/(i+2)$, $f(b_{i})=1/(i+1)$ is clearly continuous. Hence, $f$ has a continuous extension $\bar{f}: \bar{X}\rightarrow[0,1]$. Put $f_{i}=\bar{f}|\bar{A}_{i}$. As $\bar{f}$ is continuous it follows that $f_{i}$ is also continuous. Since $\bar{A}_{i}$ is compact it follows that $f_{i}$ attains both its minimum and maximum values. We may assume that $f_{i}$ attains its minimum at $a_{i}$, its maximum at $b_{i}$ and, at every other point of $A_{i}$, it takes on values other than $f_{i}(a_{i})$ and $f_{i}(b_{i})$. Let $C_{i}=f_{i}^{-1}((y_{i},\,1/(1+i)))$ where $y_{i}= \frac{2i+3}{2(i+1)(i+2)}$ is the midpoint of the interval $[1/(2+i),\,1/(1+i)]$. Clearly $C_{i}\neq\emptyset$ and by the completeness of $\bar{A}_{i}$ and the continuity of $f_{i}$ it follows that $c_{i}= \inf(C_{i})\in A_{i}$. Hence, $c=\{c_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ is a choice set for $\mathcal{A}$, finishing the proof of the theorem.

\section*{NOTE 139}

We give a proof that form 67 (MC, Multiple Choice Axiom) implies form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem). To the best of our knowledge, this result is due to David Pincus.

Suppose $X$ is a normal topological space. Then, if $A$ and $B$ are disjoint closed sets, there exist disjoint open sets $C$ and $D$ such that $A\subseteq C$ and $B\subseteq D$. MC gives us a rule for choosing a finite number of pairs $(C,\,D)$ with the above property. Since the intersection of a finite number of open sets is open, MC implies that there is a function $F$ such that for each pair of disjoint closed sets $(A,\,B)$, $F(A,\,B)=(C,\,D)$, where $C$ and $D$ are disjoint open sets such that $A\subseteq C$ and $B\subseteq D$. Thus, using the standard proof of Urysohn's lemma (see, for example, Kelley \cite{bib:1955}, p 115), there is a rule for choosing a function $f:X\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ which is zero on $A$ and one on $B$. Given this rule for choosing Urysohn's function, the standard proof of the Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem can be given in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ (See, for example, Kelley \cite{bib:1955}, p 242.).

\section*{NOTE 140}

In this note we give a proof that form 214 (For every family $A$ of infinite sets, there is a function $f$ such that $\forall y\in A,\,f(y)\subseteq y$ and $|f(y)|=\aleph_{0}.)$ implies form 152 (Every non-well orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets.)

Let $X$ be a set which cannot be well ordered and let $Y$ be the set of all infinite subsets of $X$. Form 214 implies that there is a function $f$ such that for each $y\in Y,\,f(y)\subseteq y$ and $|f(y)|=\aleph_{0}$. We define a function $g$ on the ordinals so that $g(0)=f(X)$ and $g( \alpha)=f(X\,\backslash\, \bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}g(\beta))$. Since $X$ is a set, there is an ordinal $\gamma$ such that $X\, \backslash\, \bigcup_{\beta<\gamma}g(\beta)$ is finite. We can use this function $g$ to cover $X$ with a well ordered family of pairwise disjoint denumerable sets.

\section*{NOTE 141}

In this\index{Author}{Kelley} note we give the definitions for forms [1 CE] through [1 CH], [67
K] through [67 T], [126 G] through [126 K], 173, [173 A], 232, [232 A] through [232 G], 383, and [383 A] through [383 C].

\begin{definition*} Let $(X,\,T)$ be a topological space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] $X$ is \emph{normal}\index{Subject}{normal space} if for every pair of disjoint closed sets $A$ and $B$, there exist disjoint open sets $C$ and $D$ such that $A\subseteq C$ and $B\subseteq D$.
\item[2.] $X$ satisfies \emph{Urysohn's lemma}\index{Subject}{Urysohn's lemma} iff it satisfies: If $A,\,B$ are closed and disjoint in $X$ then there exists a continuous function $f:X\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ separating $A$ and $B$. i.e., $A\subseteq f^{-1}(0)$ and $B\subseteq f^{-1}(1)$. (In the remainder of this note we shall refer to a space that satisfies Urysohn's lemma as a $U$ \emph{space}\index{Subject}{U space}.)
\item[3.] $X$ satisfies the \emph{Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem}\index{Subject}{Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem} iff it satisfies: If $A$ is closed in $X$ and $f:A\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ is a continuous function, then there exists a continuous extension $\bar{f}$ of $f$ to all of $X$ taking values in $[0,1]$. (We shall refer to a space satisfying the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem as a $T$ \emph{space}\index{Subject}{T space}.)
\item[4.] The \emph{disjoint union}\index{Subject}{disjoint union} of the disjoint family $\{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\}$ of topological spaces is the set $X=\bigcup\{X_{i}:i\in k\}$ such that $O$ is open in $X$ iff $O\cap X_{i}$ is open in $X_{i}$ for all $i\in k$.
\item[5.] A family $\mathcal{K}$ of subsets of a topological space $(X,\,T)$ is \emph{locally finite} (respectively \emph{locally countable}) iff each point of $X$ has a neighborhood meeting only a finite number (respectively countable number) of elements of $\mathcal{K}$.
\item[6.] $X$ is \emph{paracompact} (respectively \emph{para-Lindel\"{o}f}) iff $X$ is $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ and every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ has a locally finite (respectively locally countable $\rangle$ open refinement $\mathcal{V}$, (that is, $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally finite open cover of $X$ and every member of $\mathcal{V}$ is included in a member of $\mathcal{U}$).
\item[7.] A family $\mathcal{K}$ of subsets of $X$ is \emph{point finite} (respectively \emph{point countable}) iff each element of $X$ belongs to only finitely many (respectively countably many) members of $\mathcal{K}$.
\item[8.] $X$ is \emph{metacompact} (respectively \emph{meta-Lindel\"{o}f}) iff each open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ has an open point finite (respectively point countable) refinement.
\item[9.] A set $C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is $\sigma$-\emph{locally finite} (respectively $\sigma$-\emph{point finite}, $\sigma$-\emph{disjoint}, $\sigma$-\emph{discrete}) if $C= \bigcup_{n\in\omega}C_{n}$ where each $C_{n}$ is locally finite (respectively, point finite, pairwise disjoint, discrete).
\item[10.] Assume that $\gamma$ is a well ordered cardinal number, that is, $\gamma$ is an initial ordinal. A set $C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is $\gamma$-\emph{locally finite} (respectively $\gamma$-\emph{point finite}, $\gamma$-\emph{disjoint}, $\gamma$-\emph{discrete}) if $C= \bigcup_{\alpha\in\gamma}C_{\alpha}$ where each $C_{\alpha}$ is locally finite (respectively, point finite, pairwise disjoint, discrete).
\item[11.] An open cover $\mathcal{U} =\{U_{i}:i\in k\}$ of $X$ is \emph{shrinkable} iff there exists an open cover $\mathcal{V}=\{V_{i}:i\in k\}$ of non-empty sets such that $\bar{V}_{i}\subseteq U_{i}$ for all $i\in k$. $\mathcal{V}$ is also called a \emph{shrinking} of $\mathcal{U}$.
\item[12.] $X$ is a \emph{PFCS space} iff every point finite open cover of $X$ is shrinkable.
\item[13.] $D\subseteq X$ is \emph{discrete} if every $x\in X$ has a neighborhood $U$ such that $|U\,\cap\, D|=1$. A set $C\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is \emph{discrete} if $\forall x\in X$, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $U\cap A\neq\emptyset$ for at most one element $A\in C$. (Thus, $D\subseteq X$ is discrete\index{Subject}{$\sigma$-discrete} iff $\{\{d\}:d\in D\}$ is discrete.)
\item[14.] $X$ is\index{Subject}{locally finite}\index{Subject}{meta-Lindel\"{o}f}\index{Subject}{metacompact}\index{Subject}{para-Lindel\"{o}f}\index{Subject}{paracompact}\index{Subject}{point countable}\index{Subject}{point finite}\index{Subject}{$\sigma$-point finite}\index{Subject}{shrinkable} cwH (\emph{collectionwise Hausdorff})\index{Subject}{collectionwise Hausdorff} iff if $X$ is $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ and for every closed and discrete subset $D$ of $X$ there exists a family $U=\{U_{d}:d\in D\}$ of disjoint\index{Subject}{$\sigma$-disjoint} open sets such that $d\in U_{d}$ for all $d\in D$.
\item[15.] $X$ is cwH(B) (\emph{collectionwise Hausdorff with respect to the base} $B$) iff if $X$ is $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ and for every closed and discrete subset $D$ of $X$ there exists a family $U=\{U_{d}:d\in D\}$ of disjoint open sets such that $U\subseteq B$ and $d\in U_{d}$ for all $d\in D$.
\item[16.] $X$ is cwN (\emph{collectionwise normal})\index{Subject}{collectionwise normal} if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and for every discrete $C$ of pairwise disjoint closed subsets of $X$, there exists a family $U=\{U_{A}:A\in C\}$ of disjoint open sets such that $A\subseteq U_{A}$ for all $A\in C$. (cwN($B$) is defined similarly to cwH$(B)$ in 15.)
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 142}

In this note we prove that form 234 (There is a non-Ramsey set.) implies form 282 $(w\not\rightarrow (\omega)^{\omega}$).

Assume that there is a non-Ramsey set $A$. The proof will be by contradiction. We therefore assume that $\omega \rightarrow(\omega)^{\omega}$. Then (using the definitions in note 97) for every $F:\omega^{\omega}\rightarrow\{0,1\}$ there is an infinite subset $X$ of $\omega$ such that either
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(\forall g\in X^{\omega})(F(g)=0)$ or
\item[(ii)] $(\forall g\in X^{\omega})(F(g)=1)$.
\end{enumerate}

Using $A$ we define a function $F:\omega^{\omega}\rightarrow\{0,1\}$ by
\begin{equation*}
F(g)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
0\ \mbox{if}\ g\ \mbox{is strictly increasing and range}(g)\in A\\
1\ \mbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
Let $X$ be the infinite subset of $\omega$ guaranteed by $\omega\rightarrow(\omega)^{\omega}$. For each infinite subset $Y$ of $\omega$, let $g_{Y}\in \omega^{\omega}$ be the unique strictly increasing function whose range is $Y$. Then $F(g_{Y})=0$ if and only if $Y\in A$. Either (i) or (ii) must be true of $X$ and $F$. If (i) holds then for every infinite $Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega}$ so $F(g_{Y})=0$ and hence $Y\in A$. On the other hand, if (ii) holds then for every infinite $Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega}$ so $F(g_{Y})=1$ and hence $Y\not\in A$. This contradicts the assumption that $A$ is non-Ramsey.

\section*{NOTE 143}

Form [0 AM] is a form of the Hahn-Banach Theorem for separable vector spaces. We shall prove by induction that it is provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

Assume $V$ is a separable vector space, $D=\{d_{0},\,d_{1},\,\cdots\}$ is a countable dense subset of $V$, and $p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$, and $(\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x))$. Also assume that $p$ satisfies the following condition:
\begin{equation*}
\tag{$\ast$} (\forall\epsilon>0)(\forall x\in V-S)(\exists y\in D)\ \mbox{such\ that}\ (p(x-y)<\epsilon\ \mbox{and}\ p(y-x)<\epsilon.
\end{equation*}
Let $S$ be $a$ subspace of $V$ and let $f$ be a linear function from $S$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x\in S,\,f(x)\leq p(x)$. We shall define by induction a countable\index{Subject}{locally countable} set of linear functions $G=\{g_{n}:n\in \omega\}$ such that $g_{n}\subseteq g_{n+1}$ and such that the linear extension of $f,\,f^{\ast}=\bigcup\, G$, can be extended to all of $V$ by using the condition $(\ast)$.

We define $g_{0}=f$. Suppose $g_{n}$ has been defined and $S_{n}$ is the domain of $G_{n}$. In what follows, we shall let $d=d_{n+1}$ and $g=g_{n+1}$. If $d$ is in the domain of $g_{n}$, then define $g=g_{n}$. Suppose that $d$ is not in the domain of $g_{n}$. We would like to define $g$ so that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$ and any $x\in S_{n},\ g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x)\leq p(td+x)$. Then $tg(d)\leq p(td+x)-g(x)$. If $t=1,\, g(d)\leq p(d+x)-g(x)$ and if $t=-1,\,g(d)\geq g(x)-p(x-d)$. Let $s= \sup_{x\in S}(g(x)-p(x-d))$ and let $i= \inf_{x\in S}(p(d+x)-g(x))$. Then $s\leq g(d)\leq i$. Define $g(d)$ to be the mid-point of the interval $[s,\,i]$. For any $x\in S_{n}$, We define $g(x)=g_{n}(x)$ and, for each $t\in \mathbb{R}$, we define $g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x)$. Let $f^{\ast}=\bigcup\{g_{n}:n\in \omega\}$. It is clear that $f^{\ast}$ is a linear function, $f^{\ast}(x)\leq p(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain of $f^{\ast}$, and $D$ is a subset of the domain of $f^{\ast}$.

Let $\epsilon>0$ and $x\in V$. Then, by $(\ast)$, there is a $y\in D$ such that $p(x-y)<\epsilon$ and $p(y-x)<\epsilon$. If $f^{\ast}(x-y)\geq 0$, then $0\leq f^{\ast}(x-y)\leq p(x-y)<\epsilon$. If $f^{\ast}(x-y)<0$, then $0<-f^{\ast}(x-y)=f^{\ast}(y-x)\leq p(y-x)<\epsilon$. Consequently, $|f^{\ast}(x-y)|<\epsilon$ and $f^{\ast}$ can be extended to all of $V$.

\section*{NOTE 144}

A proof that dependent choice (form 43) holds in FM models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ in which the set of supports $S$ is closed under countable unions. This includes models where $S$ consists of all countable subsets of the set $A$ of atoms.

Assume that $\mathcal{N}$ is such a model and that $R$ is a relation in $\mathcal{N}$ such that for all $x\in\mathrm{dom}(R)$ there is a $y$ such that $x\ R\ y$. Then, in the ground model (where AC holds) there is a sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that $(\forall n\in\omega)(x_{n}\  R\ x_{n+1})$. If for each $n\in \omega,\,x_{n}$ has support $E_{n}$, then $\bigcup_{n\in \omega}E_{n}$ is a support for $(x_{n})_{n\in\omega}$. Hence, this sequence is in $\mathcal{N}$.

\section*{NOTE 145}

A proof that form 287 (the Hahn-Banach theorem for separable normed linear spaces) implies form 222 (there is a non-principal measure on $\omega$). This result and its proof are due to M. Morillon.

Let $E$ be the vector space of bounded sequences of reals. Let $M$ be a norm on $E$ such that the normed vector space $(E,\,M)$ is separable: for example, if $x= (x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E$ let $M(x)= \sum\nolimits_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{|x_{k}|}{(k+1)^{2}}$. Here, the normed vector space $(E,\,M)$ is separable because the set of sequences in $\mathbb{Q}^{(\mathbb{N})}$ which end in an infinite sequence of zeros is dense in E.

For every $x=(x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E$, let $p(x)=\varlimsup\{x_{k};k\in \mathbb{N}\}$. Hence, we obtain a sublinear functional $p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Using form 287, let $g:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a linear functional such that $g\leq p$. We have $p(1)=1$ and $p(-1)=-1$. Hence, $g(1)=1$. For every finite subset $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ we have $p(1_{A})=p(-1_{A})=0$, hence, $g(1_{A})=0$. Here $1_{A}$ denotes the characteristic function of the set $A$.

For every $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, lf $m(A)=g(1_{A})$, then $m:\mathcal{P}(\omega)\rightarrow[0,\,1]$ is a non-principal measure on $\omega$.

\section*{NOTE 146}

Form [43 W] is due to Claus-Peter Wirth. In this note we prove that it is equivalent to form 43. Form [43 W] is: Let $M$ be a non-empty set partially ordered by $<$ without $<$-minimal elements. Then there is a subset $C$ of $M$ which is linearly ordered by $<$ such that $C$ has no $<$-minimal element. Form 43 is the principle of dependent choice, DC. To prove [43 W] from DC let $X=M$ and define $R$ by $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $y<x$. Then the sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in \omega}$ which is guaranteed by DC is a linearly ordered subset of $M$ with no $<$-minimal elements.

To prove [43 W] implies DC, let $R$ be a relation on a set $X$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,\exists y\in X$ such that $x\,R\,y$. Let $M$ be the set of all finite sequences $(x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ of elements of $X$ such that $x_{1}\ R\ x_{2}\ R\ \ldots\ R\ x_{n}$ and define a relation $<$ on $M$ by $(x_{1},\, \ldots,\,x_{n})<(y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{m})$ if and only if $(x_{1},\,\ldots,\,x_{n})$ is $a$ proper extension of $(y_{1},\,\ldots,\,y_{m})$. $M$ has no $<$-minimal elements so by (ii) there is a $<$ chain $C$ in $M$ with no minimal element. From $C$ an infinite sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in \omega}$ can be constructed with the property that $x_{n}\ R\,x_{n+1}$ for all $n\in \omega$.

\section*{NOTE 147}

Definitions for measures on Boolean algebras\index{Subject}{measure on a Boolean algebra}.

\begin{definition*} Assume that $\mathcal{B} =(B,\,\wedge,\,\vee,\,\mathbf{1,\,0})$ is a Boolean algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[1.] A \emph{measure} or \emph{additive real valued measure} on $\mathcal{B}$ is a function $m:\mathcal{B} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $m(\mathbf{1})=1,\,(\forall x\in B)(m(x)\geq 0)$, and $(\forall x,\,y\in B)(x\wedge y=\mathbf{0}\rightarrow m(x\vee y)= m(x)+m(y))$. (It follows that $m(\mathbf{0})=0$.)
\item[2.] A \emph{two valued measure}\index{Subject}{two valued measure} on $\mathcal{B}$ is a measure on $\mathcal{B}$ whose range is $\{0,1\}$.
\item[3.] If $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{P}(X),\,\cap,\,\cup,\,X,\,\emptyset)$ then a measure $m$ on $\mathcal{B}$ is \emph{non-principal} if $m(\{x\})=0$ for every $x\in X$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition*}

\section*{NOTE 148}

We give a proof that forms 154 and [154 A] are equivalent. First, it is clear that 154 implies [154 A]. To prove the converse, assume [154 A] holds. Let $\{X_{i}:i\in \omega\}$ be a countable family of pairwise disjoint compact $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ spaces and let $Y$ be the one point compactification of $\bigcup_{i\in\omega}X_{i}$. Form [154 A] implies that $Y^{\omega}$ is compact. Since $\prod_{i\in \omega}X_{i}$ is a closed subspace of $Y^{\omega}$, it is also compact.
